title: The faces behind the feeds: Gen Z’s private lives and public posts – in pictures | Photography | The Guardian
description: For the first digital natives, there are two places to express yourself: in the comfort of your own room and online. Photographer Niccolò Rastrelli set out to find out how the identities compare
Author: Gabrielle Schwarz
Headline: For the first digital natives, there are two places to express yourself: in the comfort of your own room and online. Photographer Niccolò Rastrelli set out to find out how the identities compare
Content: Stevie, 20, Rome, photographed in his bedroom.Photograph: Niccolò Rastrelli/InstituteView image in fullscreenStevie, 20, Rome, photographed in his bedroom.Photograph: Niccolò Rastrelli/InstitutePhotographyThe faces behind the feeds: Gen Z’s private lives and public posts – in picturesFor the first digital natives, there are two places to express yourself: in the comfort of your own room and online. Photographer Niccolò Rastrelli set out to find out how the identities compareGabrielle SchwarzSat 22 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSocial media arrived just as I, a younger millennial, was on the brink of teenhood. My friends and I signed up for accounts on Facebook, Myspace and Twitter, as well as less remembered sites such as the now defunct Bebo. We didn’t know what we were doing; no one did. We posted indiscreet messages and photos on public feeds that we wouldn’t want any future employer – or really anyone, for that matter – to see. Then gradually we, and our parents and their parents, too, learned what it means to live with that world-changing phenomenon that we term social media. We started to find different ways to adapt, a process that is ongoing.But what is the experience like for gen Z, the first generation of “digital natives”, for whom the language of the internet is a mother tongue? That is the question that led the Italian photographer Niccolò Rastrelli to embark on the project IRL (the online acronym, of course, for a phrase denoting our offline existences: in real life).Rastrelli has long been interested in the way people construct their identities through self-presentation. “In the last few years, I’ve also worked a lot with younger people. I’m older and don’t have children, so I want to understand their point of view,” says the photographer, who was born in 1977, making him a member of generation X. Past works include a project exploring the rising popularity around the globe of the youth subculture of cosplay. Now he felt it was time to broaden his focus to a more ubiquitous experience: being on the “socials”.“I wanted to portray the diversity in gen Z,” Rastrelli says. He recruited subjects across the full span of the generation, from 14-year-olds to adults in their late 20s. Most were in Italy, but he also visited the UK, Morocco and France. Each portrait has two paired components. On one side the subject is photographed in their bedroom, whether in their family home or in a flatshare or university halls. They are intentionally posed, nearly always making eye-contact with the camera. S ome clutch their phones, or sit by a computer. Often there is the familiar sight of a tangle of cords and plugs in an extension cable by the bed.double quotation markWhen you’re young, your bedroom is such an important place. It’s really your first solo home“I decided to shoot in the bedroom because when you’re young it’s such an important place. It’s really your first solo home,” Rastrelli explains. “Before social media, it was also the main place where you could build your identity.” Your room and the things inside it – posters, paintings, books, an electric guitar, a barbell, a massivestuffed unicorn – tell a story about what kind of person you are and want to be.Nowadays, the same goes for social media. And so, alongside those portraits, Rastrelli asked each of his subjects to pick snapshots of their phone screens that represented their usual activity. Nearly everything is fromInstagram, one of gen Z’s main apps of choice – and many of the images are from temporary “stories” rather than posts on the feed. There are selfies with silly filters, casual snaps of friends and food, black-and-white portraits taken with film cameras. It was important to Rastrelli that the youngsters “co-curated” the selection, just as they had arranged and posed in their bedrooms.Rastrelli also gave his subjects a questionnaire about their relationship with social media. Many responses surprised him – for example, that they often maintain more than one account on a single platform. Lana, who is 16, has multiple Instagram profiles with varying levels of privacy. “Only on my most private account do I feel free to really be myself,” she told him. He was also struck by how many young people see social media less as a site of personal expression than as a work tool. The clearest example was 23-year-old web developer and social media manager Francesco, who doesn’t post on his own account. As Rastrelli observes, “It’s like when you meet chefs. They all say they don’t cook at home because they’re cooking all day in the restaurant.”Recent years have seen growing debate about the potential dangers of social media for young people. In the UK, a ban for under-16s is set to be enforced from next spring. (In Italy there are no such plans.) But from his conversations with gen Z-ers, Rastrelli doesn’t think they seem any more affected than their elders: “Many of them use social media less than people from my generation.” The primary difference is the platforms they go to. For example,Facebook, now associated with boomers, barely came up. It’s made Rastrelli consider repeating the project but focusing on the older generation instead: “We are all involved with social media.”Stevie, 20, Rome (main picture top)A student from Pennsylvania, Stevie is now studying abroad in Rome. He says he has two Instagram accounts: a public one and a private one, and tends to shift in tone and identity depending on which he’s using. He dreams of becoming a media personality.View image in fullscreenLana, 16, FlorenceView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenLana’s first smartphone – obtained aged 11 after longnegotiations with her parents – opened up a new world, from group chats to shared photos. Social media is integral to her daily life: TikTok is more of a pastime while Instagram is like a diary. Her bedroom is the place she feels most authentic, she says. She reads a lot, from YA novels to heavier authors like Dostoevsky and Freud, who help her better understand herself and the world around her.Sofia, 14,ArezzoView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenSofia attends an art school where she studies animation, a passion she discovered thanks to a digital creator who makes content about the history of cartoons. Her online life is limited: her parents have blocked Instagram and TikTok, so she uses WhatsApp to share drawings, homework and memes with friends.Roberto, 27, LondonView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenBorn in Italy to a Ghanaian family, Roberto has lived in London for the past eight years and currently works as a personal trainer and a bartender. He didn’t get his first smart-phone until around 15 or 16 – before that he used a basic phone so his parents could keep track of him. He is cautious about what he shares and views: mainly fashion and fitness content.Mark, 28, FlorenceView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenMark, who was born in Nigeria and raised in Italy, paid for his first smartphone himself aged 12, by doing odd jobs and reselling customised clothes. He used to alter his features in photos, removing elements like his nose to escape identity labels. Now, as a freelance creative, he mainly uses Instagram as a tool for research, and rarely posts.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMelina, 24, ArlesView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenMelina, who studied 3D animation, relies on Instagram for tutorials and discovering other artists. She also follows friends and humorous accounts. She shares infrequently, mostly drawings rather than photographs of herself, rarely edited beyond an occasional filter. She keeps a second account with no other followers, where she stores images to remember moments of her life.Anna, 23, GlasgowView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenWhat excited Anna most when she got her first phone, aged 11, was the ability to photograph and film the world around her. Now her dream is to work in film, and she says social media will be a useful way to share work and find opportunities. In the meantime, she uses Instagram mostly as a source of creative inspiration. When she posts, she likes to avoid putting herself at the centre of the image.Andrea, 22, FlorenceView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenAndrea maintains two separate Instagram accounts, a personal one and a professional one for his work – as well as appearing in a local theatre troupe he performs solo as a drag artist. He says his approach is consistent across both his accounts: showing himself without filters , whether beautiful or deliberately grotesque, retouching images in Photoshop only to make a scene more “editorial”.Ali, 28, RabatView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenAli’s first proper smartphone, after years spent using broken old ones, changed everything, allowing him to take and share photos for the first time. These days he works in social media marketing, helping companies and projects grow and gain visibility. He says that he sees his bedroom as a place to rest and think, while online is where he can express his personality and take inspiration from others.Silvia, 23, RomeView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenSilvia says she feels like herself both offline and online, in different ways. At home she is more quiet; on social media, more extrovert. She says her family hasn’t always approved of her lack of filter on the internet, but she continues regardless. Music is central to her life – she’s part of a techno collective and performs as a DJ.To see more images from Niccolò Rastrelli’s project, go to instituteartist.com.Explore more on these topicsPhotographySocial mediaInstagramFacebookDigital mediaSocial networkingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Is this the end of Harry and Meghan’s American dream? | Prince Harry | The Guardian
description: The Sussexes are returning to the UK with significantly reduced media deals in an industry where fame alone can no longer guarantee success
Author: Michael Savage
Headline: The Sussexes are returning to the UK with significantly reduced media deals in an industry where fame alone can no longer guarantee success
Content: Composite: Alex Mellon for the Guardian : Getty Images/EPAView image in fullscreenComposite: Alex Mellon for the Guardian : Getty Images/EPAThe Saturday readPrince HarryIs this the end of Harry and Meghan’s American dream?The Sussexes are returning to the UK with significantly reduced media deals in an industry where fame alone can no longer guarantee successMichael SavageMedia editorSat 22 Aug 2026 16.42 EDTFirst published on Sat 22 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTShareHaving settled in California in the aftermath of their dramatic decoupling from the royal family in 2020, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex announced a partnership that appeared to set a clear destination for their new lives outside the House of Windsor.With every global media stable clamouring for their signature, the couple revealed adeal with Netflix reportedly worth $100m. The ambitions were lofty and broad, including scripted and unscripted projects, shows for all ages and documentaries.A$20m podcast deal with Spotifyappeared to confirm their ambitions; the Sussexes were reinventing themselves in the competitive world of content creation, a media powerhouse in the booming universe of streaming and podcasting.As the couple now prepare to return to the UK, they do so with those mega-deals either pared back or expired, and their media plans less clear. It raises the question: is this the end of their American dream?As with all things Harry and Meghan-related, their various media forays have spawned copious amounts of reactionary content and commentary. Each appearance, commission and production has been dissected: there have been blockbuster hits, much-publicised misses and somebrutal reviewsalong the way.View image in fullscreenPrince Harry and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, being interviewed by Oprah Winfrey in 2021.Photograph: ReutersFor Harry, the pull of returning to the UK, if perhaps not permanently, has been clear for a while.He says he loves his country, andin an interview with the Guardianlast year, he admitted he hankered for home.“I have always loved the UK and I always will love the UK. It’s been good to reconnect with the causes I am passionate about. I have been able to spend some time with people that I have known for so long. It is hard to do it from far away.”Perhaps more so recently because his father, King Charles, has been ill. And on the work front, it hasn’t been easy either.Six years in the content game offers a case study in how difficult it can be to negotiate the shifting sands of a transformed media landscape, so difficult that even a Hollywood actor and a British prince are not guaranteed to succeed.double quotation markThey arrived in Hollywood with almost every advantage imaginable, but audiences now effectively have infinite choiceMatt Navarra, social media consultantThose years have proved there is one bankable aspect of the Sussex brand: their relationship with the royal family continues to be devoured on an industrial scale. However, launching lifestyle brands and philanthropic pursuits that rely purely on name recognition – even with a packed contacts book of A-list friends to help – cannot guarantee reliable success in the cut-throat era of the attention economy.“The Sussexes have kind of got caught up in the media’s awkward teenage transition,” said Evan Shapiro, a former US media executive turned leading analyst of the creator economy. “Just being famous is no longer enough … The last time Meghan Markle worked in show business [starring in the US legal drama Suits], it was a different era. It was top down: ‘We push it out, you watch it.’ That’s just how it worked.“That era has passed. It’s fucking hard [now] … the competition is literally every human on earth. Eight billion people with phones who are all competing with Meghan Markle.”The Sussexes could scarcely have had better timing for their eye-catching 2020Netflixdeal, via their Archewell Productions organisation – global streamers were scrambling for big names to lure subscribers.The pair were in demand, talking with the likes of Disney and Apple before the Netflix deal was signed.Spotifywas also pursuing big-name deals when it secured the Sussexes.While the Netflix announcement talked of a raft of potential projects, the greatest prize was always the story of the Sussexes’ relationship with the royal family. The subsequent 2022 documentary series, Harry & Meghan,duly delivered, setting record viewing figures for a documentary debut and ranking as one of its most successful docuseries ever.1:11‘They were lying to protect my brother,’ says Harry in latest Netflix trailer – videoOther Netflix projects featuring the couple followed, including the Live to Lead interview series, Harry’s Polo documentary and two series of the cooking and lifestyle show With Love, Meghan.Unsurprisingly, content without the royal intrigue could not hit the heights of Harry & Meghan. Polo failed to make Netflix’s top 10 lists around the world, while ratings for the second series of With Love, Meghan dropped off. It wasthe 1,217th most watched titleon Netflix over the second half of last year. A mooted animated children’s series, Pearl, was cancelled.Netflix also ended its partnership with Meghan’s lifestyle brand, As Ever, after seven months. The company said handing full control to Meghan was always the plan. However, the relationship endures. Netflix renewed its partnership with the Sussexes, but slimmed it down to a “first look” deal.As for podcasting, the Spotify deal wasended by mutual consent in 2023, having only produced Meghan’s 12-episode podcast Archetypes, featuring interviews with people such as the former tennis champion Serena Williams and pop star Mariah Carey.View image in fullscreenMeghan with the actor Mindy Kaling in a scene from With Love, Meghan.Photograph: APMeghan subsequently launched another podcast series, Confessions of a Female Founder, in 2025, with Lemonada Media. Only nine episodes were made. She revealed last year that there would be no second series, saying she was focusing on As Ever.In line with all of Harry and Meghan’s exploits, there have been some acerbic assessments of their media production efforts. Most notably, the Spotify executive Bill Simmons called them“fucking grifters”after the company’s deal with the couple ended.Less incendiary industry analysts point to the significant timing. The Sussexes’ narrowed Netflix deal and split with Spotify coincided with content providers cutting back on their big celebrity bets, and the chaos being wrought by the rapid rise of the creator economy.“This isn’t a story about nobody being interested in [the Sussexes],” said Matt Navarra, a social media consultant who has worked with broadcasters. “It’s quite the opposite. They can generate attention almost on demand. The harder thing is converting attention into a repeatable media proposition.“Harry and Meghan arrived in Hollywood with almost every advantage imaginable, but audiences now effectively have infinite choice. They don’t care about how expensive the deal was, or how famous the person is.“I think that’s one of the brutal lessons of the new media world: that fame can buy you the first click, but only the content earns the second … Their original Harry & Meghan series was pretty much a blockbuster. What they’ve struggled with is repeatability.”It’s Harry and Meghan in Finding Freedom 2: Back in Blighty | Marina HydeRead moreSeveral industry insiders noted the comparisons with the Obamas, whose Higher Ground production company’s multi-year deal with Netflix narrowed to a “first look” deal in 2024. Their Spotify deal also ended in 2022.Shapiro said the Sussexes had not yet proved they could draw big audiences beyond content directly related to their dealings with the royal family. “By no fault of their own, the Sussexes were not prepared for the current moment,” he said. “It turns out, other than marrying a prince, Meghan Markle just isn’t that special. Other than being born into royalty, Harry’s just not that interesting.”Navarra said: “Enormous curiosity exists around them, but curiosity about a person isn’t necessarily the same as demand for everything that person produces.Celebrityis a distribution advantage, but it isn’t a content strategy.“Harry and Meghan show that you can inherit enormous attention and still have to earn the audience every single time. To me, that is the really interesting shift.”View image in fullscreenMeghan, as Rachel Zane, with Patrick J Adams, as Michael Ross, in a scene from Suits.Photograph: USA Network/NBCU Photo Bank/Getty ImagesIt is perhaps understandable, then, that Meghan is reportedly returning to a bankable acting career that she put on ice after her marriage to Harry. Initial reports from Australia of a UK-based role for Meghan were backed up by Tina Brown, the former Vanity Fair editor and founding editor of the Daily Beast.Brown said it had been fuelled by Meghan’s positive experience as a celebrity judge on MasterChef Australia last month. “She finally realised how much easier – and more fun – it is to perform in a hit baked by someone else,”Brown wrote.“She was back on the market, and it did not take long for Hollywood’s mega-deal machine, WME, the talent agency that still represents her, to get her a role.”Sources close to the Sussexes have not denied the reports.On Friday night it was reported that Meghan was in talks to return to acting in Netflix’s series The Gentlemen. According to Variety, she was in discussions to join the third season of the Guy Ritchie-created series.On Saturday Tina Brown, the former editor-in-chief of Vanity Fair and the New Yorker, reported that Meghan’s casting had been withdrawn due to “backlash in the UK”.But the couple are not out of the media production game. Archewell has evolved into a more traditional production company. Its forthcoming Netflix projects include a polo drama and a film adaptation of the romantic novel Meet Me at the Lake. Several sources familiar with the company said there were also projects in the works beyond Netflix.In practical terms, the move back to the UK creates few issues for their media ambitions. It is not unusual for major production companies to sit outside Hollywood and make shows away from the US, and the UK remains a major production hub.As for Harry, he – or anyone else – will struggle to replicate therunaway media success of his memoir, Spare. He is focusing on his Invictus Games coming to Birmingham next year. Meanwhile, Meghan has suggested any return as a business podcaster may depend on the progress of her lifestyle brand.“I would love to bring the show back when I am at a different end of my founder journey,” she said last summer, explaining why she had put her Confessions of a Female Founder podcast on hold. “I think a different time will be so exciting to compare and contrast.”

title: Plug-in solar: could a low-cost panel cut your bills? | Energy bills | The Guardian
description: Britons will be able to buy ‘balcony’ systems they can install themselves from 27 August thanks to rule change
Author: Zoe Wood
Headline: Britons will be able to buy ‘balcony’ systems they can install themselves from 27 August thanks to rule change
Content: Plug-in systems are about a fifth of the size of a typical residential rooftop solar system.Photograph: Westend61/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPlug-in systems are about a fifth of the size of a typical residential rooftop solar system.Photograph: Westend61/Getty ImagesEnergy billsPlug-in solar: could a low-cost panel cut your bills?Britons will be able to buy ‘balcony’ systems they can install themselves from 27 August thanks to rule changeZoe WoodSat 22 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDespite this summer bringing hours of sunshine, many Britons have been unable to cash in on free electricity generated by the sun. Rooftop solar panels are usually out of the question if you live in a flat or rent your home, and the cost has made them prohibitive to many more households.However, this could be about to change because next week the first wave of low-cost “plug-in” solar panels will go on sale in Great Britain.Also known as “plug‑and‑play” or “balcony” solar, the clue to what makes them different is in the name: you can fix them to a balcony or garden wall, then plug them in like a toaster.The mini solar systems are a familiar sight on balconies in Spain and in Germany, wherethey are known as aBalkonkraftwerk(balcony power plant), but until a recent change in the law, they were not permitted in Britain.Matt Parry from the RenewableEnergyAssociation, a trade body for renewable energy, says the kits are a gamechanger. “It democratises solar and gives everyone the chance to get it,” he says.How the kits workUnlike traditional rooftop solar panels, which require a professional to install,balcony solarkits – which commonly include one or two panels – can be plugged in to a three-prong wall socket.You can fix them on a balcony railing, shed roof or garden wall – anywhere with good sun exposure and safe access.When sunlight hits the solar panels, they generate a direct current. The microinverter then converts this to an alternating current, which flows into your home’s electrical system, reducing the amount you draw from the grid.View image in fullscreenPlug-in solar panels are a familiar sight on balconies in Germany and Spain.Photograph: Ronald Rampsch/AlamyPreviously, rules around the installation of solar were what was holding people back. Butlast year the government announcedit would make it possible for plug-in solar to be used in this country.To make this a reality, it has updated wiring regulations to allow households in Great Britain to connect plug-in solar panels capable of generating up to 800 watts of power into the mains without the need for an electrician. (The rules are different in Northern Ireland.)Buying panelsBig names including B&Q, Currys, Lidl, Wickes and Amazon are lining up to sell plug-in solar.Given the size (and weight) of these devices, it is expected that many will be bought online.View image in fullscreenCurrys is one of the big high street retailers lining up to sell the panels.Photograph: May James/ReutersAlthough you may have already come across plug-in solar panels for sale, industry experts suggest waiting until the regulations take effect on 27 August before making a purchase.Electrical Safety First, the consumer safety charity, is urging shoppers to stick to reputable high street retailers and their websites to ensure the device complies with the rules.Luke Osborne, the charity’s technical director, advises people to “avoid buying these devices from third-party sellers on online marketplaces. These platforms are now not legally responsible for the safety of goods sold via their sites, exposing people to substandard versions that may put you and your home at risk.”Andrew Moore, the founder of the British solar panel brand UKSOL, says: “We are working towards making the initial products available from 27 August.”His company will initially sell 460W and 890W kits, starting at £599 and £999 respectively, and it plans to launch another four models in late September, with prices starting from £499.Sizewise, plug-in solar setups are usually smaller than rooftop options, but sizes vary. The UKSOL 460W single panel kit measures 1,762mm x 1,134mm x 30mm and weighs 25.5kg. The 890W kit comprises two panels.View image in fullscreenUKSOL’s 460W plug-in solar kit is less than two metres long.Photograph: UKSOLSetting upThe official guidance suggests that it will take about an hour to set up your system. It estimates 15-25% of people will need professional support mounting the panels, and about 15% will need minor electrical works. UKSOL suggests it takes two people to handle and position the panels, as each one weighs 25kg.Osborne says plug-in solar systems should not be connected via extension leads, cable reels, multiway adaptors, travel adaptors or plug-in RCD adaptors. “These accessories can overheat, become overloaded and create additional safety risks,” he says.View image in fullscreenThe official guidance estimates that 15-25% of people will need professional support mounting the panels.Photograph: Jeremy Poland/Getty ImagesThere is also some other housekeeping. The owner has to tell their distribution network operator that they are using them (there should be a form in the box). You can find out who it is by inputting your postcode on theEnergy Networks Associationwebsite. You will also be able to consult the ENA’s Connect Direct site for a list of approved devices, which is a good place to start before you buy.SavingsPlug-in systems are about a fifth of the size of a typical residential rooftop solar system, which means they will not provide enough energy to power a home on their own – but they could cut your bill.One drawback is that you need to be home to use the power generated because without a battery it is not being stored for later, so flows back to the grid.However, the adoption of balcony solar could, in time, pave the way for plug-in batteries in British homes, too. If paired with a plug-in solar system, households could store their own renewable electricity during the day and use it to run their appliances in the evenings. The government is reportedly considering plans to bulk-buy the devices and distribute them to low-income homes.double quotation markThe slight downside is that plug-in solar is hitting the markets as the summer’s coming to an endThe Renewable Energy Association’s Matt ParryA basic plug-in solar system costs about £400. Parry says it will “give you back, at worst, £40 a year, and at the best about £110. If it’s the worst-case scenario, it’s going to pay for itself in 10 years, but at the best-case scenario, it’s four.“If you’ve just got 800W, it’s only at its very peak that it will give you that.”He adds: “The slight downside is that plug-in solar is hitting the markets as the summer’s coming to an end. It’s going to be more use in May next year.”View image in fullscreenA basic plug-in solar system costs about £400.Photograph: amriphoto/Getty ImagesMoore says that the level of saving is affected by a number of things, including the system size, location, orientation and actually being home to use the power.He expects the 460W system his company will be selling to save a typical household about £80-£120 a year, “while the 890W system could save more”.He adds: “The greatest savings are achieved when households use appliances during daylight hours, as this increases the proportion of generated electricity used within the home.”You can buy a more expensive 2,000W kit (the inverter will only allow 800W through) to maximise your power-generating capacity, but these are more expensive.Staying safeAlthough there is no obligation to do this, before buying a kit, some experts think you should get your home electrics checked by a professional. That is because this is the first time that British residential wiring circuits will take power in via a three-point socket rather than simply being used to distribute electricity.Electrical Safety First is concerned about the impact on residual current devices, or RCDs, which sit in a household electricity box and cut off the power if someone drills through a wire or runs their lawnmower over a power cord. Electricians are concerned they may burn out when plug-in solar panels start adding electricity to the circuit.A Department for Energy Security and Net Zero spokesperson says: “Plug-in solar panels will be available to buy this summer, and stringent verification and registration checks are already in place. They are a transformative technology that can save people hundreds of pounds on their bills.”Box] RentersPlug-in solar should make it easier for tenants to take advantage of renewable energy, as any kit they buy can be moved from place to place.But if you are renting, you should ask permission from your landlord before you invest in any panels.The rules on what you can do with regard to fixing brackets to hold them, for example, may vary depending on what your tenancy agreement says.View image in fullscreenTenants can use plug-in panels as they can be moved between rental properties.Photograph: Miodrag Ignjatovic/Getty ImagesThere’s “no reason” why your landlord should be against the idea, Parry says. “He or she can look at the information and know it’s super, super safe.”Meera Chindooroy, the deputy director of campaigns, public affairs and policy at the National Residential Landlords Association, says that while the organisation supports the “principle of tenants benefiting from plug-in solar panels … landlords would first need to be satisfied that the panels meet all required safety standards”.She adds: “It would not be right for landlords to be held responsible for the safety of equipment they were not asked about in the first place.”Explore more on these topicsEnergy billsHome improvementsSolar powerConsumer affairsEnergy industryRenewable energyEnergyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Auntie v influencers: why YouTubers are ready for battle with the BBC | Public service broadcasting | The Guardian
description: Content creators are fighting proposal to boost traditional broadcasters in video platforms’ all-powerful algorithms
Author: Michael Savage
Headline: Content creators are fighting proposal to boost traditional broadcasters in video platforms’ all-powerful algorithms
Content: Ben Ebbrell filming content for his Sorted Food channel, which has 15 million viewers tuning in each month.Photograph: Sorted FoodView image in fullscreenBen Ebbrell filming content for his Sorted Food channel, which has 15 million viewers tuning in each month.Photograph: Sorted FoodPublic service broadcastingAuntie v influencers: why YouTubers are ready for battle with the BBCContent creators are fighting proposal to boost traditional broadcasters in video platforms’ all-powerful algorithmsMichael SavageMedia editorSat 22 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 22 Aug 2026 08.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe millions who subscribe to the content creator Simon Squibb’s social media channels are usually delivered tips and hacks on how to turn their dream business idea into reality. But they were recently presented with something completely different.In an Instagram post entitled “the government wants to control YOU”, Squibb issued an urgent call to arms. He asked his followers to fight against a proposal that he said could force content from theBBCand other traditional broadcasters into their social media feeds and recommendations whether they liked it or not.Squibb is one of many major UK content creators outraged by a proposal included in a government paper earlier in the summer that wouldboost content from traditional broadcasterssuch as the BBC, ITV and Channel 4 in the all-powerful algorithms of YouTube and TikTok.The idea has beenpushed collectively by public service broadcastersas a way of boosting trusted material and preserving distinctly British content.Ministers want to help them survive in a world in which audiences are ditching traditional TV for digital platforms. They prefer a voluntary deal with digital platforms, but have pointed to using legislation if necessary.Video-sharing platforms and streaming services accounted for 74% of all video time for audiences aged 16-24 in 2024-25, and 69% for 25-34s.YouTubeis the most-watched service for children aged four to 15, accounting for 28% of their video viewing.View image in fullscreenSimon Squibb is just one of many major UK content creators outraged by the proposal.Illustration: Simon GibbBut the measure has slowly but surely been causing anger and disbelief among content creators, who see it as shifting the goalposts to allow bigger players to stay on top. If the broadcasters go up the algorithm, they reason content creators will be pushed down.They have been holding private meetings, putting out emergency videos and urging viewers and fellow creators to speak out before the government’s consultation ends at the end of the month, featuring dramatic warnings about “the end of YouTube”.Squibb and others have even raised comparisons with authoritarian state control. “Russia pushes its channels that it believes the people should watch,” he said.“I just think it’s a very bad thing to push. Trust has to be earned. If the BBC is selected as one of the trusted sources, does that also mean that Dragons’ Den is going to get prominent coverage over my education and business content? You have to let the public decide.”Ben Ebbrell, whose Sorted Food channel started as a small project among friends and now has 15 million viewers tuning in each month, said the idea would undermine 16 years of investment in building an audience, a period in which the TV world ignored the growing popularity of YouTube, he said.“At first, the TV world almost looked down upon content creators, but it’s completely flipped now, where we feel like we’ve got the stardust.“It was just quite a shock when they said almost that they didn’t want to start playing the game, they wanted to move goalposts – or possibly even running off the pitch with a ball and a bit of a sulk … it’s kind of embarrassing.”Jade Beason, a creator with 310,000 YouTube subscribers who has worked with traditional broadcasters on their digital content, said they should concentrate instead on making content that works for digital platforms –something the BBC and others are trying to do.View image in fullscreenJade Beason.Photograph: YouTube“I don’t think it’s going to get them the results that they need and I think it’s going to disrupt creators in the process,” she said. “To me, it just feels like you’re pushing the queue, you’re jumping ahead.“[Traditional broadcasters] don’t need more help for people to find them … people aren’t struggling to find TV news, they know where it is. They’re choosing not to watch it. That’s the challenge we should be focusing on.”Grace Andrews, a content creator who helped set up the Diary of a CEO podcast, is among those coordinating the pushback against the idea and rounding up responses before the end of the month. YouTube has also been encouraging creators to respond.View image in fullscreenGrace Andrews.Photograph: Instagram“Now obviously [traditional broadcasters] are scrambling for eyeballs and instead of adapting to that world, they’re trying to legislate their way back into it,” she said. “Nobody who actually understands why people watch what they watch in 2026 was in the room when this document was created.“I don’t want misinformation on my feeds either, but I don’t think this is the solution. Social media works because people are choosing what they see. That’s the entire mechanic. The second that becomes something enforced instead of something they picked, they don’t trust it any more.”A spokesperson for the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport said:“We want to ensure that content from public service media providers such as the BBC, ITV, Channel 4 and others is easily discoverable on video-sharing platforms, like YouTube, and we have urged the industry to come together and move quickly on voluntary solutions.“We do not see this as a zero-sum game between traditional broadcasters, content creators and other video platforms. We want to create an environment where PSM [public service media] providers, high-quality news providers and content creators can all thrive.”Explore more on these topicsPublic service broadcastingYouTubeTikTokBBCfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: I’m known as The Black Farmer because there are so few of us in the UK. It’s one of the ways farming must change | Wilfred Emmanuel-Jones | The Guardian
description: Running a farm is tough – TV’s Clarkson’s Farm shows that – but I know many minorities would love the chance. And we would all benefit, says farmer and businessman Wilfred Emmanuel-Jones
Author: Wilfred Emmanuel-Jones
Headline: Running a farm is tough – TV’s Clarkson’s Farm shows that – but I know many minorities would love the chance. And we would all benefit, says farmer and businessman Wilfred Emmanuel-Jones
Content: In Defra’s most recent survey of England’s principal farmers and holders, 99.7% self-described as white.Photograph: Peter Cade/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIn Defra’s most recent survey of England’s principal farmers and holders, 99.7% self-described as white.Photograph: Peter Cade/Getty ImagesOpinionFarmingI’m known as The Black Farmer because there are so few of us in the UK. It’s one of the ways farming must changeWilfred Emmanuel-JonesRunning a farm is tough – TV’s Clarkson’s Farm shows that – but I know many minorities would love the chance. And we would all benefitSat 22 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 22 Aug 2026 12.46 EDTShareWho’d be a farmer?Clarkson’s Farm on Amazonis great entertainment but it also gives some indication of the stresses and challenges behind the farm gate. Would anyone who lacked the significant alternative income that Clarkson is lucky to have want that? Well, actually, yes.I’m an entrepreneur who owns a farm, as opposed to hands-on running the small one I bought 25 years ago, but as I look around the industry, I’m struck by a significant fact: the very reason I can be known as the Black Farmer is because I am such a rarity that it makes me readily identifiable.Because of what I do, people – many of them British minorities – often ask me how they can be farmers, how they can secure some land and set up for themselves. Don’t be surprised at that: among Britain’s minorities, millions have rural origins in lands abroad. It is a mistake to see people of colour as intrinsically urban – my own origins are in rural Jamaica. But when they ask me, I can’t really help them. There is no obvious route for them to follow, and there is precious little land they could possibly farm. This is the reality. In 2025, when Defra completed its most recent survey of principal farmers and holders in England, it found 99.7% of those who respondedself-described as white.I’m aware of the pitfall here. I know the danger these days of wanting to talk about diversity and being dismissed as woke. I’m hardly woke: in 2010 I fought a rural seat for the Conservatives. But in any other industry, that figure, 99.7%, would prompt some questions.Here are the problems. If you are black or Asian or a kid from another minority in London, or Manchester, or Birmingham or Newcastle, where do you start? Your parents don’t own even an acre of land. You don’t have the network, or the knowledge that comes from growing up within or adjacent to a farming family and a farming community.There is the ongoing and emotive debate about inheritance tax and whether farms should so easily be passed down from generation to generation. I’m among those who celebrate the families that have worked the same land year after year, decade after decade. That brings a knowledge and continuity essential to rural communities and our food supply. But as well as inheritance, we have to think about entry. People cannot resolve to make that commitment if they cannot see a way in.How could that be different? Think about who owns the land. The National Trust, for example, is the country’s largest farm-owner,with more than 1,300 tenant farmers. Think about the Duchy of Cornwall, the crown estate, the Church of England. Universities and local authorities also control large tracts of land. There are people and institutions that could administer properly controlled programmes to allow those from non-traditional farming backgrounds to have a go. They could create starter farms and offer affordable tenancies. They could provide mentoring, pairing experienced farmers with ambitious newcomers, and give access to equipment. Maybe there could be targeted apprenticeships, allowing people to learn the ropes on someone else’s farm – a process that may lead to them owning their own farm. One might cite 28-year-oldKaleb Cooperon Clarkson’s farm, although in that case it is clearly the younger man teaching the older how it is done.View image in fullscreenWilfred Emmanuel-Jones walking on Dartmoor.Photograph: Tim Cuff/AlamyThe supermarkets could play a role, as they wield enormous influence over British food and how it is produced. Why can’t they create routes for a new generation of growers, providing a sure path for produce to reach the public? That would be a move towards diversity with a clear economic purpose.Farmingcould do with new blood: people who question the traditions, people who know about different foods, cultures and business models – people who look at a field and can envision things that previous generations couldn’t.I think back. I grew up in Birmingham and my first experience with the land was helping my father on his allotment. My route was defiantly non-traditional. I struggled with undiagnosed dyslexia, joined the Parachute regiment and got kicked out, flipped burgers, worked as a chef and then produced cookery programmes for the BBC, which allowed me to buy a farm in Devon. Locals dubbed me “the Black Farmer”. I wish there were many more of us.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI would never want to denigrate those who work so hard, and who may have toiled for generations to run their farms, produce the food we need and sometimes – if they are lucky, if the weather permits, if the stars align – make a profit. But I also want to be just as excited by the prospect of another black kid from Birmingham getting an opportunity, or a minority kid from a council estate in Manchester becoming the first farmer in the family.Farming is key to the future, and the climate crisis is forcing us to think fast and hard about crops, water, soil and what we do with them. Old timers, new thinkers – we need both.Wilfred Emmanuel-Jones is a businessman and founder of The Black Farmer food companyExplore more on these topicsFarmingOpinionRaceFood & drink industryLand ownershipcommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘It exists only for pleasure’: does ice-cream have a future in the age of wellness fads and weight-loss drugs?  | Ice-cream and sorbet | The Guardian
description: As fitness-conscious consumers turn away from processed foods, the industry is scrambling for new ideas, including nutrient-rich lollies and protein-packed tubs. Will they take the fun out of this summer treat?
Author: Christian Sinibaldi
Headline: As fitness-conscious consumers turn away from processed foods, the industry is scrambling for new ideas, including nutrient-rich lollies and protein-packed tubs. Will they take the fun out of this summer treat?
Content: All photographs: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianPhotograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAll photographs: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianPhotograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianIce-cream and sorbet‘It exists only for pleasure’: does ice-cream have a future in the age of wellness fads and weight-loss drugs?As fitness-conscious consumers turn away from processed foods, the industry is scrambling for new ideas, including nutrient-rich lollies and protein-packed tubs. Will they take the fun out of this summer treat?Words:Kitty Drake. Photographs:Christian SinibaldiSat 22 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 22 Aug 2026 06.08 EDTShareLast month, I stood in the biggest ice-cream factory in Britain and watched a 5-metre Viennetta mint-flavoured ice-cream cake get made. The factory – which is owned by the Magnum Ice Cream Company and produces nine different brands of ice-cream – is based in an enormous building in Gloucester, where the air is thick with the scent of custard.I walked past the Twister and Solero sections on my way in, through clouds of tangy fruit, before arriving at the Viennetta assembly line, where everything smelled minty fresh. A Viennetta is built on a conveyor belt by a fully automated system, and watching it take shape was oddly hypnotic. Every few inches a nozzle attached to the belt squirted out a frilly layer of mint ice-cream, then another nozzle smoothed a flat layer of vanilla on top of that, then came a squirt of chocolate sauce, and it was back to frilly mint again. On and on it went, layer upon layer, popping out finished Viennettas at the end of the line at a rate of 200 cakes every 60 seconds.A slop bucket full of Viennetta overrun stood at the side of the conveyor belt and I fought a strong urge to squelch my fingers into it. Later, the factory operations manager allowed me to push my whole hand into the slop bucket up to the wrist and then lick my hand at a sink, before washing it and resuming the tour.View image in fullscreenA conveyor belt of Viennettas …View image in fullscreen… and Magnums in the company’s ice-cream factoryI had travelled to the factory at a tricky moment for ice-cream. Magnum – which owns Viennetta, Ben & Jerry’s, Solero and Twister, along with most of the other lollies you can buy from an ice-cream van – reported falling sales in the last quarter of 2025. The global ice-cream industry is worth £85bn and Magnum controls 20% of it, so the stakes are high.In June, Magnum was the most shorted large cap stock in Europe, with investors betting against the company because of doubts about how ice-cream will survive in the age of Ozempic. Magnum’s sales rose in the most recent quarter, driven by record temperatures, but the stock price remains volatile because investors fear people will not be eating much ice-cream in the future, says markets analyst David Hayes from Jefferies investment bank. In the US – where one in eight people are now taking GLP-1s – ice-cream sales have fallen in the past year, according to consumer research firm NielsenIQ. The British ice-cream industry looks set to suffer the same fate:1.6 million UK adultsused weight loss drugs between 2024 and 2025, and that number is predicted to jump after this month’s release of the UK’s second, and much cheaper, weight-loss pill.Such drugs are not the only problem ice-cream makers have to contend with. In recent years, as wellness culture has gained momentum, a growing obsession with protein and fibre has changed the way we eat.Protein is touted as a magical cure for all manner of ills: perimenopause, anxiety, the urge to have a nap at 3pm. The price of whey – a yellowish, dusty, protein-rich powder made from curdled milk – is at an all-time global high and the US is in the grip of a shortage of cottage cheese, which is higher in protein and lower in fat than normal cheese. Demand has become so frenzied that people trade conspiracy theories about its scarcity online.GLP-1 users eat less, but they are advised to eat more protein so they don’t lose muscle mass – which creates a problem for the ice-cream industry. (A Twister contains just half a gram of protein.) Protein mania has become so widespread, it affects even those who would never take a weight-loss drug. In the UK, one in 40 people now have gout, with some dietitians blaming the uptick on men overconsuming protein in an attempt to bulk up. On TikTok, fitness influencers chug egg whites and toy with the idea of eating dog food for its enviable protein-to-calorie ratio. In response, Magnum has developed a new range of protein- and vitamin-enriched lollies and tubs which they plan to release in the UK soon. As appetites change, can the ice-cream industry find new ways to coax us into buying treats?A few days before my trip to the factory, I travelled to Magnum’s innovation hub in Colworth, Bedfordshire, to sample the company’s new, nutrient-rich ice-creams. The hub is a sleek, wide-windowed sequence of labs where scientists and chefs experiment with new recipes. I was led into a spotless demo kitchen and seated at a conference table opposite a colour-coded model of the human brain (ice-cream “lights up” different parts of it). A chef appeared, bearing a platter with what looked like a lipstick but was actually a tiny red ice lolly, hiding inside a lipstick container.After I had finished this lolly – which I ate so greedily, I didn’t really taste it – Zbigniew Lewicki, Magnum’s chief research, design and innovation officer, spoke to me about some of the UK’s first factory-made ice-creams. Wall’s, one of the oldest brands under the Magnum umbrella, started selling ice-cream from a factory in Acton, London, in 1922. Wall’s was originally a butcher’s, and the company pivoted to ice-cream as a kind of summer-proof sausage equivalent, because meat wasn’t selling well in the heat. Ice-cream street traders have existed in the UK since the 1850s, when they used horse-drawn carts. But with the advent of mechanical refrigeration in the early 20th century, it became possible to mass-produce ice-cream. As British people began to buy freezers in the late 70s, it was rolled out to supermarkets. The 80s – which food writer Ruby Tandoh has called the “golden age” of British ice-cream – saw the invention of Twister, Viennetta, Calippo and Feast.double quotation markThis place I would compare to James Bond when he comes back and says to his science guy, ‘I need this shooting pen’View image in fullscreenChief research and design officer Zbigniew Lewicki at the Magnum’s innovation hubThe job of the innovation hub is to come up with new ice-creams that will become just as iconic as the 80s classics. Lewicki said one of the major changes he’s seeing is a new emphasis on “health and diet shifts compounded by transparency”. They are now dealing with a new kind of consumer who is deeply concerned with finding out precisely what is in their ice-cream. “A lot of people, particularly the younger generation, read labels at the moment,” he said. Lewicki is a smiley, charismatic man, and he insisted the industry has changed “mostly in a good way” – but there was a slight note of anxiety in his voice as he spoke of this new generation of label readers.Another platter appeared by my elbow and I was handed a new ice-cream Magnum is calling Hydro:Ice. Label readers scouring the back of this ice-cream packet will find a long list of vitamins and minerals: C, magnesium and so much B2, it glows in the dark. A chef invited me to place my hand holding the ice-cream inside a UV-illuminated box and I watched my lolly light up and glow neon green. Michelle Neville, a behavioural scientist employed by Magnum to get inside the heads of ice-cream eaters, talked me through the profile of the Hydro:Ice customer. “They’re very big on their appearance,” she said. “Hair is on point, nails are on point, brows on point.” Hydro:Ice launched in Ibiza last summer, with a campaign taglined “Ravers Are Athletes Too”. As I ate mine, Neville showed me a promotional video of a thin woman on a treadmill, licking an ice lolly.View image in fullscreenNew offerings include a glow-in-the-dark lolly …View image in fullscreen… and mini versions of classicsNext I was invited to sample tiny ice-creams called Bonbons – minuscule versions of Soleros and Magnums that have been specially designed for consumers who want to eat a “controlled bite”. These tiny Magnums – which look a bit like large sheep droppings – were developed before Ozempic gained popularity, and are not specifically made for GLP-1 users. Lewicki said they were more about appealing to a “collective mindset” where it had become about “the type of pleasure you can get from a relatively small amount of food”.Listening to Lewicki, now on my fifth Bonbon, I realised I had never felt so deeply aware of my own body when eating an ice-cream. For decades food companies have employed scientists to work out how to keep you eating without stopping long enough to remember you have a body.Foodtechnologists have learned how to balance carbohydrate-to-fat ratios so a food can slow down or bypass the brain’s “satiety signal” which tells you you’ve had enough. Technologists know how to design energy-dense food that dissolves so fast on your tongue, you immediately crave more. Ice-creams are usually too cold to emit odour, so Mars has worked out how to rub chocolate and caramel scent molecules into the ribbing of their ice-cream packets; they want you to begin salivating from the moment you tear one open. Magnum has hired technologists to engineer the chocolate casing on its ice-cream, so when you bite in, it doesn’t shatter into too many pieces and distract you by falling down your top. Everything has been specially designed to make you forget yourself – and your flesh – and keep chasing the next bite.double quotation markWith the birth of the 99 Flake, ice-cream became ever more connected in the British imagination with holidays and summerView image in fullscreenBy contrast, the selling point of Magnum’s new ice-creams seems to be they will keep you laser-focused on your own body. Neville explained that the brand is trying to sell ice-cream to a customer who sees their “food as medicine”. “Now, even with a basic cereal bar, some people expect it to help metabolic resilience, control glycaemic index, improve gut health,” she said. “Functionality” is a word that came up a lot during my visit to the hub; the requirement that your ice-cream should be seen to materially benefit you in some way.In a way, this pivot to selling diet food is nothing new. As the journalist Tomas Weber has written, Big Food is adept at capitalising on diet culture. In the 90s, when “fat” was the macronutrient singled out as the enemy, fast food companies sold low-fat burgers, crisps and biscuits. The Scottish brand Mackie’s released a low-fat ice-cream in 2004. But this latest drive to market ice-cream as a “functional” food – something you eat not because it tastes nice, but because you believe it has some kind of nutritious, medicinal value – still feels striking. Because more than any other food – more even than chocolate – ice-cream’s only real reason for existing is pleasure. A perfect mix of fat, sugar and at least 20% air, ice-cream was not invented to nourish you. First served in Europe in the early 1500s, it debuted in England as a magical kind of “table trick”. Guests would look on while a servant churned, and a mass of sugary ice was transformed before their eyes into a strange, sweet foam. The Victorians ate ice-cream at balls and whittled it into enormous, campy ice sculptures, modelling pineapples, huge swans and whole bunches of flowers. With the arrival of the motorised ice-cream van in the 1920s in the UK and the birth of the 99 Flake, ice-cream became ever more connected in the British imagination with holidays and summer. The fact that ice-cream is essentially frivolous is a key part of its allure. It melts, so it almost demands that the eater give themselves up to the moment. The period between unwrapping an ice-cream and it collapsing into a puddle is a window in time, specially cordoned off for pleasure. You have to enjoy it or it will disappear without you. An ice-cream is a bit like a lit cigarette in that way.View image in fullscreenIce-cream melts …View image in fullscreen… so it almost demands that the eater give themselves up to the momentThe last ice-cream I ate in the show kitchen was the Yasso, and it was the most functional of all. The Yasso looks a little like a classic Magnum, after you have peeled its chocolate casing off; it is made from Greek yoghurt and non-fat milk, and contains 4g of protein a stick. Yasso, which tastes fabulously sweet, is selling well in the US and will launch in the UK soon. Lewicki said he has grand plans to roll it out to gyms, and told me there are 100,000 across Europe: “And the best kind of nutritious ice-cream for people leaving the gym? Completely not available. Would it need to be a soft ice? Would we sell it as an ice-cream protein bar?” Lewicki’s eyes sparkled. “We have at least 10 prototypes of high-protein ice-cream, hardcore healthy formulations just to test the limits. We have ice-cream with collagen.” He gestured excitedly to the ceiling, to take in the whole of the innovation hub. “This place I would compare to James Bond when he comes back and says to his science guy, ‘I need this shooting pen.’”Curious about how nutritious Magnum’s new ice-creams really are, I called Professor Chris van Tulleken, author of the 2023 bestselling bookUltra-Processed People. In it, the doctor and academic elucidates the science that shows a diet high in ultra-processed foods – which he defines as any product containing an ingredient you could not typically find in a kitchen cupboard – causes weight gain, diabetes, heart disease, cancer and other health problems.The first chapter is largely about ice-cream, and the fact that most on the market (one notable exception being Häagen-Dazs) are ultra-processed. From the 50s on, as the ice-cream market grew, producers began to add chemicals and additives to the mix to make it more tolerant to heat, so it could be transported long distances – from the factory floor to the supermarket aisle to your home freezer – without breaking down into icy shards. To increase profit margins, expensive ingredients such as egg yolk and cream were stripped out and replaced with things like glycerine and sodium alginate, additives that mimic the effect of food but are technically not food at all. In the second half of the 20th century, ice-cream went from being a pudding you bought freshly made from a local producer to an almost indestructible substance designed to live in your freezer for years.double quotation markVitamin B2 is just put in to make an unhealthy thing seem healthy. If you want B2, eat some eggsView image in fullscreenOver the phone, Van Tulleken told me that while Magnum’s new ice-creams might appear to be healthier options, we should be suspicious of any vitamin, protein or fibre claim on an ice-cream packet. We discussed Hydro:Ice and Van Tulleken cited scientific research showing that taking supplements, unless you are prescribed them for a specific condition, has no health benefit. “There is a library of data that shows adding B2 to an ice-cream will not improve your health,” Van Tulleken said. “It’s just put in to make an unhealthy thing seem healthy. If you want B2, eat some eggs.”Next I called the food scientist Barry Smith, who used to work as a sensory consultant for fast food companies – including ice-cream makers – advising them on how to engineer food to make it as irresistible as possible. He is now a professor of philosophy and sensory expert at the University of London, and campaigns about the health risks posed by products made by some of the companies he used to work for. Smith told me when fast food companies release a diet product, they don’t remove artificial chemicals. Quite the opposite. If you strip out real sugar from an ice-cream to make a “low sugar” claim, you have to replace it with artificial sweeteners. “Quite a lot of these taste a little bitter in the finish, so they need something to mask that.” Chemical is layered upon chemical, Smith said, to counterbalance nasty side-effects and improve the texture in order to make the “healthy” treat taste bearable.Artificial sweeteners also cause the brain to expect that it will receive sugar, jacking up your insulin levels. This, Smith said, is why drinking Diet Coke with your meals might actually make you put on weight. “When the sugar doesn’t come, the body feels cheated. So it stores as much of the fat and carbohydrate from the meal as it can”. Smith has a lilting Mancunian accent and he was animated during our call. He made this last point, about Coca Cola, with the air of a conjurer producing a particularly juicy rabbit from a hat.Scoop of the year! We taste-test 99 of 2026’s most unusual ice creams, from the unbeatable to the unlickableRead moreWhile we spoke, Smith scoured the online ingredients list of the Yasso Chocolate Chip Cookie Dough ice-cream lolly. He said it has fewer artificial chemicals than a classic Magnum, but there are still some “horrors”. He pointed out guar gum and locust bean gum, which disrupt some bacterial colonies in the gut, irritating the bowel, and was particularly worried about maltodextrin – an artificial carbohydrate used to make a food product taste richer and more satisfying. The problem, Smith said, is that, unlike a real carbohydrate, maltodextrin disrupts the eater’s ability to recognise that they are full. “We tend to just want to go on eating it.” (When I put Smith and Van Tulleken’s claims to Magnum, a representative said, “We take the conversation around diet, nutrition and wellbeing extremely seriously and recognise that both consumer expectations and scientific understanding continue to evolve.”)GLP-1s have been touted as a kind of immunisation shot against the lure of ultra-processed foods because they seem to make users crave sugary, salty foods less. But when I spoke to Van Tulleken, he made the point that fast food companies are capitalising on the widespread uptake of the drugs by releasing new ultra-processed products that masquerade as health food. “We might think of this as hyper-processing,” he said. “To get around the GLP-1s and other health concerns, they’re using more and more processing and additives to keep selling food to people who want to stop eating.” Nestlé has already launched a line of frozen meals targeted at people taking GLP-1s called Vital Pursuit – and now ice-cream is cashing in on the action.When I visited the ice-cream factory a few days after speaking to Smith and Van Tulleken, I kept thinking about the futuristic ice-creams at the innovation hub. My head was full of ice lollies on treadmills. I found it hard to shake the image of soft-serve at the gym. After watching the Viennetta whiz round on its conveyor belt, I was led to another production line so I could see Soleros being dipped by robotic arms into orange sauce. Then I went to look at the Twisters. The factory manager assured me they had been selling well, but as I watched the Twisters being squeezed out of a machine and bundled into little boxes, I felt both hungry and strangely sad. They looked like a relic from a simpler time. A time when no one would ever think to scan the back of an ice lolly packet in a vain attempt to hit their macros; when an ice-cream was just an ice-cream.View image in fullscreenSoleros …View image in fullscreen… Twisters …View image in fullscreen… cardboard holders …View image in fullscreen… and lolly sticks in the Magnum’s factoryScrolling on TikTok after I got home from the factory, my algorithm was full of muscled influencers concocting their own “healthy Magnums” – ice-cream-shaped frozen slabs made from cottage cheese and chalky mountains of whey. Online, mums post videos of themselves using a viral ice-cream machine called the Ninja Creami to make “protein” ice-creams to feed to their toddlers. People competitively swap recipes in the comments section, trying to hike up the nutrient content while shaving calories. In one TikTok, viewed 85,500 times, a man shows his followers how to squeeze 40g of protein into a mud-like substance he is calling “Oreo Ice Cream”. Ice-cream’s only real appeal, in these clips, seems to be that it is soft, so you can force it down easily. Watching these videos, you get the sense that the whole experience of eating an ice-cream – and eating generally – is becoming divorced from joy.But recently I had a banana split that made me feel more positive about the future of ice-cream. On one of the hottest days of the summer, I travelled to Morelli’s Gelato in Broadstairs, which opened in 1932 and is one of the oldest ice-cream shops in the UK. Morelli’s makes all its ice-cream fresh every day in the factory beneath its shop, with no additives or ultra-processing. The ingredients for its signature vanilla ice-cream, for example, haven’t changed since the shop first opened: sugar, eggs, cream and water.As I walked down to the seafront from the train station, I could tell I was on the right track because I kept seeing people holding huge, dripping ice-cream cones. I saw a woman sitting outside the shop with her dog, who was also eating an ice-cream – out of a classic cardboard one-scoop pot. Morelli’s, which does a roaring trade with dog owners, started selling special ice-cream for dogs in 2020. Inside, everything was decorated in pink and cream, largely as it had been in the 50s. There were squishy banquette seats, and flowers arranged on some tables. It felt a bit like sitting inside a giant ice-cream.View image in fullscreenMorelli’s ice cream parlour in Broadstairs, which opened in 1932 …View image in fullscreen… and still makes all its ice-cream fresh every dayWhile I browsed the menu at a little silver table, I spoke to Chris Chalkin, who has worked at the shop since he was a teenager. Now in his late 60s, Chalkin told me customers’ ice-cream orders haven’t altered much since the 70s. “If you haven’t got chocolate, strawberry and vanilla, forget it,” he said. “You can have 20 other ice-creams, but don’t bother.” He told me he had seen trends for healthier ice-cream come and go, but “they’re all a fad”. What people want from ice-cream doesn’t change, Chalkin said. “I want it indulgent, I want it sickly!” – here he scrunched up his fists and mimed the urge to gobble an ice-cream, in a way that reminded me strongly of what I had felt right before I pushed my fingers into the slop bucket of Viennetta.High VAT rates and soaring cocoa prices make it difficult for independent ice-cream parlours to turn a profit, and the period from June to August is relied upon to keep businesses afloat. But independent ice-cream sellers aren’t as worried about weight-loss drugs as larger manufacturers are. “It’s a luxury treat for the consumer, it’s not something they have every day, so it’s not as affected by weight-loss drugs as a supermarket ice-cream,” said Catherine McNeil from the Ice Cream Alliance, the UK’s sole trade association for the industry.My banana split arrived and Chalkin talked me through the ice-creams customers keep ordering, year after year, decade after decade: knickerbocker glory, strawberry sundae, peach melba. I ate my ice-cream – which was light and sweet, and topped with airy swirls of whipped cream – and as the sugar rush hit, I felt hopeful. Perhaps our collective appetite for ice-cream, and for pleasure, is not so easy to suppress.

title: Thousands of sex offenders in England and Wales could get libido-suppressing drugs | Prisons and probation | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Voluntary use of sex drive-suppressing medication to expand to 20 prisons and expert says it could be rolled out widely by late 2028
Author: Rajeev Syal
Headline: Exclusive: Voluntary use of sex drive-suppressing medication to expand to 20 prisons and expert says it could be rolled out widely by late 2028
Content: About 15,000 prisoners in England and Wales are serving a sentence for a sexual offence.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAbout 15,000 prisoners in England and Wales are serving a sentence for a sexual offence.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesPrisons and probationThousands of sex offenders in England and Wales could get libido-suppressing drugsExclusive: Voluntary use of sex drive-suppressing medication to expand to 20 prisons and expert says it could be rolled out widely by late 2028Chemical suppression: why the UK is exploring libido control drugs to treat sex offendersRajeev SyalHome affairs editorSat 22 Aug 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 22 Aug 2026 12.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDrugs that help control the libidos of people who have committed sexual offences could be rolled out for thousands of male prisoners inEnglandand Wales from December 2028, an expert has said.Prof Belinda Winder, who has evaluated the use of sex drive-suppressing medication in prisons, said about one in four sex offenders – equating to 3,750 current prisoners – would be considered for the treatment.Government sources have told the Guardian that Andy Burnham’s administration is keen to expand the voluntary use of sex drive-suppressing drugs amid a scramble to ease the prison overcrowding crisis.However, ministers are re-evaluating whether to press ahead with Shabana Mahmood’s pledge to explore mandatory chemical castration of serious sex offenders, such as paedophiles and rapists.About 15,000 prisoners in England andWalesare serving a sentence for a sexual offence, and more than 850 men a month are arrested on suspicion of online child sexual abuse offences.A pilot programme, the medication to manage problematic sexual arousal treatment pathway (MMPSA), will be expanded from 10 to 20 prisons in November. The next phase will extend from south-west England into two additional NHS regions, the north-west and north-east.It is meant to target sex offenders who experience intrusive, persistent and intense sexual thoughts, persistent arousal, and unhealthy sexual urges and sexual behaviours. Prisoners on the trial can be offered drugs including selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), such as sertraline, which helps to limit invasive sexual thoughts, and anti-androgens, which reduce the production of testosterone and limit libido. In some cases, it reduces testosterone to pre-pubescent levels.Winder said officials could be ready to launch the drugs in prisons and probation services across England and Wales within 28 months if the pilot continued to progress.“They [the Ministry of Justice] could be ready in December 2028 to roll the programme out if the interim findings look useful,” she said.Those on the scheme would have to receive clinical support if they were to commit to taking the drugs and not reoffend, Winder said. “I am optimistic that a properly resourced, voluntary national MMPSA pathway could ultimately be developed … A good national service needs appropriately trained clinicians, clear referral routes, appropriate psychological support alongside medication,” she said.Last year Mahmood, the then justice secretary, told MPs she was exploring a national rollout ofvoluntary chemical castrationfor sex offenders and whether it could be made mandatory.Two experts have told the Guardian that the plan will not work. Winder, a co-chief investigator of a Prozac clinical trial with sex offenders, said she had significant concerns.“A mandatory approach would require screening a very large prison population to identify the much smaller group for whom treatment might actually be appropriate,” she said. “It would have substantial clinical and resource implications.”There were also concerns that if it was mandatory, there could be a breakdown of trust with offenders and it could be open to abuse, she said.“Trying to impose and monitor daily medication among people who do not necessarily want to take it could be extremely inefficient. It could also introduce a range of consequences that we simply do not yet understand, including effects on trust, disclosure, engagement and the therapeutic relationship.”She rejected characterising the drugs as a form of “chemical castration”. “People say that because some people like the idea of castrating people who commit sexual offences,” she said. “But these drugs are not permanent, unlike castration, and must be taken consistently to work.”Experts ‘would refuse to take part’ in mandatory castration for sex offendersRead moreBurnham announced earlier this month that prisoners convicted of rape, grooming and serious child sexual offences would be excluded from the early release scheme that is due to begin in October. Other sex offenders serving sentences of less than four years will still be eligible to leave prison early.There are comparatively low reoffending rates among sexual offenders compared with other cohorts.According to government data, 11.7% of sex offenders reoffended in 2023, compared with 53.9% of those with an index offence for theft.Prison campaigners have urged caution before going ahead with a national programme. Critics have previously pointed out that long-term testosterone suppression can cause osteoporosis and cardiovascular disease. There is limited data because randomised controlled trials remain scarce.Andrew Neilson, the director of campaigns at the Howard League for Penal Reform, said: “The history of prison-based treatment programmes in this area has proven troubled, which is both a reason for exploring alternatives but also a reason to exercise caution before expanding new approaches more widely. It’s also important that nobody is forced into these chemical interventions and that participation is truly voluntary.”Mark Fairhurst, the national chair of the prison officers’ union the POA, said: “Anything that potentially protects the public is welcome but I would be cautious about the rollout until we are in receipt of evidence that proves success.”A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said: “This government is determined to tackle the root causes of sex offending, which is why we’re working at pace to extend the existing pilot to a further two regions.”Additional reporting by Faisa MohamedExplore more on these topicsPrisons and probationUK criminal justiceEnglandWalesCrimeRape and sexual assaultDrugsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Seventeen-year-old girl killed in sword attack at school in Sweden | Sweden | The Guardian
description: Three other people wounded after 18-year-old man wielding sword assail students in Fagersta school
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: Three other people wounded after 18-year-old man wielding sword assail students in Fagersta school
Content: Police and emergency personnel outside the Brinell school in Fagersta, Sweden, after a 17-year-old girl was killed and several people were injured in a sword attack.Photograph: Fredrik Sandberg/TT/ReutersView image in fullscreenPolice and emergency personnel outside the Brinell school in Fagersta, Sweden, after a 17-year-old girl was killed and several people were injured in a sword attack.Photograph: Fredrik Sandberg/TT/ReutersSwedenSeventeen-year-old girl killed in sword attack at school in SwedenThree other people wounded after 18-year-old man wielding sword assail students in Fagersta schoolNadeem BadshahSat 22 Aug 2026 14.11 EDTLast modified on Sat 22 Aug 2026 15.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA 17-year-old girl has been killed after a teenager brandishing a sword attacked students at a school inSweden, police have confirmed.Three other people were wounded in the incident during classes in the central town of Fagersta on Friday afternoon, including two boys aged 12 and 17 who sustained minor injuries.The third person, who was also under 18, was also left with minor injuries and has been discharged from hospital, Swedish news agency TT reported.The parents of the 17-year-old girl told local newspaper Fagersta-Posten their daughter was killed in the attack.An 18-year-old man has been arrested over the incident at Brinell high school.View image in fullscreenArmed police officers were dispatched to Brinellskolan as an 18-year-old wielded a sword, attacking students.Photograph: Fredrik Sandberg/TT/ReutersSwedish police are investigating whether the suspect was involved in online communities promoting school violence, a police source said.Detectives are investigating whether a TikTok account that posted a picture of a sword 20 minutes before the attack belonged to the person responsible, the source told Reuters.The image appeared to have been taken in a restroom at the school, according to the Dagens Nyheter newspaper.Before the image was taken down on Friday, the month-old account contained videos that referred to two episodes of mass violence in Sweden and to the far-right mass murderer Anders Behring Breivik, who killed 77 people in Norway in 2011.One of the videos referenced a 2015 attack in which a masked swordsman killed a teaching assistant and two boys at a school in Trollhättan, western Sweden, before being shot dead by police.“The investigators are looking into various online communities that may have egged on the suspect to carry out the attack,” the police source said.Several party leaders cancelled planned speeches on Saturday, pausing campaigning ahead of Sweden’s 13 September general election.View image in fullscreenThe Swedish prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, (L) and the Social Democratic party leader, Magdalena Andersson, visit the makeshift memorial.Photograph: Magnus Lejhall/EPAThe prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, and opposition leader Magdalena Andersson travelled to Fagersta to offer
