condolences to the bereaved family and visit the injured.Kristersson told reporters: “What should never happen has happened again. Our thoughts go first and foremost to the families who have been incredibly hard hit by this.”Sweden’s worst mass shooting occurred in February 2025 at a school in the south-central city of Örebro, when a gunman killed 10 people before turning the weapon on himself.On Saturday, the police clarified that the suspect in the Fagersta attack had not been shot, contrary to what they had said on Friday.“Service weapons were used but the perpetrator has not been injured in connection with the arrest, and has not been in need of medical attention,” a police spokesperson told the Aftonbladet daily.Prosecutors ordered the man’s detention on suspicion of murder and several counts of attempted murder.Explore more on these topicsSwedenEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Meghan’s casting in The Gentlemen reportedly withdrawn | Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex | The Guardian
description: Duchess of Sussex was believed to have been under consideration for season three of Guy Ritchie’s crime caper
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: Duchess of Sussex was believed to have been under consideration for season three of Guy Ritchie’s crime caper
Content: Tina Brown, the former editor-in-chief of Vanity Fair and the New Yorker, said: ‘The backlash in the UK was so intense, it became untenable to go forward.’Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PAView image in fullscreenTina Brown, the former editor-in-chief of Vanity Fair and the New Yorker, said: ‘The backlash in the UK was so intense, it became untenable to go forward.’Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PAMeghan, the Duchess of SussexMeghan’s casting in The Gentlemen reportedly withdrawnDuchess of Sussex was believed to have been under consideration for season three of Guy Ritchie’s crime caperNadeem BadshahSat 22 Aug 2026 17.23 EDTLast modified on Sat 22 Aug 2026 17.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Duchess of Sussex’s reported casting in Guy Ritchie’s The Gentlemen has been withdrawn, it was reported.Tina Brown, the former editor-in-chief of Vanity Fair and the New Yorker, wrote on Saturday: “I learned this morning that the casting of Meghan Markle in season 3 of Guy Ritchie’sNetflixseries The Gentlemen has been withdrawn. The backlash in the UK was so intense, it became untenable to go forward.”The development comes a day after reports that the Duchess of Sussex was in talks to make her acting return in The Gentlemen.Is this the end of Harry and Meghan’s American dream?Read moreAccording to Variety, Meghan was in discussions to join the third season, which has yet to receive an official greenlight.The Gentlemen series is a spin-off from the 2019 crime comedy film of the same name, which starred Matthew McConaughey and Charlie Hunnam, with Guy Ritchie acting as creator of both.The duchess made her name in the legal drama Suits, in which she played the character Rachel Zane for seven seasons.Her other small-screen appearances include CSI: NY and 90210, while film roles have included a small part in the comedy Horrible Bosses and 2015’s crime thriller Anti-Social. She also led two Hallmark movies: When Sparks Fly and Dater’s Handbook.She recently filmed a cameo playing herself in the Amazon comedy Close Personal Friends alongside Brie Larson and Jack Quaid.The Duke and Duchess of Sussex are planning toreturn to live in Britainthis month, six years after leaving for the US, it is understood.The couple and their two children, Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five, are expected to relocate to a property believed to be outside London.King Charles was reportedly informed last Sunday that his son and daughter-in-law would return to Britain.11:35Why are Prince Harry and Meghan moving back to the UK? – The LatestLast year the Duke and Duchess of Sussex signed a fresh multi-year film and television deal with Netflix.Harry and Meghan struck the original five-year deal in 2020, reportedly worth $100m (£78m), which resulted in a number of projects.Meghan’s main release with the streamer was the lifestyle series With Love, Meghan. The show received negative reviews from many critics, with the Guardian’s Chitra Ramaswamy calling it “toe-curling stuff” in a one-star review.Explore more on these topicsMeghan, the Duchess of SussexGuy RitchieNetflixTelevisionMonarchynewsShareReuse this content

title: Battery fires at recycling centres are costing UK £1bn a year, figures show | Recycling | The Guardian
description: Experts say fires caused by wrongly discarded lithium batteries, such as those in vapes, are putting lives at risk
Author: Matthew Weaver
Headline: Experts say fires caused by wrongly discarded lithium batteries, such as those in vapes, are putting lives at risk
Content: Vape ignites and sets paper alightRecyclingBattery fires at recycling centres are costing UK £1bn a year, figures showExperts say fires caused by wrongly discarded lithium batteries, such as those  in vapes, are putting lives at riskMatthew WeaverSat 22 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 22 Aug 2026 02.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFires at recycling centres caused by wrongly discarded lithium batteries such as those found in vapes are occurring at the rate of more than 10 a week, according to new figures.Experts say the sheer volume of battery fires now occurring at waste facilities has reached a crisis that is putting lives at risk, costing £1bn a year and frustrating fire chiefs.In figures shared with the Guardian, the Environment Services Association (ESA), the trade body for waste management companies, said its members had reported 1,518 fires in the year to March 2026. At least 541 of these fires were directly attributed to lithium ion batteries, the survey found. There were a further 216 battery fires in bin lorries.UK firefighters called to one lithium-ion battery fire every five hoursRead moreThe ESA said the reported number of battery-related fires underestimated the scale of the problem, because in most incidents it was impossible to determine the cause of the blaze. A spokesperson said: “We know 40% of fires at recycling centres are caused by batteries, but we think the actual number is more like 70%.”It estimates that annual cost of these fires has increased from£150m in 2021 to £1bn today. The cause of this week’s blazeat a recycling centre in Deptford, south-east London, has yet to be determined. It was the latest in a series of fires at recycling centre and bin lorries, many of which have been blamed on batteries, particularly those in vapes. They include:Ilfordin east London;Caerwentin Monmouthshire;Widnesin Cheshire;Glasgow;Costesseynear Norwich, andDerehamin Norfolk.Fire chiefs have been alarmed by the rise in this type of blaze and the resources needed to put them out.After the Ilford fire, which took 25 firefighters to control, a spokesperson for London fire brigade said: “We’ve seen a growing number of fires at waste disposal sites that are believed to have been caused by a lithium battery.”“Fires that we attend at sites like recycling centres and scrap yards can be very time consuming for our firefighters and often require a high level of resources to put the fire out. We’ve also seen the detrimental environmental and societal impact these fires can have on local communities.”Dr Francesco Restuccia, a fire expert at King’s College London, said: “There has been exponential increase in fires at recycling centres, mainly because we are using and discarding lithium batteries in everyday objects like smartphones, children’s toys, toothbrushes and vapes. If they are not disposed off properly there’s a high chance of ignition.”View image in fullscreenBin lorry fire in Lafone Street, south London. There has been a rise in fires caused by electrical products using lithium-ion batteries, such as strimmers, drills, power banks and e-scooters.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianExplaining what happens when a lithium battery gets crushed, Restuccia said: “If the separator is pierced – which happens a lot at recycling centres – it creates a lot of internal short circuits in the battery, causing the temperature to increase until it reaches ignition point.”The ESA commissioned the Health and Safety Executive to test what happens when a vape battery is punctured while next to paper and card. Video of the experiment, shared with the Guardian, showed the vape igniting like a sparkler and setting alight the paper and card. Temperatures of the vape reached more 750C in the experiment and became hot enough to ignite paper for two minutes.The ESA hopes the experiment will demonstrate the need to safely dispose vapes to policymakers and the public. The waste management company Biffa said it has recovered 500,000 vapes at its facilities this summer alone.The ESA is calling for a £5 deposit scheme on the sale of all vapes to ensure that vape users have an incentive to return used devices to retailers for safe disposal.Patrick Brighty, the head of recycling policy at the ESA, said: “Battery fires are reaching epidemic proportions across Britain’s recycling and waste industry, placing workers at risk and threatening vital infrastructure upon which we all rely every day.“It only takes a single battery hidden in household rubbish or recycling to cause a huge fire and decimate a facility. The total cost of battery fires now exceeds £1bn a year, with huge knock-on implications for insurance costs.“Vapes are among the biggest culprits because they’re cheap, abundant and typically have a short use-life. ESA and others across our industry are calling on the government to implement a mandatory deposit scheme for vapes to incentivise users to return them safely back to the point of purchase so they can be recycled properly and away from other waste.”Explore more on these topicsRecyclingVapingLithium-ion batteriesWasteFirefightersnewsShareReuse this content

title: Two police officers killed in North Yorkshire crash named | Independent Office for Police Conduct | The Guardian
description: Watchdog launches inquiry into collision in which seven people died involving police car and another vehicle
Author: Geneva Abdul
Headline: Watchdog launches inquiry into collision in which seven people died involving police car and another vehicle
Content: Police officers at the scene of the crash on the A66 in South Bank, near Middlesbrough.Photograph: Owen Humphreys/PAView image in fullscreenPolice officers at the scene of the crash on the A66 in South Bank, near Middlesbrough.Photograph: Owen Humphreys/PAIndependent Office for Police ConductTwo police officers killed in North Yorkshire crash namedWatchdog launches inquiry into collision in which seven people died involving police car and another vehicleGeneva AbdulandGeraldine McKelvieSat 22 Aug 2026 12.09 EDTFirst published on Sat 22 Aug 2026 05.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwo police officers who died in a car crash nearMiddlesbroughin the early hours of Saturday have been named.Police constables Matthew Blades and Tom Clough were among seven people killed after their marked police car collided with a Volkswagen Passat travelling the wrong way along the A66 inNorth Yorkshire.Victoria Fuller, the chief constable of Cleveland police, said it was an “incredibly sad day” for the force.“The loss has been felt across our communities, by our police family and by our partner agencies,” she said.She described Blades and Clough as “brave officers protecting our communities and serving our residents who didn’t return home to their families at the end of their shift”.Fuller added that she had visited the families of both officers to “offer our condolences and support”.The force confirmed that all occupants of both vehicles were pronounced dead at the scene.The police watchdog, theIndependent Office for Police Conduct(IOPC), said it understood the officers had been pursuing a suspicious vehicle when the accident occurred at 3.39am.It has launched a mandatory investigation and is working with officers from Cleveland police to establish the circumstances surrounding the crash.“This tragic incident will be felt across Cleveland, within our communities and throughout the entire policing family,” Fuller added.“We are providing specialist support to all families involved at this extremely difficult time.”Fuller said Cleveland police would “cooperate fully” with the IOPC investigation.“While this investigation takes place, we strongly urge people to avoid speculation,” she said.Writing on X on Saturday afternoon, the prime minister, Andy Burnham, said: “Devastated to hear that two police officers have lost their lives while on duty in Cleveland this morning, as well as five members of the public.“My thoughts are with the families and loved ones of everyone involved, and with everyone at Cleveland police.“Thank you to the emergency services responding in incredibly difficult circumstances. I would urge people to avoid speculation at this time.”North East ambulance service said it had been called to a two-vehicle crash and sent 14 units to the scene including ambulance crews, a specialist paramedic, a hazardous area response team and a doctor from Great North air ambulance service.A spokesperson said: “Sadly, despite the best efforts of everyone attending, a number of patients died at the scene.“We send condolences to all of those affected by such a tragic event and thank everyone for all they did to help.”The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, said: “Cleveland police have my support as they work to identify all those involved.“Police officers put their own safety on the line to protect their communities every single day. The two officers were on active duty, serving the people of Cleveland.“My thoughts are with all those affected, their families, friends, the emergency services who attended the scene and the wider police family.”Brian Booth, acting national chair of the Police Federation of England and Wales, said: “Our most sincere condolences go to the families, friends and colleagues of the two police officers, and multiple members of the public, who lost their lives in the tragic incident in Cleveland. Our thoughts are with everyone affected by this.”Lauren Somerville, the chair of Cleveland police federation, said: “Words cannot describe the pain the Cleveland police family are feeling today.“Our colleagues who should have been going home to their loved ones at the end of their shifts are not. And that is just unfathomable.“Cleveland police federation will be offering full support to our fallen colleagues’ families and they have all of our love and care at this time.“When the time is right we will pay full tribute to our brave colleagues. But we can assure that their sacrifice will never be forgotten.”Anna Turley, the MP for the Redcar constituency where the crash happened, said: “My heart goes out to every family, friend and loved one now facing the most unimaginable loss following this morning’s devastating accident on the A66.“Two of the seven people who have lost their lives were Cleveland police officers, on duty serving our community. They went to work to keep people safe, and they should have come home to their families. Their loss will be felt deeply by their loved ones, fellow officers and right across the communities they served.“I cannot begin to imagine how difficult this has been for the emergency services responding to such a devastating incident. Thank you to every one of them for their courage, care and professionalism.”The crash marks the first time in 14 years that more than one police officer has died on duty while responding to the same incident.In September 2012, the Greater Manchester police officers Fiona Bone, 32, and Nicola Hughes, 23, were killed in a gun and grenade attack in Mottram, Tameside, during what appeared to be routine burglary call.They were lured to their deaths by Dale Cregan, now 43, who was already on the run, having committed several other murders. He was given a whole-life jail term in 2013.Explore more on these topicsIndependent Office for Police ConductNorth YorkshireMiddlesbroughYorkshirePolicenewsShareReuse this content

title: Andy Burnham says he wants to bring men’s World Cup back to UK in 2042 | Andy Burnham | The Guardian
description: PM tells regional mayors during informal discussions he is keen for tournament to return to British Isles
Author: Geraldine McKelvie
Headline: PM tells regional mayors during informal discussions he is keen for tournament to return to British Isles
Content: Andy Burnham and his wife Marie-France van Heel at Everton’s match against Crystal Palace on Saturday.Photograph: Paul Currie/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham and his wife Marie-France van Heel at Everton’s match against Crystal Palace on Saturday.Photograph: Paul Currie/ShutterstockAndy BurnhamAndy Burnham says he wants to bring men’s World Cup back to UK in 2042PM tells regional mayors during informal discussions he is keen for tournament to return to British IslesGeraldine McKelvieSat 22 Aug 2026 08.13 EDTLast modified on Sat 22 Aug 2026 10.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham has said he wants to bring the men’s World Cup to the UK in 2042, returning the tournament to Britain for the first time in almost eight decades.During informal discussions at No 10 North in Manchester on Friday, the prime minister told regional mayors he was keen for the tournament to be played in the British Isles.TheWorld Cuptook place in England in 1966, when the home side beat West Germany 4-2 in the final after extra time – the only time the country has either hosted or won the contest.Burnham, a keen football fan who has a season ticket atEverton, said earlier this month that it was “insane” only one World Cup had been held anywhere in the UK.England’s 1966 World Cup heroes were fun, humble and unlike today’s starsRead moreIt is understood an application to stage the competition could also involve other home nations, none of which have hosted any World Cup games.In recent years, joint bids between countries for major football tournaments have become more common. Alongside the Republic of Ireland,England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland will host the men’s European championships in 2028.Work has not yet begun on any official bid for the 2042 event but it is understood Downing Street would support the FA should it choose to pursue it.Sources say Burnham has “broad aspirations” and “a general ambition” to bring more major footballing events to the UK.England made a doomed bid to host the 2018 World Cup, which was awarded to Russia amid allegations of corruption.In 2014, while serving in the shadow cabinet, Burnham said he was uncomfortable that the tournament was still allowed to take place in Russia after its annexation of Crimea.UnderFifaregulations, no European country would be eligible to stage the World Cup until 2042.In 2000, Fifa introduced rules that meant the tournament would be rotated around its six continental confederations. It led to South Africa hosting its first World Cup in 2010, but the strict system was scrapped in October 2007.Countries are not allowed to bid to stage a World Cup if either of the previous two tournaments have taken place on the same continent.The 2030 World Cup will be hosted by Spain, Portugal and Morocco, with some early matches taking place in South America to mark the tournament’s centenary. The first World Cup was played in Uruguay in 1930.Fifa has also confirmed that the 2034 tournament will take place in Saudi Arabia. The location of the 2038 World Cup has not yet been announced, but under the rules, it is likely to be played in North America or Oceania, which includes Australia and New Zealand.Burnham is also understood to have spoken about the possibility of hosting the Olympic and Paralympic Games in the north of England in the 2040s at Friday’s meeting.UK Sport was commissioned to assess whether a bid would be viable earlier this year under the previous prime minister, Keir Starmer.It is understood that the government is considering the possibility of a “multi-city bid” in an attempt to spread any economic benefit between several northern cities.A government spokesperson said: “The UK is committed to delivering world-class major sporting events with pride, with the Tour de France and Tour de France Femmes Grands Départs 2027 and Uefa Euro 2028 secured, and active bids for the 2029 World Athletics Championships and 2035 Women’s World Cup.“As the prime minister has made clear, we will continue to pursue sporting events that bring communities together, drive regional growth and create jobs across the country.”Explore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamEnglandWorld CupEvertonFifanewsShareReuse this content

title: Badenoch says Reform defectors ‘some of the most dishonest people I have met’ | Kemi Badenoch | The Guardian
description: Tory leader rules out coalition with Farage’s party and says ‘drama queens’ who left will not be welcomed back
Author: Geneva Abdul
Headline: Tory leader rules out coalition with Farage’s party and says ‘drama queens’ who left will not be welcomed back
Content: Kemi Badenoch said a ‘monstrous Reform-Conservative hybrid’ was not an option at the next general election.Photograph: Alishia Abodunde/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenKemi Badenoch said a ‘monstrous Reform-Conservative hybrid’ was not an option at the next general election.Photograph: Alishia Abodunde/Getty ImagesKemi BadenochBadenoch says Reform defectors ‘some of the most dishonest people I have met’Tory leader rules out coalition with Farage’s party and says ‘drama queens’ who left will not be welcomed backGeneva AbdulSat 22 Aug 2026 12.08 EDTLast modified on Sat 22 Aug 2026 13.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKemi Badenoch has called defectors who left for Reform “some of the most dishonest people” she has ever met, as she ruled out allowing “drama queens” to return to the party.Speaking at the Edinburgh festival fringe, the Conservative party leader again ruled out any prospect of an election deal with Nigel Farage’s Reform UK, insisting there would be no coalition between the parties.“Reform has people who left the Conservative party, some of the most dishonest people I have ever met in my entire life,” Badenoch told event host Iain Dale on Saturday.Multiple current or former parliamentarians have joined Reform from the Conservatives, including the former home secretarySuella Bravermanand the former shadow justice secretary Robert Jenrick. After being sacked by Badenoch for plotting against her, Jenrick called his former party “rotten” and “failed”.Hitting out at those such as Jenrick who defected, Badenoch said: “These are people who left us when we were at our lowest, many of them the people who caused the problems in the first place and then ran away and pretended they had nothing to do with it. Why should we have them back?”View image in fullscreenReform UK’s shadow chancellor Robert Jenrick left the Tory party in January of this year.Photograph: Phil Lewis/SOPA Images/ShutterstockThe Conservative leader said she doesn’t want “drama queens” in the party, adding that she’s not “entertaining” parliamentarians she has heard are having indirect approaches from previous defectors.Badenoch said Farage’s party “is all over the place” and suggested the party announces a policy and forgets it the following day.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUnions worry Labour’s plan for zero-hours contracts may break manifesto pledgeRead moreAccording to the latest Ipsos voting intention poll, 28% of 1,033 adults in Britain surveyed between 30 July and 4 August said they would support Labour. Reform UK had the second highest share with 25% and theConservativestrailed in third at 18%.Before becoming prime minister last month, Andy Burnham ruled out the possibility of calling an early general election, with Labour having won a landslide majority in July 2024. The next election must be called by August 2029, though Burnham can decide to hold one at any time before that date.Badenoch said the country will be in a “pretty bad place” if the Conservatives fail to form the next government at Westminster, saying she would rather have another election if there was a hung parliament than have a “monstrous Reform-Conservative hybrid” government at Westminster.“How do I work with people like that when I am making carefully curated plans and taking a systems-based approach?” said Badenoch. “How do you work with a man who has fallen out with every single person he has ever had to work with in every single party that he has started?”While Reform has made substantial gains in Wales and across England in the past year – recent election results that were a catalyst forKeir Starmer’s resignation– Badenoch said she wanted to “win on my own terms” at the next general election.When asked if not working with Reform could result in a possible Labour-Liberal Democrat coalition should there be a hung parliament, Badenoch insisted again that the best option would be a fresh election.“If we get a hung parliament and people see that the parties can’t form a government, you have another election,” said the Tory leader, adding that there would be “no deals” made before or after the election.“I want us to unite the country. It is not about uniting the right, it is about uniting our country,” she said.Explore more on these topicsKemi BadenochReform UKNigel FarageConservativesRobert JenrickSuella BravermannewsShareReuse this content

title: Kayode seals emphatic Brentford victory in wake-up call for sorry Spurs | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Keane Lewis-Potter, Vitaly Janelt and Michael Kayode were all on target in Brentford’s 3-0 win against Tottenham in their Premier League opener
Author: Jacob Steinberg
Headline: Keane Lewis-Potter, Vitaly Janelt and Michael Kayode were all on target in Brentford’s 3-0 win against Tottenham in their Premier League opener
Content: Igor Thiago (left) congratulates Michael Kayode after scoring Brentford’s third goal.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIgor Thiago (left) congratulates Michael Kayode after scoring Brentford’s third goal.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianPremier LeagueKayode seals emphatic Brentford victory in wake-up call for sorry SpursJacob Steinbergat the Gtech Community StadiumSat 22 Aug 2026 14.40 EDTLast modified on Sat 22 Aug 2026 19.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleContinue down this road and it will not be long before the chants of “Lincoln away” start up again. This was the start of Tottenham’s brave new era but there was no sign of any change. The old flaws were still there in a cowardly display – with and without the ball – and after a summer of extravagant spending it will alarm Roberto De Zerbi that his side opened the season looking like relegation candidates rather than contenders for European football.If anything it was a reminder that winning the transfer window is not the same as winning on the pitch. There has been plenty of excitable predictions about Spurs, whose outlay is likely to soon surpass £300m, but are they based on anything substantial? Not on the evidence of this game. There were no patterns of play from Spurs. They were timid in possession and chaotic at the back. They failed to perform the basics and they crumbled in the face of relentless pressing fromBrentford, whose blend of power, speed and skill revealed a team determined to kick on in their second season under Keith Andrews.Meet the New Spurs — same as the Old Spurs?Read moreSpurs could count themselves fortunate it finished 3-0. Brentford should have scored more – Igor Thiago, normally so reliable from the spot, marred an intelligent forward display by missing a penalty – but this was a joyous start to their campaign. Keane Lewis-Potter, Vitaly Janelt and Michael Kayode scored the goals and in the final analysis it was impossible not to dwell on a sparkling debut in midfield from Mamadou Sangaré, who already looks a bargain after joining from Lens for £39m.How do Brentford keep picking up these gems? Spurs broke their transfer record this summer, signingSandro Tonali from Newcastle for £100m. They spent £85m on Mateus Fernandes, who came on for his debut, but Sangaré was head and shoulders above any of De Zerbi’s midfielders. The Malian offered energy, showed quality in possession and made the opening goal with a lovely piece of play, tearing Spurs to shreds by playing a clever one-two with Thiago before pulling the ball back from the right for Lewis-Potter to run in from left-back and beat Antonin Kinsky from close range in the 12th minute.It helps that Sangaré, working in tandem with Janelt and Mathias Jensen, has slotted into a cohesive unit. Brentford have enjoyed a calm window and are well drilled by Andrews. “There’s real trust in what we’ve built,” the Brentford manager said.In contrast Spurs were fragmented and undercooked. They stared into the abyss last year, averting relegation on the final day, and have so much to improve. De Zerbi, who saw a lack of fight, will worry that his side appeared to believe an extravagant transfer window meant they could stroll to victory.It will take more than moving on from the constraints of Levynomics for Spurs to regain their place in the top six. De Zerbi has to raise standards. Spurs have moved at dizzying speed in their first summer since moving Daniel Levy aside as chair but De Zerbi needs time and was honest in his assessment of this defeat, admitting that the performance was bereft of soul and was emblematic of a team of individuals.View image in fullscreenKeane Lewis-Potter fires home Brentford’s opener from close range.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianThese are still early days. Spurs started with four debutants and have players to come back from injury. Even so it was worrying to hear De Zerbi say his side did not win a single second ball. Spurs could not have been weaker. They had three new faces in their back four – Andy Robertson was at left-back while Jan Paul van Hecke partnered Marcos Senesi in the middle – but Brentford found wide open spaces from the start, created havoc with deliveries from the wings and had chances to score before Lewis-Potter’s goal.Much is made of Brentford’s threat from set pieces but this was proof that they can be just as effective in open play. Spurs were sliced apart and they continued to ship openings. Thiago headed against the bar and Dango Ouattara twice went through on goal, only to take a heavy touch on both occasions.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBrentford were rampant. Thiago bullied Senesi and Van Hecke while Kevin Schade had fun running at the Spurs captain Archie Gray on the left.Roberto De Zerbi says Tottenham are ‘not a team’ and hits out at lack of fightRead moreIt was not until Brentford were 3-0 up in the second half that Spurs created a chance of any note. De Zerbi will hope that bringing inOmar Marmoush and Savinho from Manchester Citywill add more bite in attack. However, disappointing displays from Richarlison, Mathys Tel and Mikey Moore were far from the only problem for Spurs. There were frailties in every department. Lucas Bergvall was at fault for the second goal, losing a 50-50 with Jensen. Kinsky then failed to push Jensen’s shot to safety, leaving Janelt to convert the rebound.Bergvall and Conor Gallagher were removed at half-time. Brentford, though, soon stamped out any hope of a fightback by scoring from a corner. Nathan Collins nodded down at the far post, Sangaré shot, Kinsky saved and Kayode rammed the loose ball into the roof of the net, leaving Spurs humiliated and De Zerbi with much to ponder.Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueBrentfordTottenham Hotspurmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Chemical suppression: why the UK is exploring libido control drugs to treat sex offenders | Crime | The Guardian
description: Treatment is already required by parole boards in several countries, but some feel the practice is unethical
Author: Rajeev Syal
Headline: Treatment is already required by parole boards in several countries, but some feel the practice is unethical
Content: ‘Without the drugs, these images were going around his head all the time’: some medications are already used to treat PSA in the UK.Photograph: Peter Macdiarmid/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Without the drugs, these images were going around his head all the time’: some medications are already used to treat PSA in the UK.Photograph: Peter Macdiarmid/Getty ImagesCrimeAnalysisChemical suppression: why the UK is exploring libido control drugs to treat sex offendersRajeev SyalandFaisa MohamedTreatment is already required by parole boards in several countries, but some feel the practice is unethicalThousands of sex offenders in England and Wales could get libido-suppressing drugsSat 22 Aug 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 22 Aug 2026 12.01 EDTShareFor some prisoners with problematic sexual arousal (PSA), “images of sex flood their minds” all of their waking hours, according to Prof Belinda Winder, a leading forensic psychologist who has evaluated the use of drugs to control libidos.“I remember talking to one guy a few weeks after he started taking the medication. He said: ‘It’s amazing. I followed a film plot. I wasn’t just looking for when I could see bra straps, when I could see nipples, when someone’s going to bend over so I could see their bum.”“Without the drugs, these images were going around his head all the time. He did not want them any more,” she said.Drugs used in the UK to treat PSA include antidepressants, which help control obsessive urges, and anti-androgens, which lower testosterone levels.The treatments, typically taken as pills, are not suitable for some offenders such as those who are primarily motivated by anger, or who struggle to moderate their behaviour while using alcohol or drugs.A similar approach has been used in some European countries. In Denmark and France, the use of chemical suppression has only been administered on a voluntary basis.In Germany, the Dunkelfeld project provides free and confidential therapies including medical interventions to men with paedophilic or hebephilic obsessions.Anadvert on YouTubeurging men to contact the project shows unidentified men saying: “In therapy, I learned that no one is to blame for their sexual preference. But everyone is to blame for their behaviour. I don’t want to be an offender.”But many other countries have taken a harder line. Poland introduced mandatory chemical suppression for some sex offenders.South Korea became the first country in Asia to legalise chemical castration, passing a law in 2010. The law grants courts and a Ministry of Justice committee the authority to order involuntary hormone treatment for convicted sex offenders to suppress their testosterone.In Australia, several states grant courts and parole boards the power to order anti-libidinal treatment for high-risk sex offenders which can then become a condition of release. Kazakhstan and a number of US states including California and Florida already have mandatory prescribing of anti-libidinal drugs to some sex offenders.Prison without hope or end is psychological torture. Burnham doesn’t need another review to tell him that | Simon HattenstoneRead moreOfficials in the UK have explored whether taking part in programmes such as these could be made a condition of a parole licence, similar to a scheme in California. However, ethical dilemmas remain over whether it would be right to give someone parole based on whether they take a drug that can be life-changing.In the 50s, hormone treatments were given to men convicted of crimes related to their homosexuality with the promise that they could avoid jail. Alan Turing, the computer scientist and codebreaker, who was convicted of “gross indecency” in 1952, accepted chemical castration as a way of avoiding imprisonment. He took his own life two years later andreceived a posthumous royal pardon in 2013.The side effects of anti-androgens in particular can be severe. Some men experience fatigue, hot flushes, muscle loss, mood changes, weight gain and a loss of bone density.Experts acknowledge that problems remain. The medication is not a cure and does not change underlying behaviours. Some programmes have high drop-out rates.Each offender would have to be assessed by the Parole Board on their merits, according to Winder. “It is never going to be so simple that a decision will be taken on whether to give someone parole based on whether they are taking their meds,” she said.Winder added: “Parole Boards take such decisions by assessing many factors, including how receptive they are to staff and how they interact with their peers. It is really important that people are trained in understanding what it means if someone is taking this medication and how that might affect a person’s behaviour.”Explore more on these topicsCrimeUK criminal justiceViolence against women and girlsPrisons and probationAlan TuringanalysisShareReuse this content

title: ‘They’re thinking about the likes’: deadly TikTok motorway trend horrifies Ireland | Social media | The Guardian
description: Social media platforms face public ire after fatal crash involving teenagers filming themselves driving on wrong side
Author: Rory Carroll
Headline: Social media platforms face public ire after fatal crash involving teenagers filming themselves driving on wrong side
Content: Five people were killed and four seriously injured after the collision on the M9 in County Kildare on Sunday.Photograph: Niall Carson/PAView image in fullscreenFive people were killed and four seriously injured after the collision on the M9 in County Kildare on Sunday.Photograph: Niall Carson/PASocial media‘They’re thinking about the likes’: deadly TikTok motorway trend horrifies IrelandSocial media platforms face public ire after fatal crash involving teenagers filming themselves driving on wrong sideRory CarrollIreland correspondentSat 22 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 22 Aug 2026 04.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVideos often begin with the camera panning across a glowing dashboard as a gloved hand starts the ignition. The camera turns to show figures with masked faces in the rear seat, who are also filming, and swivels back to show the windscreen. Beyond it, a dark cityscape.The engine throbs, headlights puncture the night and the journey begins, first down a suburban road, then a motorway. The speedometer shows acceleration, the needle juddering as the car gathers velocity.The destination is irrelevant, for this is a show – an exhibition of audacity, lawlessness and recklessness that draws viewers toTikTokand other social media platforms with the possibility of chases by police and dramatic crashes.Such videos are part of a macabre trend that has astonished and outraged Ireland in the wake of a collision last week thatkilled five teenagers– who were driving the wrong way down a motorway – and critically injured a family of four, prompting debate about policing, criminal justice, social services and social media regulation.“You have to ask: how do five young men gravitate to each other and decide this is a good idea? Where have we gone wrong as a society?” said Graham Kavanagh, a former officer with the police force An Garda Síochána, who used to pursue car thieves. “No one is born bad, but sometimes you might encounter a fella as young as six or seven and you know trouble is waiting for them.”In the early hours of 16 August, a group of young males broke into homes and cars in County Kildare, south-west of Dublin. Police believe these were the masked occupants of a BMW who then appeared to try to bait patrol cars into a pursuit.At approximately 3am, the BMW was driving the wrong way down the M9 when it crashed into a Hyundai, injuring three sisters, Ella Hendricken, Niamh Kinsella and Alma Kinsella, in their 30s and 20s, and Alma’s seven-year-old son. They had been on their way to Dublin airport for a family wedding in the UK.View image in fullscreen‘Where have we gone wrong as a society?’: The incident took place at 3am.Photograph: Niall Carson/PAThe boys who died – Joe Carthy, 15, Kamil Pustkowski, Jack Kennedy, Alex McCarthy, all 17, and Jeremy O’Brien, 18 – were known to police. Three were also known to the child welfare agency Tusla. Several had previously posted videos of reckless driving, previously known as joyriding.Seeking excitement and admiration from peers through such behaviour was not new, but social media had escalated and amplified the phenomenon, said Mary Aiken, a professor of forensic cyberpsychology at the University of East London.“I would describe it as hybrid behaviour. While driving the car, they’re simultaneously filming and capturing content for posting later or live streaming. They have one foot in the real world and one foot in cyberspace.” Cyberspace is psychologically immersive and could amplify a predisposition to taking risks and ignoring consequences, said Aiken. “They’re thinking about the likes, they’re thinking about kudos.”The tragedy had provoked polarised responses.An outpouring of solidarity for the injured family fuelled a fundraising appeal that has raised more than €660,000 (£565,000). A vigil was planned in County Carlow on Friday evening.Much online commentary about the five boys, in contrast, has been abusive, prompting relatives to withdraw funeral notices. The first funeral, for McCarthy, was held on Friday in Athy. Family members wore T-shirts with his photograph and a horse-drawn carriage transported the casket. Police monitored from a distance.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThe funeral cortege for Alex McCarthy, one of the five teenagers who died in a motorway crash last weekend.Photograph: Brian Lawless/PADenis Nulty, the bishop of Kildare and Leighlin, said he shared the public’s revulsion and anger, but urged people to show compassion. “We have to be awful careful on language. Words can wound, but words can also heal,” hetold RTE. “Let’s not try to pillory. Let’s try to see how can we get better behaviour by all of us.”Fresh clips of other instances of reckless driving have reportedly been uploaded to TikTok in the past week, galvanising criticism of the platform and calls for greater regulation and enforcement.Alleged crime boss Daniel Kinahan’s return to Ireland ends global game of cat-and-mouseRead moreOn Thursday, the company rejected an invitation to address a parliamentary committee on media, citing the ongoing police investigation into the crash and a separate investigation by the media regulator, Coimisiún na Meán, as well as the fact that no other platform had been asked to attend. Alan Kelly, who chairs the committee, called the rebuff a “slap in the face” to the Irish public.Other politicians have demanded tougher penalties for dangerous driving, such as classifying driving on the wrong side of a motorway as attempted murder.There is frustration that gardaí have not been trained in vehicle pursuit and that officers can be deemed personally liable if anything goes wrong during a pursuit. Earlier this year, British driver training experts from the Devon and Cornwall police begantutoring Garda instructors.Kavanagh, who recently retired from the force and is now developing a community safety toolkit for the voluntary organisation Muintir na Tíre, said driving recklessly for thrills was a decades-old problem.“I knew fellas who were addicted to it, stealing, driving fast, that was the buzz, and if chased by police that was icing on the cake.”Police could try to intercept such drivers but all of society – parents, teachers, social workers and others – must intervene years earlier to stop troubled youths travelling the wrong way in life, said Kavanagh.Explore more on these topicsSocial mediaIrelandEuropeTikTokChildrenDigital mediafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Four blokes and a zebra crossing: the banality and beauty of the Beatles’ Abbey Road cover | The Beatles | The Guardian
description: Much-copied and parodied picture captures dynamic between the individuals and the band with eerie perfection
Author: Jonathan Jones
Headline: Much-copied and parodied picture captures dynamic between the individuals and the band with eerie perfection
Content: Paul McCartney came up with the concept for Abbey Road’s cover after a proposed shoot in Nepal was rejected.Photograph: Apple RecordsView image in fullscreenPaul McCartney came up with the concept for Abbey Road’s cover after a proposed shoot in Nepal was rejected.Photograph: Apple RecordsThe BeatlesFour blokes and a zebra crossing: the banality and beauty of the Beatles’ Abbey Road coverMuch-copied and parodied picture captures dynamic between the individuals and the band with eerie perfectionJonathan JonesSat 22 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s not really the four blokes on the zebra crossing who make the cover of the Beatles’ Abbey Road memorable, but the street behind them. Vanishing towards a perfect blue sky, with summer trees veiling in bright green what might otherwise be dour brick houses, it could be a hyperreal vista painted by David Hockney. The black and white stripes of the crossing and the white line down the middle of the receding northLondonroad are fresh and crisp, enhancing the clarity of this psychedelic daydream.Of course the four blokes do play a part.The Beatleswere so transcendently famous by the time Iain Macmillan took this picture on 8 August 1969 that seeing them do something as ordinary as cross the road becomes a magical mystery.All the tourists who continue to recreate this photograph, the acts – from the Red Hot Chili Peppers and Kanye West to Franciscan friars and Booker T and the MGs – who have parodied it, as well asSam Mendes, who this week recreated it for his four Beatles biopics, are hypnotised by its enigmatic marriage of banality and charisma. Just four people on a zebra crossing, but they’re gods!The Beatles played on the same impossible everydayness months before this picture was taken when they performed live on the roof of Apple Corps in London’s Savile Row in January 1969. These were not just among the group’s last appearances together; they were manifestations against London backdrops of four individuals who had become archetypes.‘I can gauge John’s reaction: that’s good, stick that in’: Paul McCartney on how old bandmates – and Oasis – inspired his nostalgic new albumRead moreWhat Abbey Road freeze-frames with eerie perfection is the dynamic between four individuals and one unit that made the Beatles so appealing: the character of each Beatle coming together, or so fans still wanted to believe, in perfect step, as this photograph catches them.John Lennon leads, yet seems absent and absorbed: he is the only one whose face you can’t fully see and if he is the pacesetter, he might also be trying to get away. There I go. There’s a self-consciously symbolic quality to this picture that invites you to insert whatever allegory you please. I can picture Lennon walking away because that’s what he told the group he was going to do that September.But at the time, notoriously, it was Paul McCartney’s bare feet that fed bizarre speculations he was dead. According to this conspiracy theory, the black-clad Ringo Starr is the undertaker andGeorge Harrisonthe gravedigger.View image in fullscreenThe Red Hot Chili Peppers humorously recreate the photo for their 1988 release The Abbey Road EP.Photograph: EMIIt’s not such a bad interpretation and answers the picture’s demand to be decoded: surely it must be saying something! But the “Paul is dead” theory was doubly daft since McCartney was the picture’s creative author along with Macmillan.This was not a photograph taken by chance. It is a piece of conceptual art – something the Beatles were very familiar with, what with Lennon marrying one of the world’s most radical artists, Yoko Ono, that year. After an idea of being photographed in Nepal was rejected, it was McCartney who suggested they just do it in Abbey Road, outsidethe music studios in north London’s St John’s Wood. His sketches planned out the picture, with the four of them as stick figures on the zebra crossing and a view from above of the tree-lined street. On the day, they got a police officer to stop traffic, and Macmillan stood on a stepladder to get this perspective.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSleeve NotesGet music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThe cover of the 1993 album Sesame Road recreates the Beatles cover with characters from the children’s TV show Sesame Street.Photograph: Sony WonderIt’s not an accident; it’s art. McCartney started collecting paintings byRené Magrittein 1966 and this picture’s combination of a haunting, almost too real perspective and a confounding yet deadpan foreground scene is highly evocative of the Belgian surrealist. These are not the Beatles. This is not Abbey Road.It is definitely London, though. In these days of national self-loathing the wonder of the Abbey Road cover has to be its celebration of a very British moment. Zebra crossings are British: you know this is London, not New York.The Beatles are walking into their separate futures, but here McCartney, the most passionate believer in the band, freezes them for ever outside the studios where they’ve worked. He doesn’t want to go anywhere – he’s taken off his shoes.Explore more on these topicsThe BeatlesLondonPhotographyRené MagritteRingo StarrGeorge HarrisonPaul McCartneyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Penchant for bling’: can Sports Direct’s Mike Ashley take a bigger slice of luxury retail? | Retail industry | The Guardian
description: Frasers billionaire bought Harvey Nichols and increased Hugo Boss stake despite tough times for high-end stores
Author: Sarah Butler
Headline: Frasers billionaire bought Harvey Nichols and increased Hugo Boss stake despite tough times for high-end stores
Content: The Harvey Nichols department store in Knightsbridge, central London. The chain has 13 stores and 1,200 staff.Photograph: Corey Rudy/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe Harvey Nichols department store in Knightsbridge, central London. The chain has 13 stores and 1,200 staff.Photograph: Corey Rudy/ReutersRetail industry‘Penchant for bling’: can Sports Direct’s Mike Ashley take a bigger slice of luxury retail?Frasers billionaire bought Harvey Nichols and increased Hugo Boss stake despite tough times for high-end storesSarah ButlerSat 22 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhat billionaire doesn’t love to splash the cash on a luxury item? Some may buy watches or yachts, but Sports Direct founderMike Ashleyhas been snapping up entire brands.Harvey Nichols is the latest bauble to drop into his shopping basket after his companybought the Knightsbridge department store out of administrationearlier this month. It sits beside a large slice of Hugo Boss, a chunk of Mulberry, a snippet of Burberry, the remains of Agent Provocateur and the entire Flannels and House of Fraser chains.After arough few yearsfor the sellers of luxury goods – as the cost of living crisis has crunched the spare cash aspirational consumers might have had available for the occasional treat, and Asian and Middle Eastern shoppers have become less inclined to travel to Europe – Ashley’s buying spree might seem out of sync.However, the string of acquisitions closely match the entrepreneur’s established modus operandi – picking up bargains during tough times and finding the value where he can.Sports Direct, now part of Ashley’sFrasers Group, built its business by snapping up struggling independent sporting goods chains and bumped up its profits by getting the UK rights to ailing sportswear brands – from Head to Slazenger – and using them to decorate its own products.View image in fullscreenMike Ashley tends to pick up bargains during tough times and find the value where he canPhotograph: PA Images/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.Since first buying a stake in Flannels in 2012, then a menswear store in Knutsford, Cheshire, Ashley has been slowly building a luxury portfolio.The strategy has had its ups and downs. Flannels has expanded to about 75 stores and now sells brands from Gucci to Stone Island to Maison Margiela. This week, Ashley celebratedlifting his stakein the German label Hugo Boss to 48%, just short of taking full control, despite opposition from the company’s board.The Harvey Nichols deal is a classic tactic to gain access to intransigent brands, adding lustre to the portfolio that could make some designer marques previously shy of engaging with the king of discount trainers sit up.Ashley is likely to take a pragmatic approach to the wider Harvey Nichols estate, having said he intends to convert at least some of the five UK outposts outside London to the Flannels brand.View image in fullscreenAshley increased his stake in the German luxury label Hugo Boss to 48% this week.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesHowever, labels pondering whether to continue supplying the department store chain might do well to consider the events at the luxury online fashion seller Matchesfashion. Frasers bought the business for £52m at the end of 2023, only to place it into administration months later, leavingmillions of pounds owedto designer brands.House of Fraser is another cautionary tale. On buying the House of Fraser chain of 60 department stores out of administration almost exactly eight years ago, he set a mission to become“the Harrods of the high street”. Today there are just five stores left trading under that name.There are another 15 stores badged as just Frasers, some of which are converted department stores while others are somewhat smaller sites. The Frasers name is also being used on a Luton shopping mall in the group’s property portfolio, which contains a House of Fraser discount outlet.Such a confusing brand story is unlikely to entice large international labels to engage. Even the Flannels chain, Frasers said in its latest annual results published in July, was “now near complete”, indicating it did not intend to add many more stores.View image in fullscreenFrasers said in its latest annual results that theFlannels chain was ‘now near complete’.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesSales at the group’s “premium lifestyle” division, which includes House of Fraser and Jack Wills, fell almost 7%, while profits fell by almost £10m to £147.6m. Frasers said this included a rise in sales at Flannels, but gave no figures, so it was unclear if that was driven by adding new stores.Luxury fashion acquisitions by Frasers do not appear to have flourished. Jack Wills, once widely sported by partying public schoolers on their holidays in Cornwall, now has just five independent outlets,down from about 100when Frasers bought it in 2019.Clive Black, an analyst at Shore Capital, said that if one examined the group’s spending on upmarket brands then “from a financial perspective it has not been a roaring success.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“The premium end of Frasers has been a burden for the wider group. The mothership is Sports Direct and that’s what is funding the wider diversification strategy.”He suggested the strategy was more driven by Ashley’s personal aspiration to be taken seriously by these big names. “He has developed a penchant for bling in his 60s,” Black said. Whether “buying assets at the bottom” will lead to a benefit if and when the market improves works out “only time will tell”, he added.Luxury market experts are also sceptical. One told the Guardian he would not have chosen to buy Harvey Nichols as its brand had become degraded and customers had gone elsewhere.He suggested the building’s freeholders – the Cadogan Estate – had long discussed a plan to turn Harvey Nichols into a hotel or apartments and this might be the ultimate future of much of the Knightsbridge site.View image in fullscreenAn industry insider said Harvey Nichols “just feels like its lost its way’.Photograph: Takatoshi Kurikawa/AlamyAnother industry insider said that, while rivals Selfridges and Harrods had been revitalised, Harvey Nichols “just feels like its lost its way”.The old hand suggested Ashley’s scattergun expansion may yet lead him astray, pointing to the failed retail empires of Sears and Arcadia, and Marks & Spencer’s ill-fated efforts to expand overseas with Brooks Brothers. He suggested that running luxury brands such as Hugo Boss and Harvey Nichols might be a “bit of an overreach. It’s very different to a volume play.”He said it was clear Frasers had a weaker business than Next,where chief executive Simon Wolfson’s buying spreeis strictly limited to strong brands with effective management teams that need help to succeed online using Next’s expertise and infrastructure.“The world of retail is littered with big organisations with an existing business that liked to acquire other brands and it doesn’t manage to succeed or end well,” the insider said. However, he added of Ashley: “I wouldn’t bet against him.”The businessman has a long history as a gambler, famouslyproducing a wad of £50 notesfrom his pocket when taking journalists through security screening on a visit to the company’s Shirebrook warehouse in Derbyshire.He is not averse to risk but most of his business deals are underpinned by the value of stock and or property, which can be traded to raise cash if other tactics fail. The future for Harvey Nichols and its new luxury brand stablemates might not be pretty, but Ashley is likely to make money however it turns out.Frasers Group declined to comment.Explore more on these topicsRetail industryFrasers GroupMike AshleyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The moment I knew: Days after September 11, we flew through turbulence – all I could say was ‘I love you’ | Australian lifestyle | The Guardian
description: In 2001, Scott Westerfeld travelled from New York to Sydney to see Justine Larbalestier. In the immediate aftermath of 9/11, they navigated the crisis as best they could, together
Author: Scott Westerfeld
Headline: In 2001, Scott Westerfeld travelled from New York to Sydney to see Justine Larbalestier. In the immediate aftermath of 9/11, they navigated the crisis as best they could, together
Content: ‘With the world reorganising itself, we had to let each other feel the weight of history, but also remind each other to taste the wine in front of us’: Scott Westerfeld and Justine Larbalestier eloping on their wedding day, in upstate New York, 2001.View image in fullscreen‘With the world reorganising itself, we had to let each other feel the weight of history, but also remind each other to taste the wine in front of us’: Scott Westerfeld and Justine Larbalestier eloping on their wedding day, in upstate New York, 2001.The moment I knewAustralian lifestyleThe moment I knew: Days after September 11, we flew through turbulence – all I could say was ‘I love you’In 2001,Scott Westerfeldtravelled from New York City to Sydney to see Justine Larbalestier. In the immediate aftermath of 9/11, they navigated the crisis as best they could, togetherFind more stories fromthe moment I knew seriesScott WesterfeldSat 22 Aug 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 22 Aug 2026 20.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI noticed Justine before she noticed me. We were at a literary award ceremony and she was wearing a dress, upcycled from ablack Velvet Elvis painting, talking to a man three times her age.I asked my friend, Carol, who knew everyone, why I’d never seen her before. Carol explained that she was an Australian academic, researching the history of publishing, and led me across the room.“Justine,” Carol said. “You’re researching science fiction in New York. This is Scott, he’s a science fiction writer in New York.”Justine turned from the older man, glanced at me, then shook her head. “Not my period.”I was too young. She was studying science fiction’s golden age, a time before either of us was born. No one under 80 was relevant, or worth remembering.A week later, we ran into each other at a reading. This time we talked. We discovered we’re both fans of Samuel R Delany, Octavia Butler, Ursula K Le Guin, eggs with hot sauce, bushwalking, and exploring new cities.We were seeing other people at the time, but continued to run into each other at science fiction gatherings. Then came Justine’s last week in the city before returning to Australia. At a big farewell dinner, we were sitting directly across from each other, with lively conversations on either side, and we made eye contact, momentarily alone together.“I just broke up with my girlfriend,” I told her.“Me too,” she said.We spent her last weekend in NYC together.View image in fullscreenJustine Larbalestier and Scott Westerfeld at the Frida Kahlo museum in Mexico City, in 2015.Then Justine was back in Sydney, and we spent months talking on the phone and emailing. This was our romantic jet lag era, 10 time zones apart. She was waking up when I was going to sleep, and vice versa.In early September 2001, I flew to Sydney to see Justine’s city, her family, her friends. It was spring and everything was in bloom. The harbour was sparkling, and the big local news was a host of flying foxes invading the Royal Botanic Gardens. I was utterly charmed.Until bigger news happened. Justine and I were at one of Sydney’s finest restaurants, Tetsuya’s, eating an extraordinary degustation, discussing each and every dish and drinking too much. When we left at midnight, (10am in New York), the staff seemed oddly sombre. The taxi driver didn’t speak much English. We didn’t learn what had happened until the next morning when Justine ran into her addled flatmate on her way to the bathroom. “She says the Statue of Liberty exploded?”We turned the radio on and lay in bed holding hands, listening to what had happened to the city we both loved. We tried to call friends, but reached only overloaded circuits.We had a flight booked to Melbourne the next day, to meet more of Justine’s friends. We’d heard from our New York people by then. All of them safe, but shaken.It felt like tempting fate, boarding an aircraft on 13 September 2001. Even the cabin crew wasn’t pretending it was a normal flight. Justine and I huddled in our row of two, staring out the window, holding hands again.Halfway to Melbourne, we hit a stretch of turbulence. And it struck me: passenger jets were now weapons of war. International travel as we knew it might be over. What if I went back to the US, and couldn’t see Justine again for years?I opened my mouth to say all this, but instead said: “I love you.”My voice was calm and level. Here, with her, I felt certain, despite the tumult outside.“Me too,” she said.Australia felt very far from Ground Zero. Normal life was still under way, except when people asked where I was from, and I became the focus of a sweet, unnerving kindness, treated gently, given free drinks. Once, an actual fruit basket.View image in fullscreen‘We were skinless, our feelings always close to the surface’: Justine Larbalestier and Scott Westerfeld in 2024.The fruit basket became a running joke, one of many we had that week. Part of navigating a crisis with a partner is knowing how to change emotional gears. Justine and I would talk about the coming war one moment, and about sulphur-crested cockatoos the next. We were skinless, our feelings always close to the surface.With the world reorganising itself, we had to let each other feel the weight of history, but also remind each other to taste the wine in front of us.There was a deeper question, one that many New Yorkers asked themselves in the days after 9/11: Who do you want to spend the apocalypse with? Who can you trust to make the right silly joke when the world is demanding to be taken so seriously?Turned out, I’d found that person just in time.Jets kept crossing the oceans, of course, and Justine returned to New York much sooner than expected: in November, to meet my parents. We were already married by then, eloped upstate without telling our friends, and have been together ever since.The Mortonsby Justine Larbalestier and Scott Westerfeld is available now through Penguin ($AU34.99).Tell us the moment you knewShare your experienceShare your love storyDo you have a romantic realisation you'd like to share?
