title: Stand By Me at 40: Rob Reiner’s seminal coming-of-age saga remains a bittersweet triumph | Drama films | The Guardian
description: The late director’s sensitive and detailed adaptation of Stephen King’s novella has an authenticity that so many imitators could never replicate
Author: Scott Tobias
Headline: The late director’s sensitive and detailed adaptation of Stephen King’s novella has an authenticity that so many imitators could never replicate
Content: River Phoenix and Wil Wheaton in Stand By Me.Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Limited./AlamyView image in fullscreenRiver Phoenix and Wil Wheaton in Stand By Me.Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Limited./AlamyDrama filmsStand By Me at 40: Rob Reiner’s seminal coming-of-age saga remains a bittersweet triumphThe late director’s sensitive and detailed adaptation of Stephen King’s novella has an authenticity that so many imitators could never replicateScott TobiasSat 22 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 22 Aug 2026 16.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleComing-of-age metaphors don’t get any blunter than a group of preteen boys following a set of railroad tracks to a classmate’s dead body, a sobering testament to the fragility of life and a sign that their own futures are not guaranteed. TheStephen Kingnovella that would become Rob Reiner’s Stand By Me is simply called The Body, and there’s no doubt that commercial considerations factored into naming the film after the song that blankets the soundtrack. Yet the enduring magic of Reiner’s film lies in the tension between this bleak journey and the nostalgia and warmth that keeps complicating our feelings about it. Between those two poles is a bittersweet tone that perfectly suits the material, the rare example of an adaptation that benefits from softened edges.Stand By Me review – Rob Reiner’s nostalgic look at friendship and the loss of innocence still grips tightRead moreThough Reiner kicked off his career on a legendary heater that opened with This is Spinal Tap and would go on to include The Princess Bride, When Harry Met Sally … and A Few Good Men, Stand By Me was just his third feature and an early showcase of his versatility. His deft comic touch is not only essential in maintaining tonal balance, but important in suggesting what these four wayward boys mean to each other. Between the loose talk about Annette Funicello’s expanding bust on The Mickey Mouse Club and a Wurlitzer soundtrack of novelty singles like Lollipop and Yakety Yak, it can be easy to forget the anger, pain and dread that’s always simmering close to the surface. They laugh to keep from crying and occasionally don’t succeed.Though set a few years earlier than American Graffiti, Stand By Me feels like a natural companion to it, another radio-friendly nostalgia piece about a transitional moment for male friends in small-town America. Both films are death-haunted but the difference is that the characters in American Graffiti, who are reaching young adulthood at the cusp of the Vietnam war, don’t know what the future holds and writer-director George Lucas saves that bummer news for the epilogue. The boys in Reiner’s film know what lies at the end of a 20- to 30-mile hike down the tracks and their attraction to the novelty and notoriety of seeing a dead peer turns morbid. Their steps grow heavier by the hour.The more direct tie-in to American Graffiti is Richard Dreyfuss as Gordie LaChance, who narrates his memories as a novelist and father who’s gotten the perspective he and his buddies lacked as 12-year-olds. Flashing back to Labor Day weekend in 1959, the film casts Wil Wheaton as young Gordie, whose intellect and storytelling wizardry already puts some distance between him and his three troublemaking friends, who are bound for trade school at best. There’s not much to do in the Oregon backwater of Castle Rock, so when Gordie’s pal Vern (Jerry O’Connell) overhears his older brother talking about where they found the body of missing boy, the group’s curiosity is piqued. The two other no-goodniks in the gang, Chris (River Phoenix) and Teddy (Corey Feldman), come from broken homes, so they’re all too happy to lie to their parents and join the hunt. They figure they’ll be stars on the local news.Even when he’s writing horror novels around this period, like the first half of It or 11/22/63, King’s affection for the late ‘50s and early ‘60s of his own adolescence is boundless and those fond memories flow through Stand By Me. (Between this and his 1990 adaptation of Misery, which plays off an author’s relationship with his fans, Reiner would become King’s unofficial screen biographer.) Small details like the boys singing the theme song to the TV western Have Gun – Will Travel or musing about cherry-flavored Pez or “what Goofy is” fill out the milieu before the fun pops like bubblegum. As Dreyfuss describes it, a jovial night around the campfire featured “the kind of talk that seemed important until you discover girls”.I watched Stand By Me with Rob Reiner. Both film and man changed my lifeRead moreReiner stages some fun scrapes along the way, like a confrontation with a notably meek junkyard dog and a mad dash across a bridge as a train unexpectedly bears down on them. His work with his exceptionally talented young cast, too, establishes a relaxed camaraderie that pays huge emotional dividends later, when they’re closer to the end of the line. Much has been made about how Feldman’s angst about his troubles offscreen feeds into his startling reserves of anger as Teddy, a boy whose father once held his face to the stove. Wheaton, too, has affecting moments as the lesser son of parents who grieve his late older brother (played in flashbacks by John Cusack) and make him feel like the wrong kid died.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: c Columbia/Everett/Rex FeatureYet Stand By Me is another reminder of how generationally special Phoenix was as an actor, here in just his second feature after appearing with young Ethan Hawke in Explorers a year earlier. His Chris is a tough kid who seems to fit the mould of a sadistic greaser like the one played here by Kiefer Sutherland, but Phoenix plays him with astounding sensitivity, especially when Gordie needs a lift. Chris, Gordie and their buddies are expected to mask their vulnerabilities, and one of the film’s most effective gambits is how it contrasts these boys with Sutherland’s gang, who are inevitably cowed by his leadership. Phoenix’s Chris charts a more empathetic course.There are times when Reiner tilts too far into sentimentality, especially when Dreyfuss’ narration reaches for emotions the film might better grasp without a personal story seeming like grist for a novelist’s mill. Yet Stand By Me does well to preserve the R-rated saltiness of King’s world – it’s always more bracingly profane than you remember – and that helps it land more authentically than popular TV imitators like The Wonder Years and Stranger Things. These innocent boys strike out looking for a taste of adulthood and the film captures the feeling in all its pungency.Stand By Me is available on HBO Max in the US, Now TV in the UK and Tubi in AustraliaExplore more on these topicsDrama filmsRob ReinerStephen KingRiver PhoenixfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Perfect for kids’: the best (and worst) supermarket ketchup, tested and rated | Sauces and gravies | The Guardian
description: It’s a saviour at family mealtimes, but which bottle of red sauce does our reviewer relish the most? (Spoiler: it’s not Heinz)
Author: Tom Hunt
Headline: It’s a saviour at family mealtimes, but which bottle of red sauce does our reviewer relish the most? (Spoiler: it’s not Heinz)
Content: Feeling saucy? Not all tomato ketchups are created equal.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Loïc Parisot.View image in fullscreenFeeling saucy? Not all tomato ketchups are created equal.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Loïc Parisot.Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterSauces and graviesReview‘Perfect for kids’: the best (and worst) supermarket ketchup, tested and ratedIt’s a saviour at family mealtimes, but which bottle of red sauce does our reviewer relish the most? (Spoiler: it’s not Heinz)The best supermarket mayonnaiseTom HuntSat 22 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIwas that kid who put ketchup on everything, from fries to french toast, and if my parents wanted me to eat vegetables, they’d have to cover them in the stuff (the sugar cravings of my youth have subsided, but I still love ketchup mixed into peas). So I was pleasantly surprised by this test group, because even the most economical sauces performed well.Tomato content varied greatly (though not always in line with price), with the most tomato-heavy products containing almost twice as much fruit as the least. This information is presented in two ways: the first is the amount of raw tomato used before the sauce is cooked down into puree (more than 200g per 100g of finished product is high, less than 150g is low); the second is a straight percentage of tomato puree used, which is a more transparent measure (above 50% is high, while less than that I’d consider low, so check the label if you want more fruit in your sauce). Products made with fewer tomatoes are sometimes thickened with modified maize starch. I’ve also listed the total sugar content.Ultimately, every product did “what it says on the tin”, and while not necessarily delicious straight from the spoon, all were great with chips. Some of the top-end sauces suit a more mature palate, with a richer, spiced flavour, but they still have that classic burst of umami-sweet-sour tang.The best supermarket tomato ketchupsBest overall:Rubies in the Rubble Ketchup but GooderView image in fullscreen£3 for 485g at Tesco (62p/100g)£3.30 for 485g at Ocado (68p/100g)★★★★☆A squeezy bottle of vivid red sauce with a sweet and complex aroma. Contains a high percentage of fruit – 242g per 100g (tomatoes, plus surplus pears/apples) – which adds sweetness and a fruity depth layered with spice. Contains the preservative potassium sorbate and 20% total sugars.Best bargain:Bramwells Original tomato ketchupView image in fullscreen89p for 550g at Aldi (16p/100g), in store only★★★☆☆A squeezy bottle of thin and smooth puree, with a classic, inoffensive and unremarkable flavour profile (sweet-sour, tomato), making it perfect for kids. A simple, additive-free formula with 16.4% total sugars.And the rest …Co-op On the Side tomato ketchupView image in fullscreen89p for 550g at Co-op (16p/100g)★★★☆☆A squeezy bottle of thick, deep red sauce that’s sharp on the nose but with a tempting, savoury aroma. Sweet and easy on the palate, too, with a slightly higher total sugar content of 22% and a ratio of 167g tomatoes per 100g sauce. Contains modified maize starch.Sainsbury’s So Organic tomato ketchupView image in fullscreen£2.10 for 460g at Sainsbury’s (46p/100g)★★★☆☆A squeezy bottle with a clean tomato puree aroma, rich colour and that classic, sharp-yet-sweet umami flavour. Total sugars stand at 20.9%, plus, at 38%, a relatively low percentage of tomato puree. Certified organic.Mr Organic Italian organic tomato ketchupView image in fullscreen£3.75 for 480g at Ocado (78p/100g)★★★☆☆A glass bottle of very thick, smooth ketchup with the comforting and uncomplicated aroma of cooked tomatoes. Lively on the tongue yet classic and simply flavoured, with a dominant sweet-and-sour tomato flavour. A high percentage (80%) of tomato, too, and 16% total sugars.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionM&S Only 8 Ingredients tomato ketchupView image in fullscreen£2.50 for 250ml at Ocado (£1/100ml)★★★☆☆A thick puree with a little separation that’s sharp and lively on the palate with a subtle, spicy complexity. The sweetest sauce in the test, with 23.9% total sugars (it’s sweetened with agave syrup). It also has a high tomato content, with 281g of tomatoes per 100g.Heinz tomato ketchupView image in fullscreen£3.30 for 460g at Morrisons (72p/100g)£3.30 for 460g at Tesco (72p/100g)★★★☆☆The classic, fire-brick-red ketchup is a thick yet very smooth puree with a spiced, acidic, tomatoey aroma. Candy-sweet with a sour twang and good depth, but with 22.8% total sugars and a low 148g of tomatoes per 100g sauce. A simple, additive-free formula, though.Essential Waitrose & Partners tomato ketchupView image in fullscreen£1 for 470g at Waitrose (21p/100g)★★☆☆☆A squeezy bottle with a thick, mousse-like texture, a classic sweet taste, and a clear sharpness. At 75%, a high percentage of tomato puree. Contains modified maize starch and 21.5% total sugars.Asda Classic tomato ketchupView image in fullscreen£1.13 for 550g at Asda (21p/100g)★★☆☆☆A squeezy bottle of Venetian-red, perfectly smooth and thick puree. A mousse-like texture and a plain, sweet-forward flavour with that classic sour twang. Sugar is at 21%, and the tomato ratio is on the low side (148g per 100g ketchup). Contains modified maize starch.Tesco tomato ketchupView image in fullscreen£1.15 for 555g at Tesco (21p/100g)★★☆☆☆Sweet on the nose, with a thin consistency and a slimy texture from the modified maize starch. Low in total sugars (17.9%), while 148g tomatoes per 100g sauce is also on the low side.For more, read thebest supermarket mayonnaiseand thebest supermarket English mustardExplore more on these topicsSauces and graviesThe FilterFoodFamilyTomatoesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Thomasina Miers’ recipes for spiced lamb-stuffed aubergine with aleppo chilli butter, and berry ripple ice-cream | Lamb | The Guardian
description: A meaty, Middle Eastern style stuffed vegetable feast finished off with an ice-cold berry dessert
Author: Thomasina Miers
Headline: A meaty, Middle Eastern style stuffed vegetable feast finished off with an ice-cold berry dessert
Content: Thomasina Miers’ spiced lamb-stuffed aubergine with aleppo chilli butter.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Mandy Thompson.View image in fullscreenThomasina Miers’ spiced lamb-stuffed aubergine with aleppo chilli butter.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Mandy Thompson.Thomasina Miers recipesLambThomasina Miers’ recipes for spiced lamb-stuffed aubergine with aleppo chilli butter, and berry ripple ice-creamA meaty, Middle Eastern style stuffed vegetable feast finished off with an ice-cold berry dessertThomasina MiersSat 22 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere’s something delightfully retro about stuffed vegetables. They take me back toDelia Smith’s iconic Summer Collection cookbook, which blew my tiny mind when it came out in my early teens. Too sheltered to know about the e rage that had inspired Delia, I delved into my mother’s vegetable crisper with reverence, stuffing courgettes, tomatoes and aubergines with a zeal that had escaped me at school. How could the roasting, reducing and condensing of ingredients create such explosions of flavour? I was hooked. I have recently been returning to this technique with glee, a simple solution for turning seasonal vegetables into feasts.Spiced lamb-stuffed aubergine with aleppo chilli butterWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appServe these richly seasoned aubergines with warm, herb-flecked bulgur, rice or flatbreads, and a parsley and onion salad.Prep15 minSalt20 minCook1 hr 30 minServes4-65 medium auberginesSalt and black pepperOlive oil400g lamb mince2 small onions, peeled and finely chopped2 garlic cloves, peeled and crushed1 green pepper, halved, stalk, pith and seeds removed and discarded, flesh cut into 1cm dice200g cherry tomatoes, chopped2 tsp ground cumin1 tsp ground cinnamon3 tspaleppo chilli2 tbsp Turkish red pepper paste, or tomato paste400g tinfinely chopped tomatoes1 bunchflat-leaf parsley, picked and chopped50g unsalted butter200gGreek yoghurt, to serveCut the aubergines in half lengthways, then slice a lattice of crisscrosses over the flesh of each cut side, being careful not to cut down through the skin. Lay the aubergines flesh side up on a baking dish, sprinkle generously with salt, and leave for 20 minutes. Meanwhile, heat the oven to 220C (200C fan)/425F/gas 7.Using kitchen paper, blot away any moisture from the aubergine flesh, then drizzle over a tablespoon or two of olive oil. Roast for 30 minutes, until browned and softened, then remove and leave to cool.Meanwhile, make the filling. Put a large pan on a medium-high heat, then add a tablespoon of olive oil and the lamb. Season generously with salt and pepper and saute for seven to eight minutes, until the meat starts to catch and brown. Stir in the onions and garlic, turn down the heat down to medium and cook, stirring often, for 10-12 minutes, until the onions have softened.Add the green pepper, cherry tomatoes, cumin, cinnamon and one teaspoon of aleppo chilli, and cook for another 10 minutes. Add the pepper paste and half the chopped tomatoes, and cook for a further 20 minutes. Taste and adjust the seasoning, then stir in half the chopped parsley.Carefully spoon the filling over each aubergine half. Mix the remaining half-tin of chopped tomatoes with 200ml boiling water and season with salt and pepper. Pour the mixture around the aubergines in the tin, cover with foil and bake for 20 minutes. Remove the foil and bake for a further 10 minutes.In the last 10 minutes of cooking, put the butter in a small saucepan over a medium-high heat. Once sizzling, cook for 30 seconds before adding a generous pinch of salt and the remaining two teaspoons of aleppo chilli. Pour the butter over the baked aubergines, sprinkle on the remaining parsley and serve with the yoghurt.Iced berry-ripple tahini creamWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appView image in fullscreenThomasina Miers’ iced berry-ripple tahini cream.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Mandy Thompson.An easy, no-churn ice-cream to finish; the tahini adds a nutty, salty note against the backdrop of intense berry deliciousness.Prep5 minCook25 minFreeze4 hr+Serves4-6200g mixed berries(blackcurrants, redcurrants, raspberries, say),thoroughly washed2 tbsp runny honey100ml tahini2 tsp vanilla essence150ml condensed milk200ggreek yoghurt400ml double creamTo serveYour favourite biscuits2 tsp toasted sesame seeds(optional)Pop the berries in a saucepan with the honey and cook over a low heat for eight to 10 minutes, until they start to break down. Take off the heat and leave to cool.Spoon the tahini into a small bowl and slowly whisk in the vanilla essence, followed by the condensed milk. Fold through half of the yoghurt, then fold in the rest.In a second bowl, whisk the cream to soft peaks, being careful not to over-whisk. With a large spoon, fold in the yoghurt mix little by little, until well combined.Spoon half the tahini cream into a freezable container, then pour over half of the berry sauce create a ripple effect with the blade of a knife. Repeat with the rest of the cream and sauce in a second layer, and ripple that, too. Freeze overnight, or for at least four hours, then serve with your favourite biscuits on the side and perhaps a sprinkle of sesame seeds.Explore more on these topicsLambThomasina Miers recipesFoodMeatMiddle Eastern food and drinkMain courseIce-cream and sorbetDessertrecipesShareReuse this content

title: From Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma to Brandon Flowers: your complete entertainment guide to the week ahead | Culture | The Guardian
description: A film-maker’s attempt to reboot a horror movie franchise is derailed by her wild relationship with its former star, and the Killers frontman gets rustic
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A film-maker’s attempt to reboot a horror movie franchise is derailed by her wild relationship with its former star, and the Killers frontman gets rustic
Content: Director’s cult … Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma.Photograph:  MUBIView image in fullscreenDirector’s cult … Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma.Photograph:  MUBIGoing out, staying inCultureFrom Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma to Brandon Flowers: your complete entertainment guide to the week aheadA film-maker’s attempt to reboot a horror movie franchise is derailed by her wild relationship with its former star, and the Killers frontman gets rusticSat 22 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleContents1Going out: Cinema2Going out: Gigs3Going out: Art4Going out: Stage5Staying in: Streaming6Staying in: Games7Staying in: Albums8Staying in: Brain foodView image in fullscreenGoing out:CinemaTeenage Sex and Death at Camp MiasmaOut nowJane Schoenbrun’s third feature builds on their interest in queer horror, with a story about the fictional Camp Miasma slasher franchise, set to be resurrected by an up-and-coming director (Hannah Einbinder), who enters into a wild relationship with the star of the originals (Gillian Anderson).MutinyOut nowJason Statham is back in his favourite niche of action thriller: one guy pitted against a system or conspiracy, which he will try to unravel, and when that doesn’t work, smash it to bits. This time, he’s framed for the murder of his boss. Annabelle Wallis and Adrian Lester also star.Spa WeekendOut nowA buddy comedy in the vein of Bridesmaids: Leslie Mann, Isla Fisher, Michelle Buteau and Anna Faris star in a tale of three childhood BFFs reunited for a fabulous weekend getaway, only to find a former friend, a total hot mess, gatecrashing their pampering sesh.Insidious: Out of the FurtherOut nowIn case you haven’t been keeping up, this is the sixth instalment in the Insidious franchise, which began in 2010 with a relatively simple haunted-house story. In this latest outing, a young mother discovers she can bring back supernatural demons. Spooksome.Catherine BrayGoing out:GigsView image in fullscreenArt on her sleeve … Rochelle Jordan.Photograph: Elise KRochelle JordanDublin,25 August; Manchester,26 AugustBritish-born, Canada-raised dance music maven Rochelle Jordan arrives in the UK and Ireland in support of last year’s excellent third album, Through the Wall. With a five-EP series of remixes slowly being released, expect these shows to be head-knocking, sweat-soaked affairs.Michael CraggTyler, the CreatorVictoria Park, London,28& 29 AugustThe mercurial rapper, singer, actor and fashion designer headlines two dates at this year’s east London-based All Points East series. Expect a zigzagging setlist careening between hip-hop, funk and electro, plus support across the two shows from the likes of Turnstile, Dijon and Rex Orange County.MCLondon Symphony Orchestra/PappanoSnape MaltingsConcert Hall, Snape,28 AugustThe Proms may be London’s symphonic main stage in August, but one of the capital’s finest orchestras is decamping to East Anglia, armed with Bruckner’s thrilling Symphony No 9 and Gubaidulina’s Viola Concerto. Antonio Pappano conducts, with Norwegian violist Eivind Ringstad.Flora WillsonTom Barford QuintetPeggy’s Skylight, Nottingham,22 August;East Side Jazz Club, London,25 AugustYoung UK musician Tom Barford won the prestigious Kenny Wheeler prize in 2017 for his edgily inviting compositions – but is just as notable for his sax virtuosity. Expect vivacious Barford originals mixed with hip tributes to the music of sax legend Joe Henderson.John FordhamGoing out:ArtView image in fullscreenSimón Vega’s Tourist Prospero Reflects, 2024.Photograph: Courtesy of Simón Vega and Elizabeth Xi Bauer, London.Our Place in These WorldsElizabeth Xi Bauer, London,to 27 SeptemberA roving, constantly evolving exhibition that has been growing and touring since 2023, featuring work about migration, colonialism and collective identity by artists Esvin Alarcón Lam, Antonio Pichillá Quiacaín and Simón Vega.Hot Snakes Night ClubTaco!, London,22 Augustto 13 SeptemberThis hip experimental gallery in south-east London is being transformed into a cabaret club by artist Chloe Langlois for three weeks of live performances, workshops and experimental music, starting with a 24-hour occult marathon.Gender StoriesWalkerArtGallery, Liverpool,to 31 AugustWith works by major artists such as David Hockney, Catherine Opie, Grayson Perry and Zanele Muholi, this show looks at how art can help us figure out the meaning of gender, and how it shapes our everyday lives.Simeon BarclayJohn Hansard Gallery, Southampton,to 29 AugustThe British conceptualist celebrates his nomination for this year’s Turner prize with a complex exhibition about barriers, gatekeeping, pop culture, fashion, bus seats and giant inflatable mascots.Eddy FrankelGoing out:StageView image in fullscreenUneasy listening … Frankie Thompson: Horrible Things.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianFrankie ThompsonBeside at Pleasance Courtyard, Edinburgh, to 30 AugustSomewhere between character comedy, performance art and drag, Thompson’s latest show, Horrible Things, is a riot of lip-syncing (often to unsettling archive recordings), audience interaction and contemporary clowning.Rachel AroestiA Slow FireJermyn Streettheatre, London, to 26 SeptemberThe UK premiere of Simon Stephens’s post-apocalyptic play stars a fierce trio of Irish actors and sees two men trapped in a bunker – before they meet a mysterious stranger.Miriam GillinsonSauna Sessions Arts ClubSummerhall, Edinburgh, to 31 AugustThis year’s Edinburgh festival fringe hosts the UK’s first arts centre set inside a sauna: the 80-seater venue will host a series of immersive performances – including a morning rave, a ritualistic storytelling experience and a reworking of Virginia Woolf’s The Waves, with towel-based choreography.MGDan Daw: ExxyKing’stheatre, Edinburgh,23 AugustExxy (it’s Australian slang for expensive) is the follow-up to the uncompromising and acclaimed Dan Daw Show, as seen at last year’s Edinburgh international festival. Hugo Weaving and The Pitt’s Shabana Azeez star.Dog ParkU,24 AugustAlso from down under, this cute canine-dominated dramedy is TV at its most wholesome and nuanced. With production by Swedish pop producer Klas Åhlund (Robyn, Katy Perry) and hip-hop wizard Kenny Beats, plus a guest spot from alt-rockers Wednesday, it’s another perfect mix of existential angst and frat anthems.Brandon Flowers – ThrasherOut nowWith Mr Brightside still bobbing around the UK Top 100, where it has now spent more than 500 weeks (!), the Killers frontman returns with a third solo album. title: Roberto De Zerbi says Tottenham are ‘not a team’ and hits out at lack of fight | Tottenham Hotspur | The Guardian
description: The manager said ‘we are not in the right physical condition for a lot of reasons’ after Tottenham’s 3-0 Premier League defeat by Brentford
Author: Jacob Steinberg
Headline: The manager said ‘we are not in the right physical condition for a lot of reasons’ after Tottenham’s 3-0 Premier League defeat by Brentford
Content: Roberto De Zerbi (right) handed debuts to five players in the defeat at Brentford.Photograph: John Walton/PAView image in fullscreenRoberto De Zerbi (right) handed debuts to five players in the defeat at Brentford.Photograph: John Walton/PATottenham HotspurRoberto De Zerbi says Tottenham are ‘not a team’ and hits out at lack of fight‘We are not in the right physical condition’Spurs beaten 3-0 at Brentford in Premier League openerJacob Steinbergat the Gtech Community StadiumSat 22 Aug 2026 16.27 EDTLast modified on Sat 22 Aug 2026 16.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRoberto De Zerbi said that Tottenham are “not a team” after they opened their season with a humiliating 3-0 defeat away toBrentford.Spurs are looking to kick on after almost going down last season and are expected to spend more than £300m this summer but they were handed a rude awakening at the Gtech Community Stadium. Brentford outclassed the north Londoners and left De Zerbi rueing a lack of fight from his players, bemoaning his side’s physical conditioning and suggesting that the pre-season tour of Australia was less than ideal.Kayode seals emphatic Brentford victory in wake-up call for sorry SpursRead more“We are not a team yet for a lot of reasons,” the Tottenham manager said. “Before you become a team you can’t say what you can do. We are not in the right physical condition for a lot of reasons. Some players came back late from the World Cup. In Australia we don’t work in the right way but it is not excuses. It is a normal situation when building a new project.“I don’t want time but we have to pass through these problems. I cannot lose confidence in my players. I believe in my players, my club, myself. We are working well. We have to improve quickly. We could fight stronger than we did today. We lost too many duels today. We arrived second in the second balls. We didn’t win one second ball, one duel, one tackle.”Spurs handed debuts to Andy Robertson, Jan Paul van Hecke, Marcos Senesi, Mateus Fernandes and Sandro Tonali. They are close to strengthening their attack by signing Omar Marmoush and Savinho from Manchester City but De Zerbi needs to build a collective.“There are steps to become better,” he said. “Now the target is to become a team. You can’t become a team from the transfer market on paper. You become a team when the players find a connection, a spirit, a soul. It’s a project.”De Zerbi pointed out that he was without Pedro Porro, Kevin Danso and Micky van de Ven. He said that Rodrigo Bentancur, who started on the bench, came back late in pre-season.It was a fine way for Brentford to start their second year under Keith Andrews. Keane Lewis-Potter, Vitaly Janelt and Michael Kayode scored and there was an outstanding debut in midfield from Mamadou Sangaré, the £39m signing from Lens.“The club deserve a lot of credit for getting that deal done,” Andrews said of Sangaré. “You’ve seen today what he’s capable of, the attributes he has. It adds to a talented midfield. I really enjoyed his performance today. He’s slotted in really well. He’s a humble young man who’s very, very hungry.”Explore more on these topicsTottenham HotspurBrentfordPremier LeaguenewsShareReuse this content

title: Carrick tells Manchester United to keep calm and carry on after Hull humbling | Michael Carrick | The Guardian
description: Michael Carrick insists he is not panicking after going down 2-0 in their opening Premier League game of the season at promoted Hull
Author: Will Unwin
Headline: Michael Carrick insists he is not panicking after going down 2-0 in their opening Premier League game of the season at promoted Hull
Content: Michael Carrick said he and his Manchester United players were ‘hurting inside’ after defeat at Hull.Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPAView image in fullscreenMichael Carrick said he and his Manchester United players were ‘hurting inside’ after defeat at Hull.Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPAMichael CarrickCarrick tells Manchester United to keep calm and carry on after Hull humblingBruno Fernandes: ‘We gave too much of the ball to them’Sergej Jakirovic happy Hull proved critics wrongWill Unwinat the MKM StadiumSat 22 Aug 2026 11.41 EDTLast modified on Sat 22 Aug 2026 11.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMichael Carrick says he will not overreact, but has called for improvement afterManchester Unitedstarted the season with a 2-0 defeat at Hull. United lost their opening game for the fourth time in the past seven years as Semi Ajayi and Nobel Mendy took advantage of poor defending from set-pieces.The United head coach presented a professional exterior despite United’s performance not reaching the desired standard as they were deservedly beaten by Hull, who finished sixth in the Championship last season.Ajayi and Mendy give Hull dream start against misfiring Manchester UnitedRead more“I’m talking to you quite calmly, but I’m not exactly calm inside and enjoying the day, so there’s a big difference,” he said. “I played [for United] for a long time. You don’t get to play here for a long time without just going day by day, the results, the ups and downs, but you just carry on as normal.“It’s 100% not that, and trust me, it’s not that. It just doesn’t mean that we all have to shout and scream and come out and create some chaos just because of it. Inside we’re hurting and we need to get better. But the calmness doesn’t mean there’s no emotion in it, for sure.”He added: “The result’s the result. We got beat, we’re hurt and it’s not a nice feeling. It doesn’t mean it’s going to change the whole direction of how we’re going as a team or as a football club.“It’s one game and results can happen in football, we all understand that. It’s not nice when they do, but it does happen.”View image in fullscreenManchester United’s Bruno Fernandes (left) looks dejected after the match against Hull CityPhotograph: Lee Smith/Action Images/ReutersUnited barely threatened throughout the 90 minutes. “Same mistakes as we did last season, every away game,” Bruno Fernandes said. “We gave too much of the ball to them, in the first 20 minutes the goalkeeper had more touches on the ball, too much time. We need to press a little bit more, be more aggressive, and set-plays – we need to work on it, to be more aggressive and try not to concede these types of goals.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHull’s head coach, Sergej Jakirovic, said he and his backroom staff had spotted a weakness in the way United defended set-pieces, but would not divulge his “secret” that helped to expose it.Hull are strongly tipped for relegation and their supporters sung “are you watching Joe Cole?” during the match after the pundit mocked their chances of survival. “I don’t have any problems with critics with opinions,” Jakirovic said. “We tried to prove them wrong and today we won the game. Now it’s 37 to go, so we will try to continue like this. I’m very, very happy because of all the people in the club.”Explore more on these topicsMichael CarrickHull CityManchester UnitednewsShareReuse this content

title: Infantino angers Concacaf nations by hijacking meeting in Caribbean | Fifa | The Guardian
description: Gianni Infantino has angered many of the Concacaf nations, whose support he is seeking in his re-election campaign, by hijacking a meeting of the Caribbean Football Union
Author: Matt Hughes
Headline: Gianni Infantino has angered many of the Concacaf nations, whose support he is seeking in his re-election campaign, by hijacking a meeting of the Caribbean Football Union
Content: Gianni Infantino’s behaviour in the Dominican Republic infuriated many Concacaf nations.Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PAView image in fullscreenGianni Infantino’s behaviour in the Dominican Republic infuriated many Concacaf nations.Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PAFifaInfantino angers Concacaf nations by hijacking meeting in CaribbeanGianni Infantino used opportunity to lobby for supportFifa president was asked to stay away from CFU meetingExclusive byMatt HughesandNick AmesSat 22 Aug 2026 14.02 EDTLast modified on Sat 22 Aug 2026 15.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGianni Infantino has risked alienating numerous Concacaf nations, whose support he is seeking in his re-election campaign, by hijacking a meeting of the Caribbean Football Union (CFU) to announce Fifa-funded development projects for the region with millions of dollars that had been delayed for months.‘See you at the hairdresser’s’: Gianni Infantino’s bizarre reply to bald reporterRead moreMultiple sources attending the CFU meeting in the Dominican Republic said many of the Concacaf members were infuriated by Infantino’s behaviour, particularly as he had been asked to stay away by their president, Victor Montagliani.The Concacaf position echoes previous complaints about Fifa’s operations from the Jordan FA, whose president, Prince Ali bin al-Hussein, accused Infantino of bribery this month when he claimedthey have not received prize moneyfrom last year’s Arab Cup due to the country’s failure to endorse the president.Infantino appears to have seen the CFU meeting as an opportunity to lobby for election votes among Caribbean countries in the hope of causing a split within Concacaf, who have aligned with Uefa and the Asian Football Confederationin demanding his resignationafter the World Cup sell-off debacle.In a letter addressed to Infantino on Friday, Montagliani had asked theFifapresident “in the name of football to reconsider your attendance”, pointing out his presence would take the spotlight away from a regional under-14 tournament being held alongside the meeting.Despite that entreaty, Infantino is understand to have turned up at the resort of Punta Cana with a large Fifa entourage including the secretary general, Mattias Grafström, and Elkhan Mammadov, a staunch ally who is responsible for maintaining good relations with the 211 members in his role as director of member associations.Before making funding pledges in the CFU meeting, Infantino’s team are understood to have approached individual member associations lobbying for support. Mammadov has played a central role in attempts to keep them onside since theFifa Forward Enterprise scandal brokeand his insistent approach has caused disquiet in some quarters.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFifa general secretary Mattias Grafström sounded out about standing against InfantinoRead moreOne source said the official Fifa party had attempted to portray their governance crisis as a private dispute between Infantino and Montagliani. The Canadian businessman has not commented since news of the proposed Fifa Forward Enterprise emerged, but has been widely touted in Europe as a possible contender to replace Infantino.The pair met briefly and shook hands before the CFU meeting in an exchange captured by Infantino’s personal camera crew.While Mexico, Grenada and St Kitts and Nevis have all broken with Concacaf and declared their support for Infantino, the majority of their 41 members are understood to back the alliance with Uefa advocated by Montagliani.The Uefa/Concacaf pact extends beyond attempts to unseat Infantino, with the two confederations in talks aboutsetting up a joint Nations Leaguein 2028 that could develop further into a new global competition.Explore more on these topicsFifaGianni InfantinoFootball politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: José Mourinho marks Real Madrid return with late drama and touch of humility | José Mourinho | The Guardian
description: The old master is back at Madrid as he begins with celebrations, frustrations and finally relief at Espanyol
Author: Sid Lowe
Headline: The old master is back at Madrid as he begins with celebrations, frustrations and finally relief at Espanyol
Content: José Mourinho enjoys a giggle with Vinícius Júnior after Real’s dramatic 2-1 win at Espanyol.Photograph: Pablo Morano/ReutersView image in fullscreenJosé Mourinho enjoys a giggle with Vinícius Júnior after Real’s dramatic 2-1 win at Espanyol.Photograph: Pablo Morano/ReutersJosé MourinhoJosé Mourinho marks Real Madrid return with late drama and touch of humilityThe old master is back at Madrid as he begins with celebrations, frustrations and finally relief at EspanyolSid Loweat the RCDE StadiumSat 22 Aug 2026 19.21 EDTLast modified on Sat 22 Aug 2026 19.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJosé Mourinho says he is calmer now so when the rest of the bench emptied, sprinting down the touchline to celebrate the 90th-minute goal that finally delivered victory on his first game in charge of Real Madrid in 4,380 days, he didn’t set off with them. Instead, he clenched his fists, got to his feet and walked down the touchline behind the subs, watching them head, shouting, towards Carlos Espí. As they piled on down in the corner, he pulled over his captain Fede Valverde for a word. Which might just have been:phew.For all those stars; for all that Mourinho’s main task might just have been been to find a way to fit Kylian Mbappé, Vinícius Júnior and Jude Bellingham together; for all that he had introducedYan Diomande, the most expensive player in the club’s history, it was a 21-year-old, unknown six months ago and unexpectedly signed from Levante, who got the goal that secured victory upon the coach’s second coming.Espí, whose goals had rescued Levante from relegation last season and who is still living at Madrid’s Valdebebas training ground like his coach, the two of them sharing breakfast every morning, was signed for pretty much this: to be a different type of striker, an old-school No 9, with a presence in the area. And when a scrappy, broken-up move ended with Mbappé seeing the ball run away from him in the area, there he was to force it over the line. Perhaps even to pose a question: is his a profile they could do with and not just in reserve? This time, at least, it had worked.View image in fullscreenCarlos Espí celebrates the late winner for Real Madrid.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesMourinho’s first game since a 4-2 win over Osasuna in May 2013 began with the photographers abandoning their places behind the goal to surround him on the bench, no doubt what the attraction was; it ended with him hugging theEspanyolcoach Manolo González, high-fiving the referee and ducking down the tunnel. In between time, reality was revealed, which he surely always imagined it would be: it is early, solutions are never immediate, and he had said that Espanyol were a good side. At times, they showed it too. Madrid had more chances, but Manolo’s team had largely succeeded in limiting the visitors.On a night where Madrid exhibited some of the old flaws, there were doubts still – it is the first day after all – but they were at least allayed for a little while. There will be other days, sterner tests of this team; there will also be sterner tests of Mourinho’s temperament, of course.When Madrid faced Benfica in the spring, Mourinho had described his time there as “three hard, intense, sometimes violent years”. But the thing about nostalgia is that as the bad slips into the distance, only the good remains. Mourinho said that he is “not the kind of man who misses anything”, someone who has “regrets”; plenty though had missed him, the president Florentino Pérez first among them. In his world view, managers are mostly a necessary evil; the Portuguese is virtually the only coach he had ever truly liked.Interviewing José Mourinho: ego, charisma, talent and his ‘rucksack of pain’Read moreThere are those who had longed for exactly that intensity, violence even: for a hard man to lead them, some kind of iron surgeon to fix them and go to war with their rivals, someone with the personality to impose. For all that by the end they really could not go on, at some level Pérez had always been drawn to Mourinho’s return. He clung to the idea that their success after his departure – six Champions League wins in 11 years – was down to him, that he had made it possible. He had shown the way.Mourinho told a story on the eve of this game revealing that after every trophy Madrid won he would have got a call from Pérez. “I always said no, no, no, it was nothing to do with me,” he said, which was a neat way of saying it kind of was. This was not a confidence betrayed: Pérez had said much the same. It took the president 13 years to attend to his urge, but now Mourinho was back.And, perhaps, why not? The last returnees had done rather well, while all the others had failed. There was a moment at the end of that story when Mourinho said the trophies belonged to Zinedine Zidane and Carlo Ancelotti, not him, andinnocentlychecked that they were the only men to have won anything. The diagnosis of their ills, the challenge before them, required his surgery too. Like in 2010, Madrid had fallen behind Barcelona. They have not won a major title in two years, and that was about culture as well as football.View image in fullscreenA first look of Yan Diomande in action for Real Madrid against Espanyol.Photograph: Quality Sport Images/Getty ImagesIt may not be as simple aseffortbut that is a start. “We have to try not to negotiate things that are non-negotiable,” Mourinho said. “Commitment can’t be missing.” Mourinho has the authority to change that, or so it goes. He would be afforded it, anyway. That at least is the theory. Habits had been changed, demands made. Sessions had improved, or the attitude towards them. Diomande had said he was ready to “die” for his coach, who insisted that was just a phrase, but he could not help but be pleased with that.There were other reasons to be optimistic. Vinícius’s future had been resolved at last, no lingering doubts over status or resentment. The World Cup is out the way, no other priority on the horizon. Mourinho noted that Brazil, France and England had found a way to get the best out of Vinícius, Mbappe and Bellingham, but that getting the best of all three is different. “I don’t think they’re incompatible,” he insisted; last year it often looked like they were, Bellingham, admitting that they find themselves occupying the same spaces at times.Here, they all started. Bellingham was at No 10, Vinícius tight to the touchline. “For me this is his [Jude’s] position: the connection with the forwards, he can score goals. He has to play close to the goal. Playing at 6 or 8 we’re losing his closeness to the goal,” said Mourinho.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBellingham had an immediate impact, the first goal of this new era coming from a dead ball and after nine minutes. Vinícius was fouled, which was already looking like becoming a pattern – Alex Calatrava had already given him a kick in the back, prompting Mourinho to raise his arms – and from the left, Arda Guler delivered a superb cross. Bellingham leapt highest to head past Marko Dimitrovic.View image in fullscreenJude Bellingham celebrates after giving Real the lead.Photograph: David Ramos/Getty ImagesThis time, sitting on the left end of the bench, Mourinho barely flinched. He got up, put his hands in his pockets and walked along the touchline to the other end where the rest of his sizeable staff sat in the overspill in the stand beyond the other end. There, he shook hands with Sami Khedira, the in-house assistant Madrid have provided him, and Roberto Merella, the analyst.And that, it was tempting to assume, was that. The gap between the teams looked insurmountable. Madrid were pressing high, Espanyol barely able to find a way out. Here was a glimpse, they might have hoped, of the future. Instead, the intensity dropped again and that was an invitation for Espanyol.When Dean Huijsen needed attention for a cut, Madrid’s players came to Mourinho for instructions but the game started to slip from them a little. Espanyol took a step forward and soon had an equaliser. Thibaut Courtois saved from Riedel, Roberto Fernández unable to keep down the follow-up. Then a lovely move concluded with Tuy Dolan and Javi Hernández setting up Calatrava to score. Mourinho sat almost motionless.Twice Mbappé escaped to force saves from Dimitrovic, one on each side of the area, but it was Espanyol who should have led at the break. Again, the ball was worked into position. From the right, Omar El Hilali provided a superb cross. Dolan couldn’t quite get to it, inside the six-yard box, and Fernández headed it straight at his own feet. Mbappé may wonder how he didn’t put Madrid into the lead just after the break. From Guler’s corner, Bellingham headed against the bar, via Dimitrovic’s hand, and the ball dropped to the Frenchman right by the post. Somehow, it went wide.Valverde hit the post, Mbappé shot wide, but there was no way through. Mourinho turned to the men behind him – Cucurella, Diomande, Camavinga, Alexander-Arnold, Espí – until, at last, he saw them dash past him, given a reprieve on his return.“I think we deserved to win, but Espanyol didn’t deserve to lose,” Mourinho said as he ended the night with a touch of humility.Explore more on these topicsJosé MourinhoReal MadridEspanyolLa LigaEuropean club footballfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Arthur Fils blasts past Flavio Cobolli to reach first Masters final in landmark win | Tennis | The Guardian
description: Arthur Fils marched into his first Masters 1000 final at the Cincinnati Open with an impressive 6-3, 6-4 victory against Flavio Cobolli
Author: Tumaini Carayol
Headline: Arthur Fils marched into his first Masters 1000 final at the Cincinnati Open with an impressive 6-3, 6-4 victory against Flavio Cobolli
Content: Arthur Fils showed athleticism, explosiveness and audacity in his 6-3, 6-4 victory against Flavio Cobolli in Cincinnati.Photograph: Wally Nell/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenArthur Fils showed athleticism, explosiveness and audacity in his 6-3, 6-4 victory against Flavio Cobolli in Cincinnati.Photograph: Wally Nell/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockTennisArthur Fils blasts past Flavio Cobolli to reach first Masters final in landmark winFrench youngster beats No 7 seed 6-3, 6-4 in CincinnatiJessica Pegula battles past Swiatek to reach women’s finalTumaini Carayolin CincinnatiSat 22 Aug 2026 19.16 EDTLast modified on Sat 22 Aug 2026 19.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the middle of a tense, erratic start to a rain-delayed semi-final day in Cincinnati, Arthur Fils found himself locked in defence and miles behind the baseline on his serve at 3-3. He scurried from sideline to sideline, lunging toward the ball at full stretch, seemingly with no real chance of turning things around. As Flavio Cobolli swept to the net with the intention of finishing Fils off, however, the Italian soon learned that his opponent had another gear to reach. From far wide of the court, Fils pulverised a forehand passing shot winner beyond his astounded opponent, drawing a roar from the crowd.That one point alone provided evidence of the athleticism, explosiveness and sheer audacity that have long marked Fils as such a rare, exciting talent, and it also set the tone for a monumental victory. From that moment onwards, Fils took control of the match and he marched into his first Masters 1000 final at the Cincinnati Open with a supreme performance, defeating Cobolli, the No 7 seed, 6-3, 6-4.Can Aryna Sabalenka find a way to repair her collapsed form? | Tumaini CarayolRead moreFils has now reached a final, two semi-finals and two other quarter-finals in his five completed Masters 1000 tournaments this year. He also won his fourth title at the Barcelona Open 500 event and he has won four of his last six matches against top 10 opponents. As he seeks his first Masters 1000, he now sits at No 6 in the race to the ATP Finals. He will rise to a career high ranking of No 11.Fils has played some incredible tennis this year, and it is far from surprising for such a talented 22-year-old player taking the next step in his career. His problem, simply, is how infrequently he has been able to play. In spring last year, Fils suffered a stress fracture in his back that forced him to retire from Roland Garros, his home grand slam tournament, and essentially sidelined him for nine months. During his time away, Fils made countless changes to his game, including altering his forehand and serve technique, learning how to slide into his backhand on hard courts and dropping weight.He returned to competition a far better player, producing the best tennis of his career early in his comeback. However, just as it seemed like he had found his way back, his body betrayed him again. A week after his run to the Madrid Open semi-final, Fils suffered a hip injury at the beginning of his opening round match at the Italian Open that forced him to again withdraw from Roland Garros. His performances this season showed beyond doubt that he was capable of achieving great things, but it remained unclear if his body would allow it. “I was feeling great, but you just got to take it,” he said. “Some things are happening for a purpose. It’s OK.”View image in fullscreenFlavio Cobolli stretches during his straight sets defeat against Arthur Fils in the Cincinnati Open.Photograph: Wally Nell/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockFils’ minimal preparation was reflected in his second-round loss at Wimbledon. After that, it was again time for him to rebuild his form, level and physicality. As at the beginning of the season, it is a reflection of Fils’ talent that it has taken him no time at all to find his best level again. One of the most impressive aspects of these comebacks have been the positivity he has maintained throughout. “If I’m sad, there is no way I can make it,” he said. “If I’m positive, then I give myself a shot, at least. When I’m sad, if I’m going crying into my bed, there is no way I can wake up and play some good tennis. If I’m going happy and blessed that now I’m able to play tennis, then after, it’s working well.”In his last three matches, dominant straight sets wins over the fifth seed, Alex de Minaur, Thiago Agustín Tirante, Novak Djokovic’s conqueror, and Cobolli, Fils’s level has been immaculate. In terms of its immense speed and wicked spin, his forehand is the heaviest groundstroke in the game. He has spent the past 10 days demolishing the ball off both wings and dominating the baseline while also serving well, moving spectacularly and maintaining his composure. At his best, Fils is also one of the most charismatic and extroverted players on the tour, but part of his development has been adopting a more composed approach.“I’m a bit less crazy,” he said. “Miami was nice, I was in the semis, but I lost so much energy in this tournament. I was screaming ‘Come on’, ‘Vamos’ after every point. Now here it’s completely different. And I think also when you do it, you start to do it a couple of times, the tournaments, those big runs, then you start to get a bit used to [it], and you don’t need anymore to go crazy, to pump yourself. I think I’m already pumped enough, especially with my team also. They are very pumped, so I don’t need to go that crazy anymore.”Fils awaits Saturday night’s all-American semi-final between Frances Tiafoe, the 2024 finalist here, and Brandon Nakashima, who reached his first Masters 1000 final a week ago at the Canadian Open in Montreal.In the women’s draw,Jessica Peguladefeated Iga Swiatek 7-5, 4-6, 6-4 to reach the final. The American rallied from a break down in the final set to subdue Swiatek in a tense, rain-delayed battle that lasted two hours and 47 minutes.Pegula will face either her compatriot Coco Gauff or unseeded Czech player Sara Bejlek in Sunday’s final. The world No 3 is chasing her third WTA title of 2026 having won in Dubai and also lifted the trophy in Charleston.Elsewhere,Serena Williamsand Carlos Alcaraz will team up in the revamped US Open mixed doubles tournament. The US Open will mark Alcaraz’s first tournament back after a serious wrist injury that sidelined the 23-year-old for four months, while the 44-year-old Williams returned to professional tennis this summer after being retired for four years.After her singles return at Wimbledon, where she lost in three sets in the first round to Maya Joint and sustained a knee injury, Williams will not compete in singles at the US Open. She is likely to compete in the women’s doubles alongside her sister, Venus, after the pair played together this week in Cincinnati.Explore more on these topicsTennisSerena WilliamsCarlos AlcarazUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I was rooting for Josh’: Pogacar wins Vuelta opening stage with Tarling third | Vuelta a España | The Guardian
description: The Tour de France champion held off Ethan Hayter to win the Monaco time trial, but had hoped Josh Tarling could earn an emotional victory
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The Tour de France champion held off Ethan Hayter to win the Monaco time trial, but had hoped Josh Tarling could earn an emotional victory
Content: Tadej Pogacar is chasing a Vuelta a España overall victory that would complete his Grand Tour treble.Photograph: Philippe Magoni/APView image in fullscreenTadej Pogacar is chasing a Vuelta a España overall victory that would complete his Grand Tour treble.Photograph: Philippe Magoni/APVuelta a España‘I was rooting for Josh’: Pogacar wins Vuelta opening stage with Tarling thirdPogacar edges out Ethan Hayter in Monaco time trialJosh Tarling third a week after death of brother FinlayAFPSat 22 Aug 2026 14.27 EDTLast modified on Sat 22 Aug 2026 19.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTadej Pogacar stormed to victory in the individual time trial to claim the leader’s red jersey after the first stage of theVuelta a Españaon Saturday.The overwhelming favourite,aiming to complete a career Grand Tour treble, completed the 9.4km ride just 0.09 seconds faster than Britain’s Ethan Hayter.Wiebes wins Tour of Britain Women stage four as Le Court maintains overall leadRead moreJoshua Tarling finished third, four seconds behind the top two, to complete the podium a week after his younger brother,Finlay, died in a road accidentwhile racing in the Tour of Portugal.Pogacar clocked 10min 57sec for the short and technical course through the streets of Monaco, where he now lives, in the opening stage of the 81st edition of the Vuelta. Pogacar, who won theTour de France for the fifth timelast month andtriumphed in the Giro d’Italia in 2024, is expected to finish in the red jersey in Granada on 13 September.“It’s a weird feeling to win the time trial on the first stage and by such a small margin,” said Pogacar. “I was not expecting it. I’m really happy. This red is a really nice colour.”The Slovenian said home advantage was the key to his victory. “That 0.09 happened when I passed my apartment because that was the most technical part, and I walk and cycle there every day.”View image in fullscreenJoshua Tarling finished in third place a week after his brother Finlay died during the Tour of Portugal.Photograph: Miguel Medina/AFP/Getty ImagesPogacar said he had been hoping Tarling could win the stage after his brother’s death. “When I was going to the start line I saw that Josh had the best time. I was really wishing he would win today. I was going to give my best, but it was a strange moment, I was really rooting for Josh as well.“Then I came to the intermediate point and I hear a different name. I hear Ethan Hayter is in front of me by three seconds. So I thought: I will give it everything, but no risks – I’ll see what happens.”A Vuelta victory would make Pogacar the fourth rider to complete the Tour-Vuelta double in the same season, while only eight riders have won all three Grand Tours. His compatriot, Primoz Roglic, is chasing a record-equalling fifth Vuelta victory, but came in 24th.Tarling (Netcompany Ineos) had been among the leading contenders for the opening stage, on a route designed to favour specialists, and moved into the lead before Hayter (Soudal Quick-Step) and Pogacar (UAE Team Emirates) usurped him.The race continues on Sunday with a gruelling 214.3km stage from Monaco to Manosque in France. Monday’s stage runs 174km from Gruissan to Aude in southern France, with stage four taking place in Andorra before the race returns to Spain.Explore more on these topicsVuelta a EspañaTadej PogacarCyclingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Jordan double stuns South Africa as New Zealand clinch statement victory | Rugby union | The Guardian
description: Will Jordan scored twice for the All Blacks in their dominant 33-16 victory in South Africa as the world champions lost the opening match of their series
Author: Gerard Meagher
Headline: Will Jordan scored twice for the All Blacks in their dominant 33-16 victory in South Africa as the world champions lost the opening match of their series
Content: Will Jordan continued his stunning scoring rate with two tries in New Zealand’s impressive win against South Africa.Photograph: Gianluigi Guercia/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWill Jordan continued his stunning scoring rate with two tries in New Zealand’s impressive win against South Africa.Photograph: Gianluigi Guercia/AFP/Getty ImagesRugby unionJordan double stuns South Africa as New Zealand clinch statement victoryFirst Test: South Africa 16-33 New ZealandAll Blacks score five tries against world championsGerard MeagherSat 22 Aug 2026 13.28 EDTLast modified on Sat 22 Aug 2026 16.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs first courses go, this was a delicious appetiser to a series that looks set to live up to its billing. First blood goes to New Zealand, who withstood a barrage of South Africa scrum pressure and demonstrated a slicknessthe double world championscould not live with, clinching a first win at Ellis Park since 2022.It wasn’t a classic, but a statement victory by the All Blacks to which South Africa must respond in the coming weeks. By the end, South Africa had two men in the sin-bin and, given their status as the world’s leading side, this must go down as a disintegration. There will be a backlash – it is hard to remember a time when South Africa were so inaccurate with the ball in hand – but credit New Zealand for producing a masterclass at weathering the storm and taking their chances. It is 30 years since Sean Fitzpatrick led the All Blacks to a first series victory in South Africa, but the class of 2026 are off to a flying start.South Africa 16-33 New Zealand: rugby union first Test – as it happenedRead moreThe All Blacks chalked up five tries to South Africa’s one and they were even calling for scrums late in the second half, having found parity to nullify the Springboks’ only threat on the day. The last meeting between these sidesin Wellington ended 43-10in South Africa’s favour. This was some revenge mission.South Africa, for their part, may wonder how New Zealand kept 15 men on the field during a period of sustained pressure near their line early in the second half. Their profligacy in the New Zealand 22 should be of more concern to Rassie Erasmus and his assistant coaches, however.The pre-match verbals had all centred around speed. New Zealand wanted a fast-paced game, South Africa supposedly wanted to slow it down. It matters little what tempo you play at if you cannot catch the ball.Quick GuideSouth Africa 16-33 New Zealand: teams and scorersShowSouth AfricaWillemse; Kolbe (Reinach 57), Kriel, De Allende; Arendse (Esterhuizen 10; Libbok 62); Feinberg-Mngomezulu, Williams; Nche (Steenekamp 46; Wessels 67), Marx, Louw (Porten 60, Etzebeth, Nortje, De Villiers (Van Staden 61), Du Toit (capt), J WieseTriesEsterhuizenConsKolbe Pens Kolbe 2Sin-binVan Staden 70, Reinach 70New ZealandMcKenzie, Jordan, Tupaea (Lienert-Brown 75), J Barrett; Moorby (Carter 63); Love, Roigard (Preston 75); De Groot (Bower 38), Taylor (Aumua 54), Lomax (Newell 50), Lord (Parker 38), Holland, Vaa’i, Jacobson (Lakai 75), Savea (capt)TriesJordan 2, Moorby, Holland, JacobsonConsLove 4Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Three of New Zealand’s five tries came in the right corner – targeting the scrum-half Grant Williams’ position was clearly a pre-planned strategy – but this was a victory founded on defensive courage. South Africa’s handling was woeful, but their powerful runners, led by the No 8, Jasper Wiese, and their ruthless scrum gave them a platform in the middle 40 minutes of the game that would have been enough to brush aside most teams. That New Zealand survived before ruthlessly taking their chances is some feather in the cap for Dave Rennie’s side.It was a stop-start first half – injuries and ill-discipline ensuring the whistle was rarely far from the lips of the referee, Matt Carley. New Zealand were the first to cross the tryline – Will Jordan continuing his stunning scoring rate by finishing in the right corner past Williams. Cheslin Kolbe had kicked South Africa into a 3-0 lead and the Boks were in front again when André Esterhuizen – on after 10 minutes for the injured Kurt-Lee Arendse – powered through Josh Moorby all too easily to score.Moorby atoned with a sharp finish, gathering a delightful offload from Tupou Vaa’i at the second attempt for New Zealand’s second try, but another Kolbe penalty edged the Springboks back in front on 26 minutes.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe BreakdownThe latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenWill Jordan dives over to score one of his two tries for the All Blacks.Photograph: Kim Ludbrook/EPASouth Africa turned the screw thereafter, but wasted three visits to the All Blacks’ 22 – Malcolm Marx the most culpable when knocking on just short of the line, though credit to Jordie Barrett, who did remarkably well to force the error.The second half began in a similar vein and Kolbe further extended South Africa’s lead with another penalty, awarded for further scrum dominance, but the Springboks scrum-half was charged down by Fabian Holland at the restart and the Dutch-born New Zealand lock had the simplest of scores.South Africa responded with another scrum barragebut their inaccuracy in the New Zealand 22 again let them down and Carley awarded a scrum penalty to the All Blacks on their own line, immediately alleviating the pressure It typified their heart shown and soon after Luke Jacobson was over from close range – territory brought about after a scything run down the middle from Damian McKenzie. Ruben Love converted for a 10-point lead.The Springboks were desperate by this stage, unable to get on the right side of Carley, and the humiliation was complete when the replacements Marco van Staden and Cobus Reinach were sent to the sin-bin for infringing near their own line in quick succession. Jordan’s second, again out on the right, put the exclamation mark on a thoroughly deserved victory.Explore more on these topicsRugby unionSouth Africa rugby teamNew Zealand rugby union teammatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Women’s Super League 2026-27 preview No 2: Aston Villa  | Aston Villa Women | The Guardian
description: Defensive tightness and replacing a key goal scorer are Natalia Arroyo’s focus in her second season in charge
Author: Sophie Downey
Headline: Defensive tightness and replacing a key goal scorer are Natalia Arroyo’s focus in her second season in charge
Content: Natalia Arroyo has built a squad that suits her direct style of play. Photograph: AVFC/Getty ImagesDefensive tightness and replacing a key goal scorer are Natalia Arroyo’s focus in her second season in chargeBySophie DowneySat 22 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Sat 22 Aug 2026 19.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGuardian writers’ predicted position:9th (NB: this is not necessarily Sophie Downey’s prediction but the average of our writers’ tips)Last season’s position:9thProspectsLast season was a frustrating one for Aston Villa and a ninth-place finish will have been disappointing for the club and fans. Nevertheless, under Natalia Arroyo, there has always been something about Villa that catches the eye – a work in progress that is full of youthful exuberance, far from the finished product yet clearly full of potential. It is that promise that means there will again be considerable excitement going into Arroyo’s second season in charge.Aston Villa’s Rachel Daly: ‘It’s given me more of a focus: club football is my one job’Read moreIt has been a summer of change that has allowed the Spaniard to continue to rebuild the team in her image, one that will suit the distinct brand of direct football she favours. Several stalwarts have moved on, with Sarah Mayling, Sabrina D’Angelo and Ebony Salmon departing and Lucy Staniforth retiring. Young talents such as Akane Okuma, Kamilla Melgård and Mia McAulay have been recruited, while England Under-20 international Lily Murphy has come in on loan.The big blow for Arroyo will have been the departure of Kirsty Hanson. The 28-year-old was responsible for almost 43% of Villa’s goals last season and figuring out how to replace that output will be the head coach’s biggest task. The return ofRachel Dalyto full fitness is a boost while the experience of Amalie Vangsgaard is a useful acquisition. Defensively is where the biggest questions continue to lie. Villa possessed the second-leakiest backline in the division last season – they will need to tighten up to have any hope of moving up the table.InteractiveOff-field pictureVilla’s work away from the pitch continues to grow, with the women’s team operating as an independent entity. The managing director, Maggie Murphy, said that reconnecting with the fanbase has been at the forefront of the club’s efforts and that has been evident. Last season brought collaborations with Level Playing Field, an International Women’s Day event and a women’s clothing range launched with AFTA Studios. Saathi House, a foundation working to empower women, young people and migrant communities in Birmingham, featured on the front of the shirt during the World Sevens Tournament.The managerArroyo’s first 18 months in the Women’s Super League have been full of ups and downs, but there is no doubt the charismatic head coach brings something different. She is a constant bundle of energy, living every moment in her technical area. Arroyo has a clear vision for what she wants and her direct style of in-possession play, using pacy forwards to attack the spaces behind the opposition, has been well-defined. She is unafraid to put her faith in young players, illustrated by the emergence of Lucia Kendall and Rachel Maltby last season.Star signingThe arrival of Mathilde Harviken is a strong solution to Villa’s defensive woes given the Norway centre-back’s front-foot approach to defending and good distribution. Despite being only 24, she brings with her a wealth of experience. She signed from Juventus, where she made close to 50 appearances and lifted the Serie A title in 2024-2025. Harviken has represented her country since the age of 20, featuring at the 2023 World Cup and 2025 Euros.View image in fullscreenMathilde Harviken has made 44 appearances for Norway.Photograph: Vitalii Kliuiev/Getty ImagesStat attackVilla have work to do defensively. While only five teams scored more WSL goals last season, relegated Leicester were the only side with a worse defensive record. The penalty area appears to be the problem; 75.9% of the shots Villa conceded were in the area, against a division-wide average of 68.6%. Their league-worst rate helps to explain why they allowed more goals from within their penalty area than Leicester.GraphSet for a breakthroughAged 20, Melgård is among a crop of young talents that have emerged from Norway in the past few years. She joins Villa after two years in Liga F with Madrid CFF. A versatile midfielder, Melgård can play in the centre or on the wing and has an eye for goal, as shown in Villa’s recent friendly against Paris FC. She has represented Norway from under-16 level and is now part of their under-23 contingent.What they say …“You can feel that we are building an honest team, a hard-working team, players that are committed to the idea, they understand that we are facing an important year for us,” – Arroyo.Where are they playing their home games?Villa Park remains home for all WSL fixtures, while Hednesford’s Keys Park Stadium will host cup games. There has been plenty of initiatives around ticketing for Villa Park this summer, with prices frozen, a new 18-25 category, a new four-match bundle offer and the return of the 82 Champions Club hospitality. Drinks, alcoholic and non-alcoholic, will continue to be allowed inside the stadium, with an alcohol-free zone established.Explore more on these topicsWSL season previews 2026-27Aston Villa WomenWomen's Super LeagueWomen's footballfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Lando Norris surges past Russell and Antonelli to snatch Dutch GP pole | Formula One 2026 | The Guardian
description: Lando Norris came back at the last to seal pole position at the Dutch Grand Prix, with George Russell finishing second and Kimi Antonelli third
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: Lando Norris came back at the last to seal pole position at the Dutch Grand Prix, with George Russell finishing second and Kimi Antonelli third
Content: Lando Norris claimed pole position for the second grand prix in succession.Photograph: Jakub Porzycki/ReutersView image in fullscreenLando Norris claimed pole position for the second grand prix in succession.Photograph: Jakub Porzycki/ReutersFormula One 2026Lando Norris surges past Russell and Antonelli to snatch Dutch GP poleNorris outperforms Mercedes pair against the oddsGeorge Russell wins the sprint race convincinglyGiles Richardsat ZandvoortSat 22 Aug 2026 11.42 EDTLast modified on Sat 22 Aug 2026 16.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhat a title fight Formula One would have on its hands if McLaren could make the final steps with their car. This was demonstrated to dramatic effect on Saturday asLando Norrishurled his ride around Zandvoort to claim pole position for the Dutch Grand Prix. It was a prize secured against the odds and his own expectations, hours after he had bemoaned being in no position to fulfil his hopes of mounting a successful title defence.The McLaren car is immensely quick through the fast corners, perhaps the class of the field, but is haemorrhaging time through the slow stuff, the package not quite complete, or suboptimal as Ron Dennis would have had it. Yet Norris managed to eke out its very best across the circuit to see off the Mercedes of George Russell and Kimi Antonelli into second and third place. The season’s dominant car was subdued by Norris in qualifying for the second race in succession, after hetook pole in Hungary.Formula One 2026: Lando Norris takes pole for Dutch GP after George Russell wins sprint race – liveRead moreEarlier in the day the defending world champion was disgruntled at best with his ride. Russell had won the sprint race with a controlled dominance from pole position, but Norris had gone from second to third, struggling for grip and pace, passed late on by Charles Leclerc. His assessment was blunt.“We don’t have the pace in general, slow-speed corners we struggle so much compared to others. There is nothing we can do,” he said. “The upgrades have all worked and they allowed me to be P3 today, but we need more if we want to be fighting for a championship.”A turnaround had not been expected, but with fresh tyres and low fuel theMcLarenwas a less recalcitrant beast and Norris delivered a mighty lap in the final runs to see off Russell and Antonelli by a tenth of a second.“Our biggest losses were still the same places, the same corners, as it was this morning,” he said. “It’s just new tyres, low fuel. It just seems to mask quite a few of our issues and that was probably still the case today. I just drove well, I put a lot of things together.”Which sets up an intriguing prospect for Sunday’s race. With tyre wear and fat with fuel he will have to fight hard to keep the two Mercedes behind him.Quick GuideDutch F1 qualifyingShow1Lando Norris🇬🇧McLaren1:11.1632George Russell🇬🇧Mercedes1:11.2653Kimi Antonelli🇮🇹Mercedes1:11.2964Oscar Piastri🇦🇺McLaren1:11.3055Lewis Hamilton🇬🇧Ferrari1:11.4946Charles Leclerc🇲🇨Ferrari1:11.5587Max Verstappen🇳🇱Red Bull1:11.6188Liam Lawson🇫🇷Red Bull1:11.7339Gabriel Bortoleto🇧🇷Audi1:12.07910Arvid Lindblad🇬🇧Racing Bulls1:12.185Q2 eliminations11Pierre Gasly🇫🇷Alpine1:12.61612Yuki Tsunoda🇯🇵Racing Bulls1:12.62713Nico Hülkenberg🇩🇪Audi1:12.79714Franco Colapinto🇦🇷Alpine1:12.80015Esteban Ocon🇫🇷Haas1:13.13716Alexander Albon🇹🇭Williams1:13.182Q1 eliminations17Carlos Sainz🇪🇸Williams1:13.57418Fernando Alonso🇪🇸Aston Martin1:13.65019Lance Stroll🇨🇦Aston Martin1:13.81820Oliver Bearman🇬🇧Haas1:13.82621Valtteri Bottas🇫🇮Cadillac1:14.37122Sergio Pérez🇲🇽Cadillac1:14.600Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.With Russell’s sprint victory and Antonelli only fourth, the Briton trails his teammate by 56 points, in third place in the championship. Lewis Hamilton is 53 points back in second and Norris 90 points in arrears.Most notable is how much more comfortable Russell has looked in the car this weekend, after struggling with problems around its energy deployment that had left him frustrated and examining his driving style. Having said he intended to drive more instinctively here he came into the weekend confident, took pole and then victory in the sprint race. While he was beaten to pole in qualifying, Russell was quicker than his teammate.Certainly he appeared to be enjoying himself once more. “I just feel way more relaxed. I don’t feel like I’ve got anything to lose. The pressure’s off,” he said. “I’m just going to go out and enjoy it. I don’t even really feel in a fight. It’s not mine to lose. It’s mine to gain. So that’s the mentality I’ve got, I feel it’s going to help me, I’m just enjoying driving.”View image in fullscreenLando Norris secured his second pole at the Dutch GP and the 18th of his career.Photograph: Clive Rose/Getty ImagesNorris went on to win from pole in Hungary and with Piastri taking the win here last year and Norris in 2024, McLaren may still make it three in a row, which would be a testament to their impressive work. Their car development has been ferocious and most importantly effective, including another swathe of developments brought here, fulfilling the expectations of the team principal, Andrea Stella, whose calm assurance at the helm has once more been a striking piece of management as the team adjusted to the new regulations.All of which may yet shake down into a tense title fight and the teenager Antonelli was aware his rivals were watching closely to see how he handles it, a task which comes with the territory. “It was a very good wake-up call this weekend, that you can never lower your guard,” he said. “When you do that, I made a mistake yesterday and today I made a mistake in Q3.“It’s not that I’m driving more tense or anything but I feel this weekend is a good wake-up call to just put things in the right place at the right time and deliver the result when it counts.”It all sets the scene for a showdown beside the North Sea on Sunday.Explore more on these topicsFormula One 2026Formula OneMotor sportGeorge RussellLando NorrisMercedes GPMcLarennewsShareReuse this content

title: Drinks are on Daiquiri Bay at York after Ebor win: horse racing – as it happened | Sport | The Guardian
description: Alan King was ‘blown away’ after Daiquiri Bay’s fast finish delivered a memorable victory in Europe’s richest handicap
Author: Greg Wood
Headline: Alan King was ‘blown away’ after Daiquiri Bay’s fast finish delivered a memorable victory in Europe’s richest handicap
