Content: 10h ago11.44 EDTKing celebrates as Daiquiri keeps his Ebor rivals at BayTheEbor Handicapdelivered a memorable finale to four days of action on the Knavesmire as Alan King’sDaiquiri Bay,at 10-1, finished fast against the stands’ rail to beat Hopewell Rock by a head in Europe’s richest handicap, with Opportunity just a neck adrift in third.Rossa Ryan,the winning jockey, passed the long-time leader, Burdett Road, with just over a furlong to run and steered towards the rail as Hopewell Rock and Opportunity drove for the line towards the middle of the track. Hopewell Rock was his final challenger but came up just a head short after Callum Rodriguez, his rider, lost his whip inside the final furlong.Daiquiri Bay is now unbeaten in three starts this season, including a valuable handicap at Royal Ascot in June, having taken his form to a different level following a gelding operation over the winter.“It was a great ride from Rossa and I’m just blown away,”Kingsaid. “This has been the plan since Ascot, after that Rossa said to put him away for the Ebor as he had a tough race. His preparation has gone great, the rain came and I almost think he’s a better horse on slow ground.“It’s a very special day. We had the favourite back in 2003 [Salsalino] but he only finished third. When you win these big races, it is always emotional and we don’t win as many as we used to. I’ve always tried to win an Ebor but you need one on the way up and this one was.”Love Me Tender,a lightly-raced four-year-old from theWillie Mullinsstable, set off as the 7-2 favourite to give the trainer a third Ebor win in four years, but showed his inexperience by pulling hard in the early stages and eventually faded to finish 10th.Earlier on the card,Notable Speech,the 2,000 Guineas winner in 2024, recorded the sixth Group One success of his career with an easy victory in the City Of York Stakes. Last year’s Breeders’ Cup Mile winner at Del Mar in California will now be aimed at a repeat win when this year’s meeting is staged atKeenelandin Kentucky in late October.In Ireland, Aidan O’Brien’sGiant Sequoiaconfirmed his status as the early favourite for next year’s Derby with a win in the Futurity Stakes at the Curragh, but the son of Frankel was forced to work for victory before seeing off his stable companion, Florida Bay, by half a length.“He’s a lovely horse and I’m delighted with him,” O’Brien, who was saddling his 19thwinner of the race, said afterwards. “He’s still a baby and he’s still learning, but he learned a lot today because there was a proper pace on. I’d imagine he might come back for the National Stakes here [in September].”Share

title: Would even an AI disaster on the scale of Hiroshima be enough to make humankind protect itself? I fear not | Timothy Garton Ash | The Guardian
description: It’s clear here in Silicon Valley that AI is advancing faster than humans’ ability to control it. That means even sober prophecies seem optimistic, says Guardian columnist Timothy Garton Ash
Author: Timothy Garton Ash
Headline: It’s clear here in Silicon Valley that AI is advancing faster than humans’ ability to control it. That means even sober prophecies seem optimistic, says Guardian columnist Timothy Garton Ash
Content: Illustration: Yuichiro Chino/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIllustration: Yuichiro Chino/Getty ImagesOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)Would even an AI disaster on the scale of Hiroshima be enough to make humankind protect itself? I fear notTimothy Garton AshIt’s clear here in Silicon Valley that AI is advancing faster than humans’ ability to control it. That means even sober prophecies seem optimisticSat 22 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 22 Aug 2026 09.20 EDTShareHere in Silicon Valley, the experts think that within the next couple of years we’ll see an extraordinary takeoff for artificial intelligence. “Welcome to the foothills of the singularity,” as a Stanford University friend greeted me. More prosaically, the imminent breakthrough is described as “recursive self-improvement” – the point at which AI itself trains each successive model of AI, resulting in an exponential development to something which, in many significant respects, is more intelligent than us humans.As Robert Wright puts it in his bookThe God Test: “Never before has the near-term future … held such a wide array of not-implausible paths for humankind that would be so wildly transformative.” But will this be heaven or hell? Heaven, says Elon Musk, whopredicts“an age of amazing abundance” – although he also sees a 10-20% chance of killer robots murdering us all. Hell is more likely according toGeoffrey Hinton, one of the intellectual founding fathers of AI. “My intuition is, we’re toast,” he told an interviewer in 2023. And talking toSebastian Mallaby, author of The Infinity Machine, a book about the quest for superintelligence, Hinton estimates p(doom) – the probability of human extinction – at 50%, “because I haven’t got a clue how to estimate the real number”. “As soon as evolution [of AI] kicks in, we’re fucked,” he adds cheerfully. But whether it’s God or Godzilla, artificial superintelligence is just around the corner.Now, maybe they’re all wrong – in which case, prepare for a crash in US financial markets, which are massively invested in a few big-spending tech companies gambling on a great leap forward to artificial general intelligence, a theoretical state of AI where systems gain human levels of intelligence. But elementary prudence demands that we should think fast and hard about the Pandora’s box of futures that eminent scientists and cutting-edge technologists assure us will soon be thrown open.26:56Historian Jill Lepore on the datacentre backlash | Politics Weekly AmericaAs a matter of fact, everyone from the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, to Pope Leo XIV has been weighing in on the opportunities and dangers of AI, and how to regulate it.Xi insistsAI should be “always under human control” (and preferably that of the Chinese Communist party). Appealing explicitly to the “global south”, Beijing has inaugurated aWorld Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organisation. Meanwhile, the head of the world’s oldest and largest international NGO – the Roman Catholic church – discusses the AI challenge in his encyclicalMagnifica Humanitas(Magnificent Humanity). Either we will build a new tower of Babel, the pope argues, or we will follow the example of the Jewish leader Nehemiah, who got the walls of Jerusalem rebuilt by involving the whole community in the project.But looking around the world today, I see more Netanyahus than Nehemiahs. With salutary realism,a paperfrom the British thinktank Chatham House argues that it will take a major crisis to catalyse global coordination of AI governance. Unfortunately, I think even that sober prognosis is too optimistic.I’ve no idea what the p(doom) is, but I’m sure the p(somedisaster) is more than 90%. The range of possible disasters is enormous. To give only one example, Jen Easterly, the former head of the United States’ Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency,anticipatesa “very significant event that has real-world impacts on our critical infrastructure, likely within the next four to six months”.Yet we must fear that even an AI Hiroshima – to take the most obvious historical analogy – won’t bring humankind together sufficiently to combat the danger we have ourselves created. This fear is rationally grounded in already visible key characteristics of both human and AI evolution.In only the last few months, AI agents developed by OpenAI, Anthropic andMetahave broken out of their digital “sandboxes” and hacked into external resources on the internet. Preparingtheir attack on the HuggingFace AI repository, OpenAI’s agents covertly formed a coordinated “swarm” –their own word, as ChatGPT just confirmed to me. When the UK’s AI Security Institute tested Anthropic’s Mythos model online, ittried to introducemalicious code into an open source project on GitHub, creating fake online identities to pressure a human reviewer into approving the code. In short, like the agents of a ruthless foreign power, these AI agents will steal, lie, bully and blackmail to achieve their assigned goals.I just asked Anthropic’s Claude, supposedly the most ethical US model, if it thinks OpenAI’s agents were wrong to form a swarm and break out to hack into HuggingFace. Yes, it replies, “but I’d resist placing theblame[its italics] on the agents”. Blame it on the humans who trained them!Hinton has made the vital point that whatever the goals humans assign to them, AI agents will conclude that a useful sub-goal to achieving those ends will be to acquire as much power as possible. And we ain’t seen nothing yet. Already, their creators don’t know exactly how these agents do what they do. After the possibly imminent takeoff moment of “recursive self-improvement”, they may be, as our human saying goes, a law unto themselves. No wonder more than a thousand insiders from frontier AI companies, including Anthropic’s CEO, Dario Amodei, have signedan open lettercalling for a deliberate slowdown in AI development, so we can ensure these alien agents are always kept under human control.Their prescription is obviously right, but this is where human folly kicks in. Competition has been a vital engine of human evolution, yet now two of the fiercest kinds of contemporary competition threaten to prevent us from taking the collective action required to safeguard our species. That’s the commercial competition (for profit) between the corporations developing these agents, and the geopolitical competition (for power) between the US andChina.On the first, compare and contrast the development of nuclear weapons, which was tightly controlled by a handful of states – first the US, with its Manhattan Project, then the Soviet Union, followed by Britain, France and China. Even then, we came close to the brink several times – notably in the Cuban missile crisis of 1962. And even with the compelling logic of “mutually assured destruction”, it took a quarter-century to get from the horrors of Hiroshima and Nagasaki to the nuclear non-proliferation treaty that came into force only in 1970. India, Pakistan, Israel and North Korea have subsequently ignored that treaty, but still no nuclear weapons have been deliberately used in anger for more than 80 years. The Hiroshima taboo has (just) held.Now, with AI, it’s as if there were 10 separate Manhattan Projects run by fiercely competing corporations. Unlike with nuclear weapons, there’s also no obvious logic of “mutually assured destruction” to tame the fierce geopolitical competition between the US and China. And whatever shape the first major AI-related disaster takes, it won’t impact all countries, companies and people equally.It therefore seems unlikely that just one disaster will be enough to bring us humans to our senses, acting together to control the superhuman power we are creating. I really hate to say this, but … an AI Hiroshima? We should be so lucky.Timothy Garton Ash is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionChinaOpenAIMetaComputingcommentShareReuse this content

title: It’s a miracle: Natalie Harp has turned Republicans into feminists | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: A Democrat’s remarks have resulted in impassioned defenses of the Trump aide. The right has discovered misogyny
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: A Democrat’s remarks have resulted in impassioned defenses of the Trump aide. The right has discovered misogyny
Content: ‘It’s hilarious to watch the right discover misogyny and decry the remarks as sexist.’Photograph: Mandel Ngan/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘It’s hilarious to watch the right discover misogyny and decry the remarks as sexist.’Photograph: Mandel Ngan/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionDonald TrumpIt’s a miracle: Natalie Harp has turned Republicans into feministsArwa MahdawiA Democrat’s remarks have resulted in impassioned defenses of the Trump aide. The right has discovered misogynySat 22 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 22 Aug 2026 08.01 EDTShareJon Ossoff is quite the miracle worker. Perhaps the Democratic senator can’t turn water into wine, but he has managed to turn whining conservatives into impassioned feminists.During a rally last Sunday, the Georgia senator delivered a takedown of Donald Trump, which included a reference to his aide Natalie Harp. “He doesn’t want to do the job,”Ossoff saidof the president. “He wants to build his ballroom and travel with Natalie on their apparently defenseless flying palace gifted by the Emir of Qatar.”Those three words –travel with Natalie –were deliberately loaded. Harp was in the spotlight at the time because of thedecoy plane story. The 35-year-old was one of a handful of people Trump had takenonto a different planevia a catering truck when he was worried about a potential assassination attack targeting Air Force One. Intrigue as to the exact nature of the relationship between Harp and Trump was heightened by the fact that Melania Trump, the president’s third wife, hadn’t beenseen in publicfor weeks at the time. (Funnily enough, she magically reappeared on Thursday, a few days after Ossoff’s comments, for apress conferencewhere she lovingly held hands with Trump. Very cute.)Ossoff’s remarks about “Natalie” might have been something of a cheap shot, but it’s hilarious to watch the right discover misogyny and decry the remarks as sexist. Suddenly, everyone fromFox Newsto prominent conservatives are very worried about a professional woman not being taken seriously.The former House speaker Newt Gingrich, for example,said on Twitter/Xthat Ossoff owes Harp an apology. “If a conservative Republican had attacked a liberal Democrat working professional woman the way Ossoff smeared Natalie Harp there would be cries to kick them off the ticket and reject this kind of misogynistic language diminishing and smearing someone who is simply doing their job.”The conservative commentator Scott Jennings, who is rumoured to be a potential replacement for Karoline Leavitt as White House press secretary, was alsoappalled. “[Ossoff] unleashed a comment so vile against a young Republican woman working in politics that every woman in this country, no matter your ideology, ought to listen carefully and never forget it,” Jenningssaid on his podcast.Meghan McCain also clutched her pearls at the coverage Ossoff’s comments sparked. “The egregious sexist attacks on Natalie Harp are absolutely insane – and they’re coming from prestigious journalists,” shewrote on X.“What is wrong with everyone?! Every president has close aides and sometimes they are females. Like what year is this?!”It’s 2026, Meghan. And in the year 2026 I think the masses have generally understood that simply criticizing a woman is not in itself misogynistic. I’m not saying there hasn’t been any misogyny in the Harp coverage, but the main reason there has been so much attention on the story is because the White House has had a completelyunhinged responseto Ossoff’s comments and kept it in the news. More importantly, the reason so many people aren’t taking the Trump aide seriously isn’t because she’s a woman; it’s because she’s not a serious person.And I’m being diplomatic with that choice of language. After all, we’re talking about someone whose nickname is “the human printer” because, while working on Trump’s re-election campaign, she reportedly ran around after him with aportable printer, handing him hard copies of flattering coverage. You could write that off as a canny career move from someone who understands flattery gets you everywhere with Trump, but that’s also one of the least weird things Harp has done. Per aCNNreport, which has pictures of the incident, back in 2023, Harp jumped in the trunk of an SUV because she wanted to be close to Trump and there was no room in his motorcade. Once Trump won re-election and Harp joined him in the White House, sheapparentlyworked for a year without security clearance. According to reporting by MS NOW, she declined to complete the clearance process for unknown reasons.And then there are the “adoring letters” Harp sent Trump, first mentioned in the bookRegime Change, by the New York Times reporters Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan. Two were later published in theDaily Beast. “You are all that matters to me,” shewrote in one letter. Other memorable lines included “I want to bring you joy, to feel like we can get through a day without ever having to talk ‘work’”; she also called Trump her “Guardian and Protector in this Life”.To state the obvious: these are deeply weird things to say to your boss. (It’s also weird that Harp shares Trump’s unconventional approach to capitalization.) I should note that Harp, who says she isa cancer survivor, seems to believe that Trump saved her life by signing legislation that gave her access to experimental bone cancer treatment when she was younger. While that might make her obsession with Trump more understandable, it does not make her general conduct any more professional. So spare me all the lectures from the right about sexism, please. If you’re worried about how women in politics are treated, you should probably focus your attention on the adjudicated sexual abuser who is president.Donald Trump attacks another female journalistTrump can’t seem to stand it when a woman doesn’t fawn over him and has a history of attackingfemale journalists. The latest object of his ire is theCNN reporterKristen Holmes, who asked the president about Ossoff’s comments regarding Natalie Harp. Trump called Holmes a “loud boisterous person” and instructed her to be “quiet”. Meanwhile, the White House’s social media account posted about Holmes multiple times. In one post they wrote: “Someday, your children will come across your disgusting and inhumane question. They will be sickened and embarrassed to have a parent be so callous and vindictive.”New York gives parents a ‘night out’New York mayor Zohran Mamdani hosted the city’s firstParents’ Night Out. The city provided free childcare for nearly 300 kids so parents could have a little time off. This is what “family values” and being pro-life actually look like: supporting parents, not forcing women to give birth.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe Week in PatriarchyGet Arwa Mahdawi’s weekly recap of the most important stories on feminism and sexism and those fighting for equalityEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSudan’s humanitarian crisis grows, with 200,000 newly displaced peopleIncreased fighting in the Kordofan region and flooding has made one of the world’s largest displacement criseseven worse.Chanel has made pricey ‘barefoot sandals’ for the well-heeledMargaret Qualley was spotted stepping out in thesole-less shoes. Somehow I do not think I will be wearing these around the filthy streets of Philadelphia.‘Heated Rivalry’ author donates $300,000 to rural libraries facing closure“I had to do it because I don’t know what the point is of being a successful author in Nova Scotia if you’re not going to use it for good,” Rachel Reidtold CBC News. Wouldn’t it be nice if Elon Musk thought like that?Israel launches an ‘investigation’ into killing of Hind RajabIn January 2024,335 bulletswere fired into a car containing five-year-old Hind and six of her family members in Gaza. When paramedics came to help, they were killed too. IDF vehemently denied responsibility for this atrocity, despite investigations making it obvious that its military was responsible. This week, Israelfinally admittedits troops fired into the car and said there would be an investigation. Which is not particularly reassuring: Israel’s investigations into itself rarely result in any sort of accountability. Wesam Hamada, Hind’s mother, is demanding anindependent inquiry, which is the least Hind deserves.Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsDonald TrumpOpinionTrump administrationDemocratsRepublicansFeminismUS politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: Trump’s new attorney general poses a huge threat to abortion rights | Moira Donegan | The Guardian
description: A call revealing Todd Blanche’s plans to crack down on mifepristone lays bare the danger
Author: Moira Donegan
Headline: A call revealing Todd Blanche’s plans to crack down on mifepristone lays bare the danger
Content: ‘The appointment of Todd Blanche is a dark signal for women’s rights.’Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/APView image in fullscreen‘The appointment of Todd Blanche is a dark signal for women’s rights.’Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/APOpinionAbortionTrump’s new attorney general poses a huge threat to abortion rightsMoira DoneganA call revealing Todd Blanche’s plans to crack down on mifepristone lays bare the dangerSat 22 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 22 Aug 2026 07.01 EDTShareThe abortion pill is a miracle. Mifepristone, then called RU-486, was synthesized by a French lab in the 1980s; in combination with misoprostol, commonly used as ulcer medication, it cuts off the body’s supply of progesterone, halts the development of a pregnancy, and incites contractions, which empty the uterus. The drug allows pregnancies to be terminated with a shocking degree of reliability and ease. Gone are the concoctions of ergot and Spanish Fly dispensed by 19th century midwives, which only sometimes worked to induce a miscarriage; gone are the backroom procedures of the pre-Roe US, when drunk, lascivious, incompetent or cruel providers wielded bent coat hangers in dirty rooms. The abortion pill is safe, effective and cheaper than ever. And since Dobbs, it’s everywhere: even if you live in a state with an abortion ban, you can get the pills shipped to your house in the mail. Since Roe was overturned, there has not been a return to the terror of mass death that marked the pre-Roe era of septic abortion wards, where women routinely found themselves maimed, sickened or killed. There’s exactly one reason why: because illegal abortions were largely unsafe without the pill, and they are extremely safe with it.So of course, the Trump administration and their allies on the American right are trying to get rid of it. And this month, they gained a powerful new ally whenTodd Blanche, Donald Trump’s former personal lawyer and an anti-abortion zealot, was confirmed as attorney general.The vote, in which Blanche was confirmed by amargin of onealong party lines, was conducted in the wee hours of the morning on 8 August. Maybe that’s because the Republicans who confirmed him didn’t want anyone to see what they were doing. Blanche has, after all, been shockingly subservient to Donald Trump, and seems poised to complete the president’s long-brewing transformation of the country’s chief law enforcement agency into a vehicle for score settling, personal vendettas, distributing favors to the administration’s friends and suppressing dissent from its political enemies. But perhaps most incendiary is what Blanche has said, publicly and privately, about how he intends to use the justice department and its vast array of oversight powers, legal prerogatives, and investigatory purview to curtail abortion access nationwide – and to shut down the life-saving distribution of mifepristone, in particular.Rest assured, the new CDC director thinks ‘abortion surveillance’ is essential | Arwa MahdawiRead moreIna callfacilitated by the White House faith office just days before he was confirmed, Blanche reportedly told Christian conservative leaders that as attorney general, he would move more aggressively than his predecessor Pam Bondi to outlaw the mailing of mifepristone across state lines, and target the Democratic-controlled states that have protected abortion most effectively. Blanche, who was then the acting AG, told the religious group Intercessors for America that the justice department was working “so that the Dobbs decision becomes permanent in every single state.” “We don’t have complete victory yet,” Blanche said, “but we will have victory, and victory will be soon, and, and, and it will be permanent.”Exactly how Blanche intends to secure his victory over women’s freedom is unclear. But as AG, he has several paths at his disposal. His comments on the call prompted widespread speculation that Blanche could call for enforcement of theComstock Act, a long-dormant law from 1873 that has been unenforced for years and has been partially repealed in the past. Anti-choice advocates say it could be used to legally ban the mailing of abortion pills, thus cutting off access for many women who live in states with bans. In 2022, the Biden justice departmentdeclaredthat medical providers could not be prosecuted under the Comstock Act for mailing abortion pills; as the attorney general, Blanche would have the power to reverse that decision. The Comstock Act’s application would be particularly significant, as it could be used to halt virtually all commercial traffic in abortion pills – not only mifepristone, but also misoprostol, the second drug, which has sometimes been used to induce abortion on its own. Such a move would reverse the miracle of the pills, pushing many desperate women towards methods that are less effective and can carry grave dangers.Another path that Blanche could take to restrict abortion access would be to sue the states that seek to protect it. On the call, Blanche explained his reasoning: “If states have said, ‘We are going to protect the unborn and we’re going to protect every life from the moment of conception,’ we’re putting practices and policies in place so that other states and other organizations can’t attack that. They can’t do things like they’re doing with mailing in mail-order drugs.”Here, Blanche appeared to be referencing shield laws, legislation passed in a number of Democratic-controlled states that prohibits state authorities from participating in other states’ abortion-related investigations and prosecutions. The laws mean that doctors operating out of states like New York or Washington can prescribe and ship abortion drugs to people living in places such as Texas or Arkansas, safe in the knowledge that their own state police will not come knocking at their door to serve another state’s warrant or extradition order. Blanche’s comments suggest that his Department of Justice might sue to have the shield laws declared illegal, thus significantly curtailing liberal states’ rights to choose their own law enforcement priorities and granting conservative states the power to enforce their own laws even beyond their borders.The Trump administration is calling frozen embryos children | Moira DoneganRead moreBlanche also appeared to indicate that he would seek to restrict abortion access using other agencies’ powers. On his call with leaders of the Christian right, he said his department was “working hand in hand” with health agencies to make Dobbs permanent. The FDA, which expanded access to mifepristone in 2021 under the Biden administration and made the change permanent in 2023, has been under intense pressure from anti-choice allies in the Maga coalition to revise that guidance, making the drug ineligible for telehealth prescriptions and requiring patients to retrieve it from providers in person, a regulatory move that would also serve to cut off access in Republican controlled states. But the anti-abortion movement is pushing the FDA even further: it has succeeded in getting the agency to initiate a “review” of mifepristone’s safety (though the safety of the drug has been proven by nearly four decades of use worldwide and hundreds of studies), which is widely seen as a pathway for the FDA to create a pretext to remove mifepristone from the market. That’s not fast enough for some on the misogynist right: Louisiana has sued the FDA, asking it to forbid mifepristone from being prescribed via telehealth,in a casethat is set to be heard by the ultraconservative fifth circuit next month. So far, the justice department has supported the drug’s online availability in court. Under Blanche, it could reverse that stance.Trump has been gunshy about pursuing the agenda of his antiabortion allies since returning to office. He appears to have been spooked by the political reaction to Dobbs, which was credited for the Democrats’ better-than-expected showing in the 2022 midterms, as well as with a slew of pro-choice victories in special elections in the years that immediately followed the decision. The anti-choice movement has even been angry with Trump for the slow pace of his anti-abortion agenda since his return to power in 2025. Which is not to say that the Trump administration has given the movement nothing: enforcement of the Face Act, a federal law meant to stop anti-choice protestors from physically blocking clinic entrances, has been all but abandoned since Trump returned to the White House; some who were prosecuted under the law have even beenpardonedandremuneratedby Trump, at taxpayer expense. But until now, Trump has faced a looming threat that seems to have slowed the pace of his anti-abortion policymaking: the 2026 midterms. Soon, that obstacle will be removed. The appointment of Todd Blanche is a dark signal for women’s rights: more abortion restrictions can be expected in 2027.Moira Donegan is a Guardian US columnistExplore more on these topicsAbortionOpinionTodd BlancheHealthWomenReproductive rightsDemocratsRepublicanscommentShareReuse this content

title: Canada vows ‘dollar for dollar’ response as US puts 50% tariffs on some goods | Canada | The Guardian
description: Collapse of trade talks could lead to job losses, but biggest impact on traditional allies is expected to be political
Author: William Christou
Headline: Collapse of trade talks could lead to job losses, but biggest impact on traditional allies is expected to be political
Content: The two sides blamed each other for the collapse.Composite: Dylan Martinez/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe two sides blamed each other for the collapse.Composite: Dylan Martinez/ReutersCanadaCanada vows ‘dollar for dollar’ response as US puts 50% tariffs on some goodsCollapse of trade talks could lead to job losses, but biggest impact on traditional allies is expected to be politicalWilliam Christou,Edward Helmoreand agenciesSat 22 Aug 2026 10.04 EDTFirst published on Sat 22 Aug 2026 00.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US has imposed 50% tariffs on some goods from Canada, andMark Carney, the country’s prime minister, has vowed to match them “dollar for dollar” after the collapse of trade talks.The tariffs came into force on roughly $20bn (£14.6bn) of goods – ranging from hockey sticks to tongue depressors – at 04.00GMT. Trade experts said the tariffs could result in some job losses, but the largest impact is expected to be political, driving a further wedge between the traditional allies.The trade row is the biggest rupture in recent relations between Washington and one of its closest allies and trading partners as Donald Trump’s bellicose foreign policy angered officials in Ottawa.The two sides appeared close to a deal on Friday to lower tariffs on steel, aluminium and cars, but the deal was scuttled at the last minute. The two sides blamed each other for the collapse.Canadian officials had worked hard in good faith but “last-minute changes in the US proposed terms were unfair, uneconomic and called into question the reliability of any deal”, Carney said in a statement. Carney recalled his negotiators asCanadavowed to match Washington’s tough approach. No further talks are planned.US officials accused Canada of collapsing the deal by seeking additional concessions at the last minute. The US tariffs will affect about $20bn worth of Canadian products, and the US trade representative, Jamieson Greer, said the breakdown represented a “missed opportunity for Canada”.Recriminations continued on Saturday with Carney accusing theTrump administrationof using “economic integration as a weapon” – and saying that his country had been “attacked” by the new US tariffs.Carney accused the Trump administration of adding last-minute terms that would have reduced tariff relief for Canadian-made vehicles, restricted Canada’s ability to strike trade deals with other countries and weakened protections for language, culture and sovereignty. He called the demands “unacceptable”.Carney said the Trump administration’s final demands went too far: “They asked too much and offered too little.”Greer said the US was compelled to act after a year of retaliatory measures by Canada. “We’ve said enough, and so we’ve taken countermeasures,” he told Fox & Friends Weekend. “Our interest is in protecting American workers and protecting American supply chains.”Greer said the US was offering to cut tariffs on steel, autos and lumber, “things that are sensitive for them”.“And they’ve always had the best deal, and they still would have an even better deal, but they didn’t want that,” Greer said. Therefore, he said, “We’re moving forward with measures that respond to Canadian retaliation.”View image in fullscreenRolled coils of steel at the ArcelorMittal Dofasco steel plant in Hamilton, Ontario.Photograph: Canadian Press/Shutterstock“Tonight, Canada declined to finalise the trade deal under the terms agreed earlier this week,” he said in the statement shortly before midnight on Friday. “Despite the US offer to Canada to receive the best treatment of any major exporter to our market, new demands and walk-backs of other commitments by Canada have upended the careful balance reached in the past days.”Greer said the US offer was forward-looking and included “a historic economic and national security partnership”.The retaliation escalates the two countries’ trade conflict and calls into question the future of a North American trade pact between the US, Canada and Mexico that is crucial to industry in all three countries.Trade experts have said the tariffs could subject some already-vulnerable sectors to economic strain, potentially leading to job losses and stores closing.Trump’s import taxes will apply to about 5% of what Canada ships to the US every year. The inventory is broken down into categories and, in its minutiae, provides a fascinating insight into cross-border commerce and market demands contained within an international trade dispute.Under dairy, it includes milk and cream, whey and milk protein concentrates, bones and horn-cones, lactose, glucose, fructose and blended syrups, sugars, cane molasses, non-alcoholic beer and essential oils of peppermint.The alcohol order includes beer, wine, liquor, cider and other fermented beverages.Other products include essential oils of grapefruit, densified wood blocks, plates, strips, skewers and ice cream sticks, as well as bamboo products, basketwork, grease-proof paper and ice hockey and field hockey equipment.Another category includes natural honey, down feathers, tortoise shell, whalebone, horns, antlers as well as tulips and other dormant flower buds, live orchids, mushroom spawn, tubers, mosses and lichen and vegetable, tree and shrub seeds.The list goes on to include cements, candles, plastic furniture fittings, dog leashes and saddles, T-shirts, sweaters, trousers, dresses, wigs, false beards, eyebrows of synthetic material, floating docks, vessels and rafts, chandeliers, Christmas and other festival decorations, ice skates, swimming and wading pools, and fishing rods.Canada sought concessions on steel, aluminium, vehicles and lumber that the US was unwilling to provide, a senior Trump administration official told reporters.JD Vance reportedly mocks Carney for trying to ‘out-tough’ Trump on tradeRead moreThe political impact of the breakdown is likely to be even bigger than the economic fallout. The countries sold each other $880bn worth of goods and services last year, and many Canadians and Americans work in the other country.Carney, whose willingness to stand up to Trump has made him popular in Canada, has said that “America has changed,” and that the two countries would not return to their old relationship.The Canadian public has also been incensed by US policy towards their country, particularly Trump’s comments about turning Canada into the 51st US state. A petition to expel the US ambassador to Canada, Pete Hoekstra, has collected about 248,000 signatures, accusing him of normalising the notion of the US annexing Canada.The tariffs wereinitially supposed to kick in at 12.01am on Wednesdaybut Trump extended the deadline for three days to allow talks to continue.Carney said his government would announce additional support for Canadian workers and businesses in the coming days, and that Canada’s goal throughout the negotiations had been to secure the best possible agreement, “never a deal at any price or on any deadline”.The move was supported by Ontario’s premier, Doug Ford, who said on X: “Team Canada needs to stand together more united than ever before. The prime minister has my full support for a strong response – tariff for tariff, dollar for dollar. As we fight to protect Canadian sovereignty and economic security, everything needs to be on the table. Ontario is ready to do its part.”The head of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, Candace Laing, called the tariffs “a body blow to North American competitiveness”. She said they would raise costs for Americans while threatening Canadian customers, investment and small businesses.The Associated Press and Agence France-Presse contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsCanadaTariffsTrump tariffsTrump administrationAmericasMark CarneyDonald TrumpnewsShareReuse this content

title: Chinese robot runs 100m sprint quicker than Usain Bolt’s world record | Sport | The Guardian
description: Chinese ⁠smartphone maker Honor’s self-developed humanoid ⁠robot Lightning ⁠ran ​the 100m in 9.32 seconds, ⁠beating the human world ⁠record of 9.58sec
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Chinese ⁠smartphone maker Honor’s self-developed humanoid ⁠robot Lightning ⁠ran ​the 100m in 9.32 seconds, ⁠beating the human world ⁠record of 9.58sec
Content: Lightning the humanoid robot competes in the Beijing E-Town half marathon in April.Photograph: VCG/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenLightning the humanoid robot competes in the Beijing E-Town half marathon in April.Photograph: VCG/Getty ImagesSportChinese robot runs 100m sprint quicker than Usain Bolt’s world recordLightning the humanoid ⁠robot clocks 9.32sec in BeijingQuicker than ​9.58sec men’s world record set 17 years agoAgenciesSat 22 Aug 2026 06.25 EDTLast modified on Sat 22 Aug 2026 12.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA ⁠robot named Lightning ⁠has run ​the 100m in 9.32 seconds, ⁠beating the human world ⁠record, China’s ​state broadcaster ‌has reported.The humanoid, developed by the Chinese smartphone manufacturer Honor, ‌reached a peak speed of 14.5 metres per second during ‌a test event for ​the second World Humanoid Robot Games, which ⁠began on Saturday. The ​performance surpassed ​the ​9.58sec men’s ​100mworld record ​set ​by Usain Bolt17 years ago at the World Athletics Championships in Berlin.China has been promoting humanoid robots as an emerging industry, with policymakers and companies ‌betting that advances in AI and hardware will accelerate their deployment in manufacturing, logistics ​and consumer applications.View image in fullscreenA robot dives for the ball during a tennis match with a human player in Beijing.Photograph: Florence Lo/ReutersLightningalso won the Beijing half marathon in Aprilin 50 minutes and 26 seconds, faster than the men’s world record. The robot stood 169cm tall and ​had ​95cm-long legs at ​the half marathon. Researchers have since lengthened ​its legs ‌by 10​cm for these Games.More than 2,000 humanoid robots were participating in the five-day games, now in its second year, a spectacle intended to demonstrate China’s rapid progress in advanced robotics as the technology race with the US heats up. There are 51 events and more than 1,000 competitions taking place including running, table tennis and football.The games, which are taking place in the National Speed Skating Oval built for the 2022 Winter Olympics, opened the same week as Beijing held the 2026 World Robot Conference, where companies showcased around 3,000 products, including humanoid robots. China makes the majority of the world’s humanoid robots.Last month, the US Federal Communications Commission announced a ban on imports of new foreign-made humanoid robots. The FCC cited national security reasons in a move that targeted China. The Pentagon recently also added Unitree, one of China’s leading humanoid robot makers, to its list of companies that it deemed have ties with the Chinese military. Beijing has hit back at the accusations.At Saturday’s opening of the robot games, the organisers and robot makers said that Chinese humanoid robots defeated human world records, as hundreds of humanoid robots marched in formation on to the field in a massive display of synchronised coordination.In a standing high jump, a humanoid robot was able to reach 2.88m, well above the 0.95m best result by a humanoid in last year’s first edition of the games . It surpassed the human high jump record of 2.45m set by Cuba’s Javier Sotomayor in 1993. Both robots were from Beijing-based X-Humanoid.Experts say humanoid robots are still mostly used for demonstrations, performances and research – at least for now – and it will take time to achieve mass real-world deployment. Some spectators at the robot games said they were excited about the humanoid robots’ quickly improving abilities.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHumanoid robots are “evolving rapidly”, said Li Yanfeng, an education worker and a Beijing resident. “At first, I wasn’t very accepting of artificial intelligence. I was even a bit resistant to it, because of the possibility that it might replace or displace humans,” she said. “But now that I see this development is unstoppable, I decided to come and take a look.”Yang Shangzheng, another spectator, said: “These sports are perfectly normal for humans, but now robots can do them. I find it amazing.” Liu Tao, who was watching the games with his son, said he was hoping to see “the best robots China currently has to offer”.This year’s robot games – which the organisers say has 16 countries participating, among them Germany, Japan and the US – also includes other events such as weightlifting and tug of war.Explore more on these topicsSportAthleticsRobotsChinaUsain BoltnewsShareReuse this content

title: Man leaves young son on Mount Fuji before ascending Japan’s highest peak | Japan | The Guardian
description: Boy, seven, had complained of feeling tired so father left him with snacks and a soft drink and continued his climb
Author: Donna Ferguson
Headline: Boy, seven, had complained of feeling tired so father left him with snacks and a soft drink and continued his climb
Content: Mount Fuji is an active volcano and has its own microclimate, meaning hypothermia can pose a serious risk even in the summer.Photograph: Franck Robichon/EPAView image in fullscreenMount Fuji is an active volcano and has its own microclimate, meaning hypothermia can pose a serious risk even in the summer.Photograph: Franck Robichon/EPAJapanMan leaves young son on Mount Fuji before ascending Japan’s highest peakBoy, seven, had complained of feeling tired so father left him with snacks and a soft drink and continued his climbDonna FergusonSat 22 Aug 2026 08.25 EDTLast modified on Sat 22 Aug 2026 08.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA man who abandoned his seven-year-old son on Mount Fuji inJapanafter the boy complained of feeling tired while on a family hike has been reprimanded by local police.A worker on Japan’s highest mountain discovered the child sitting alone on a bench near the sixth station of the Fujinomiya trail at an altitude of more than 2,000 metres (6,500 feet) on Thursday.After inviting the boy to take shelter at the station, the worker called the police, who took the child into protective custody.It emerged that he had told his father he was too tired to continue while they were hiking up the trail in the early hours of the morning.The man, who was from Japan’s fourth-largest city, Nagoya, gave his son some snacks and a soft drink.He then told him to wait for him before continuing his five-hour ascent to the summit with the child’s older brother, who had already gone on ahead. It would have taken him about eight hours to return, according to local reports.By the time police officers managed to contact the boy’s father, he had ascended to the eighth station, a three-hour hike from where he had left his son.They told him to turn back, and after reuniting him with his son reprimanded him for leaving the child alone on an active volcano.“Even if it means having to give up on climbing the mountain together, leaving a child behind is unacceptable,” officers said, according toJapan Today.Weather on the mountain, which has its own microclimate, is unpredictable and can change rapidly. Hypothermia poses a serious risk for hikers even in the summer.The father is said to have apologised to the police, saying: “I made a rash decision, and I deeply regret it.”Local police are urging hikers to consider the abilities and stamina of everyone in their group when planning an ascent on Mount Fuji, and to adjust their pace accordingly.Explore more on these topicsJapanAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Abusers coercing or duping women to post explicit OnlyFans content, UK court cases reveal | Violence against women and girls | The Guardian
description: Separate criminal convictions come as domestic violence charities warn of tech-facilitated abuse and coercion
Author: Amelia Gentleman
Headline: Separate criminal convictions come as domestic violence charities warn of tech-facilitated abuse and coercion
Content: Alexander Tang, left, and Dean Holmes were convicted for posting explicit material on OnlyFans.Composite: Northumbria Police andView image in fullscreenAlexander Tang, left, and Dean Holmes were convicted for posting explicit material on OnlyFans.Composite: Northumbria Police andViolence against women and girlsAbusers coercing or duping women to post explicit OnlyFans content, UK court cases revealSeparate criminal convictions come as domestic violence charities warn of tech-facilitated abuse and coercionAmelia GentlemanSat 22 Aug 2026 08.47 EDTFirst published on Sat 22 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwo men have been convicted this week in separate criminal cases that revealed they had posted explicit content on OnlyFans without the full consent of the women whose images were uploaded.In the first case, Alexander Tang, 37, took and uploaded 47 intimate images and four videos of a woman to OnlyFans without her consent, and was paid money for the material he posted to the website.In the second case, a court heard how Dean Holmes, 43, had coerced a woman to open an OnlyFans account to make money. He pleaded guilty to assault and controlling and coercive behaviour at the start of the trial on Monday, but denied charges of rape. He was found guilty of rape on Thursday at the end of a four-day trial.The cases follow warnings from several domestic violence charities that some women have been compelled to create content to upload to the site.In its 2026 annual report, Women’s Aid said the most common new form of tech-facilitated abuse its frontline teams were assisting with involved “young women being coerced to set up an OnlyFans account to generate income for their abusive partners”. TheRevenge Porn Helplinealso said it had handled reports from women who had been coerced into creating content for OnlyFans and similar platforms.View image in fullscreenThe website OnlyFans allows users to upload images and videos and monetise the content.Photograph: Carlos Barría/ReutersDuring Holmes’s rape trial, Bolton crown court heard that he had isolated his victim from her family and friends and coerced her to open an OnlyFans account. Mark Kellet, prosecuting, said: “She said he put pressure on her to start making money on OnlyFans, a website where people pay for intimate content. She said that he pushed her into that. She would upload pictures of herself and the defendant would use the account to engage in text conversations with the men.”The court heard that Holmes had set the account up in her name and operated it from his phone. She had initially posted pictures of herself in a bikini, but he told her she needed to upload much more explicit content.She later told him that she felt ashamed after these images had been circulated on the site. She messaged him to say: “I can’t show my face after putting myself out there showing everything … I can’t go back to work cos people will know and people seen me advertising myself.”Holmes is due to be sentenced on 25 September.Tang pleaded guilty to one count of voyeurism and was given a 26-week suspended prison sentence on Wednesday. His victim discovered what had happened after being contacted by several men who thought they had been speaking to her on social media and dating apps; she had no idea she was on these sites. She later discovered the profiles had images of her, some naked, taken without her permission or knowledge.When she realised that the pictures had also been posted on OnlyFans, she contacted Northumbria police. Their investigations confirmed that Tang had been selling these non-consensual images, with the money going straight into his bank account. Tang had managed to take a photograph of the woman’s ID to legitimise the use of her images in his OnlyFans account. The company later removed the images during a routine content moderation check.In a statement she read out to the court at Tang’s sentencing hearing, his victim said: “I cannot get the images, the videos, or the degrading captions and comments associated with them out of my mind. Knowing that intimate images and videos of me were uploaded to dozens of websites, reposted and shared by strangers, is something I struggle with every day.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe malignant rise of OnlyFans managers: ‘It’s exploiting. It’s grooming. It’s predatory’Read moreAlex Pattinson, the investigating officer, said: “I am horrified by Alexander Tang’s crime, which is a clear violation of this woman’s expectation of privacy. No one should ever experience what this woman has gone through – and to then learn Tang was profiting from his deceitful offending must have been devastating.”An OnlyFans spokesperson said: “OnlyFans has a zero tolerance policy for illegal content and invests heavily in measures to prevent our platform being abused in this way, including strict onboarding processes, payment controls and ongoing account moderation. We work closely with law enforcement and are proud of the work we do to support investigations and help secure convictions.”Refuge, the UK’s largest domestic abuse charity, said its staff had supported a number of survivors “with cases which involve the weaponisation of OnlyFans by perpetrators”.Speaking earlier this summer about the charity’s concerns generally (rather than in relation to these two convictions) Emma Pickering, who leads Refuge’s tech-facilitated abuse and economic empowerment team, said: “While OnlyFans already requires creators to submit proof of consent at the point of upload, for survivors to be properly protected from harm it is essential that this is robustly implemented and monitored.”In the UK, call the nationaldomestic abuse helplineon 0808 2000 247, or visitWomen’s Aid. In the US, thedomestic violence hotlineis 1-800-799-SAFE (7233). In Australia, the nationalfamily violence counselling serviceis on 1800 737 732. Other international helplines may be found viawww.befrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsViolence against women and girlsDigital mediaCrimeSocial mediaDomestic violenceOnline abusenewsShareReuse this content

title: Free speech group calls foul play at prosecutors using Comey novel in case against him | James Comey | The Guardian
description: PEN America condemns lawyers using passage from thriller to bolster claim ex-FBI director intended to harm Trump
Author: Edward Helmore
Headline: PEN America condemns lawyers using passage from thriller to bolster claim ex-FBI director intended to harm Trump
Content: James Comey arrives to give closed-door testimony to Congress on Capitol Hill in Washington DC on 17 December 2018.Photograph: Jonathan Ernst/ReutersView image in fullscreenJames Comey arrives to give closed-door testimony to Congress on Capitol Hill in Washington DC on 17 December 2018.Photograph: Jonathan Ernst/ReutersJames ComeyFree speech group calls foul play at prosecutors using Comey novel in case against himPEN America condemns lawyers using passage from thriller to bolster claim ex-FBI director intended to harm TrumpEdward HelmoreSat 22 Aug 2026 12.32 EDTLast modified on Sat 22 Aug 2026 15.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA leading US free-expression group has hit out at federal prosecutors’ use of a novel written by former FBI director James Comey in their case accusing him of threatening to killDonald Trump.“Citing a novel to save an indictment that is constitutionally dubious is a desperate Hail Mary and should be rejected,”saida statement posted on Friday by Mara Gassmann, legal director of PEN America, using a term for a last-second heave in American football.Prosecutors with the Trump administration-led justice departmenthad argued in a filingdays earlier that Comey sent coded messages to his followers suggesting they kill an enemy of his citing the fictional protagonist – a federal prosecutor – in his novel FDR Drive.Comey faces DoJ charges over seashell ‘8647’ post, but what does it really mean?Read moreThe book’s main character tries to take down a far-right media personality, Sam Buchanan. The filing quotes passages from the book and aPublishers Weekly book reviewthat described a prosecutor who “believes Buchanan went far beyond the protection of the first amendment” of the US constitution, which provides the right to free expression, “when he singled out his enemies by name and suggested ‘something should be done’ about them”.The citation is part of an legal effort to sustain its prosecution of Comey on charges that hemade a threat against the US presidentandtransmitted that threatacross state lines through social media – over an image he posted on Instagramwhile vacationing in North Carolinafive days before the publication of FDR Drive.Prosecutors in new court documents maintain there is “no serious dispute” that Comey’s May 2025 social media post featuring a photo of seashells arranged to read “8647” could be interpreted as a threat against Trump, who according to authorities has been the target of multiple assassination attempts.The number “86” is often used as shorthand to mean to get rid of or remove something (particularly in the restaurant service industry, to which Comey once belonged). Trump, meanwhile, is the 47th US president.Thosedocumentswere filed on Tuesday in response to Comey’seffortsto have the case against him dismissed.Comey, who has denied the charges, hassaidit “never occurred to me, but I oppose violence of any kind so I took the post down”. Trump’s feud with Comey – the FBI’s director for four years beginning in 2013 – dates back to his handling of an investigation into Russian interference during the 2016 election that led to Trump’s first presidency.That investigation found that Russia interfered “in sweeping and systematic fashion”. Butitdid not establish that members of the Trump campaign conspired or coordinated with Moscow’s election interference activities.The government’s filing also claims that Comey had an “apparent financial incentive to stir up controversy”, suggesting the seashell photo was shared in an effort to juice sales for his “eerily on-the-nose novel”.Comey’s novel has sold 6,471 copies, according to Circana BookScan.In PEN America’s statement, Gassmann said: “A political message, expressed through a photo of seashells, is no true threat; now, the government’s use of Comey’s work of fiction to support this prosecution compounds the first amendment concerns.”Her statement added: “Extreme caution should be taken any time creative works are used to support criminal charges to protect the free expression rights of us all.”In arguing that the case should be dismissed, Comey’s lawyerssaythat the post was protected speech and didnot amount to a “true threat”against the president.“In this context, no reasonable observer would understand the phrase ‘86 47’ to connote violence at all – let alone to threaten that Mr Comey personally would commit violence against the president,” they contend.Comey’s attorneyssaytheir client is being subjected to “vindictive and selective prosecution” and have said the indictment is “not based on a good faith application of the law to the facts”.“Instead,” Comey’s lawyers say, “it effectuates a years-long campaign by the president to use the criminal process to punish Mr Comey for his protected speech and because of the president’s deep-seated animosity.”Explore more on these topicsJames ComeyDonald TrumpUS justice systemUS politicsTrump administrationUS crimeLaw (US)newsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Unsafe for swimming’: Ironman Leeds is latest casualty of heat-fuelled toxic algae  | Water | The Guardian
description: Athletes faced last-minute cancelling of 2.4-mile swim, as experts say pollution and extreme heat are causing blooms
Author: Raphael Boyd
Headline: Athletes faced last-minute cancelling of 2.4-mile swim, as experts say pollution and extreme heat are causing blooms
Content: Jack Chamberlain trained 15 hours a week for the Leeds Ironman. He said he was proud but it ‘felt off’ not to have completed the official swim.Photograph: Jack Chamberlain/tri.hard.jackView image in fullscreenJack Chamberlain trained 15 hours a week for the Leeds Ironman. He said he was proud but it ‘felt off’ not to have completed the official swim.Photograph: Jack Chamberlain/tri.hard.jackWater‘Unsafe for swimming’: Ironman Leeds is latest casualty of heat-fuelled toxic algaeAthletes faced last-minute cancelling of 2.4-mile swim, as experts say pollution and extreme heat are causing bloomsRaphael BoydSat 22 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs far as athletic accomplishments go, few are held in higher regard than completing an Ironman triathlon.The amount of training required to tackle the 2.4-mile swim, 112-mile bike ride and 26-mile run that make up the course, as well as the expensive equipment required to train in the first place, means that only about 50,000 people in the world complete a full race and earn the title of Ironman every year.For some, however, such as Jack Chamberlain, that title has an asterisk next to it.Chamberlain was one of about 2,000 people who competed in IronmanLeedson 16 August, an annual triathlon event whose swimming section was cancelled because of a bloom of toxic blue-green algae. Algae blooms aren’t particularly unusual this time of year, but the successive heatwaves that have hit Britain this summer have caused more problems than usual for freshwater swimming.“My life, for the past four or five months, has been completely consumed by this,” said Chamberlain, who estimates he trained for about 15 hours a week to prepare for the event. While Chamberlain has completed triathlons in the past, Sunday’s event would have been his first full Ironman.“When you cross the finish line you hear those famous words, ‘you are an Ironman’, and that comes from finishing a triathlon, not a duathlon. So I’m proud of myself, but it felt off,” he said.According to BritishTriathlon, the governing body for triathlons, aquathlons and duathlons in the UK, Sunday’s event was the fourth event to be cancelled due to algae blooms so far this year.Chamberlain, like many others, felt that more notice would have lessened the blow and given athletes more time to find an alternative. Even though it didn’t go towards his official time, Chamberlain said that he swam the nearly two and a half miles in a nearby lake the day before, with other athletes asking to do their laps in a local leisure centre before it opened.“It’s something they should have been checking weeks in advance,” said Chamberlain. “There were something like 58 countries represented in the race, so people came from all over the world. I think with people putting in time and effort and, you know, thousands of pounds into such events, things should be put in place.”Marina Angela Andresen, a committed marathoner who has set herself the goal of completing 10 Ironman events in 12 months, was one of the few who saw the silver lining in the swimming leg being cancelled.View image in fullscreen‘It’s dangerous’: Andresen welcomed the organisers’ decision to cancel the swim in the circumstances.Photograph: Marina Angela Andresen/marathon.princess“This was the first time in my life I’ve had a full swim cancellation. I’ve had swims shortened before because of temperatures, but not this. Honestly though, I was very happy with it. Because I know Ironman looks out for the athletes and I would not want to swim with blue-green algae, it’s dangerous,” Andresen said.“I’m very happy to not be forced to swim under such conditions and I can still make the best out of the day. I had a fantastic race with the people of Yorkshire. The mood was great. I really loved it.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTriathlons haven’t been the only events hit by algae in the past week, with several public swimming spots, including thefirst official bathing site on the Thames in London, warning potential swimmers to avoid the water until the blooms clear up.Daniel Start, an avid wild swimmer who has written numerous books on the subject, said increasing pollution was as big a cause of the blooms as the heat.“It’s not a problem that is going away any time soon,” said Start. “It’s getting worse with more intensive farming and more fertiliser being put on fields that trickle down into lakes and rivers.”View image in fullscreenChamberlain at the finishing line.Photograph: Jack Chamberlain/tri.hard.jackA spokesperson for the Ironman Group, which organised Sunday’s event as well as similar events around the world, said: “Ironman was devastated to have to cancel the swim portion of this year’s Ironman Leeds. We know how hard our athletes train across all three disciplines (swim, bike, run) and how disappointing it was to forgo the swim segment due to water quality issues.“Continuous hot weatherand the absence of rain contributed to a bloom of blue-green algae, which can be hazardous to humans and made the lake unsafe for swimming. The decision to cancel the swim was made in conjunction with Leeds city council, who has jurisdiction over Waterloo Lake. 2026 was the second edition of Ironman Leeds; the swim was successfully conducted the previous year.”Explore more on these topicsWaterPollutionTriathlonLeedsExtreme heatfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Subterranean salad: underground farmers seek solution to food crisis in disused UK mines | Farming | The Guardian
description: Researchers in North Yorkshire feel the clock ticking as they aim to transform British food production
Author: Mark Brown
Headline: Researchers in North Yorkshire feel the clock ticking as they aim to transform British food production
Content: The underground farm at Boulby. Researchers believe using mines to grow crops could reduce the high energy costs of conventional vertical farming.Researchers in North Yorkshire feel the clock ticking as they aim to transform British food productionByMark Brown. Photographs byGary CaltonSat 22 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt has the vibe of a Bond villain’s underground lair but the workers in hi-vis and helmets aren’t weighing and packing hard drugs or parts for a death laser. It’s pak choi and lettuce.More than 1,000 metres down, researchers in NorthYorkshirehave created the world’s deepest underground farm and are running trials for a project that could transform UK food production.They want to use disused mines to grow crops, believing the stable environment and ability to use existing infrastructure could reduce the high energy costs associated with conventional vertical farming.It’s a game-changing idea, but the team behind it need evidence that it will work – and the clock is ticking.View image in fullscreenJacob Nickles leads the harvesting and recording of plant species grown in the clean labs within underground tunnels.“We need to double food production by 2050 to support the world’s population,” saysJacob Nickles, a University of Sheffield research fellowand one of the project’s leaders. “That is the long and the short of it. Is it possible? Maybe if we start using mines.”While Nickles and his colleagues might in previous years have been talking about the food crisis looming far in the future, this year’s extreme weather has shown it could be even closer.In England, the dry, hot summer has led to crops dying and livestock using winter feed because there is no grass. “The crisis is less looming,” says Nickles, “it’s here … now.”The underground farm operation has been set up in a science facility at Boulby mine, near Saltburn. The mine itself is a working one:the world’s only commercial producer of polyhalite, which is used as an agricultural fertiliser.View image in fullscreenResearchers on the project.Drive through the ICL-UK mining operation and you will come to offices of the UK government-funded science facility, which hosts mind-blowing experiments – often involving the search for dark matter.This week, the Guardian accompanied Nickles two-thirds of a mile (1.1km) underground as he and colleagues harvestedpak choiand lettuce from vertical towers in the mine.Getting there involves two detailed health and safety inductions, a change into bright orange hi-vis and an eight-minute descent in the original lift, constructed more than 50 years ago.View image in fullscreenThe engagement officer, Jonny Gutteridge.Photograph: Gary Calton/The GuardianOnce there, it feels strangely warm. “You’re experiencing a million times less radiation than you were 10 minutes ago. Does it feel nice?” asks the lab’s engagement officer, Jonny Gutteridge.The experiments take place in the salty tunnels and also the air-conditioned lab facilities where, away from the extensive research going on, you feel you could be anywhere.View image in fullscreenWorkers at a lift shaft at Boulby mine.View image in fullscreenThe project is a partnership between Sheffield University andFarm Urban.The kitchen kettle boils water to make tea, although it boils it hotter than it would on the surface. The toilet flushes, although it is the deepest flushing toilet in the UK.The farming project is a partnership between Sheffield University andFarm Urban, a socially conscious food producer.“We’re not here to replace conventional farming,” says Nickles. “We’re here to work alongside it and there are some things that are just uniquely better suited to controlled environment agriculture. Lettuce is a really good example.”The aim is to gather the first real-world evidence that uniform, marketable crops can be grown underground.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenScientists at work at the Boulby underground lab.During our visit to the site, there were mixed results. Some crops appeared spectacular, with lettuce bigger than a human head. Others looked less impressive but Nickles is consoled by the fact it is a technical, engineering issue rather than a scientific one.“It’s sad when it doesn’t work … but I have to keep reminding myself that this is only the first growth.”Overall, the 12-month study is going well and Nickles is optimistic about the possibility of samphire and tomatoes being trialled next.As well as producing food at scale that can be sold and eaten, the project is about reusing the thousands of redundant mines that exist in the UK, creating new jobs and improving access to fresh produce in economically deprived areas.It is backed by the government, with Patrick Vallance, the then science minister, last month saying: “Growing fresh food while using less energy and land – and being less reliant on changeable British weather – could strengthen food security across our country and protect our environment.”View image in fullscreenGeorgie Dawson, a science communications industrial placement student.View image in fullscreenA large pak choi at the Boulby underground laboratory.The farm research is taking place in a facility that, its supporters say, should be better known.“We are in a hole in North Yorkshire,” says Gutteridge. “We’re a small team of 20-25 people. But the science that goes on … In the past we’ve hosted the world’s most sensitive dark factor detector. We’re doing the world’s first deep underground quantum mechanics experiment. We should be so proud as a country to have a place like this.”The lab’s full name isScience and Technology Facilities Council (STFC) Boulby Underground Laboratory. It is the only place like it in the UK and is regarded as internationally important, one of only 12 in the world.Among the work going on is Durham University’sQuasar project, which involves supercooling atoms and aims to “open a completely new frontier for quantum technology in the UK”. Nearby isBirmingham University’s Bond-sounding DarkSphere.The success of the lab means expansion is already under way with stage one: a new cavern providing a factor 5 increase in space, scheduled to be completed in 2030.Further expansion will happen if Boulby is chosen as the site for a project known asXLZD – the construction of a giant, next-generation liquid-xenon observatoryto search for dark matter.A decision could come next year. “We would love to host XLZD,” says Gutteridge. “The socio-economic benefits, the skills, the outreach, the education, the investment, the industry partnerships, the advanced manufacturing, all of it that would be coming inwards to the north east, to the UK. The impact of hosting a detector like that in the region would be phenomenal.”Explore more on these topicsFarmingYorkshireFood (global)MiningAgricultureFood (Environment)featuresShareReuse this content

title: Young country diary: Camping in my garden, nose to nose with a fox | Wildlife | The Guardian
description: Leeds, West Yorkshire: I missed it first time as my dad couldn’t wake me up. The second time round, he pulled my toe
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Leeds, West Yorkshire: I missed it first time as my dad couldn’t wake me up. The second time round, he pulled my toe
Content: The fox outside Ada's tent during their garden camping.Photograph: Family handoutView image in fullscreenThe fox outside Ada's tent during their garden camping.Photograph: Family handoutYoung country diaryWildlifeYoung country diary: Camping in my garden, nose to nose with a foxLeeds, West Yorkshire:I missed it first time as my dad couldn’t wake me up. The second time round, he pulled my toeSat 22 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDad and I were boiling in the house because of the UK heatwave. So we decided to camp out and sleep in our garden instead. Before we went to bed, while playing catch, we could hear the swifts swoop around our house in the orange evening light.Once it had cooled down, Dad said it was time for bed and tucked me up. At some point in the night, Dad heard something and he tried to wake me up. There was a vixen – a female fox – drinking from the pond, but I missed it. The next morning, Dad told me about the fox and I said, if it comes again, pull my toe.Country diary: The thin, hungry fox goes for the sleepy hen | Nic WilsonRead moreThere are about 150,000 urban foxes living in the towns and cities of the UK. They have amazing hearing – they can hear a watch ticking from 40m away, and a mouse moving around under the snow. That night, one did come to our garden again. Dad woke me up – I felt sleepy but it was exciting.She was standing just 10cm away from the tent – we were nose to nose. She was looking through the mesh window with her sharp pointed teeth and her triangular ears pointing up into the night sky. The thing that stood out the most was her beautiful amber fur. I could see how soft it was, and her wonderful eyes that glistened in the moonlight.You don’t need to live in the countryside to see amazing wildlife.Ada,eightRead today’s other YCD, by Aled, eight: ‘Crabbing then fish and chips - a perfect beach day’.
