title: ‘We fear lessons will not be learned’: Chloe Moffat’s parents on their fight to hold Treasury to account | Civil service | The Guardian
description: Couple considering suing for wrongful death after coroner found disciplinary process materially contributed to suicide
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: Couple considering suing for wrongful death after coroner found disciplinary process materially contributed to suicide
Content: Anne and David Moffat: ‘We need to grieve. The inquest has delayed that.’Photograph: Chris de Bode/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAnne and David Moffat: ‘We need to grieve. The inquest has delayed that.’Photograph: Chris de Bode/The GuardianCivil service‘We fear lessons will not be learned’: Chloe Moffat’s parents on their fight to hold Treasury to accountCouple considering suing for wrongful death after coroner found disciplinary process materially contributed to suicideHelena HortonSat 22 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen a coroner ruled this month that the Treasury“materially contributed” to Chloe Moffat’s death, her parents breathed out in bittersweet relief. For a year, David and Anne Moffat had been forced to become detectives in the worst case any parent could have to solve: why their daughter took her own life.Chloe, 26, went to her job as a personal assistant at the Treasury on a Monday last May “happy as Larry” after a weekend she’d told her friends was a “10 out of 10”. She was planning a holiday with her sister, Alice, and arranging for friends to come for a dinner party the next weekend. She was, according to her father, living “the best life”.That afternoon, however, she was sent to asurprise disciplinary meetingwith her manager and her manager’s manager, which the coroner found left her distressed and convinced she was going to lose her job. The following morning, Chloe was dead.Anne, 64, who is retired and used to work as the head of care at a children’s hospice, said: “When she first did it, we had to question Chloe. We had to question what might have driven Chloe to this.” She paused, and David added: “Criminality? Fraud? All sorts of things. Because why would somebody take their own life if they were the person that we expected?”Anne interjected: “Are they on drugs? Are they in debt? Everything. And so we searched and questioned our own daughter.”None of this was the case. After trawling through emails, talking to Chloe’s friends and colleagues and holding the Treasury to account in a gruelling, multi-day coroner’s court hearing, they found out their daughter had been mistreated by her employer.“After our investigations, it was clear it was literally that one-to-one meeting,” Anne said. “Chloe never recovered. She walked out of that meeting absolutely destroyed and never recovered and went down a black hole.”View image in fullscreenChloe Moffat had worked at the Treasury as a personal assistant for almost three years.Photograph: Family handoutSpeaking from their house in the French Alps, which they bought to be near Alice, who lives there and recently had a daughter, the couple seem exhausted. If the Moffats had not fought their daughter’s case, it is likely the coroner would have explained Chloe’s death with one word: suicide. Instead, she made a narrative finding, explaining the circumstances that led up to the death and laying blame partly at the Treasury’s door.Since that finding two weeks ago, the Moffats have had no contact from the Treasury to offer condolences or an apology. “Now that the inquest has said that the coroner has found them responsible for Chloe’s death, we would have expected for them to have written to us,” David said.Chloe was described as cheerful, popular and funny, and a person who took her job seriously. “I think Chloe was always looking to serve,” David said. Anne added: “I didn’t realise, but people like Chloe, who are bright, confident perfectionists, when they’re given a piece of shocking news such as they might lose their job, can be very vulnerable.”The young woman was blindsided after being presented with anonymous complaints that she had shared confidential information at work, which she denied. She was not reassured that her job was safe even though she was unlikely to be dismissed, or offered a third party in the meeting to give her support or advice.“If Chloe had known that it shouldn’t have happened, if she’d known her rights, she could have walked in and said: ‘I’m not having this meeting’, and walked out. But of course she didn’t. She didn’t know that, she was a people pleaser,” David said.The coroner found Chloe was denied her rights at work, such as being told what the likely outcome of the disciplinary process would have been, which was a written warning, and that she could bring a supporter with her. Instead, she felt ambushed and was convinced she would lose the job she had worked so hard for.Anne said: “I don’t know about the original complaints about Chloe, if they were malicious or to bring her down a peg or two – she was a big personality in the office.”View image in fullscreen‘We do want Chloe remembered for the Chloe that she was.’Photograph: Anne MoffatHer parents are considering suing the Treasury for wrongful death, particularly as they have had no response from the ministry since the finding. “If that’s the only way we’re going to get recognition, it’s a possibility,” David said.The Treasury is obliged to give the coroner a response to the prevention of future deaths report she issued to the civil service. The coroner found there was a risk of further deaths at the Treasury because of how the department handled disciplinary cases.The department brought a team of lawyers to the inquest, who pushed for Chloe’s death to be recorded as an unexplained suicide.“We definitely want to be in touch with the Treasury because we do want Chloe remembered for the Chloe that she was,” Anne said. “And be that a bench in her name or whatever, but we want her to be remembered, but we do fear that she is going to be brushed under the carpet and lessons will not be learned.”Unusually for an inquest, the small, drab room in Surrey was full of young people in their early to mid-20s – Chloe’s friends and colleagues, who wept throughout. Those who attended from the Treasury were not given bereavement leave to attend the inquest into their friend’s death. “They didn’t get any time off from the Treasury or support for that horrible ordeal they had gone through,” Anne said.The couple said they hoped the Treasury acknowledged Chloe and issued a satisfactory response to the prevention of future deaths report, so this nightmarish chapter could be closed and they could begin to grieve.“We need to grieve. And I’m not sure that we have. I think the inquest has delayed that,” Anne said.David said: “The hole it’s left in our lives is just enormous. We’re only still coming to terms with that. Sometimes we don’t feel we can attend family events because we’ve got something missing. We are a tight-knit family, we’ve all holidayed together. But now we don’t have Chloe.”They said they hoped Chloe’s case could help prevent other parents from going through the same experience. And they wanted to remember their daughter as the grinning, popular, confident, adventurous woman she was.“We have got so many happy memories. So that’s what we have to be positive about,” Anne said. “I think: ‘At least she didn’t have cancer,’ you know, and suffer. She was literally happy up until that meeting.”David said: “I think for sure we will continue to want to ensure that we spread the word of what we have learned from all this.”A Treasury spokesperson said: “Our deepest sympathies continue to be with Chloe’s family, and the department continues to mourn Chloe’s death.“We are taking all concerns extremely seriously and are considering the coroner’s findings carefully. We have introduced improvements to guidance, support and wellbeing arrangements but recognise we must continue to take action to prevent this happening again.”In the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the988 Suicide & Crisis Lifelineat 988 or chat at988lifeline.org. In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsCivil serviceEnglandWork & careersnewsShareReuse this content

title: Nancy Kassebaum Baker, former US senator from Kansas, dies aged 94 | US politics | The Guardian
description: Kassebaum Baker became the first woman elected to the US Senate without following a spouse into office
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Kassebaum Baker became the first woman elected to the US Senate without following a spouse into office
Content: Nancy Kassebaum Baker in Washington DC on 21 March 2012.Photograph: Carolyn Kaster/APView image in fullscreenNancy Kassebaum Baker in Washington DC on 21 March 2012.Photograph: Carolyn Kaster/APUS politicsNancy Kassebaum Baker, former US senator from Kansas, dies aged 94Kassebaum Baker became the first woman elected to the US Senate without following a spouse into officeAssociated PressSat 22 Aug 2026 16.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNancy Kassebaum Baker, aKansasgovernor’s daughter who became the first woman elected to the US Senate without following a spouse into office, has died. She was 94.Kassebaum Baker died on Friday of natural causes, according to her son, Bill Kassebaum.“She loved Kansas. She loved people from Kansas and representing Kansas for 18 years in theUS Senate,” he told the Associated Press. “She was an independent-minded Republican who was willing to stand up for what she thought was right, even if that meant going against the party.”She was elected to theUS Senatein 1978 and served three terms. Her modest demeanor endeared her to voters of all political stripes, though she shared the progressive Republican politics of her father, Kansas governor Alf Landon, the unsuccessful 1936 Republican nominee for president. Even after leaving the Senate early in 1997, she continued taking on public service roles.She married the former US senator Howard Baker, a Tennessee Republican, in 1996. He died in 2014.Kassebaum Baker remained an icon for Kansans generally. She could work with Senate colleagues of all political philosophies, and a 1996 health insurance law bore her name, along with that of liberal US senator Ted Kennedy of Massachusetts.View image in fullscreenNancy Kassebaum, as she was known then, reflects on her first year as the junior senator from Kansas in her Washington DC office, on 21 December 1979.Photograph: Charles W Harrity/APHer election to the Senate brought her immediate national attention. When she announced her retirement, she was among eight senators who were women and the only one to chair a Senate committee, the labor and human resources panel.She was also in a dwindling bloc of moderate-to-liberal Republicans, having supported, for example, a ban on assault weapons championed by Democratic president Bill Clinton.Yet she never polarizedKansasconservatives as other GOP moderates did. She connected with voters because she never seemed caught up in the trappings of power, and when she retired, she acknowledged: “I’d rather cuddle up and do needlepoint all day.”Kassebaum Baker broke with the Republican party as it became more conservative later in her life, endorsing Democratic candidates for Kansas governor and US senator, including Democratic governor Laura Kelly, who was elected in 2018 and re-elected in 2022. Kelly’s 2022 Republican opponent, then state attorney general Derek Schmidt, had worked on Kassebaum Baker’s Senate staff.She also declared in 2021 that Donald Trump should be impeached after supporters attacked the US Capitol toward the end of his first presidency hoping to stop congressional certification of his defeat by Joe Biden in the 2020 White House election.“This just has gone too far,” shetoldKansas City’s KMBC news station.Explore more on these topicsUS politicsKansasUS SenatenewsShareReuse this content

title: 40,000 bottles of eye drops across the US recalled over issues with sterility of product | Product recalls | The Guardian
description: Prestige Brand Holdings has voluntarily recalled a batch of its Clear Eyes eye drops after FDA alert
Author: Marina Dunbar
Headline: Prestige Brand Holdings has voluntarily recalled a batch of its Clear Eyes eye drops after FDA alert
Content: The FDA classified the action as a Class II recall, defined on the agency’s website as a moderate-risk situation.Photograph: José Luis Magaña/APView image in fullscreenThe FDA classified the action as a Class II recall, defined on the agency’s website as a moderate-risk situation.Photograph: José Luis Magaña/APProduct recalls40,000 bottles of eye drops across the US recalled over issues with sterility of productPrestige Brand Holdings has voluntarily recalled a batch of its Clear Eyes eye drops after FDA alertMarina DunbarSat 22 Aug 2026 11.44 EDTLast modified on Sat 22 Aug 2026 11.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNearly 40,000 bottles of eye drops are being pulled from store shelves across the US over concerns about potential contamination, according to the Food and Drug Administration (FDA).Prestige Brand Holdings, based in Tarrytown,New York, has voluntarily recalled 39,060 bottles of Clear Eyes Maximum Itchy Eye Relief eye drops because of a “lack of assurance of sterility”, an FDAenforcement reportstates. The FDA classified the action as a Class II recall, defined on the agency’swebsiteas a moderate-risk situation “in which use of or exposure to a violative product may cause temporary or medically reversible adverse health consequences or where the probability of serious adverse health consequences is remote”.The recall specifically covers 15ml bottles carrying lot code 2552A and an expiration date of 30 September 2027. The eye drops were distributed by Medtech Products Inc, a Prestige Consumer Healthcare company.Massive egg recall in US south and south-west due to salmonella outbreakRead moreClear Eyes Maximum Itchy Eye Relief is marketed on its packaging as an astringent/lubricant redness-reliever eye drop intended to provide relief from redness, itching, burning and watery eyes.The product is sold at major retailers including Walmart, Target, Kroger, Giant Eagle, Meijer, Dollar General and Family Dollar stores.Consumers are being advised to stop using the recalled eye drops and return them for a refund. Anyone concerned about possible effects from the product is encouraged to contact a pharmacist or healthcare provider.Eye drop and other related medicinal product recalls have become relatively less common compared with the continuing food safety crisis in the US, which under the Trump administration has recently been grappling with one of thelargest recordedfoodborne illness outbreaks in the nation’s history. Still, eye drop recalls do happen.In 2023, for instance, the FDA recalled EzriCare Artificial Tears after the eye drops werelinkedto an outbreak ofPseudomonas aeruginosa, a drug-resistant bacterial contamination. That outbreak may have resulted in one death and injuries to 68 other people.A small number of those sickened had to have the affected eye surgically removed.Explore more on these topicsProduct recallsConsumer affairsHealthnewsShareReuse this content

title: Former world boxing champion, 38, shot dead outside home in South Africa | South Africa | The Guardian
description: Zolani Tete was arriving at his house in Eastern Cape when two men in balaclavas got out of a car and shot him
Author: William Christou
Headline: Zolani Tete was arriving at his house in Eastern Cape when two men in balaclavas got out of a car and shot him
Content: Police said the motive behind the 38-year-old athlete’s murder remains unclear, but said they have started investigations.Photograph: Jason Cairnduff/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenPolice said the motive behind the 38-year-old athlete’s murder remains unclear, but said they have started investigations.Photograph: Jason Cairnduff/Action Images/ReutersSouth AfricaFormer world boxing champion, 38, shot dead outside home in South AfricaZolani Tete was arriving at his house in Eastern Cape when two men in balaclavas got out of a car and shot himWilliam ChristouSat 22 Aug 2026 06.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe former boxing world champion Zolani “Last Born” Tete was shot dead outside his home inSouth Africaon Friday amid rampant violence in the country, which has one of the world’s highest murder rates.The 38-year-old athlete was arriving at his house in the Mdantsane township, Eastern Cape province, when two men in balaclavas got out of a car and shot him. He was declared dead at the scene. A 27-year-old woman with Tete was also shot multiple times and taken to hospital.Police said the motive remains unclear, but that they have started investigations, asking the public for assistance.The killing of the boxer brought renewed attention to South Africa’s widespread violent crime. The country has recently had a decline in homicides, but remains one of the world’s murder capitals.View image in fullscreenA forensic pathologist outside the home of Zolani Tete after the fatal shooting in Mdantsane in the Eastern Cape province.Photograph: ReutersAn average of 58 people per daywere murderedin South Africa in the first four months of 2026, according to government data. The UK recorded an average of 1.5 murders per day in 2025.The boxer’s death led to an outpouring of grief and tributes. Tete fought in 34 matches over the course of his career. He was a two-time title winner, winning the IBF junior-bantamweight title in 2014, and the bantamweight title in 2017. He also held the Guinness world record for the fastest knockout in a title fight.Gayton McKenzie, the minister of sports, arts and culture in South Africa, said: “South Africa has lost one of the finest fighters it has ever produced … There are no words I can offer tonight that will be equal to what [the family] has lost.”Tete was training to return to the ring, according to McKenzie, who said the boxer believed “he still had something to give his country.”The world boxing council published a tribute of Tete, offering their “deepest condolences” to his family and praising his “remarkable career.”Explore more on these topicsSouth AfricaBoxingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Nebraska school district asks police to stop using shock gloves on students | Nebraska | The Guardian
description: Omaha police agreed to stop carrying electric shock gloves in the halls of state’s largest public school district
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Omaha police agreed to stop carrying electric shock gloves in the halls of state’s largest public school district
Content: A jailer in Nelson county, Kentucky, with an electric shock glove on 13 August 2026.Photograph: Dylan Lovan/APView image in fullscreenA jailer in Nelson county, Kentucky, with an electric shock glove on 13 August 2026.Photograph: Dylan Lovan/APNebraskaNebraska school district asks police to stop using shock gloves on studentsOmaha police agreed to stop carrying electric shock gloves in the halls of state’s largest public school districtAssociated PressSat 22 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOmahapolice recently agreed to stop carrying gloves that can deliver electric shocks to students in the halls ofNebraska’s largest public school district.The decision affecting most Omaha middle and high schools came after the Associated Press first revealed Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE)’s plan to give officers the “Gloves” – or “generated low output voltage emitters”. The devices have also been used in recent years by some jails.The superintendent of Omaha public schools, Matthew Ray, on 18 August requested that police working in the schools, known as school resource officers, stop using the gloves. Omaha police agreed two days later.Their cities dropped Flock surveillance cameras. They’re still being watchedRead moreHowever, the suburban Bellevue police department that patrols two Omaha schools and the large Bellevue district said its officers will continue carrying the gloves. Three other large school districts in the metro area that have Omaha school resource officers assigned to their buildings have not taken action to stop police from using the devices.The AP left messages seeking comment from the Millard, Elkhorn and Westside districts that are also patrolled by Omaha officers.Bellevue schools spokesperson Amanda Oliver said the district has a great relationship with Bellevue police and doesn’t see a need to alter anything.“We’ve got a great communication and dialogue that we have with them consistently. And so for us right now, no changes are being made,” Oliver said.Ray said in a school board meeting on 17 August and in a letter to the public schools community that he’d only learned about the gloves the previous week. But local television station KETV found emails from 2023, when Omaha police notified the districts that the department planned to equip officers with the gloves, and an official with the Omaha district said they were already familiar with them because Bellevue police had them at two Omaha schools.Students in all the Omaha area districts have gone back to class over the past two weeks.Before halting the use of the gloves, the Omaha police department held a news conference in which an officer demonstrated how they can help an officer quickly get control of someone who is refusing commands.Omaha police used the gloves twice during the 2025-26 school year. And Bellevue police have also used them twice in previous years.At the school board meeting, about 30 people spoke out against police using the gloves. Residents and board members alike said they were appalled at the practice. No one spoke in favor of it.“I can’t even imagine walking down the hallway and seeing a peer of mine being electrocuted in a place that is supposed to be a safe space for students,” said Nora Wessel, a senior at Omaha Central high school. “Yet, this is now a very real possibility. These are adults we are supposed to be able to trust, but these weapons create a barrier for our students to turn to resource officers when needed.”Ken Trump, president of the consulting firm National School Safety and Security Services, said before schools allow police to bring in technology like shock gloves, there should be a careful discussion of questions like how school resource officers will respond to students with disabilities or special medical needs, how parents will be informed and under what circumstances the gloves can be used.“Less than lethal doesn’t mean low risk,” Trump said.Ray said the district recognized longstanding relationships with law enforcement partners and the important role school resource officers have in promoting school safety. Continued use of the gloves “would be counterproductive to our work together”, Ray said.Omaha’s mayor, John Ewing Jr, who helped oversee creating the school resource officer program when he was on the police force, said the department has honored the school district’s decision to “opt out”. The Omaha police department said officers will continue to carry stun guns, batons, pepper spray and firearms.Most of the Omaha police department’s 34 school resource officers had been trained and were allowed to use the gloves, the mayor and the police chief, Todd Schmaderer, said in a statement.“We believe it is the safest use-of-force option in the rare times when it is used,” the statement said.In 2025, Omaha police agreed to pay Compliant Technologies LLC, which manufactures the gloves, about $66,000 for 40 gloves, according to the contract.Officers were expected to give warning before using the gloves and then touch the person for up to 15 seconds while the electric shock was delivered, the statement said.Bellevue’s police chief, Ken Clary, said his officers will continue carrying the gloves, which they have had for more than three years.“I am not comfortable having our officers give up a tool that has repeatedly proven to be safe, effective and less harmful than the alternatives,” Clary said in a statement.The devices activate when an officer presses a button. The gloves must touch someone’s skin directly to produce voltage that causes pain, which is intended to make people stop resisting officers. Unlike stun guns, they do not leave burn or contact marks.In the 2025-26 school year, an Omaha officer used the glove in one case to stop a high school student from another school from trying to escape after fighting with a security guard, according to the statement. In a second case, the glove was used on a student at the Omaha district’s integrated learning center for special education students. Police said that student made verbal threats and threw a chair at a school security guard, striking the guard in the head. The student also punched the guard in the head, according to the statement.Bellevue police didn’t immediately have details about when its officers have used the gloves. Clary said the devices have been an extremely effective tool that sometimes make students cooperate on sight even without shocking a student.Omaha public schools is Nebraska’s largest school district and serves more than 50,000 students, its website says. The metro area’s other districts are also among the biggest in the state.Explore more on these topicsNebraskaUS policingSchoolsUS educationnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It brings me joy’: how young people are making CDs cool again | Music industry | The Guardian
description: Compact discs are back, with searches for players up 96% at John Lewis and popular models sold out online
Author: Lauren Cochrane
Headline: Compact discs are back, with searches for players up 96% at John Lewis and popular models sold out online
Content: The CD revival is part of a wider fashion for retro tech.Photograph: pixdeluxe/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe CD revival is part of a wider fashion for retro tech.Photograph: pixdeluxe/Getty ImagesMusic industry‘It brings me joy’: how young people are making CDs cool againCompact discs are back, with searches for players up 96% at John Lewis and popular models sold out onlineLauren CochraneSat 22 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWith more than800 million peoplesubscribing to a music streaming service, wireless speakers have become a familiar sight in homes. But expect to get reacquainted with a different object to play music soon: the CD player, once consigned to obsolescence, is back.John Lewis report that searches for CD players are up 96% since July, possibly owing to students heading to university and buying the systems for their rooms. The£79 Crosley Voyager, and the£129 Pure Classic C-D6are both sold out online, with the Voyager scheduled to return in October. Portable CD players are also popular.This tallies, of course, with sales of CDs themselves. Areportthis year found that the growth of CD sales is up 16%, compared with vinyl’s 2.4%. HMV reports that sales of CDs are up 10% year on year – thanks to artists often providing unique content on the format. “K-pop has been a massive driver, with BTS the most obvious example of artists that have led the resurgence,” says the managing director, Phil Halliday. “But it goes much wider than that. We’re seeing very strong CD demand around artists like Olivia Rodrigo, Ariana Grande and Olivia Dean.”View image in fullscreenThe fact that a CD is so much cheaper that vinyl is a factor in their return.Photograph: Phynart Studio/Getty ImagesThe fact that a vinyl record is about £35, compared with £12 for a CD, is no doubt a factor.Tom Morgan-Freelander, the deputy editor of the technology magazine Stuff, has noticed the change over the past two years. He puts it down to consumers wanting to move away from using their phone, a better audio quality, and limited disposable income. “It’s: ‘I don’t want to spend money on a turntable and the speakers that go with it. I want to spend £150 on an all-in-one system that comes with the CD player,’” he says.In the CD aisle of an HMV in London on a weekday morning, people in their teens and twenties are browsing. Fourteen-year-old Milo Georgeaux-Healy has chosen two Dua Lipa albums as well as Brat by Charli xcx to play on an “old boombox”. “I like them because they’re cheaper,” she says. “They’re a lot more compact [than vinyl], and I find that they have better quality than your phone.” Adel Alsehi, 27, is visiting from Riyadh. He has selected a Madonna greatest hits, a Kacey Musgraves album and Private Dancer by Tina Turner. “It gives me a different feeling,” he says of CDs. “I feel like I’m listening to an artist’s work. It brings me joy.”View image in fullscreenThe sold-out Crosley Voyager CD player: better quality than streaming without shelling out for a high-end system.Photograph: John LewisRichard Farnell runsVinylExchange in Manchester, where they also sell CDs. He says the people buying CDs are now younger, and cost is a big part of this. “The record labels started to up the price of vinyl and it became largely unaffordable for this demographic,” he says. “A copy of Oasis’s Definitely Maybe on original UK “Damont” pressing can sell for between £150 and £250, depending upon condition. The standard vinyl reissue will be around £25-£30, but in our shop the CD version will only be £4.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSleeve NotesGet music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn an era of frictionless digital experiences, there’s something magical about obsolete technology | Tansy GardamRead moreThe CD revival is part of a wider fashion for retro tech. As well as the vinyl resurgence andcassettes becoming popular items to buy, there’s the vogue forwearing wired earphonesover AirPods. “The vinyl revival re-established our appetite for analogue, and now we’re seeing that broader love for physical music drive a genuine surge in CD players,” confirms Katrina Mills, the category buying lead for audio and imaging at John Lewis.Part of this is about optics. “Someone walking around with a portable CD player and wired headphones is signalling their sense of taste and cultural capital,” says brand strategist Alexi Gunner. He has labelled this trend“performative audiophilia”.Gunner argues that the return to the physical for music is a kind of rebellion. “The status quo is streaming platforms and wireless audio on identical iPhones,” he says. “All this has taken away the haptic, sensorial quality of listening to music.”View image in fullscreenChoosing an album rather than being directed by an algorithm has growing appeal for young music lovers.Photograph: Stephen Frost/AlamyJ’Nae Phillips, who writes about Gen Z trends on her SubstackFashion Tingz, agrees. “When music is effectively infinite and frictionless, something is appealing about having to choose an album, put a disc in and listen to it from beginning to end,” she says, and echoes Gunner’s point: “There’s a certain cultural cachet in showing that you’re interested in music as an object and an experience, rather than simply consuming whatever happens to be recommended by an algorithm.”Arguably, the CD is the final revival available to young people – it’s the last format for music before the MP3 arrived in the early 2000s. However, Gunner suggests there may be a different object waiting in the wings: the USB stick. Fred Again named his 2025 tour after the portable drive. “It’s the most common format that a DJ will carry their music to a gig on,” explains Gunner. “In the frame of performative audiophilia, you’re showing that you’re not just listening to music, you are possibly a DJ, you are a tastemaker … it’s something that will become more popular.”Explore more on these topicsMusic industryYoung peopleRetail industryStudentsVinylnewsShareReuse this content

title: Hook, hold, harvest and hide: Meta’s alleged strategy laid out in first week of landmark trial  | Meta | The Guardian
description: In trial that opened on Tuesday, California and 28 other states accused the company of designing addictive sites and violating laws protecting children’s privacy
Author: Dara Kerr
Headline: In trial that opened on Tuesday, California and 28 other states accused the company of designing addictive sites and violating laws protecting children’s privacy
Content: ‘Meta’s business model worked especially well for kids.’Photograph: Vicki Behringer/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘Meta’s business model worked especially well for kids.’Photograph: Vicki Behringer/ReutersMetaHook, hold, harvest and hide: Meta’s alleged strategy laid out in first week of landmark trialIn trial that opened on Tuesday, California and 28 other states accused the company of designing addictive sites and violating laws protecting children’s privacyDara KerrSat 22 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 22 Aug 2026 04.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMeta’s business can be boiled down to four words that begin with the letter H: hook, hold, harvest, hide, according to a lawyer who is prosecuting the world’s largest social media company.The owner of Facebook andInstagram“hooks” in users, “holds” them on its platforms for as long as possible, “harvests” their data and then “hides” the truth from the public, she argued.“Meta’s business model worked especially well for kids,” said Megan O’Neill, a lawyer for the state ofCalifornia.Her accusation opened theblockbuster trialagainst the US tech company on Tuesday in Oakland, California, just north of Meta’s headquarters in Silicon Valley. California has joined 28 other US states in suing the £1tn ($1.36tn) company for allegedly designing addictive products that lead to children being harmed.View image in fullscreenLennon Torres of Heat Initiative holds a banner with the names of young people who died as a result of social media outside the Ronald V Dellums federal building on 18 August.Photograph: Noah Berger/APEight jurors heard from O’Neill and attorneys for Meta this week, along with testimony from former employees and a psychologist. The lawsuit centers on allegations that the company violated US federal child privacy laws and state-level consumer protection laws by collecting data on children under the age of 13 without parental permission. Over the course of the trial, the jury is additionally expected to hear from Meta CEOMark Zuckerbergand Instagram CEO Adam Mosseri.The threat to Meta is existential. If the company is found liable, damages could be as high as $200bn – an amount equivalent to the company’s 2025 annual revenue. The states are also asking that Meta be forced to change the design of its products to make them safer for children, which could have permanent effects on the company’s business model and how its social media platforms operate.Meta has denied all allegations. Liza Crenshaw, a spokesperson for the company, said: “Rather than sticking to the facts or the law, the states have instead decided to chase an outlandish payout.”During opening statements, Paul Schmidt, an attorney for Meta, said there is “no dispute” people can struggle with social media, but that Meta had “come up with tools to try and address that”. He added the company does not allow children under the age of 13 to register for accounts on its social networks and that it had disabled more than 1m accounts of those young users.View image in fullscreenPaul Schmidt, lead attorney for Meta, leaves the courthouse as Meta is on trial over social media addiction in Oakland on 19 August.Photograph: Karl Mondon/AFP/Getty ImagesThe trial is expected to last six to eight weeks. The proceedings will be led by attorneys for the states of California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey. The jury’s role is advisory, which means they will give recommendations to the presiding judge, Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers, who will make the final decision on the verdict and damages.Meta faces thousands of similar US lawsuits brought by families, school districts and other attorneys general. The company lost the first two of those cases to go to trial in March. In the first, the company was ordered topay nearly $1bnto the state of New Mexico for allowing child sexual exploitation on its platforms; and in the second, it was found liable for deliberately designing addictive products thathooked one young womanand was ordered to pay her more than $4m.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionNew Mexico’s attorney general pushes new social media safety laws after $900m court victory over MetaRead moreThestar witness to take the standin the trial’s first week was Arturo Béjar, a safety engineer at Meta who worked there in two separate stints between 2009 and 2021. Since leaving, Béjar has been an outspoken critic of the company, testifying before a US Senate committee and serving as an expert witness in other cases that involve social media’s harm to children.In Oakland, Béjar testified that his motivation for pursuing solutions for harms to children was his own teenage daughter’s treatment on Instagram. He said she received unwanted sexual advances and photos of male genitals as well as misogynistic insults. Later, she told her father that reporting these abuses through Instagram’s established processes was either ineffective or not possible.“Meta is taking a ‘don’t ask, don’t tell’ strategy” when it comes to child safety, Béjar testified.View image in fullscreenArturo Bejar, a former Meta safety engineer and consultant, leaves the courthouse as Meta faces trial over claims that they illegally collected and used children’s data.Photograph: Manuel Orbegozo/ReutersBéjar said that his job often included briefing Zuckerberg and that he had spoken with the CEO more than 100 times in the course of his work.During Béjar’s testimony, attorneys for the government showed the jury an email he sent Zuckerberg in 2021, which outlined a survey he had conducted of teens’ experiences on Instagram. The results showed 51% of users said “yes” to having bad or harmful experiences within the previous seven days and that content was taken down only 0.02% of the time.Béjar testified he sent that data to Zuckerberg because, “in my experience, when Mark makes something a priority, mountains move.”“Did he ever respond to you?” the attorney asked.“No,” Béjar replied. “I didn’t hear back from him.”Meta fought to bar Béjar from testifying at the trial, filing a series of motions to strike his exhibits and prevent him from taking the stand, all of which were rejected. In an email to reporters on Wednesday, Meta continued to hound him. The company’s statement said Béjar’s testimony was not credible or reliable because he overinflated his role at the company and took credit for work he didn’t do.After Béjar’s testimony wrapped, the jury heard recorded depositions from Elena Davis and Natalie Troxel – both former user experience researchers for Meta. Jean Twenge, a psychology professor at San Diego State University, also briefly took the stand, with testimony scheduled to continue next week.Explore more on these topicsMetaFacebookInstagramMark ZuckerbergCaliforniaSocial mediaDigital mediafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘The worst part is the guilt’: the owners who fear dog food caused pets’ eye problems | Retail industry | The Guardian
description: In the week that Years recalled all of its fresh meals, concerns grow about a potential link to dogs’ health conditions
Author: Rupert Jones
Headline: In the week that Years recalled all of its fresh meals, concerns grow about a potential link to dogs’ health conditions
Content: Phoebe the cavalier King Charles spaniel before and after being affected with dry eye.Photograph: Pets MagazineView image in fullscreenPhoebe the cavalier King Charles spaniel before and after being affected with dry eye.Photograph: Pets MagazineRetail industry‘The worst part is the guilt’: the owners who fear dog food caused pets’ eye problemsIn the week that Years recalled all of its fresh meals, concerns grow about a potential link to dogs’ health conditionsRupert JonesSat 22 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 22 Aug 2026 03.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“It’s been horrible – Chester developed sudden red and gunky eyes in May,” said Elizabeth, whose six-year-old cavachon “can’t open his eyes” on many days.The 29-year-old civil servant is one of a number of people who contacted the Guardian because they are concerned about a potential link between a recalled dog food and their pet’s eye condition.Elizabeth, who did not want to give her surname, said she and Chester had been to see vets more than 10 times in recent months, and they had all been “totally stumped”. Chester was initially treated for conjunctivitis, before Elizabeth was told it could be hay fever because of the lack of rain and high pollen count, and then the vet thought her pet might have an autoimmune disorder.Then came the news this week that the dog food brand Years wasrecalling all its fresh mealsafter reports that a recipe change may have caused some animals to develop a condition called sudden bilateral dry eye. Also known as keratoconjunctivitis sicca, or KCS, dry eye occurs when a dog is unable to produce tears, making their eyes very sore. If left untreated, it can lead to sight loss.View image in fullscreenChester’s owner, Elizabeth, says her six-year-old cavachon has been to the vet more than 10 times in recent months.Photograph: Elizabeth/Guardian CommunityThe company said its investigation was “currently focused on potential contamination within a portion of buckwheat supply”. Buckwheat was added to the company’s meals several months ago.Years said it began receiving reports late last month of dogs experiencing sudden bilateral dry eye and, as of Tuesday evening, 192 customers had reported “potential, as yet unverified, eye issues”.Chester had been fed on Years food for about 18 months, and Elizabeth said her vet had told her “they are fairly confident of a link” between the recalled dog food and Chester’s eye condition.She said one theory was that there had been “a toxic chemical reaction” of some sort, adding that the vets “are unsure if just taking him off the food is going to be sufficient”.Elizabeth, who lives in north London, said the vet trips and treatments had cost her hundreds of pounds “and Chester has been miserable for months”, adding: “I fear what long-term damage has been done and whether this is reversible.”Marie Carter-Robb’s seven-year-old cavalier King Charles spaniel, Phoebe, was formally diagnosed with dry eye – the condition linked to the Years recall – during a visit to the vet on Thursday.Phoebe is one of her three dogs. All three have eaten Years meals regularly as part of their diet since her subscription with the company began in April 2025, but Phoebe is the only one who has developed these eye problems.“Her symptoms began in June,” said Carter-Robb, who is the editor ofPetsMagazine. “She had never suffered from allergies before this summer and, until discovering the Years recall, I had assumed we were dealing with some sort of new allergy or an ordinary eye problem.”Since then, Phoebe has had repeated vet examinations and treatment.Speaking just before Thursday’s vet examination, Carter-Robb said that, having reviewed the Years recall information, “my vet has subsequently told me that the information is concerning and could suggest the food as a possible cause. He said that if the timing of the introduction of buckwheat correlates with the onset of Phoebe’s symptoms, he would be suspicious of it as the inciting cause.”The emotional impact has been considerable, she added.“The worst part is the guilt. I had absolutely no reason to suspect her food. I thought we were dealing with an allergy or an ordinary eye problem, and I carried on feeding Years to all three dogs. Finding the recall by chance at 11pm at night and suddenly looking back at everything Phoebe has been through was horrible.”She said that as a first priority she wants Phoebe to recover fully, and then she wants to understand exactly what happened and whether the condition is linked to diet.Phoebe has now been prescribed an eye ointment to treat the dry eye and will need treatment for at least the next few months, meaning examination and medication costs, Carter-Robb added.Adele Chaplin, 50, who lives in Suffolk, said her eight-year-old greyhound, Lettuce, was first diagnosed with bilateral dry eye and eye ulcers in March this year. He has been eating Years dog food for “a good couple of years”.View image in fullscreenLettuce the greyhound’s owner, Adele Chaplin, says: ‘Frankly, he’s miserable. His eyes itch and are painful; he rubs them against anything he can – sofas, legs, curtains.’Photograph: Adele Chaplin/Guardian CommunityChaplin said: “He has undergone treatment from our local vet and was referred to a specialist vet ophthalmologist in April with the severe warning that he may well lose his eyes. The specialist vet has been seeing him since and, fortunately, his eyes are safe for now, but he still had zero tear production when he was last tested and vast amounts of discharge.“Frankly, he’s miserable. His eyes itch and are painful; he rubs them against anything he can (sofas, legs, curtains), and now he has a gruelling daily regime of oils, cream and drops which are administered hourly. Add to that the sudden need to switch him to an entirely new food (something you are always recommended to avoid – you should always do that gradually) and he’s a very confused dog.”Chaplin said that since the details of the recall had emerged, she had been in communication with the vet ophthalmologist, who told her to immediately stop feeding the Years food to Lettuce.“I’m hopeful we’ll get a reduction in symptoms, but it’s too early to say,” she added.“So far, this has cost thousands in treatment and medication, not to mention the travel back and forth to the specialist vet, which is an hour away from our home … Greyhounds live to about 14, so we could have another six years of treatment and medication costs, along with the increased insurance (which has already doubled as a result of this issue).”A Years spokesperson said: “Years exists for one reason: to give people more time with their dogs, and the reports we have received are deeply upsetting to everyone here. As a result of the reports, we took the step to voluntarily recall our fresh meals because, while the evidence is still developing, we are not prepared to take chances with the dogs people trust us to feed.“Our investigation is currently focused on potential contamination within a portion of buckwheat supply, rather than buckwheat itself, although a definitive cause has not yet been established.“Independent laboratory testing is under way, alongside our wider investigation, to understand exactly what has happened. We want to give customers clear, evidence-based answers rather than speculate while that work continues, and we will communicate the findings as soon as the investigation is complete. In the meantime, customers are encouraged to visitwww.years.com/pages/carefor more detailed information.”Explore more on these topicsRetail industryFood & drink industryDogsProduct recallsPetsConsumer affairsAnimalsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Premium bonds: more chance of win as NS&I ups prize fund rate again | Savings | The Guardian
description: Savings bank estimates there will be 308,000 more prizes available in September draw than the month before
Author: Rupert Jones
Headline: Savings bank estimates there will be 308,000 more prizes available in September draw than the month before
Content: When you buy premium bonds, you are entered into a monthly prize draw in which you can win tax-free sums between £25 and £1m.Photograph: Justin Long/AlamyView image in fullscreenWhen you buy premium bonds, you are entered into a monthly prize draw in which you can win tax-free sums between £25 and £1m.Photograph: Justin Long/AlamySavingsPremium bonds: more chance of win as NS&I ups prize fund rate againSavings bank estimates there will be 308,000 more prizes available in September draw than the month beforeRupert JonesSat 22 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePremium bond holders will have more chances of winning prizes after changes announced this week.From September there will be more prizes up for grabs for the 22 million people who hold the government-backed savings bonds.This is the second time in two months NationalSavingsand Investments (NS&I) has upped the premium bond prize fund rate, with one expert saying that the UK government’s savings bank is “pulling out all the stops” to attract more cash.When you buy premium bonds, you are entered into a monthly prize draw in which you can win tax-free sums between £25 and £1m.NS&I is increasing the prize fund rate – the proportion of the total invested amount paid out in prizes – from 3.8% to 4.35% a year with effect from September’s draw. It was previously upped from 3.3% to 3.8% with effect from July.As a result of the latest change, the odds of winning with each £1 bond number will improve from 22,000-1 to 21,000-1.NS&I estimates there will be 308,000 more prizes up for grabs in the September draw than there were in this month’s draw, with the prize pot increasing by about £63m to £497m.Crucially, it has boosted the number of higher-value prizes and trimmed the number of £25 ones.For example, the number of £100,000 prizes will rise from 83 this month to an estimated 95 in September, while the number of £50,000 payouts is going from 165 to 192. Meanwhile, the number of £25 prizes is being cut from just under 2.3m to about 1.7m.One of the advantages of premium bonds is that they are tax free, which is particularly good for higher-rate taxpayers. If you held the maximum amount of bonds – £50,000 worth – and won the equivalent of 4.35%, that would amount to £2,175 tax free.But one big downside is that they do not pay any interest and so are more vulnerable to inflation than other savings.And while you could strike it lucky and scoop a life-changing sum, there is no guarantee you will win anything at all.View image in fullscreenAn AJ Bell freedom of information request revealed that 62% of all premium bond holders had never won a prize.Photograph: Finnbarr Webster/AlamyA freedom of information (FoI) request submitted by the investment platform AJ Bell earlier this year revealed that almost two-thirds (62%) of all premium bond holdershad never won a prize.If you want a guaranteed return, you should shop around for a decent bank or building society savings account. This week, there were easy-access savings accounts available paying up to 5% interest.Premium bonds may be particularly appealing to savers who have already used up their Isa allowance or who are likely to go over their personal savings allowance, says Caitlyn Eastell, an analyst at the data websiteMoneyfactscompare.co.uk.The personal savings allowance is the amount of interest you can receive from non-Isa savings accounts without having to pay tax on it. The allowance is £1,000 for basic-rate taxpayers and £500 for higher-rate ones (and up to £5,000 if you earn less than £17,570 a year).But, says Eastell, despite the improved odds, premium bonds are a game of chance, and the 4.35% quoted figure “shouldn’t be mistaken for a headline rate”.She adds: “With the cost of living continuing to weigh on household budgets, it’s understandable savers may not want to leave their returns to chance.”Sarah Coles at AJ Bell says the prize fund rate has been upped by a decent amount and has been accompanied by a welcome shortening of the odds. But “it doesn’t change the fact that in an average month the average bond holder will win nothing”.Those with smaller amounts are even less likely to see anything resembling a return, she adds. AJ Bell’s FoI revealed that fewer than 1% of all prizes handed out between February 2025 and January 2026 went to accounts with a holding worth less than £1,000.Nevertheless, some experts believe cuts to the cash Isa allowance taking effect next spring may see more people put money into premium bonds.Every tax year you can save up to £20,000 in one Isa or split the allowance across multipleIsas, putting as much of that as you want into either cash or stocks and shares.But from 6 April 2027, the rules on where the money can go will change for anyone aged under 65. Instead of being able to put all of the money into a cash Isa, that elementwill be capped at £12,000.Explore more on these topicsSavingsConsumer affairsIsasCash IsasBanks and building societiesnewsShareReuse this content

title: The film Apollo 13 taught me how to survive heartbreak | Culture | The Guardian
description: After my engagement ended, I found myself repeatedly watching a movie about three astronauts trapped in a damaged spacecraft. It helped me see that sometimes the mere act of getting home is the success
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: After my engagement ended, I found myself repeatedly watching a movie about three astronauts trapped in a damaged spacecraft. It helped me see that sometimes the mere act of getting home is the success
Content: Illustration: Martin O'Neill/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Martin O'Neill/The GuardianMy cultural awakeningCultureThe film Apollo 13 taught me how to survive heartbreakAfter my engagement ended, I found myself repeatedly watching a movie about three astronauts trapped in a damaged spacecraft. It helped me see that sometimes the mere act of getting home is the successElf LyonsSat 22 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Failure is not an option” has always been my family’s catchphrase; it’s flight director Gene Kranz’s famous line in the film Apollo 13. When I tell people it’s our family motto, they often joke, “That’s healthy.” But it isn’t about being the best. It’s about refusing to stop being.I’ve loved Apollo 13 since I was a child. To me, Ron Howard’s 1995 adaptation of one of humanity’s greatest rescue missions is the perfect film to watch when you feel you might implode – because they got home. It is a film about a successful failure. When the Nasa director warns: “This could be the worst disaster Nasa’s ever experienced,” Kranz replies: “I believe this is going to be our finest hour.” Every time I watch that scene, I start crying.Since I was little, if I couldn’t understand an emotion, I used scientific examples and historical events as analogies and metaphors to explain my emotional state. For this reason, it was never the trapped floating astronauts led by Tom Hanks’s Jim Lovell who fascinated me. It was the white-shirted, spectacled, chain-smoking engineers and scientists in Mission Control.It was sexy, crew-cut Ed Harris saying: “Let’s work the problem, people. Let’s not make things worse by guessing.” It was Gary Sinise as Ken Mattingly refusing to take a break (“If they don’t get one, I don’t get one!”) as he tried to get his friends home.Mission Control embodied everything I loved about humanity and learning: teamwork, creativity, rationality, calmness and respect for the data and the facts. This was why, in 2025, when my own systems module exploded, Apollo 13 became my breakup movie. On a balmy night in Australia in April 2025, my relationship with my fiance ended in a concrete hotel room under a flightpathin Sydney, 15 minutes before I was due to perform to 2,000 people.double quotation markThe astronauts survive because they trust Mission Control … Mission Control became every WhatsApp group on my phoneInstantly, my brain shut down and went into survival mode. I moved into my own dreamlike Lunar Module (the lifeboat that saved the astronauts). I worked flat out but on reduced power. In 2025, that meant touring Australia and the UK with a show in which I pretended to be a horse, while also relearning three shows for the Edinburgh fringe.People suggested tragic weepies to watch: Call Me By Your Name, Twilight, Blue Valentine. They said: “You should let it out.” No, thank you. I have to be a horse later! Give me a film where there is categoricallyno chance of people having sex at all.I don’t need romance films full of tears. Words mean nothing to a depressed mime artist! Life isn’t romantic declarations. It is actions that matter. It is waking up, brushing your teeth and putting your clothes on. Survival is Ed Harris declaring, “We are not losing the crew!”The immediate explosion passed; survival mode lasted much longer. I was operational, but only just. The astronauts survive because they trust Mission Control. During the second half of 2025, Mission Control became every WhatsApp group on my phone. My friends and family made sure I ate, drove me to every show. My sister let me borrow and subsequently lose most of her clothes. My brother told me he loved me more than he had in his entire life. Everyone lied about my new haircut. They kept me on the right trajectory. They found the duct tape and rebuilt my lifeboat while I concentrated on putting one hoof in front of the other.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA kids’ film taught me the power of delusion – and helped me chase my standup dreamsRead moreWhenever I felt I couldn’t keep going, I returned to the film and revelled in the knowledge that it was based on truth. If Mission Control could get three men home from the other side of the moon, I could rebuild my confidence, travel the world as a horse and prepare for the Edinburgh fringe.Now, when people ask how I am, I tell them I’m like the crew of Apollo 13. I’m home. I had a rupture, but I landed – and, like Mission Control, I am focusing on the next mission.Because failure is not an option.Elf Lyons Is the Woman on the Edgeis at Pleasance Courtyard, Edinburgh, to 31 August.Share your cultural awakeningsYou can tell us how a cultural moment has prompted you to make a major life change by filling in the form below or emailing us on cultural.awakening@theguardian.com.Please share your story if you are 18 or over, anonymously if you wish.
