title: Dog Park: a delightful sitcom that will fill the Colin from Accounts shaped hole in your life | Television | The Guardian
description: This snort-aloud Australian comedy is sweet, hilarious – and a surprising examination of male loneliness and mid-life crisis. Who’s a good show then?!
Author: Rhik Samadder
Headline: This snort-aloud Australian comedy is sweet, hilarious – and a surprising examination of male loneliness and mid-life crisis. Who’s a good show then?!
Content: Park life … Grace Chow as Pamelia with little friend Big in Dog Park.Photograph: PRView image in fullscreenPark life … Grace Chow as Pamelia with little friend Big in Dog Park.Photograph: PRThe watcherTelevisionDog Park: a delightful sitcom that will fill the Colin from Accounts shaped hole in your lifeThis snort-aloud Australian comedy is sweet, hilarious – and a surprising examination of male loneliness and mid-life crisis. Who’s a good show then?!Rhik SamadderSat 22 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhenever I’m watching a programme that features an animal and I realise I’m expected to have a specific reaction to that animal, I run into a problem. I call it the Cuteness Assumptive Theory: Subjectivity inTelevisionissue (CATSIT for short). It boils down to this: if the success of your show relies on my finding your lead actor scrumptious-wumptious, you’ve already failed. We all like different things.The theory applies equally to humans. We all know that moment when some interchangeable heartthrob walks into the scene on a US sitcom. All the characters lose their minds, this being apparently the hottest person on Earth, while you’re sitting thinking, ‘Huh?’ It happens with child stars too. Casting directors have a narrow spectrum of children they think will elicit an “awww” response from audiences. The response usually elicited in me is “Couldn’t they find a better actor?” I’m not trying to be liked here! Anyway, it’s the animal version that came to mind this week, watching Dog Park.Dog Park(U, from Monday 24 August) centres on Roland, a misanthrope whose partner Emma has gone overseas for work. He’s been left in charge of their child, plus Beattie, a white poodle he never wanted. A neighbour, Sam, kidnaps Beattie to take her to the park to play with her friends. Roland’s wife has arranged this; she knows Roland will be a terrible dog-dad, only taking Beattie on joyless solo jogs if at all. Forced into the company of walkers, Roland comes to realise the importance of community and the joy of pooches. It sounds as trite as trifle, but hear me out.This downbeat comedy set in Victoria, Australia, is a surprisingly mature examination of male loneliness and midlife crisis. Roland is a borderline alcoholic grammar pedant who is quite literally running from depression. Working as a careers counsellor at a college, he encourages his young wards to write their future gravestones, a hilariously uninspiring exercise. He’s not thriving. You know how in Studio Ghibli films, you get interstitial shots of grass rustling or beetles creeping? Dog Park’s scenes are cut with moments of Roland getting annoyed at people in the grocery store or losing his rag at an Alexa. All worryingly relatable.His relationship might need one of those headstones. Roland and Emma are circling a breakup. They hurt each other and fumble to repair, while failing to hide this from their daughter. Rather than stock moments sketching such a breakdown, the show inhabits the barbed jokes, retyped texts, egg-shell conversations and frustrating phonecalls that feel painfully real. The show is sold as a comedy – and there are snort-aloud moments – yet more often I felt the prick of tears.View image in fullscreenJogging on … writer and co-creator Leon Ford as Roland in Dog Park.Photograph: PRBeing only at the start of the series, I don’t know if Roland and Emma make it. Perhaps theirs is a drawn-out game of fetch and return? However, I’m pretty sure his irascibility will be mellowed by the “dog park divas”, an eccentric band of gregarious day drinkers. Chief among these “dog tragics”, as Roland thinks of them, is Sam. Kind-eyed, gently provocative, she’s played by a radiant Celia Pacquola. If romance is in the air, it will surely come with a side order of pain and messiness. Or maybe Dog Park is playing a different game altogether.Writer and co-creator Leon Ford gives a thorny, moving performance as Roland, who distrusts joy and shuns friendship. “How’s your more interesting significant other?” joshes a colleague. “Dead, actually. She died,” he shoots back. This saltiness feels highly Australian. It put me in mind ofPatrick Brammall, who co-wroteColin from Accounts: another Aussie comedy about a dog I worried I wouldn’t find cute, the name of which I hated to boot. That show became my most beloved of recent years.And, actually, the dog is cute. Beattie has a sweet face, and ears that look like pigtails. I’m just delighted the show doesn’t rely on them. Unearned sentiment is what I struggle with, but Dog Park skips this hurdle, like an Australian kelpie at Crufts. Funny and frequently beautiful, it’s for dog people, but mostly it’s for people people. Who’s a good show? You’re a good show!Explore more on these topicsTelevisionThe watcherShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: The Voice gets a shake-up with new judge Kelly Rowland  | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: The Destiny’s Child star joins the hit singing contest. Plus: the essential BBC Four drama about America’s exit from Kabul. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: The Destiny’s Child star joins the hit singing contest. Plus: the essential BBC Four drama about America’s exit from Kabul. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Sing for survival …The Voice on ITV1.Photograph: Rachel Joseph/ITVView image in fullscreenSing for survival …The Voice on ITV1.Photograph: Rachel Joseph/ITVTV tonightTelevision & radioTV tonight: The Voice gets a shake-up with new judge Kelly RowlandThe Destiny’s Child star joins the hit singing contest. Plus: the essential BBC Four drama about America’s exit from Kabul. Here’s what to watch this eveningHollie Richardson,Hannah Verdier,Graeme Virtue,Ali Catterall,Phil HarrisonandSimon WardellSat 22 Aug 2026 01.15 EDTLast modified on Sat 22 Aug 2026 02.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Voice UK7pm, ITV1A new series calls for a new judge! Kelly Rowland will take a seat in the swivelling chairs for this year’s talent show, alongside Tom Jones, will.i.am, Tom Fletcher and Danny Jones. Emma Willis is back on hosting duties, though this could well be her last time. And there’s another fancy new feature: a “rewind” button that gives the judges an opportunity to bring back a contestant they regret letting go.Hollie RichardsonDeal Or No Deal: Celebrity Special6pm, ITV1Comedian and actor Katherine Ryan has faced the infamous Banker before, but she’s back again for more drama. With no shortage of celebrity friends and a history of taking home the cash for charity, she’s as ready as anyone to open those 22 red boxes in the right order as Stephen Mulhern tries to keep up.Hannah VerdierAlan Carr’s Picture Slam6.30pm, BBC OneEyes front for Carr’s breezy “say what you see” quiz in which competing duos must correctly identify images against the clock. If the aim is to get the entire family shouting at the telly, the show’s arbitrary pick’n’mix – from classic Hollywood to smartphone app icons – is its secret weapon.Graeme VirtueMarvin Gaye: A Tribute at the Proms8pm, BBC TwoView image in fullscreenLet’s get it on … Marvin Gaye: A Tribute at the Proms on BBC Two.Photograph: BBC/ Andy ParadiseEdwin Outwater conducts, and guest singers including Luke James are on tonsil duty for the BBC Concert Orchestra’s celebration of the soul icon. Andi Oliver hosts proceedings, with new arrangements of I Heard It Through the Grapevine, Sexual Healing and Ain’t No Mountain High Enough.Ali CatterallKabul9pm, BBC FourThis essential drama about the fallout from the American decision to abandon Kabul in 2021 continues. As panic spreads, Gilles attempts to negotiate with the Taliban – but with no trust on either side, it seems risky. Meanwhile, Amina decides to flee, but can she keep Nooria safe in the meantime?PHNigel Farage: Where Does the Money Come From?9.30pm, Channel 5Reform’s taste for litigation arguably makes idle speculation about this question unwise. But Channel 5 are up for it anyway in this documentary which puts Farage’s finances under the microscope, exploring his donors and examining his various lucrative sidelines as a broadcaster and speaker.PHFilm choiceWe Dive at Dawn,1.25pm, BBC TwoView image in fullscreenLife or death … We Drive at Dawn on BBC Two.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyDespite dutifully fulfilling its propaganda brief, this 1943 film from Anthony Asquith works superbly in its own right as a tense wartime thriller. John Mills, that era’s go-to everyman, stars as the captain of the fictional submarine Sea Tiger. Sent on a mission to attack a new German battleship, he and his crew find themselves out on their own in the Baltic, facing mines, undersea nets and destroyers. Naturally, a can-do attitude prevails, but the tangled personal lives of the crew provide a comic distraction to the life-and-death stuff of winning the war.Simon WardellDoctor Strange, 8pm, Channel 4This is the movie that, for better or worse, introduced the multiverse to Marvel’s superhero franchise. It also chucked magic into the otherwise muscle-based mix – as practised by Benedict Cumberbatch’s arrogant brain surgeon turned wielder of the mystic arts. This gives the film an enjoyably psychedelic feel, as Strange battles rogue sorcerer Kaecilius (Mads Mikkelsen), and is oddly reminiscent of Christopher Nolan’s Inception and Tenet (it was released between the two) in its architecture-twisting, time-reversing spectacle.SWLive sportTest Cricket: England v Pakistan, 10.15am, Sky Sports CricketDay four of the first Test. The second Test at Lord’s starts on Thu at 10am on Sky Sports Main Event.Premier League Football: Hull v Man United, 11am, TNT Sports 1Followed by Brentford v Tottenham at 5pm on Sky Sports Main Event. Man City v Bournemouth is on Sun at 1pm on Sky Sports Main Event followed by Newcastle v Liverpool.Women’s Cycling: Tour of Britain, 12.15am, TNT Sports 2Stage four of the Tour of Britain from Llanidloes to Hay-on-Wye.Gymnastics: European Championships 2026, 3pm, BBC TwoDay four of the men’s event, with the individual apparatus finals.Men’s Cycling: La Vuelta a España, 3.15pm, TNT Sports 1Stage one is a time trial in Monaco, with Oscar Onley leading the British representation.Explore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV tonightfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Meet Fat Papi, the little-known NZ rapper catapulted to Billboard 100 fame | New Zealand | The Guardian
description: Kurdish New Zealander Baban Hussain has gained global fame with online hit he created with Australian producer
Author: Eva Corlett
Headline: Kurdish New Zealander Baban Hussain has gained global fame with online hit he created with Australian producer
Content: New Zealand rapper Fat Papi shot to fame after an influencer used his music as backing to a video about haircut.Photograph: Ahmed Gaber/The GuardianView image in fullscreenNew Zealand rapper Fat Papi shot to fame after an influencer used his music as backing to a video about haircut.Photograph: Ahmed Gaber/The GuardianNew ZealandMeet Fat Papi, the little-known NZ rapper catapulted to Billboard 100 fameKurdish New Zealander Baban Hussain has gained global fame with online hit he created with Australian producerEva Corlettin WellingtonFri 21 Aug 2026 20.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 22.56 EDTShareTwo months ago, Baban Hussain, a 22-year-old Kurdish New Zealander, was working from a self-run studio in Auckland, putting out music to a few thousand followers as little-known rapper Fat Papi.Then, as modern fairytales go, he made a viral hit that has amassed over 7.5bn views across YouTube, gained him nearly 10m new monthly listeners on Spotify, and catapulted him on to global charts – including the US Billboard Hot 100.The last feat made history: Hussain is the first Kurdish artist to land on the Billboard Hot 100, and only the second New Zealand rapper to do so.“It’s a whirlwind,” Hussain tells the Guardian on a video call from a hotel in New York City where he has been promoting his music and meeting with industry. “My life is completely different. It’s a very intense time and honestly amazing and everything we have ever wanted.”Hussain seems candid and relaxed despite having only spoken to media a handful of times. He is joined on the call by producer Owen Omen, an Australian-based artist known as Prodshushy, who is beaming in from Perth.Their now-viral song Freaked Out was released in May and initially got little attention.“It was doing terrible numbers,” Hussain says. After various attempts at promoting it online, Prodshushy released a short dance video, backed by a clip of the song where Fat Papi raps “Get that bag, you ain’t ever comin’ last.”It quickly clocked up 1.5m views and a couple of days later caught the attention of a UK-based TikTok influencer, Jocelyn Meiere, or Miss Diva Bob, who posted a video to her 3.1m followers of her slick bob haircut, using the song as a backing track.View image in fullscreenOwen Omen, who produces music under the name Prodshushy.Photograph: Emily Nettle“We look back a week later and it’s growing and growing,” Hussain says. “From that point, it was over, it was everywhere, it was insane.”TikTok has been flooded with copycat videos of people shaking their haircuts to Freaked Out, including British artist Raye. US rapper Megan Thee Stallion posted a video of her making enchiladas as she mouths the words.The song became number one on Shazam globally; hit the UK, Australia and US charts; and then debuted at 88 on the Billboard Hot 100.Omen, who is of Papua New Guinea and Solomon Islands descent, says it was “a surreal moment”.“No one where I’m from has ever reached this point in their career, like music producing-wise. It was such a big moment for me and also my people back home.”The song’s success has been similarly moving for Hussain, whose parents fled Iraq as refugees in 1999. He grew up within a tiny Kurdish community in Auckland, and was the only Kurdish student at his school.“It’s history, it’s insane,” he says. “I think that’s a big thing – actually just representing people and our home towns. Being able to do that for my people was insane. I still struggle to find the words to show love for that.”The duo only began working together four months ago, and met in person for the first time in July. Their collaboration came about after Hussain rapped over one of Prodshushy’s beats and sent it back to him.“I didn’t expect him to reply – he had 20,000 followers at the time, I had 800,” Hussain says. “But I was like, OK, I’m going to shoot my shot … and he really liked it.”The pair say they have an incredible “flow state” when working together, with Hussain praising Prodshushy’s mixing skills and wide array of influences – including hip-hop, trap and afro-beat – and Prodshushy lauding Fat Papi’s ability “to flow over any beat”.View image in fullscreenFat Papi says growing up listening to Kurdish music shaped his ear for different styles.Photograph: Ahmed Gaber/The GuardianHussain is drawn to the sounds of 2015 club music, US rapper Kid Ink, US record producer Mustard, as well as west coast, New York and New Jersey hip-hop. He believes growing up listening exclusively to Kurdish music shaped his ear for different styles.Gaining viral fame means every door is now open, Hussain says. “There is nothing too far away or anything we won’t reach for.”They have management and record deals, a new single dropping in September, and are scheduled to play at Australia’s four-date Spilt Milk festival in December. They aspire to one day play at Coachella, and to collaborate with other artists.To make this viral moment into something “bigger, forever” will require hard work, Hussain says. “Even if it doesn’t happen, we’ll definitely give it our best go, and we’ve got that confidence with us.”

title: From Booker-listed Marlon James to a memoir by Michael Douglas – the biggest books this autumn | Books | The Guardian
description: Midlife meditations from Barbara Kingsolver; musical portraits by Jonathan Coe and Yiyun Li; plus memoirs from Dustin Hoffman and Judi Dench – all among the coming season’s highlights
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Midlife meditations from Barbara Kingsolver; musical portraits by Jonathan Coe and Yiyun Li; plus memoirs from Dustin Hoffman and Judi Dench – all among the coming season’s highlights
Content: Illustration: Simon Pemberton/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Simon Pemberton/The GuardianBooksFrom Booker-listed Marlon James to a memoir by Michael Douglas – the biggest books this autumnMidlife meditations from Barbara Kingsolver; musical portraits by Jonathan Coe and Yiyun Li; plus memoirs from Dustin Hoffman and Judi Dench – all among the coming season’s highlightsSat 22 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTShareFictionThe DisappearersbyMarlon JamesHamish Hamilton, 3 SeptemberAfter a detour into mythic fantasy, the author of the Booker-winning A Brief History of Seven Killings returns to Jamaica. This account of a brutal homophobic attack on a group of gay actors in 1980s Kingston has already been longlisted for this year’s prize.The BridgebyColm TóibínPicador, 3 SeptemberTwenty years on, this short novel is a sequel to Tóibín’s exquisite story A Long Winter, set around a family tragedy in the isolated Pyrenees. Now the building of a bridge brings modernity, possibility and threat to a father and son, in a spare chronicle of longing and grief.The Golden HoursbyLouisa YoungMantle, 3 SeptemberYoung continues her aunt Elizabeth Jane Howard’s much-loved Cazalet Chronicles, bringing her story of a sprawling upper-middle-class English family into the swinging 60s.SwitzybyEmma ClineChatto & Windus, 10 SeptemberWith dementia making him increasingly confused, David is on his way to a clinic in Zurich to end his life while he still has the capacity to make a choice. Longlisted for the Booker prize, this is a bravura portrait of a failing mind, told from the inside.The RousebyChina MiévillePicador, 17 SeptemberA leading light of the New Weird, Miéville has been working on this stonking 1,000-page supernatural fantasy for two decades. Political intrigue, continent-hopping global conspiracy and uncanny mysteries unfold.View image in fullscreenThe HousekeeperbyRose TremainChatto & Windus, 17 SeptemberAn origin story for Daphne du Maurier’s enduring bestseller Rebecca is told from the perspective of the novelist’s secret lover Danni, housekeeper in a Cornish mansion, who is outraged to find herself recast on the page as the malevolent Mrs Danvers.StationsbyLouise KennedyBloomsbury, 24 SeptemberThe author of bestselling 2022 debut novel Trespasses, a Troubles-set love story recently adapted into a C4 drama starring Gillian Anderson, returns with a tale of friendship and loss. Róisín and Red meet in small-town Ireland in the 1980s and reconnect in a London squat, before Red is caught up in a cycle of poverty and addiction.Doom PaintingbyAK BlakemoreGranta, 24 SeptemberOne of our most exciting historical novelists takes on the peasants’ revolt, in a blow-by-blow account of unlikely leader Wat Tyler and the 16 days in 1381 that turned England upside down. With cinematic action and a relish for medieval vocabulary, it’s a punky successor to Hilary Mantel.View image in fullscreen(Left to right) Barbara Kingsolver, Marlon James, Bonnie Garmus,  Jonathan Coe, Yiyun Li and Emma Cline.Composite: Getty/Christopher L Proctor/Ricky Sai and Simon PembertonzAmerican HagwonbyMin Jin Lee4th Estate, 29 SeptemberThe hagwon or cram school is a symbol of Korea’s stress on education. This new saga from the Pachinko author follows a middle-class family, their life in ruins after the 1997 Asian financial crisis, who move to Sydney and then California in search of a better future for their children.PartitabyBarbara KingsolverFaber, 6 OctoberAfter the Pulitzer-winning Demon Copperhead, a retelling of David Copperfield set in Appalachia, Kingsolver returns with a quieter tale of midlife longing and regret. A gifted pianist, Livia used music to escape the sadness of her family life in rural Tennessee, but having married and resettled in her home town, an unexpected call from a former lover drags her back into the past.Life Out of OrderbyAudrey NiffeneggerJonathan Cape, 13 OctoberSet a quarter of a century on, this long-awaited sequel focuses on the daughter of the couple in The Time Traveler’s Wife. Alba has inherited her father’s extraordinary condition, jumping unpredictably across the decades, from a United States in turmoil to a dystopian future London. She’s torn between two lovers – one anchored in the present, and one a time traveller like herself.Peck & PeckbyBonnie GarmusManilla, 13 OctoberIn the follow-up to global bestseller Lessons in Chemistry, it’s 1982 New York and young Batter Gray lands a job at the eponymous poetry periodical, run by feuding twin brothers. Expect charm, quirk and literary rabbit holes.View image in fullscreenIn One Brief MomentAll EternitybyElif ShafakViking, 15 OctoberFrom the Booker and Women’s prize-shortlisted author, a study of French writer Gustave Flaubert refracted through the lives of the women around him, including his most iconic creation: Madame Bovary.Music Against the NightbyYiyun Li4th Estate, 22 OctoberSet at the end of the 18th century, against a background of global tumult, the Pulitzer winner’s historical epic is inspired by the lives of two musicians: Adelaide Percheron, born in French India, and the Irish John Field, the inventor of the nocturne, who will be brought together by love and talent.Lessons in HarmonybyJonathan CoeViking, 12 NovemberMusic is in the air this autumn: Coe’s latest follows the friendship between French dandy Maurice Ravel and English traditionalist Ralph Vaughan Williams, exploring creativity and national identity against the encroaching shadow of the first world war.Crime and thrillersSherlock Holmes, Miss Marple and George Smiley returnView image in fullscreenAutumn is back-to-school season for series authors, with William Boyd on the third of his cold war espionage novels starring travel writer Gabriel Dax. InCold Sunset(Viking, 3 September) our reluctant spy is on his way to Russia, to tussle with the KGB. Richard Osman serves up number two in his We Solve Murders franchise:We Chase Shadows(Viking, 10 September) sees Steve, Amy and Rosie – retired cop, private security officer and bestselling crime author respectively – investigate after a body is found in the Italian hills. Five years on, Janice Hallett publishes a sequel to her hit am-dram debut The Appeal, as the Fairway Players’ new production of Agatha Christie leads to murder inThe Silent Appeal(Viper, 3 September). The vigorous afterlife of the queen of crime continues elsewhere, with the first official new outing for Miss Marple,Murder at the Grand Alpine Hotelby Lucy Foley (HarperCollins, 22 September). A varied cast list, death on the mountaintop and plenty of suspects are guaranteed.Ian Rankin, known for his grumpy Edinburgh detective John Rebus, takes a new direction inThe Heights(Orion, 8 October), a standalone thriller set in a luxurious central London high-rise. And there’s a return to the world of John le Carré’s Circus in the latest from his son Nick Harkaway: inThe Taper Man(Viking, 5 November), George Smiley finds himself navigating the unlikely terrain of 1960s LA in search of a communist sleeper agent.Finally, a festive treat: 10 new adventures for the world’s most famous detective in short story anthologySherlock(Simon & Schuster, 5 November), with contributors including Sarah Perry, Joe Hill, Abir Mukherjee and Kate Mosse.NonfictionSwan Song: Diana, My SisterbyCharles SpencerPenguin Michael Joseph, 22 SeptemberThirty years after Princess Diana was killed in a car crash, her brother – whose euology at her funeral echoed around the world – tells the story of their upbringing and recounts the devastating week of her death.The CastlebyJon RonsonViking, 20 AugustA concerning late-night call from his teenage son marks the start of a strange journey into modern masculinity for the journalist and author of The Psychopath Test and So You’ve Been Publicly Shamed.The Future StartsWith UsbyGordon BrownSimon & Schuster, 1 SeptemberThe former PM tries to join the dots between two seemingly disparate political phenomena: the erosion of the international rules-based order, exacerbated by war and climate breakdown, and the fragmentation of the tight-knit communities that keep us connected at a local level.View image in fullscreenThe Great Dictator: A Life of Barbara CartlandbyMatthew SweetHodder & Stoughton, 10 SeptemberThe queen of romance novels wrote a scarcely believable 723 of them during her career – with a little help from an amanuensis or two. Historian Sweet tells the extraordinary story of a woman born into an upper‑middle-class family fallen on hard times, who navigated scandal and opprobrium to become one of the bestselling writers of the 20th century.Queens and Kings: An Unusually Personal HistorybyLucy WorsleyHodder & Stoughton, 3 SeptemberThe historian and chief curator of royal palaces brings a personal touch to some of British history’s pivotal moments, focusing on the places in which they unfolded, and in which Worsley herself has worked: Hampton Court, Kensington Palace and the Tower of London.All the Wrong MovesbyAnthony ScaramucciBodley Head, 17 SeptemberNot many political figures are able to give Liz Truss a run for her money in the shortest-ever-tenure stakes, but Scaramucci, Trump’s press secretary for just 10 days, is one of them. Since then he’s reinvented himself as one of the administration’s sharpest critics. His first book is an attempt to chart how the US went from stable postwar consensus to today’s “shitshow politics”.End Times FascismbyNaomi Kleinand Astra TaylorAllen Lane,15 SeptemberThinkers and activists Klein and Taylor have identified a distinctive strand of rightwing nihilism: the kind that seeks to reshape the world in its image, even as it devours the natural resources on which our survival depends (certain tech barons and authoritarian leaders may feel particularly seen). Here they offer both a diagnosis and a plan for resistance.Profits, Prophets, Coaches and Kings:(When) Do Leaders Make a Difference?byJared DiamondMariner, 22 SeptemberThe author of Guns, Germs and Steel, known for his analyses of the grand, impersonal forces that shape human destiny, returns with a timely book on the role of prominent individuals. What difference does a sports coach, a CEO or an erratic president really make to the fortunes of teams, companies and global civilisation?An Unexpected Life: A MemoirbyGloria SteinemEbury, 22 SeptemberA totemic figure in American feminism, Steinem sought to carry the momentum of the civil rights era into what became known as the women’s liberation movement. Here she writes about her childhood and political awakening, and reflects from the present moment on nearly 60 years of activism.View image in fullscreen(Left to right) Joe Biden, Colin Kaepernick, Naomi Klein, Malcolm Gladwell and Judi Dench.Composite: Getty and Simon PembertonHawking: His Life and WorkbyGraham FarmeloJohn Murray, 24 SeptemberIn the first authorised biography of Stephen Hawking, Farmelo paints an intimate portrait of the acclaimed physicist based on unique access to his diaries and letters, as well as interviews with family and close associates.The American Way of Killing:The Invention of an EpidemicbyMalcolm GladwellAbacus,29 SeptemberThe author of The Tipping Point asks why the United States has ended up being so much more violent than comparable countries around the world. From a Chicago ER to a 17th-century court case, he explores stories that may hold the key to what he describes as “the most pressing of all American social problems”.View image in fullscreenBlockers: Rebels in the Deep Stateby Michael LewisAllen Lane, 6 OctoberLewis’s pacy, high-stakes nonfiction has been drawing readers since 1989’s Liar’s Poker, an account of his time on Wall Street in the 1980s. Here he deploys his powers of narration to tell the story of how the US Department of Government Efficiency (Doge) sought to dismantle the state – though his real subject is the principled civil servants who stood in the way of Elon Musk’s campaign of vandalism.Requiem for GazabyJoe Sacco and Chris HedgesJonathan Cape, 8 OctoberThe master of graphic reportage and author of Palestine teams up with veteran war correspondent Hedges to document the devastating Israeli war on Gaza and its human impact. Interviewing 29 displaced Palestinian families, Sacco and Hedges tell stories of death, destruction and resilience.The Perilous FightbyColin KaepernickGrand Central Publishing, 8 OctoberThe NFL quarterback made history in 2016 when he knelt for the US national anthem, rather than standing. Since that time, “taking the knee” has become an emblem of the fight for racial justice, in the US and beyond. In his memoir, Kaepernick traces the relationships and experiences that culminated in a pivotal sporting and political moment.Promise Me, AmericabyJoe BidenJohn Murray, 17 NovemberA year on from 107 Days, in which former vice-president Kamala Harris detailed her boss’s failure to get out of the way, Joe Biden tells his side of the story in a book which promises to reveal “the deeply agonising calculation behind his decision … to step aside from the presidential race”.Pay Attentionby Laura KuenssbergCorsair,5 NovemberThe former BBC political editor’s first book reflects on 20 years of upheaval in British politics, and what the broadcaster perceives as being at the root of it all: a failure by the political class to really listen to what people have actually been saying.Holding Lightning: The Life, Loves and Artof Whitney HoustonbyEmily LordiWhite Rabbit,1 OctoberEnglish professor Lordi treats the career of one of pop’s greatest stars with the seriousness it deserves, but with emotional intelligence too, tracing the arc of Houston’s life from global success to personal tragedy.MemoirFrom Hollywood hijinks to political scandal – life stories to look out forView image in fullscreenIt’s another bumper autumn for Hollywood stars with plenty of tales to tell – though this year skews male. Michael Douglas’sOne Helluva Ride(Headline, 6 October) includes details of “affairs with some of the most celebrated actresses in Hollywood” and the “serious drug addiction that threatened to destroy his first marriage and career”. If you’re still in the mood for testosterone-laced hijinks after that, there’s Sylvester Stallone’sThe Steps(Seven Dials, 29 September), which charts the Rocky star’s 1970s journey from homelessness to the Oscars. For a more multilayered take on acting and fame, tryFictional Selvesby Kyle MacLachlan (Century, 29 September), whose talent in picking idiosyncratic roles such as such as Agent Cooper in Twin Peaks has earned him a cult following. And then there’s screen icon Dustin Hoffman, whose first memoirLook at Me(Gallery, 10 November), published as he prepares to enter his 10th decade, covers the pressures of being dubbed the “voice of a generation” after The Graduate, and his many acting roles since that extraordinary breakthrough. It would make a neat pairing with Watergate reporter Bob Woodward’s memoirSecrets(Simon & Schuster, 24 November): that era-defining scoop was dramatised in All the President’s Men, with Hoffman playing Woodward’s partner, Carl Bernstein.On the other side of the Atlantic, Judi Dench reminisces about a 70-year career inIs It Too Late to Make a Run for It?(Michael Joseph, 22 October). InVigilauntie(W&N, 3 September) actor and co-creator of the groundbreaking sketch show Goodness Gracious Me, Meera Syal, writes about family, frustration and making it as an Asian woman on TV, while another veteran of the small screen, Russell T Davies, charts a writing career that has spanned Coronation Street and Doctor Who inThe Queerest of Folk(Bantam, 8 October). Everyone’s favourite communist standup Alexei Sayle gets political inHow I’ve Tried to Change the World(W&N, 3 September), a memoir of protest through the decades, while actual politician and scourge of the BNP in her Barking constituency, Margaret Hodge, shares the lessons of a life on the frontlines inBattle Axe(William Collins, 10 September).

title: Hang Time review – a chilling picture of the horrors of racial violence | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Three men bicker and reflect like they’re chatting at a bar – yet this grimly beautiful piece of theatre at the Edinburgh international festival won’t let you forget their fate
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: Three men bicker and reflect like they’re chatting at a bar – yet this grimly beautiful piece of theatre at the Edinburgh international festival won’t let you forget their fate
Content: Full of life … Julian Rozzell, Bryce Foley and Kamal Bolden in Hang Time.Photograph: Danté Charles CrichlowView image in fullscreenFull of life … Julian Rozzell, Bryce Foley and Kamal Bolden in Hang Time.Photograph: Danté Charles CrichlowEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewHang Time review – a chilling picture of the horrors of racial violenceRoyal Lyceum theatre, EdinburghThree men bicker and reflect like they’re chatting at a bar – yet this grimly beautiful piece of theatre at the Edinburgh international festival won’t let you forget their fateMark FisherSat 22 Aug 2026 06.14 EDTLast modified on Sat 22 Aug 2026 06.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThree men are shooting the breeze. “We’re just talking – man to man to man,” says Slim (Kamal Bolden), an ex-con who believes in looking after number one. In a literal sense, he is right. They are just talking. In this short, grimly beautiful production, written and directed by Zora Howard for New York’sFlea theatre, they have the kind of all-male conversation you might hear in any bar – at turns needling, teasing, argumentative, romantic, trivial and spiky. They like nothing more than when an attractive woman walks by.Where Slim is always out for personal gain – a quick buck, a sexual misadventure – Bird (Julian Rozzell) carries the wisdom of age. He scorns Slim’s quick-fix philosophy, favouring old-fashioned values of loyalty, decency and privacy. Blood (Bryce Foley), the youngest of the three, is the romantic: the one who dreams of life beyond streets that seem to have stripped a community of ambition.Unhurried, they bicker about blues musicians: Slim is backingFreddie King, Bird sticking up forMuddy Waters, each winding the other up on a topic of little consequence. Their backchat is frequently funny, but they can be reflective, too: their failings as fathers and the role of the fathers who failed them. Most poignant is the talk about those they have lost. “A lot of ways to lose someone,” says Slim, whose time behind bars has made him a stranger to his family.Angels in America review – Tony Kushner’s five-hour fever dream predicts and reflects the US at 250Read moreAll this comes in bursts, as if we were overhearing snatches from afar. But although Slim is right to say they are just talking, in a theatrical sense, he is wrong. Thanks to the austere set design by Neal Wilkinson and the stark illumination of Reza Behjat’s lighting, we can never forget that these men, seemingly unknown to themselves, have beenlynched.Rigid and constrained, they dangle in space. At intervals between the conversation, Megan Culley’s sound design swells and the buzz of cicadas becomes a grating industrial ring. Their bodies droop and spasm. These men are at once full of life and deprived of life, killed by racist ideology. Hang Time is a dark and chilling testament.AtRoyal Lyceum theatre, Edinburgh, until 23 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026TheatreEdinburgh festivalRacereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Elouise Eftos: Aphrodite review – ‘Australia’s first attractive comedian’ asks if love is real | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Heckling herself in character as the Greek goddess, the standup delivers an intelligent, in-your-face show about sex and expectations
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: Heckling herself in character as the Greek goddess, the standup delivers an intelligent, in-your-face show about sex and expectations
Content: Ticklish gags … Elouise Eftos at Sydney comedy festival.Photograph: Ashley MarView image in fullscreenTicklish gags … Elouise Eftos at Sydney comedy festival.Photograph: Ashley MarEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewElouise Eftos: Aphrodite review – ‘Australia’s first attractive comedian’ asks if love is realPleasance Dome, EdinburghHeckling herself in character as the Greek goddess, the standup delivers an intelligent, in-your-face show about sex and expectationsBrian LoganSat 22 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou can’t argue with the opening gambit of Aphrodite: “I’ve never been in love and I don’t think it’s real.” Consider me grabbed. This is the follow-up to Elouise Eftos’s fantastically provocative 2025 debut,Australia’s First Attractive Comedian, and it’s another intelligent, in-your-face hour about men and women, sex and expectations. OK, so it doesn’t administer the shock of the new quite like its predecessor, and Eftos’s argument about love is not as authoritative as her impossibly high status requires. But Aphrodite consolidates Eftos as a gripping new presence on the comedy scene.View image in fullscreenEftos ends Aphrodite by dancing with her audienceIt starts with a steamy pop video, with theGreek-Australian Eftosin character as goddess of love Aphrodite – who then heckles the comic in interrupting voiceovers for the remainder of the show. Eftos has an Aphrodite side, she tells us, but an Athena too –andshe wants to be funny. That’s a combination forbidden to women, she posits, certainly if they want to find love with (whisper it) heterosexual men. That latter disappointing category of human is mocked here for its privilege, its fear of dancing, and because “being a straight man is a little bit gay”.All of this is delivered with amusing hauteur by an act who styles herself as infinitely sexier and cleverer than we riffraff in the audience. There’s arresting material about the Eftos approach to flirting, the historical roots of misogyny (in medicine, in the church) and, as her tone turns more serious, about violent porn too. Visibly emotional, Eftos also tells the story of the life her grandmother led, one of brutally narrow marital and professional horizons.Courtney Büchner: One of the Girls review – all aboard for a rollercoaster relationshipRead moreThat tells a powerful tale of gender injustice, and contextualises the comic’s scepticism of romance in a world where true equality is beyond us. But that’s an argument Eftos never quite lands, as she insists on being both equalandworshipped, bringing the show to a slightly indistinct end. But if Aphrodite doesn’t scale Olympian heights, it does offer us trenchant feminist thinking, all sorts of sass, and lots of ticklish gags aboutGomez Addamsand the secret sauciness of bus travel.AtPleasance Dome, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Comedy (Stage)Edinburgh festivalComedy (Culture)FeminismWomen (Life and style)Women (Society)reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Dirty Dancer review – Swayze stan is like a whirlwind as she replays 80s favourite | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Melissa Firlit recreates Dirty Dancing in a one-woman show that mixes trivia, personal memories and a singalong
Author: Chris Wiegand
Headline: Melissa Firlit recreates Dirty Dancing in a one-woman show that mixes trivia, personal memories and a singalong
Content: Dirty Dancer, written and performed by Melissa Firlit.Photograph: Bjorn BolinderView image in fullscreenDirty Dancer, written and performed by Melissa Firlit.Photograph: Bjorn BolinderEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewDirty Dancer review – Swayze stan is like a whirlwind as she replays 80s favouriteUnderbelly Cowgate, EdinburghMelissa Firlit recreates Dirty Dancing in a one-woman show that mixes trivia, personal memories and a singalongChris WiegandSat 22 Aug 2026 04.15 EDTLast modified on Sat 22 Aug 2026 05.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDirty Dancing was the first VHS in our house: snazzy purple box, pure 80s brushstroke title, alluring 15 certificate – and all that slo-mo, black-and-white grinding to the Ronettes before it even begins. I’m not the only one who remembers their first viewing. Melissa Firlit watched the film again and again. Now she recreates the whole thing, from the drive to the Catskills resort, toPatrick Swayzeand Jennifer Grey’s lift, in this fizzy one-woman show.With a coat stand for costumes and a box of props (yes, she’s carried a watermelon), Firlit strikes a fangirl pose as she whirls us through the film that “changed the trajectory of all films for ever forward”. Going scene by scene, sometimes line by line (“nobody puts Baby in a corner!”), she steps through each mambo, salsa, cha-cha-cha and merengue, with movement direction by Kristyn Pope. Firlit salutes Cynthia Rhodes’ lightning legs, recruits audience members to teach them the Swayze swivel and leads us in a slow handclap for smarmy Neil (played on screen by Lonny Price, who co-directs the fringe musicalThe Real Kyle McCarrenacross town).View image in fullscreenMelissa Firlit with the ‘Johnny Castle’ jacket.Photograph: Elaine WongTonight’s audience isn’t the liveliest and doesn’t seem to know the words for a singalong of the soundtrack, yet Firlit isn’t deterred. Directed by Michael Thomas Walker, she puts herself in the shoes of Grey’s naive Baby, casting a leather jacket as Swayze’s rebellious Johnny Castle, and channels her inner teenager. She also draws early parallels with her own coming of age, yet these are swiftly sidelined. You want to know more about her – and screenwriter Eleanor Bergstein, who was inspired by her own family holidays to the Catskills.Courtney Büchner: One of the Girls review – all aboard for a rollercoaster relationshipRead moreIt plays like a trivia-packed podcast or viewing party, steadfastly following the film’s chronology. Amid some hit-and-miss tomfoolery, Firlit brings a starkness to the abortion plot and is sharp on the class structure at Kellerman’s. Pop-culture segues include cameos for detective Briscoe from Law & Order, another character played by Baby’s father, Jerry Orbach. (Sadly, no waspish appearances for Emily from Gilmore Girls, portrayed by Baby’s mother,Kelly Bishop.)With a literally uplifting ending, it’s an uptempo night – to misquote Swayze, she’s like a whirlwind – and there’s plenty of audience participation. If that fills you with dread, just put yourself in a corner.AtUnderbelly Cowgate, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026TheatreDirty DancingPatrick SwayzeComedy (Stage)DanceComedy (Culture)reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Wiping My Mother’s Arse review – confusion and subterfuge in a care home | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Iain Heggie’s rejigged 2001 play – now ensconced in the world of voice notes and vapes – is very funny, but the lighter moments jar with some sobering subtexts
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: Iain Heggie’s rejigged 2001 play – now ensconced in the world of voice notes and vapes – is very funny, but the lighter moments jar with some sobering subtexts
Content: Care package … Anne Kidd and David Rankine in Wiping My Mother’s Arse.Photograph: Tommy Ga-Ken WanView image in fullscreenCare package … Anne Kidd and David Rankine in Wiping My Mother’s Arse.Photograph: Tommy Ga-Ken WanTheatreReviewWiping My Mother’s Arse review – confusion and subterfuge in a care homePitlochry Festival theatreIain Heggie’s rejigged 2001 play – now ensconced in the world of voice notes and vapes – is very funny, but the lighter moments jar with some sobering subtextsMark FisherSat 22 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThese days, shows about care homes, dementia and end of life are very common, but when Iain Heggie’s splendidly named Wiping My Mother’s Arsepremiered in 2001, it was ahead of the curve. It is set in an overstretched nursing home where Andrene (Anne Kidd) has developed a close relationship with her care worker, Larry (Johnny McKnight), little realising he previously spent five years living with her son, Derek (David Rankine). Cue the comedy of confusion and subterfuge.The play’s fault line runs through questions of care, compassion and money. The emotionally detached Derek has been happy to farm out the care of his mother while he lives at the other end of the country. He shows less interest in her welfare than he does in her bank account.Any compassion comes from Larry, who has the measure of Andrene’s short-term memory lapses, as well as the sense to recognise her moments of lucidity. Derek’s new love interest, Kath (Lisa Livingstone), also unaware of his history with Larry, is torn between empathy and acquisitiveness: if she sticks with Derek she could be in for a tidy inheritance.A History of Paper review – Shirley Henderson and Alan Cumming sing a fragile romanceRead moreIf this were a play to wear its politics on its sleeve, it would be about the monetisation of care. Even the unworldly Larry makes constant reference to money, either playing teasing games with Andrene – who has lost all sense of the price of things – or, more riskily, flushing out his ex-partner by making suspicious bank withdrawals. Andrene can only complain about her lot in a place where everything is about efficiency and routine, and nothing about family and home.These ideas are there, but it is not that kind of a play. Updated by Heggie to the era of podcasts, vapes and voice messages, it falls awkwardly between farce and drama. Sam Hardie’s spirited production is frequently funny, whether it is the running bad-taste amputee gag or Andrene’s “catastrophe bag” malapropisms. But it also has more sobering concerns about abusive relationships, homophobia and alienation that are at odds with the playwright’s lighter tone. It is a play of some charm that never quite lives up to the subversive promise of its title.AtPitlochry Festival theatreuntil 5 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsTheatrePitlochry Festival theatreDementiaComedy (Stage)Comedy (Culture)Care workersSocial carereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Shabana Azeez: ‘The most disgusting thing I’ve seen on The Pitt? American coffee’ | Television | The Guardian
description: The Australian actor on posing as a patient for medical schools, having multiple birthdays on The Airport Chaplain and the song ‘nobody likes’ by the Strokes
Author: Rafqa Touma
Headline: The Australian actor on posing as a patient for medical schools, having multiple birthdays on The Airport Chaplain and the song ‘nobody likes’ by the Strokes
Content: 7:15The most disgusting thing Shabana Azeez did on The Pitt | 10 chaotic questions – video10 Chaotic QuestionsTelevisionShabana Azeez: ‘The most disgusting thing I’ve seen on The Pitt? American coffee’The Australian actor on posing as a patient for medical schools, having multiple birthdays on The Airport Chaplain and the song ‘nobody likes’ by the StrokesRafqa ToumaSat 22 Aug 2026 18.00 EDTFirst published on Wed 22 Jul 2026 11.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhat is the most disgusting thing you saw on the set ofThe Pitt?I mean, American coffee. It’s bad over there. The de-gloved leg was gross. I saw a full vaginal birth. I drilled into a skull!Did you enjoy that?I did like that. I really liked that. But, actually, I broke the rig. I haven’t spoken about this publicly, actually. It was, like, a US$75,000 rig.When you shoot, you shoot the same thing over again … and we’re shooting my coverage on my face. We’re not looking at the rig, so I have to fake it, right? So I faked it a bunch of times. And then we were shooting the rig’s coverage, and they went: “Do it.” And I only knew how tough it is to drill through an actual human skull because I’d talked to a bunch of doctors [about] how much force I should be putting on it. So I start doing it like I would a human skull. But this thing on the inside is made of styrofoam or something. So I go clean into that guy’s head. And it’s just silent.So it looked like you’d torn a human head apart?It was horrible. In a car crash, I wouldn’t have that much adrenaline. I regret everything.View image in fullscreen(L-R):  Azeez with Noah Wyle and Supriya Ganesh in The Pitt.Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyYou run an airport in your new show The Airport Chaplain. Who would be the worst two people to be sat in between on an airplane?Sorry, Elmo. I love Elmo, I really do. But imagine that guy laughing for 15 hours straight from one side of you. Kermit on the other side – no no no no no. Kermit and Miss Piggy. And they’ve just had a divorce.What has been your most cringe-worthy run-in with a celebrity?When we started shooting The Pitt season one, I’d never been to LA before. I didn’t know celebrities were real … It was post-strike, post-Covid. It was empty. Then Abbott Elementary started shooting, and I love Abbott Elementary. Quinta Brunson makes that show, she’s amazing. She just worked really hard and she represents really good stuff to me. And she walked past me one day. I came out of the sound station, she walked past me and I went “AH!”, I screamed and I fell to my knees. And Jalen [Thomas Brooks, who plays Mateo] came running out of his trailer and was like, “What happened? Who died? Who’s hurt?” And it was just Quinta Brunson walking past me.If you could shrink any person to have them sit on your shoulder for the rest of your life, who would you pick?Is that like a punishment?!No, they are a willing companion. They want to hang out with you!If they’re willing, it could be somebody I don’t know. Martin Scorsese. And then I start directing, and I’m really good.View image in fullscreen‘I actually had three birthdays on the set of The Airport Chaplain’ … Hugo Weaving and Shabana Azeez in The Airport Chaplain.Photograph: Ben King/SBSTell us about your most recently played song.I get really obsessed with songs. I’ll just listen to one song for two weeks straight. Right now, one of my favourite songs from my childhood is Machu Picchu by the Strokes. Nobody likes that song by the Strokes. It’s not one of their most popular songs but, for me, it tickles a part of my brain.What is the strangest job you’ve ever had?I was a simulated patient for medical schools. It was different every day. Some days you have appendicitis, so you’d have reflex pain or tenderness. When they figured out I could cry on cue, they’d give me a silicone baby and my baby would be sick and I would just cry. You’d be in a room with a one-way mirror, like an interrogation room. All the students would sit in the tutorial room and I would sit in the other room, and students would come in three at a time and try to navigate the situation. Everybody thinks they can handle it, and then you start crying in front of them and they panic. It was really fun.What is your secret talent?[Azeez tries to juggle using ourcamera lens caps and some scrunched-up pieces of paper. She does not necessarily succeed but must be commended for the valiant effort.]Do you have a nemesis?Honestly, me from five minutes ago. It’s so hard being alive and I have to live with me. Do you know what I’m saying?Adam Liaw: ‘The most famous person I’ve cooked for? Gordon Ramsay. My wife spilled a jug of water over him’Read moreWhen was the last time you lied?I lie all the time. I love it. I think it’s so fun. Never genuine lies. But I’ll just be like: “I’m 45 years old.” And I’ll double down until they believe me. I actually had three birthdays on the set of The Airport Chaplain. That was fun. That was a good week. I had three birthdays in one week. And eventually I was the boy who cried wolf. By the time it was actually my birthday, nobody cared.What is your most controversial pop culture opinion?I think we should care less about pop culture. I’m so sorry but what is it contributing to us? There’s war, there are things happening in the world that matter. And then there are people being like, “Who wore this dress better?” Who cares? Who actually cares?Comedy has a place. Art has a place. I don’t want to do pop culture a discredit by being like, “It’s all vapid”, because it’s not. Pop culture can illuminate our culture in a way. It’s like holding up a mirror to who we actually are. What do we care about? What are we doing? We can have genuine conversations about this. But, “We like this girl because she is pretty”, is a waste of everybody’s time.Do you see your work as part of that pop culture that illuminates?I’ve been very lucky. My bigger projects have been really impact-driven. My first film was about coercive control and gendered violence in domestic relationships. My second film was about queer joy. It was really fun and silly, and a different way of having impact. My first big TV show is about gun control in season one, and then violence against healthcare workers in season two. So there’s a real political impact-driven statement there.The Airport Chaplain is on SBS and SBS On Demand in Australia and Netflix globally from 26 AugustExplore more on these topicsTelevision10 Chaotic QuestionsAustralian televisionThe PittfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘It was dark and deserted. I was drawn by the light’: Christine Rodgers’ best phone picture | Photography | The Guardian
description: A man at a bank counter in a border town in northern India, tension in the air: how could any photographer resist?
Author: Grace Holliday
Headline: A man at a bank counter in a border town in northern India, tension in the air: how could any photographer resist?
Content: Late Night Banking, 2024, shot on Samsung Galaxy S21.Photograph: Christine RodgersView image in fullscreenLate Night Banking, 2024, shot on Samsung Galaxy S21.Photograph: Christine RodgersSmart shotPhotography‘It was dark and deserted. I was drawn by the light’: Christine Rodgers’ best phone pictureA man at a bank counter in a border town in northern India, tension in the air: how could any photographer resist?Grace HollidaySat 22 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOver the last decade, Lancashire-born, London-based Christine Rodgers has trekked in Bhutan, Nepal and the Indian states and regions of Uttarakhand, Ladakh and Sikkim. “I’ve developed something of a passion for the Himalayas,” she says. “I love being in the mountains; not climbing, but walking and camping at altitude, in sight of the wonderful range of peaks.”Rodgers used to rely on her Olympus camera to take photographs on her trips, but has since switched predominantly to using her phone. “I love the immediacy,” she notes. “I did miss having a viewfinder at first, but I now feel completely at home with the screen.”‘The machine turned into a lonely character gazing at an empty beach’: Alon Goldsmith’s best phone pictureRead moreThis photograph was taken in 2024 in Melli, a town on the West Bengal-Sikkim border in northern India. It was after midnight when she arrived; her guide had stopped at the police station to collect passes for the area they would be trekking through.“Melli was mostly dark and deserted, apart from the police station and this bank branch. I was drawn initially by the light, and the blocks of colours of paint, then by the stillness of the man at the counter. There seems to be some kind of tension in the air, caused by a customer waiting there alone at this hour of night.”The shot is displayed in this year’sSummer Exhibition at the Royal Academyin London, one of three Rodgers took before quickly moving on. She never did find out the reason for the unease she sensed before stepping back into the night.Explore more on these topicsPhotographySmart shotfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Guide #257: What we lose when a medium ​built for the ear surrender​s to the camera | Culture | The Guardian
description: In this week’s newsletter: As platforms chase ​s​ubscribers, podcasts are losing their off‑screen charm​, leaving listeners to wonder whether the intimacy of audio can survive the studio lights
Author: Gwilym Mumford
Headline: In this week’s newsletter: As platforms chase ​s​ubscribers, podcasts are losing their off‑screen charm​, leaving listeners to wonder whether the intimacy of audio can survive the studio lights
Content: Seeing is believing … Amy Poehler and Olivia Coleman chat on Good Hang with Amy Poehler.Photograph: YouTubeView image in fullscreenSeeing is believing … Amy Poehler and Olivia Coleman chat on Good Hang with Amy Poehler.Photograph: YouTubeThe Guide newsletterCultureThe Guide #257: What we lose when a medium ​built for the ear surrender​s to the cameraIn this week’s newsletter: As platforms chase ​s​ubscribers, podcasts are losing their off‑screen charm​, leaving listeners to wonder whether the intimacy of audio can survive the studio lightsDon’t get The Guide delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereGwilym MumfordSat 22 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 22 Aug 2026 02.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis has been the year that podcasting properly, unapologetically “pivoted to video”. Yes, it’s been a progression that has been in the making for quite a while, arguably ever since Joe Rogan first trained a webcam at himself and whichever guest he was smoking weed with in his studio back in 2009 – but in 2026 the medium’s transformation from purely aural to audio/visual (often with more of an emphasis on the visual) is truly complete.In January, Netflix startedbroadcasting video versions of popular podcastsfrom The Ringer, iHeartMedia, Barstool and more, as well as continuing to make video pods of their own. That landgrab was a slightly desperate response to YouTube’s phenomenal success with visualised pods; after becoming the preferred podcast platform for most Americans in 2024, it managed the same featin the UK in 2026, overtaking Spotify. No wonder, then, that Spotify has – as part of a wider push to get people sticking to its platform for pods – continued to bolster viewing capabilities for its own pods too.Meanwhile, more and more podcast creators are running into the arms of video, wheeling cameras into studios that often resemble an Ikea showroom circa 2008, with their felt throw cushions and chairs that are absurdly poorly suited to facing someone and having an actual conversation with them. (I’m concerned about what all this pivoting to video is doing to these poor podcasters’ backs; they all seem to be sitting so uncomfortably, swivelling between guest and camera.)You might have guessed from the slightly sniffy tone that I’m not entirely on board with podcasting’s video pivot.Podcastshave long had a clearly defined role in my life: they are there for when I’m ironing, on my commute, at the gym or the ever-shrinking bit of time not glued to a screen. Adding video complicates that. If people are performing to camera as much as to microphone, you start to feel like watching them is the only way to get the whole picture. And some podcasters are just not suited to camera: I don’t want their true gift for audio to be diluted by them having to constantly think about the lens pointed squarely at their face. Let podcasts be podcasts, I say!But lately I’ve realised that my King Canute stance against this tide is futile. I need to learn to stop worrying and love – well, tolerate at least – the video pod. This is a permanent revolution – and one that does have its advantages. Making a show visual as well as aural allows podcasters to clip up their best bits and share them for potential new fans on social media, a crucial arrow in the quiver of smaller podcasts that lack the marketing budgets of their bigger competitors. It feels a bit churlish of me to deny them that out of sheer podcast purism.View image in fullscreenSee the shock … John Robins’s credit score meltdown from Elis James and John Robins podcast.Photograph: YouTubeWorse still for my militant anti-video pod stance, I have to shamefully concede that some of them work pretty well visually. Who would have thunk it, but it turns out that comedians, in particular, are good with a camera pointed at them: I’ll regularly try to catch a good moment from Elis James and John Robins that I enjoyed in audio form on video later on – just to see the redness of John’s face (pictured above), and the reality of his contempt as he embarks on awhite-hot rageat having a less than perfect credit score rating, say.Other podcasts, for example some of the Ringer stable, are starting to skilfully knit in clips and stills from the shows and films they are talking about, which is definitely an improvement over watching two people talk at each other over a desk for an hour. (The Rest is History’s own attempts – flashing up the odd picture of a historical figure mid chat – is a little less slick but just about does the job.)I still have quibbles. Many of these video podcasts will never look to me like anything other than bargain-basement daytime chatshows, causing them to shed the aura of their audio form. And I will never stop being infuriated by podcasters who forget that they have a listening audience as well as one watching on a screen. Gesticulations are completely useless to those who can’t see them, and please, if something funny happens in the studio, explain it to listeners rather than just bursting into guffaws and moving on. Maddening!skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhat I’m trying to say is: I still want most podcasts to stay podcasts, nattering away amiably in my ear while I’m at the supermarket. But I will concede that the video podcast isn’t a totally terrible idea, particularly when set against, say,AI-generated podcasts. But that’s a rant for another newsletter …To read the complete version of this newsletterplease subscribeto receive The Guide in your inbox every FridayExplore more on these topicsCultureThe Guide newsletterPodcastingPodcastsDigital medianewslettersShareReuse this content

title: ‘Embryonic’: lost novel by French film-maker Éric Rohmer is republished  | Movies | The Guardian
description: English translation of Élisabeth, the New Wave director’s 1946 book about young lovers in prewar Paris, receives rave reviews as precursor to auteur’s cinematic work
Author: Xan Brooks
Headline: English translation of Élisabeth, the New Wave director’s 1946 book about young lovers in prewar Paris, receives rave reviews as precursor to auteur’s cinematic work
Content: ‘He was always hiding his profession from his mother’ … Éric Rohmer on the set of Full Moon in Paris in 1984.Photograph: Photo 12/Photo12/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘He was always hiding his profession from his mother’ … Éric Rohmer on the set of Full Moon in Paris in 1984.Photograph: Photo 12/Photo12/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesMovies‘Embryonic’: lost novel by French film-maker Éric Rohmer is republishedEnglish translation of Élisabeth, the New Wave director’s 1946 book about young lovers in prewar Paris, receives rave reviews as precursor to auteur’s cinematic workXan BrooksSat 22 Aug 2026 05.54 EDTLast modified on Sat 22 Aug 2026 05.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the dog days of the second world war, 24-year-old Maurice Schérer wrote a tale of young lovers in prewar small-townFrance. He described lazy August swims in the Marne River east of Paris. He wrote about age-gap affairs and semi-incestuous flirtations. Schérer gallantly used a nom de plume, Gilbert Cordier, to shield his Catholic family from scandal, but he needn’t have bothered as his concerns were unfounded. The finished novel, Élisabeth, barely made a ripple and quickly slipped out of print. Undeterred, Scherer adopted a second pseudonym – Éric Rohmer – and decided to try his luck as a film-maker instead.Now – eight decades on from its first publication, 16 years on fromits author’s death– Élisabeth belatedly returns from the cold. Republished in an English-language translation by Aaron Kerner, Rohmer’s book has been greeted with glowing reviews, hailed as a lost modernist classic and a crucial origin story for the award-winning director of Claire’s Knee, The Green Ray and My Night at Maud’s. “It would be a rewarding, exciting read even if the identity of its author were unfamiliar,” wrote Richard Brody in the New Yorker. The fact that it’s by Rohmer? That’s the icing on the cake.View image in fullscreenThe new edition of Élisabeth by Éric Rohmer.Photograph: McNally Editions“On the one hand, to be honest, the book is a footnote,” says the novelist André Aciman, a longtime Rohmer fan who wrote the foreword to the new edition. “But it is also embryonic and full of Rohmerian moments. It takes on all the themes that will become more developed, complex and impactful in his films.”Rohmer was working as a freelance journalist in Nazi-occupied Paris when he wrote Élisabeth, which follows a loose-knit group of dreamers in the pregnant summer of 1939. Stung by the book’s failure, he moved on to film criticism and finally to directing, becoming an older member of a generation of French New Wave film-makers that included Claude Chabrol, Jean-Luc Godard and François Truffaut. “I didn’t believe in literature any longer,” he would later say. “I felt its time had passed [and] that cinema had supplanted it.”Cinema, Aciman says, provided Rohmer with his natural home. Plot elements that feel formulaic in Élisabeth are more honest and lively in his films. “There is something in his work that has always captured me,” he says. “The study of human behaviour and our unpredictable natures. Two people who are dying to sleep with each other but don’t. That’s probably why I project myself on to every character in every Rohmer film. I think, ‘Oh my God, I could be this man or this woman. That’s what I’d do or say in that situation.’”The critic Adrian Martin, an expert on New Wave cinema, says that Rohmer’s use of improvisation helped give his films a sense of freshness and freedom. “He shot with a very small crew, sometimes three or four people,” Martin says. “And what was important to him was the spontaneity of the actors and the dialogue. He didn’t like to do multiple takes. He didn’t even like to direct the actors very much. Sometimes he’d be off in the next room while the scene was being shot. He’d yell: ‘Just do it!’ and whatever the actors gave him was mostly what he wanted.”In person, by contrast, Rohmer remained private and secretive. Sometimes he claimed that he was born in Tulle and sometimes in Nancy; sometimes that his real name was Maurice and sometimes Jean-Marie. “Basically he was always hiding his profession from his mother,” Martin says. “She would have been ashamed and seen film-making as a bit of a dirty profession. His parents thought he was a teacher and that was seen as OK and respectable. But they never knew that he was writing about films and eventually directing them. It’s mind-boggling to think of anyone doing that now. His whole adult life was a complete secret to them.”View image in fullscreen‘The missteps and confusions of footloose French youth’ … Éric Rohmer’s 1983 film Pauline à la Plage.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyRohmer’s best-loved works – Claire’s Knee (1970),Pauline à la Plage(1983), the Tales of the Four Seasons (1990-1998) series – chiefly focus on the missteps and confusions of footloose French youth. His people are articulate and self-questioning, invariably to a fault. “My heroes, a little like Don Quixote, take themselves for characters in a novel,” the director once said. “But perhaps there is no novel.” The republished Élisabeth at least puts that notion to bed. Filled with sparky dialogue and crisp stage directions, it is the literary ancestor of Rohmer’s arthouse filmography and as close to a screenplay as a novel can get.“The thing about Rohmer is that he dug his own field,” Martin says. “He’s constantly telling the same story, just with these little variations. It’s always about friendship, love affairs, games of desire and flirtation. It’s never simply a matter of one person loving another person. They’re thinking: ‘Do I want to love this person – and why?’ They’re hyper-rationalising all the time. That’s the same field that Élisabeth is digging. The basic dynamic is already there.”“I don’t think it’s a great novel,” Martin adds. “It might even be too much to call it a wellspring. But it’s still fascinating. It’s the seeds, germ and kernel of everything he went on to achieve.”Explore more on these topicsFilmEric RohmerPublishingFranceEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Nigel Havers: ‘My biggest disappointment? Not playing James Bond’ | Life and style | The Guardian

Content: Nigel Havers: ‘The last lie I told? “We must have lunch sometime.”’Photograph: Stills Press/AlamyView image in fullscreenNigel Havers: ‘The last lie I told? “We must have lunch sometime.”’Photograph: Stills Press/AlamyThe Q&ALife and styleInterviewNigel Havers: ‘My biggest disappointment? He is married, has a daughter and lives in London.What is your greatest fear?Every actor has the same fear – ie, you’re never going to work again.What is your earliest memory?Being in a pram in London and there being a road accident ahead and saying to my mother, “Go quickly, I want to see what’s happened.”Which living person do you most admire, and why?The king – because he’s been through quite a bit and I think he’s come out the other side brilliantly.What is the trait you most deplore in yourself?I’m over-tidy.What is the trait you most deplore in others?When they don’t tell the truth.What was your most embarrassing moment?I was about six years old in a market square in Italy and my dad said, “Oh, those shorts would look perfect on you.” So he whipped my trousers off and I hadn’t got any knickers on.What is your most treasured possession?My new lawnmower.Stockard Channing: ‘I cried at the election of Joe Biden, thinking we were out of the woods. Wrong!’Read moreDescribe yourself in three wordsI am here.What scares you about getting older?Everything.Who is your celebrity crush?Julia Roberts.Would you choose fame or anonymity?A hard question for an actor to answer.What was the last lie that you told?“We must have lunch sometime.” Who was it? I’m not telling you.To whom would you most like to say sorry, and why?My first wife, because I left her.What or who is the greatest love of your life?My wife.What does love feel like?Cosy and warm.What was the best kiss of your life?I’m not telling you.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine.
