title: Could the macadamias hidden in Queensland’s rainforests be the key to saving ‘the world’s finest nut’? | Australian food and drink | The Guardian
description: While grown in huge numbers commercially, macadamias are a vulnerable crop. A group of wild Australian nut hunters is seeking to change that
Author: Susan Chenery
Headline: While grown in huge numbers commercially, macadamias are a vulnerable crop. A group of wild Australian nut hunters is seeking to change that
Content: Ian McConachie and traditional owner and Kabi Kabi man Russell Bennet. Australia did not start commercial production of macadamias until the 1960s.Photograph: Krystle Wright/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIan McConachie and traditional owner and Kabi Kabi man Russell Bennet. Australia did not start commercial production of macadamias until the 1960s.Photograph: Krystle Wright/The GuardianAustralian food and drinkCould the macadamias hidden in Queensland’s rainforests be the key to saving ‘the world’s finest nut’?While grown in huge numbers commercially, macadamias are a vulnerable crop. A group of wild Australian nut hunters is seeking to change thatSusan ChenerySat 22 Aug 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 22 Aug 2026 20.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWe are bouncing over a rough, steep gravel road on the hunt for macadamia trees in the wild. Here in the tangled rainforest at Mary’s Creek inQueenslandis the macadamia’s main ancestral home.Ian McConachie has always been partial to a macadamia nut. As a boy inBrisbanein the 1940s he used to climb fences to steal them from people’s backyards. “We’d put them in a little hole in the concrete under the house and hit them with a hammer.”Now 90, he has spent much of his life devoted to the nut, including developing a tree that has raised $2m in royalties for the Macadamia Conservation Trust, which seeks to preserve this scrappy rainforest plant.View image in fullscreenIan McConachie is a pioneer of the commercialisation of macadamia nuts.Photograph: Krystle Wright/The GuardianToday macadamias are a $2bn global industry, grown in industrial quantities in subtropical climates in Hawaii, the Americas, Africa and Asia. But there was a time when Aboriginal people traded them for rum and tobacco with the white settlers here on this country.“It is the world’s finest nut,” McConachie says. “It is an Australian icon and our only native plant that has become a commercial food.”A couple of kilometres from here livesMacadamia integrifolia, which genetic testing has shown is the genesis tree of 70% of macadamia trees grown commercially around the world.There are three other species:M. tetraphyllais also grown commercially, whileM. ternifoliaandM. janseniiare almost inedible, wild and rare.Macadamias have been cultivated commercially since the 1920s, starting in Hawaii. Australia didn’t start commercial production until the 1960s. Only two to three generations out of the wild is “terribly young in the world of horticulture”, McConachie says. “So we simply don’t know what the potential of the wild macadamia tree is.”After graduating from industrial chemistry and business management with a focus on food, McConachie spent 35 years in businesses involving macadamia nuts. Later, he developed 20 macadamia orchards in Gympie and Bundaberg for investor-owners. Australia was behind Hawaii in growing commercial crops, with the first domestic processing plant only opening in 1954.View image in fullscreenMcConachie with his published book on macadamias. He has spent decades walking the remnant rainforests to find and document wild macadamias in situ.Photograph: Krystle Wright/The GuardianGrowers were given a tax deduction to help establish a local industry, McConachie says. This also attracted organised crime, seeking to launder money. “I’ve got wonderful stories which can never be printed. A guy working for us was charged with murder.”All four macadamia species are native to a tiny patch of Australian subtropical rainforest in south-east Queensland and northern NSW. “Which is pretty much where everyone wants to live,” says Denise Bond, executive director of Wild Macadamia Conservation. “They [the trees] like expensive real estate, which makes them incredibly endangered because we’ve got so little rainforest left.”Wild trees may hold the key to the next generation of climate- and disease-resilient nuts. McConachie says for commercial macadamia farming, “one of the very few things Australia has got going for it is the wild trees and their genetic potential”.View image in fullscreenTraditional owner Russell Bennet says the wild macadamia trees’ modest appearance ‘is their problem – they get dozed over’.Photograph: Krystle Wright/The GuardianBut more than 80% of the habitat that these trees evolved in over 120m years is reduced to remnant now.One of the macadamia species,M. jansenii, is seriously endangered, so rare “a bushfire could totally wipe them out”, McConachie says. Their locations are kept secret to protect them. While the nuts are too bitter to eat, “it could be a major tool in terms of climate change because it is so hardy”. The other three species are listed as threatened or vulnerable.McConachie has spent decades walking the remnant rainforests not far from where he lives, to find and document wild macadamias in situ. In August, he and fellow macadamia conservationist Russell Bennet take me on one of their hunts.Bennet, a Kabi Kabi man, custodian and elder, who is driving, is known for his ability to spot them. “It’s some genetic ability handed down through the ancestors, I reckon,” he says.First Nations Australians, though, have received vanishingly little financial benefit from the nut’s global popularity.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFive Great ReadsEach week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhen he finds a new undocumented tree, Bennet says, “it’s almost like finding gold. You can go through a lot of rainforest and not see one.” Except in September, when they flower and put on a show. The rest of the year, their dark leaves retreat into the rainforest, easily overlooked.View image in fullscreenM. ternifolia, commonly known as the gympie nut, in bloom.Photograph: Krystle Wright/The Guardian“They’re quite cryptic,” says Bond, with a couple of trees scattered here and there.Their modesty, says Bennet, “is their problem – they get dozed over”.McConachie is “shocked” by the degradation of the trees we find. An invasive creeper called cat’s claw has been smothering them; some have been smashed by storms.We come to a sudden halt at a “Keep Out” sign. Behind it is logging machinery. The hills are denuded, the small macadamia trees struggling in the dust. “The rainforest is tired,” McConachie says. “Whether the remaining trees are still there is unknown.”View image in fullscreen‘One of the goals in the future will be to find out if we can store the genetics of the wild macadamias, so that they’re available for breeding for conservation,’ McConachie says.Photograph: Krystle Wright/The GuardianCultivated trees have significantly less genetic diversity than their wild counterparts, making those that remain “a genetic bank,” says Bond. “If anything were to happen, like a root rot fungus go through the commercial population, or any sort of pest or disease that commercial nuts can’t survive, if all the wild trees are gone you can’t go back and say, lets breed some resistance into the crop.”They should be safe in the state forests of Mary’s Creek, Amamoor and Imbil, the largest continuous area of habitat – “but they’re not,” says McConachie.View image in fullscreenAt his home, McConachie has handwritten descriptions of the four different types of macadamia.Photograph: Krystle Wright/The Guardian“We can conserve DNA, but we can’t regenerate it. So one of the goals in the future will be to find out if we can store the genetics of the wild macadamias, so that they’re available for breeding for conservation.”In 1981, McConachie and his wife, Jan, bought a rundown dairy farm near Wolvi. He flirted with other trees, mangoes, lychees, stone fruit, but quickly came back to his great love. After an extensive selection trial, he found a particularly hardy and accommodating tree, named it MCTI and secured planter breeding rights. “It has sold about a million and a half trees,” he says, “and raised about $2m in royalties.” All of that has been gifted to Wild Macadamia Conservation.“We’re probably all a bit eccentric,” he says of the group, “but we’re passionate about the need to conserve the wild genetics.”Explore more on these topicsAustralian food and drinkFoodQueenslandNative ingredients (Australia)AgriculturePlantsFarmingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Meera Sodha’s recipe for blackberry and almond cake | Food | The Guardian
description: Rich, velvety nuts are offset by zippy, seasonal berries in a cake for all occasions
Author: Meera Sodha
Headline: Rich, velvety nuts are offset by zippy, seasonal berries in a cake for all occasions
Content: ‘I never regret a slice’: Meera Sodha's blackberry and almond cake.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Mandy Thompson.View image in fullscreen‘I never regret a slice’: Meera Sodha's blackberry and almond cake.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Mandy Thompson.Meera Sodha recipesFoodMeera Sodha’s recipe for blackberry and almond cakeRich, velvety nuts are offset by zippy, seasonal berries in a cake for all occasionsMeera SodhaSat 22 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMost cakes I can take or leave, but I never regret a slice of almond cake. The density! The chewy crumb! The way it romances butter and other flavours! The ultimate almond cake, in the Sodha house, at least, isClaudia Roden’s orange and almond cake, which is made religiously for special occasions (of which there are many from December to March), but I wanted a more seasonal cake for a good friend’s August birthday. Blackberries are perfect (not least because we’re drowning in them right now), because they provide an excellent, zippy contrast to the almond’s velvety nature.Blackberry and almond cakeWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appPrep10 minCook1 hr 15 min, plus coolingServes8-10180g unsalted butter, melted, plus extra for greasing180g caster sugar150g ground almonds80g plain flour1 lemon, zest finely grated to get 1 tbsp1 tsp baking powder½ tsp fine sea salt500g blackberries, washed3 large eggs1½ tsp vanilla extract200g icing sugarHeat the oven to 190C (170C fan)/375F/gas 5, and grease and line a 20cm springform cake tin with baking paper.Put the sugar, almonds, flour, lemon zest, baking powder and salt in a bowl and whisk to combine. Sprinkle in 300g of the blackberries and stir to coat them in the dry ingredients. In a second bowl, mix the eggs, melted butter and vanilla extract, then pour into the bowl of dry ingredients and gently fold in until you have a smooth batter.Pour this into the lined tin, then bake for 45-55 minutes, until a skewer inserted into the centre comes out clean. Remove and leave to cool in the tin.While the cake is cooling, mash 150g of the remaining blackberries in a small bowl, then push them through a small sieve (or tea strainer) to extract the juice (eat or discard the pulp and seeds). Put the icing sugar in a small bowl, add three tablespoons of the blackberry juice, mix well until smooth, then mix in up to another tablespoon of blackberry juice, until the glaze is the thickness of double cream.Once the cake is cool, remove it from the tin and put on a plate. Slowly pour over the icing, then gently press in the remaining 50g blackberries to decorate. The cake will keep in the fridge for up to three days.Explore more on these topicsFoodMeera Sodha recipesFruitCakeBakingSummer food and drinkBritish food and drinkEggsrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Blind date: ‘There was a mature, polite peck on departure at a busy Manchester Piccadilly station’ | Dating | The Guardian
description: Susan, 74, a retired careers adviser, meets Pete, 72, a retired Methodist minister
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Susan, 74, a retired careers adviser, meets Pete, 72, a retired Methodist minister
Content:
Composite: Photography  by Anderson & Fabio De PaolaView image in fullscreenComposite: Photography  by Anderson & Fabio De PaolaBlind dateDatingBlind date: ‘There was a mature, polite peck on departure at a busy Manchester Piccadilly station’Susan, 74, a retired careers adviser, meets Pete, 72, a retired Methodist ministerSat 22 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleView image in fullscreenSusan on PeteWhat were you hoping for?A relaxed, friendly lunch with good and fun conversation.First impressionsPete was immediately welcoming and relaxed. I felt at ease pretty quickly.What did you talk about?An awful lot! Our optimism around our new PM. There was a good deal of common ground, including that I had twins, while he was a twin, and we both fall asleep at night listening to Radio 4 podcasts!Most awkward moment?There weren’t really any, except perhaps my revelation that I didn’t eat red meat … but that didn’t prove to be a problem.Good table manners?Impeccable.Best thing about Pete?His obvious kindness and sociability. His clear ability to have put his thoughts and beliefs into positive, meaningful action.Describe Pete in three words?Humanitarian, genuine, interesting.Q&AFancy a blind date?ShowBlind date is Saturday’s dating column: every week, two 
strangers are paired up for dinner and drinks, and then spill the beans 
to us, answering a set of questions. This runs, with a photograph we 
take of each dater before the date, in Saturday magazine (in the
 UK) and online attheguardian.comevery Saturday. It’s been running since 2009 – you canread all about how we put it together here.What questions will I be asked?We
 ask about age, location, occupation, hobbies, interests and the type of
 person you are looking to meet. If you do not think these questions 
cover everything you would like to know, tell us what’s on your mind.Can I choose who I match with?No,
 it’s a blind date! But we do ask you a bit about your interests, 
preferences, etc – the more you tell us, the better the match is likely 
to be.Can I pick the photograph?No, but don't worry: we'll choose the nicest ones.What personal details will appear?Your first name, job and age.How should I answer?Honestly
 but respectfully. Be mindful of how it will read to your date, and that
 Blind date reaches a large audience, in print and online.Will I see the other person’s answers?No. We may edit yours and theirs for a range of reasons, including length, and we may ask you for more details.Will you find me The One?We’ll try! Marriage! Babies!Can I do it in my home town?Only if it’s in the UK. Many of our applicants live in London, but we would love to hear from people living elsewhere.How to applyEmailblind.date@theguardian.comWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Would you introduce Pete to your friends?No reason why not – but to be honest, my family would be more important. He is very easy to get on with.What do you think Petemade of you?Well, I guess I will find that out here!Did you go on somewhere?No.And … did you kiss?A mature, polite peck on departure at a busy Manchester Piccadilly station.If you could change one thing about the afternoon what would it be?There were areas of conversation I would have liked to have gone a bit deeper, but it didn’t seem the occasion to do so.Marks out of 10?For a lunchtime out in excellent company and meeting my hopes, a very strong 8.Would you meet again?We exchanged numbers but there was no romantic spark … and I think my agnosticism would be a sticking point.View image in fullscreenSusan and Pete on their dateView image in fullscreenPete on SusanWhat were you hoping for?At the least, an interesting afternoon … possibly more.First impressions?Susan has a lovely smile.What did you talk about?What didn’t we talk about? Walking in the Peak District. Running half marathons. Family. A little about religion. The Labour party. Sailing. Cancer … the time went so quickly.Most awkward moment?Perhaps after getting the menu and noting that Susan is pescatarian.Good table manners?Very. We shared most of the lovely dishes brought for us.Best thing about Susan?She is very easy to talk with.Describe Susan in three words?Fascinating, attractive, lovely.Would you introduce Susan to your friends?Yes. She would get on well.What do you think Susan made of you?Someone who has travelled a lot – and perhaps talks too much.Did you go on somewhere?Only a walk back to the railway station together.Blind date: ‘I got the impression he liked me well enough, but who knows?’Read moreAnd … did you kiss?No. There was no spark of that kind.If you could change one thing about the afternoon what would it be?Not much. I had excellent company and great food. We were the last to leave the restaurant.Marks out of 10?8.5.Would you meet again?If I were in the areas of the Peak District we both know and love, we might go for a walk.Susan and Pete ate atStowin Manchester. title: I’d heard ringing in my ears before. This time, it didn’t stop | Health | The Guardian
description: Miranda Luby was only 36 years old when her tinnitus arrived in the middle of the night, without warning and for no clear reason
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Miranda Luby was only 36 years old when her tinnitus arrived in the middle of the night, without warning and for no clear reason
Content: ‘Tinnitus can be torturous for anyone, but for someone who worships the first birdcall breaking through a soundless dawn, who owns two dog-eared and underlined copies of Sara Maitland’s A Book of Silence, it felt especially cruel,’ writes Miranda Luby.Photograph: Carol Yepes/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Tinnitus can be torturous for anyone, but for someone who worships the first birdcall breaking through a soundless dawn, who owns two dog-eared and underlined copies of Sara Maitland’s A Book of Silence, it felt especially cruel,’ writes Miranda Luby.Photograph: Carol Yepes/Getty ImagesHealthI’d heard ringing in my ears before. This time, it didn’t stopMiranda Luby was only 36 years old when her tinnitus arrived in the middle of the night, without warning and for no clear reasonMiranda LubySat 22 Aug 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 22 Aug 2026 16.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne night two years ago I was lying in bed when I began to hear a high-pitched, electronic hum. The scene that followed would be comical if it wasn’t so traumatic. I roamed around the house in my PJs, frantically pressing my ears against various electrical appliances. It took half an hour to realise the sound was coming from inside my own head.I’d heard ringing in my ears before, rising then falling, like a one-note crescendo of an orchestra. As a kid I used to believe the myth it was the sound of dying ear cells, playing a swan song for a frequency I’d never hear again. This was different. This time, it didn’t stop.Fiona’s 14-year-old son Max was bright and gave enormous bear hugs. She lost him in an instant when his heart suddenly stoppedRead moreTinnitus is common, with a global burden similar to migraines. Fourteen per cent of adults experience tinnitus with 2% experiencing a severe form. It’s often triggered by age-related or noise-induced hearing loss, but I was only 36 and a trip to the audiologist revealed my hearing was perfect – the Kings Cross nightclubbing of my youth hadn’t come back to haunt me. Another trigger is stress.The first few days after the ringing began felt increasingly claustrophobic. The alarm-like sound that no one else could hear followed me everywhere: to my writing desk, to coffee with a friend, into the shower and, worst of all, back into bed.Tinnitus can be torturous for anyone, but for someone who worships the first birdcall breaking through a soundless dawn, who owns two dog-eared and underlined copies of Sara Maitland’s A Book of Silence– an exquisite manifesto of solitude and quiet– it felt especially cruel.My GP thought I might have an ear infection. I cried in her office, tears of relief. “I’ve never been so happy to have an infection,” I told her. She gave me drops, a thick mucousy liquid that blocked both ears and made the ringing significantly louder. My days were a constant battle against steadily rising panic. Meditation was useless, for obvious reasons.I drove to the ocean and sat there for hours. The dull roar of whitewater drowned out the sound and, there, I could breathe. I took the sea back to bed with me, a 10-hour playlist of deep-blue bliss. I dreamed about waves, but also about a bright light piercing the fog of sleep.View image in fullscreen‘The alarm-like sound that no one else could hear followed me everywhere: to my writing desk, to coffee with a friend, into the shower and, worst of all, back into bed.’Photograph: Tero Vesalainen/Getty Images/iStockphotoThe drops dried up. If there was an infection it was gone. Weeks passed, but the ringing remained. I fell down the research rabbit hole.Like all chronic conditions, you could spend a lot of money on trying to find a fix: supplements, acupuncture, hypnosis, antidepressants (not as a cure but a way to cope). But the most common advice is to just try to ignore it. To learn to live with it.Because here’s the most disconcerting thing about tinnitus: the sound doesn’t exist outside your perception of it. It’s a type of false alarm, created by your nervous systems and brain rather than an actual wave of sound in the air, and – like the way we aren’t bothered by our clothes brushing our skin all day long – the less you pay attention to it the less you hear it.double quotation markI raged, I cried, I begged the universe. I didn’t want to live with thisTrust me when I say this does not feel helpful, or at all believable, when a semi-trailer’s brakes have been squealing in your ears for two months. I raged, I cried, I begged the universe. I didn’t want to live with this. Icouldn’tlive with this. There had to be something physical happening to me that a professional could fix.It took seven excruciating weeks to get into an ENT. He performed test after test in his office before turning to me with a stern but sympathetic look. “There’s nothing wrong with you,” he said. And there was something in his voice. It felt like a magic spell, or some kind of blessing. Stop fighting this, it told me, you’re already free.Over the following months, slowly but surely, my tinnitus began to soften around the edges. Through both natural habituation and intentionally training my attention, my nervous system learned to focus on more important, beautiful and interesting things. Sometimes, while watching the sun rise or reading a book, I didn’t hear it at all.These days, although tinnitus is still my near-constant companion, I’ve stopped wishing things were different. Because when you remove hope and fear, some suffering transforms into a kind of melancholic but peaceful surrender.I didn’t think I could learn to live with tinnitus, but every day is more proof that I can.Now when stress causes the ringing to spike, or if I listen too hard for a silence that isn’t there, I refocus my attention on something I love and the sound soon stops bothering me. My new version of tranquility returns.Explore more on these topicsHealthfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Icons, new stars and First Nations excellence: 10 key shows from New Zealand fashion week | Fashion weeks | The Guardian
description: The event feted its 25 year anniversary with labels like Zambesi, promising emerging designers and an explosion of Māori and Indigenous culture
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The event feted its 25 year anniversary with labels like Zambesi, promising emerging designers and an explosion of Māori and Indigenous culture
Content: Twenty-Seven NamesPhotograph: Supplied by NZ Fashion WeekView image in fullscreenTwenty-Seven NamesPhotograph: Supplied by NZ Fashion WeekFashion weeksIcons, new stars and First Nations excellence: 10 key shows from New Zealand fashion weekThe event feted its 25 year anniversary with labels like Zambesi, promising emerging designers and an explosion of Māori and Indigenous culturePatty HuntingtonFri 21 Aug 2026 20.00 EDTShareNew Zealand fashion week took place in Auckland this week at the heritage-listed Shed 10 on Waitemata harbour and other venues across the city. Founded by Dame Pieter Stewart in 2001, now run by entrepreneur Feroz Ali, the 25th anniversary featured a mix of established names, exciting newcomers and a dramatically enhanced Indigenous program. The event boasted three separate group showcases of creatives from not just the Pacific region, but India, Taiwan and the US, in addition to the inauguralNew ZealandIndigenous fashion symposium.Karen WalkerView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenThe queen of Kiwi cool, Karen Walker, staged a takeover of the Auckland Art Gallery Toi o Tamaki on Wednesday evening to present a showcase called the Grand Tour which featured “current, future and archival” looks from the Karen Walker label, alongside sneakers and streetwear designed for her longtime collaborators Adidas Originals and Levi’s, including customised Japanese denim pieces for Levi’s Blue Tab line.Claudia LiView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenAotearoa’s most exciting “new” fashion name, Claudia Li is a Chinese-New Zealander who studied at London’s Central Saint Martins and later worked with JW Anderson and Brandon Maxwell on the Haus of Gaga label, before launching her eponymous line in New York in 2015. Her label has been worn by notables including Michelle Obama, Bella Hadid and Lady Gaga. Li now calls Auckland home once again, after returning during the Covid-19 pandemic. Known for her romantic, full-blown silhouettes, she unveiled a brand new made to order collection of sculptural silk taffeta wedding dresses and occasion wear.By KaiView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenMakaira Lee, an Auckland-based stylist and art director who has worked with brands including Ruby and YOUKNOW,unveiled her first collection on Thursday under the brand name By Kai. Tapping into her Fijian heritage, the minimalist women’s and men’s cotton and silk resort wear line came in a palette of ecru, khaki and olive green, with pops of canary yellow and a vintage blue and white floral fabric. It was styled back with accessories made from traditional Fijian woven voivoi (pandanus). Of note: a standout khaki safari jacket with a Nehru collar, teamed with matching cargo pants featuring deep side pockets.Jung-YingView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenOriginally from Canberra, William Fitzgerald moved to Wellington in 2012 to further his dance studies and two years later joined the Royal New Zealand Ballet Company. There, his other passion – making his own clothes – caught the attention of, among others, choreographer Loughlin Prior, who commissioned him to make costumes. The Australian-born designer ditched dancing in 2018 to work for Zambesi, then attended the Whitecliffe school of fashion and sustainability. Jung-Ying is the name of his new menswear label, a nod to his Chinese-Malaysian heritage (and in fact his middle name). Collection One, which features fluid tailoring crafted from deadstock and upcycled fabrics, is being sold at Auckland multi-brand concept boutique The Shelter.Iti ClothesView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenAnother of the week’s revelations – also with Australian connections – is Iti Clothes, founded by Christchurch native Jeorge Bradford in 2023. A graduate of University of Technology Sydney and now based in Moss Vale in the NSW Southern Highlands, he makes every garment himself, in a back yard studio. An elevated, genderless streetwear brand made entirely out of cotton drill and poplin, in vibrant primary colours, all Iti Clothing designs come in one size. From boxy short-sleeved shirts to voluminous balloon pants and shorts, the pieces often feature intricate woven panels and cotton tape trims.Kahui CollectiveView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenKāhui Collective, founded by Kiri Nathan, staged their biggest group show to date on Thursday. The nearly two-hour presentation showcased 16 Māori and Indigenous designers from places including Australia, Fiji, Taiwan and Alaska. Highlights included the McQueen of Māori fashion, veteran artist, designer and weaver Shona Tāwhiao, who sadly said it may be her last runway presentation. There was also a debut collection from Āhuru, a label from Māori designer Natalie Robb, which features labour-intensive knits crafted using generational hand-spinning techniques.Twenty Seven NamesView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenTwenty-Seven Names hasn’t shown at NZFW since 2018. For their big runway return founders Rachel Easting and Anjali Burnett went back to school – incidentally the duo originally met at primary school in Wellington. The collection was replete with collegiate references, from varsity jerseys to tunics layered over blouses with schoolgirlish Peter Pan collars and academic gowns for the finale. A striking series made from deadstock fabrics included a mid century-look miniskirt suit in mint green and a limemid calf-length trapeze coat made from 100% nylon.ZambesiView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenThe weather shined on Auckland this week, with sun every day. For Zambesi, clear skies injected absolute wow factor to their Friday morning show at an events space called Okahu, with near 360 degree views of Auckland harbour. The adjacent 200-metre-long Ōrakei Wharf became Zambesi’s runway, providing the perfect backdrop to their spring 2026 collection, Song to the Siren. Featuring featherlight tunics and separates in soft tulle, mesh and silk in a delicate colour palette of sea foam, aqua and mint green. They were layered with fluid tailoring accented with fringing and raffia details, which fluttered in the breeze. Pure magic.Nom*D and PlumeView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenMargi Robertson – sister of Zambesi creative director Liz Findlay - held an intimate show inside Kingy restaurant. The presentation was split in two: first up, showing new pieces at Robertson’s iconic Dunedin multi-brand boutique Plume, from international names including Ann Demeulemeester, Comme des Garçons and Undercover. Then came Robertson’s own Nom*D line, its milestone 81st collection, which popped with primary colours and superhero-style cartoon graphics. Retro swing jackets, trench coats and bombers were teamed with two-tone sack dresses, boxy skirts and culottes and some adorable Brady Bunch striped skinny knits.Beach BrainsView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenIt’s been a while since a Stolen Girlfriends Club show rocked New Zealand. Lately, SGC co-founder Dan Gosling has teamed up with Jody Coggan to grow lowkey local brand Beach Brains. The new label’s very first NZFW show definitely had the same vibe as Stolen Girlfriends Club’s wild punk runway presentations. Totally packed, the audience pumped, models charged out to a deafening soundtrack in a collection of relaxed tailoring, workwear, grungy plaid flannels and patent leather jackets, shirts and shorts. Designed “for the space between the beach and the city”, this elevated streetwear line only makes menswear, but women are buying it, Gosling said backstage. We also hear someone threw up in the front row. Party on.

title: Island-hopping through stone-age history in Ireland, Wales and the Isle of Man | Heritage | The Guardian
description: Exploring prehistory sites around the Irish Sea – that were old even before the pyramids were built – throws a magical light on our ancestors
Author: Kevin Rushby
Headline: Exploring prehistory sites around the Irish Sea – that were old even before the pyramids were built – throws a magical light on our ancestors
Content: The Memorial Cross on a hillside on the Isle of Man.Photograph: Jan Treger/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe Memorial Cross on a hillside on the Isle of Man.Photograph: Jan Treger/AlamyGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.HeritageIsland-hopping through stone-age history in Ireland, Wales and the Isle of ManExploring prehistory sites around the Irish Sea – that were old even before the pyramids were built – throws a magical light on our ancestorsKevin RushbySat 22 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 22 Aug 2026 06.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe guide was adamant. “I’ve picked human teeth out of there and I’m not doing it again.” The small group of tourists looked suitably aghast, except the boy. He was jiggling the wellington boots on his feet and singing to himself. He looked about 14. I sensed that he was the catalyst, the one to make things happen.“So, if anyone is planning to leave human remains in this ancient place,” went on the guide, throwing the boy a stern look, “I say, DON’T.”We had arrived on the visitor centre bus from nearby Knowth, the first stop on our tour ofNewgrange Neolithic site, 30 miles (50km) north of Dublin. I was on a circuit of the Irish Sea, a ferry and road trip to see the best ancient sites that ring this salty mere at the heart of these islands. It was here, around 5,100 years ago, that a new people arrived and, capitalising on the sea as a cultural superhighway, constructed a dazzling array of stone monuments. Some of Europe’s finest Neolithic passage tombs are here, notably at Newgrange, the only one you can enter. But as the guide was sternly pointing out, some modern folk are irresistibly drawn to leave the ashes of deceased relatives inside, especially at Newgrange.View image in fullscreenNewgrange is more than 5,000 years old.Photograph: Ruben Galvez/AlamyThe plush visitor centre had been informative but had not conveyed the deep atavistic intensity that drives such tributes. There was magic here. I wanted to feel it. I had a hunch this boy was in touch with it.“As for pets,” said our guide, “I want no dog or cat ashes either.”The boy was drumming his hands on his knees, hearing an unheard rhythm. We were about to walk up to the hallowed tumulus with its 19-metre-long passageway that leads to the central chamber, but our guide was determined to get that boy’s attention. “There,” she shouted. The boy’s head shot up. She was pointing at a set of wheelie bins in the corner. “I can promise you,” she went on, grimly, “that if I find your granny’s remains inside my Neolithic chamber, then her last resting place will be that green wheelie bin.”There was a stunned silence among the tourists. But not the boy. He immediately ran over to the bin, opened the lid and stared inside.“Nothing,” he reported, slamming it down. “She’s not there.”The guide looked nonplussed, then marched away towards the hill that is a tomb. “Follow me,” she commanded. “Do not leave the path.”Everyone obeyed, except the boy. He ran in a great arc off the path, arms flapping like shamanic wings.We had started our huge circular journey around the Irish Sea at Pentre Ifan, a magnificent tomb from 3500BC, sited on the same Pembrokeshire ridge that provided the bluestone for Stonehenge. I was travelling with my partner, Sophie, and our dog, Stevie, who had gone through complex hoops to prove he was not carrying either rabies or tapeworm into Ireland. He liked the first ferry, from Pembroke Dock to Rosslare; it had an excellent pet lounge, but what fascinated him was the sea. He could not stop staring. His reaction made me pay more attention to him. Could dogs, I wondered, also help connect us with the deep past? After all, their wolf heritage is 30,000 years old, yet they relive it every minute of their lives. If anyone could remember the Neolithic age, it was Stevie.double quotation markInside, Newgrange looks haphazard, but is perfect, a Rolex assembled by FlintstonesHe had been well cared for initially. We stayed near Wexford, in a dog-friendly hotel,Marlfield House, with superb gardens. Then we toured the ruins of the greatest Irish saint of them all, Kevin. His sixth-century seat atGlendalough, in County Wicklow, is now a busy pilgrimage site. Twelfth-centuryTrim Castlein County Meath was next, followed by the Hill of Tara with its ancient standing stone, the Lia Fáil. Here all the pagan kings of Ireland were crowned, so the legend goes.At its base, visitors had laid a collection of apples, flowers and coins. That puzzled me. Were the apples significant? Or had that gang of girls carrying hurling sticks just donated their unwanted snacks? Some people, it was clear, wanted such places to mean something, not simply be dusty artefacts.I persuaded Stevie to lie down on a nearby grassy mound. Under us was theMound of the Hostages, a chambered tomb that was already ancient when the Great Pyramid was built. Time slipped away. Those Neolithic people are so distant and mysterious. What we know for certain is almost nothing. They had cows … and dogs. I opened one eye. Stevie had gone. He’d given up communing with the stone age and gone after the hurling sticks.That night, we stayed in another excellent dog-friendly hotel,Bellinter House, and visitedMarcie Regan’sin Trim, a vibrant, dog-loving pub. Not until Newgrange did we meet the dreaded sign, NO DOGS. I’d been forced to leave him in the car, my dæmon, my conduit to the ancient.Our guide stopped us at the entrance to the great megalithic structure, a turf-topped hill walled with white quartz. Discovered largely intact in 1699, the entrance was guarded by the same five-tonne stone that sits there now, covered in mysterious swirling patterns. Behind was a narrow entrance and a passage that lay under 200,000 tonnes of stone and earth.View image in fullscreenPentre Ifan tomb in Pembrokeshire, which is on the same site that provided the bluestone for Stonehenge.Photograph: Paul Williams/Alamy“If you get claustrophobic,” said the guide, “you can leave at any time. Do not touch the carvings.”Out the corner of my eye, I saw the boy come running. He had done a lap of the monument, chanting to himself, his little sister close behind. The guide bowed her head and disappeared inside. The boy ran his fingertips over the carvings and followed. I went in next. My unsatisfied desire for stone age magic was about to be fulfilled.The tunnel is slightly kinked and rises imperceptibly. You don’t see the final chamber. The mystery grows. There are patterns on some stones. A deep silence descends. I thought of Stevie back in the car. They found the bones of a dog in here, and its DNA showed traces of wolf from both Europe and Asia. Stevie’s Neolithic moment, however, would have to wait.At the end of the corridor, we arrived in a small chamber. Above, the roof was made of massive stones. In more than 5,000 years, it has not leaked. It looks haphazard, but is perfect, a Rolex assembled by Flintstones. The most impressive thing, however, was not understood untilProf Michael O’Kellycame and stood in this chamber on 21 December 1967. Our guide was now going to recreate that event, and what has happened at dawn on every winter solstice since about 3150BC.double quotation markManx ancient monuments do not come with visitor centres and guides, they come only with a cast iron sign, ‘Ancient Monument’We were in complete darkness. The boy had pressed himself into a niche where a huge stone basin sat. Human remains, ancient ones, had been found there. And then, the guide touched a hidden switch and a golden light came creeping up the passageway towards us, finally illuminating a triple spiral of megalithic art carved into one giant stone. It was like hearing a deep harmonic chord, or the haunting cry of a night bird, something profound and enigmatic. I forgave the bus, the tickets, the gift shop – all the paraphernalia of the tourism business – and saw the genius of this recreation.Light slowly filled the chamber. We were all dumbstruck, except the boy. He spoke out loud and bold. “Question. Are there aliens here?”The guide shook her head impatiently. “I won’t have any talk of aliens.”The boy nodded and turned to his little sister. “That means there are.”Then he was gone, scurrying down the tunnel in a half crouch, humming to himself.A huge storm came in that night, downing trees and flooding roads. We drove through it to Belfast and hunkered down in ourhotel.View image in fullscreenKevin Rushby’s dog Stevie on the Isle of Man.Photograph: Kevin RushbyNext day, thankfully in calm weather, we sailed for the Isle of Man. Landing here was like travelling back in time, to around AD1950. Manx ancient monuments do not come with visitor centres and guides, they come only with a cast iron sign, “Ancient Monument”. We climbed the highest peak, Snaefell, visited several fabulous Celtic crosses and spent ages in the wonderfulManx Museum.Then, one afternoon, we left the car and walked through fields to the island’s most important Neolithic monument,Cashtal yn Ard. It was in a tussocky field behind a kissing gate and a small sign. No ticket required, only some imagination and, if possible, a stone age scent hound. Behind were ranged the dark hills. The monument itself is a collapsed passage tomb that has left the ghostly imprint of its shape in rows of pale stones, marking the entrance, the tunnel, and finally, a low portal into what is left of the central chamber. Nevertheless, Stevie seemed to know the layout. He ran to the entrance, bounded down the tunnel, dodged through the portal and stopped dead. We lay on our backs and watched the skies. After a few minutes, I sneaked a look at the dog. He was curled up asleep at the exact centre of the vanished chamber.Travel was provided byDiscover Ferries, the industry body for 12 ferry companies.Irish Ferries sails Pembroke to Rosslarefrom £190 forcar plus two (pets travel free).Isle of Man Steam Packet Companysails Belfast to Isle of Man from £179.50 for a car plus two (pets in cars free, pet-accessible cabins £75).Taking a dog to Irelandrequires micro-chipping, rabies jab and tapeworm treatment (Stevie’s documents were checked at Rosslare).Further information fromTourism Ireland,Fáilte Ireland, Tourism Northern IrelandandVisit Isle of ManExplore more on these topicsHeritageIreland holidaysIsle of ManWales holidaysEurope holidaysPembrokeshire holidaysCultural tripsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘My ability to cope was unravelling’: how I navigated ADHD and childbirth – and seven things I learned | Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder | The Guardian
description: Neurodivergence can make an already challenging process far trickier — and in the UK support isn’t automatically available. A new book aims to help mothers prepare
Author: Sarah Marsh
Headline: Neurodivergence can make an already challenging process far trickier — and in the UK support isn’t automatically available. A new book aims to help mothers prepare
Content: Sarah Marsh with her children.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSarah Marsh with her children.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianAttention deficit hyperactivity disorder‘My ability to cope was unravelling’: how I navigated ADHD and childbirth – and seven things I learnedNeurodivergence can make an already challenging process far trickier — and in the UK support isn’t automatically available. A new book aims to help mothers prepareSarah MarshSat 22 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 22 Aug 2026 00.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s 7am in a postnatal ward. I’ve been brought here having given birth around four hours earlier. I’m hot and have not slept since arriving at the hospital at 9pm for an induction, only to go into labour spontaneously before it could begin. All around me is incandescent hospital light and the sound of crying newborns. This would be challenging enough for someone who isn’t neurodivergent, but coupled with my attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) I could feel my ability to cope unravelling.I remember looking around, crying, unable to shut off the noise in my brain. “What if I don’t ever sleep again,” the little voice asked. I shut my eyes and the noise grew. Then there was my newborn son, lying next to me in a cot, and the fact that I had absolutely no idea how to look after him. I pressed the emergency buzzer and told the midwife who arrived that I could not breathe and needed to be discharged immediately. She said they couldn’t do that because I was under the mental health team and needed to speak to them first. I cried more.The rest of my stay in hospital is a blur. I begged anyone who came near my bed for sleeping pills. Eventually, with the help of my midwife and the mental health team, I was sent home that day.It was only a year later, when I learned I was neurodivergent, that my struggles that day finally made sense. Certain parts of becoming a parent are simply harder with ADHD. Birth itself strips away any sense of predictability, and ADHD brains often manage anxiety by controlling their environment – being on a postnatal ward, with its constant lights, noises, and the feeling of being trapped inside, can be sensory overload.View image in fullscreen‘Having ADHD has made me resilient.’Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianThe NHS currently has no consistent, ADHD-specific maternity pathway, so support for women with ADHD during childbirth varies widely and often depends on individual clinicians recognising and accommodating their needs, rather than on a standardised system.When I gave birth, I was told afterwards that nothing really exists to support women and research is limited. It prompted me to write a book about ADHD and becoming a parent to help other women. Here’s a summary of what I learned.Hormones affect those with ADHD moreScientists believe that ADHD symptoms can be affected by hormones, and astudy by King’s College London is aiming to look at exactly that.Oestrogen and progesterone are the two main female hormones, and both rise rapidly in pregnancy. Oestrogen has a stimulating effect on the brain – it boosts dopamine and serotonin, the chemicals behind focus, mood, and motivation – so when it’s high, ADHD symptoms tend to ease. Progesterone, which rises after ovulation and in pregnancy, may have an opposing effect on dopamine signalling to oestrogen and can even make ADHD medication less effective.In the first trimester, both hormones rise fast. Things often improve in the second trimester, when oestrogen levels are higher and more stable. Anecdotally, I heard from psychiatrists I interviewed that some women find their ADHD symptoms ease in pregnancy as a result. For others, this isn’t the case. There’s no universal rule, as hormones are complicated.A large study found that women with ADHD were over five times more likely to be diagnosed with postpartum depression than women without ADHD, because hormone levels drop suddenly after birth. In terms of coping, simply being aware of these changes is valuable – it lets you protect yourself during the periods when your endocrine system is affected most. Staying active can help as it releases endorphins and is a natural mood booster, as can putting together a postnatal plan in advance, to relieve pressure and make sure you have as much support as you need after birth.MedicationFor those with ADHD, the more pressing concern might be whether they can continue taking medication.When I was pregnant with my son, I continued taking the antidepressant citalopram. My psychiatrist explained that the potential risks associated with the drug were relatively small, and that the evidence linking it to harm was inconclusive. I weighed things up and decided that, for me, the risks of stopping a medication I’d been taking for seven years were greater than the potential risks of continuing it.As for ADHD medication, there isn’t a tremendous amount of research on its use during pregnancy, mainly due to the ethical challenges of studying pregnant women. Dr Catherine Durkin, joint presidential lead for women and mental health at the Royal College of Psychiatrists, says the key is to balance risk. “What are we treating? What are the risks of not treating it?” she says. Durkin also says that data on ADHD medication and breastfeeding is limited, and recommends discussing the matter with your specialist.Know your rightsView image in fullscreenFor people with ADHD, knowing how to access mental health support is vital.Photograph: FatCamera/Getty ImagesIf you have ADHD, you have more power and agency in the healthcare system than you might think. Not every healthcare professional understands ADHD, so it’s vital to know where to access appropriate perinatal mental health support if you need it. People with ADHD may be more vulnerable to experiencing mental health difficulties during pregnancy and the postnatal period, making appropriate support particularly important. Victoria White, a doula who specialises in helping those who are neurodivergent, says that under the Equality Act 2010, anyone with a chronic illness or disability can request reasonable adjustments to their care. “Neurodivergence falls under that,” she says. “Technically, self-diagnosis should count too, though that can be more difficult.”A reasonable adjustment could be as simple as visiting the birthing suite in advance to reduce anxiety. Laura Spence, a midwife who trained in Scotland 14 years ago, says: “Women have the right to most things; it’s their birth, their body, their baby. Nothing is set in stone.”Create a birth planMy son was measuring small, and my obstetrician wanted him to be born by 39 weeks because they were concerned he might not be growing as well as he should. His estimated size had dropped from the 14th to the 10th percentile – in other words, he was now smaller than approximately 90% of babies at the same stage of pregnancy. To help encourage labour to start, I was given a membrane sweep, a procedure where a midwife or doctor gently separates the membranes surrounding the baby from the cervix.Three days later my waters broke and I was told I had 24 hours for labour to start before they would need to induce me due to the increased risk of infection that comes with the waters being broken for too long. Luckily, moments before my booked induction, contractions started. Labour progressed quickly and was around five hours in total.If you have ADHD, do what you need to get through birth. Neurodivergent individuals may require more control, knowing when and how things will unfold. Or less. Ask for what you need.Plan for the postnatal periodView image in fullscreenMake a plan before bringing your baby home.Photograph: mihailomilovanovic/Getty ImagesIn the car on the way home from the hospital, I kept looking over at my son, worrying about every bump in the road and whether his tiny body could withstand it. My partner and I had no plan for what life would look like now. We hadn’t thought about a sleep schedule and barely had all the essentials such as a cot and a pram. In hindsight, a plan would have been smart. If I could go back, I’d focus on five key areas: sleep, feeding, changing clothes and nappies, stimulation, and love. That’s all your baby needs early on. I would have made a plan about how to manage each of these.It’s also helpful to note down essential appointments in advance: vaccinations, health checks and registering with a GP. Delegate this type of admin to your partner or a family member. You’ll be recovering. If you need mental health support, arrange it in advance.Ignore unhelpful expectationsThe idea of the perfect mother is a myth, but those with ADHD may feel the sting of falling short more acutely. After all, if you have ADHD, you’ve likely been criticised your whole life for doing things “wrong”. Focus on your strengths, whatever they may be. Having ADHD has made me resilient and I am much more able to cope than I give myself credit for.Watch out for burnoutReturning to work after having a child can sometimes mean the end of the workday simply marks the start of another shift – managing the household, bedtime routines and family needs. It can be hard to balance work, family and a social life. This challenge is amplified for those with ADHD, who tend to overcommit and then burn out. Watch for the key signs of burnout – exhaustion and fatigue, sadness and depression, a lack of motivation, and general disconnection from others – and prioritise your self-care. If you start to feel as if you might be about to hit a wall, then make more time for yourself.Mum, Interrupted by Sarah Marsh is out now (Jessica Kingsley, £14.99). To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. title: Tim Dowling: my working holiday just isn’t working | Family | The Guardian
description: The weather is unrelentingly glorious, the views are amazing, but I cling to the freelancer’s habit of never quite admitting I’m on holiday
Author: Tim Dowling
Headline: The weather is unrelentingly glorious, the views are amazing, but I cling to the freelancer’s habit of never quite admitting I’m on holiday
Content: Illustration: Selman Hosgor/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Selman Hosgor/The GuardianThe Tim Dowling columnFamilyTim Dowling: my working holiday just isn’t workingThe weather is unrelentingly glorious, the views are amazing, but I cling to the freelancer’s habit of never quite admitting I’m on holidayTim DowlingSat 22 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 22 Aug 2026 16.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the summer of 1995, I went on a family holiday to Portugal. On the first day I got a call from a UK magazine, asking if I would be interested in interviewing Meg Ryan, in three days’ time. I looked out to the pool, where my wife and my mother-in-law were pushing my infant son across the water in an inflatable ring.“Sure,” I said. I broke the news, packed my things, flew to London and, the next day, to LA.While no one who knows me would suggest I am overburdened by ambition, I still cling to the freelancer’s habit of never quite admitting to being on holiday: I bring work with me, I still accept assignments while I’m away, and I’m always a little cagey regarding my whereabouts.On Friday an email arrives, asking if I’m available to go on the radio next week. I know I should admit that I’m on holiday in the country, in a remote cottage with no phone reception and ropey internet, poorly tethered to civilisation by a mile of copper wire. And so, on balance, no thanks, maybe next time.“I can do it,” I type back.Over the weekend guests arrive, friends on their way somewhere else. The weather is unrelentingly glorious, the views are amazing and I’m worrying about how I’m going to manage a live radio interview three days hence.double quotation markMidweek more friends arrive… but negotiating the use of the single shower proves easier than rationing the limited bandwidth“How long are you here for?” our friend asks.“Nearly two weeks,” my wife says.“How lucky!” our friend says.“The thing about him,” my wife says, pointing at me, “is he can work anywhere.”“I mean, I’m sort of working now,” I say, indicating the laptop in front of me.“You’ve been online all morning,” my wife says. “When are we going out?”“That’s the thing about slow internet,” I say. “Everything takes longer.” In truth, I am trying to download a crossword puzzle.On Wednesday morning everyone goes to the beach while I stay with the dog. At the appointed hour I click the link the radio programme sent me. A technician comes on the line.“Hi,” I say. “Can you hear me?”“You sound weird,” he says.Tim Dowling: how many electricians does it take to install an electric car charger?Read more“Do I?”“Never mind, at least the line’s clear,” he says. “You’re on at 20 past, so just keep the link open until then.”I think: the whole time?My wife and our friends return two hours later.“The sea is unbelievable,” she says. “How was your radio thing?”“Fine,” I say. “The link held, and Janet Street-Porter did most of the talking anyway.”“That’s lucky,” she says. “What’s for lunch?”More friends arrive, and there is some overlap, but negotiating the use of the single shower proves easier than rationing the limited bandwidth. Even when people aren’t using their phones, their phones are using the internet.“Two weeks! How amazing!” says a new arrival.“The thing about him is, he can work anywhere,” my wife says.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“At the moment, I can’t even send a text,” I say.The weekend comes. Our first visitors depart. New friends arrive for Sunday lunch.“Were you on the radio last week?” says one. “With Janet Street-Porter?”“Yeah,” I say. “Did I sound weird?”“No more than usual,” the friend says.double quotation markAt six we take a car to the beach, dog included. The tide is out, the sea is warm and the phone signal is amazing“I’m suggesting an evening swim,” my wife says, turning to me. “Are you coming this time?”“Sure,” I say, thinking: I can probably send texts from the beach.At six we take a car to the beach, dog included. The tide is out, the sea is warm and the phone signal is amazing. Within the hour we’re driving back down the long track to the cottage. I’ve got sand in my hair, salt on my skin, and a wet dog on my lap. My email inbox is up to date.My wife hits the brakes suddenly. Ahead a tree is lying across the track.“When did that happen?” I say.“While we were out,” my wife says. “We could have been under it.”We all climb over the tree and walk down to the cottage. When my wife tries to call someone about the problem, a further problem presents itself; a trip back to the car confirms it.“The tree took the phone line down with it,” I say.“No internet,” my wife says.“Trapped like rats,” I say.“Don’t be like that,” she says.“How am I going to work?” I say. “I’ll have to walk half a mile just to get a signal!”“You used to do that all the time,” she says.First thing Monday morning, trudging uphill through a flock of sheep with my laptop held open, I think: she’s right; I used to do this a lot.Explore more on these topicsFamilyThe Tim Dowling columnfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: What is the pan-European emergency telephone number? The Saturday quiz | Quiz and trivia games | The Guardian
description: From Adventure Galley and Queen Anne’s Revenge to a bus station that’s a classic of brutalist architecture, test your knowledge with the Saturday quiz
Author: Thomas Eaton

title: Ebola frontline workers missing wages as outbreak spreads ‘exponentially’ | Ebola | The Guardian
description: People fighting to contain rapidly growing outbreak in Democratic Republic of the Congo describe the obstacles and dangers they face
Author: Rachel Savage
Headline: People fighting to contain rapidly growing outbreak in Democratic Republic of the Congo describe the obstacles and dangers they face
Content: A health worker preparing to disinfect the area during the burial of suspected Ebola victims in Bunia. Photograph: Gradel Muyisa Mumbere/ReutersPeople fighting to contain rapidly growing outbreak in Democratic Republic of the Congo describe the obstacles and dangers they faceByProsper Heri Ngorora in Bunia andRachel SavageSat 22 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 22 Aug 2026 05.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEvery day, Sophie Mwadawa Kabundo goes to her job as a nurse at an Ebola treatment centre in the north-east of theDemocratic Republic of the Congo, afraid she will contract the virus and pass it to her family and friends.“More and more confirmed cases are being admitted here … Some of our colleagues have died,” said Kabundo. “We fear that, despite our vigilance, workplace accidents may occur and put us in ever greater danger … We go to sleep already worrying about the days ahead, as patients continue to pour in.”View image in fullscreenA health worker’s protective gear is disinfected after handling the body of a suspected Ebola victim in Bunia.Photograph: Gradel Muyisa Mumbere/ReutersMartin Bolombi, her colleague at the Elikya treatment centre in Bunia, the capital of the hardest-hit province, Ituri, holds similar fears. “Personally, this outbreak is causing me a lot of stress,” he said. “But I have no choice but to pluck up my courage and ensure that the situation is brought under control first, before it can stabilise.”Ebola outbreak: five big questionsRead moreThat courage is all the more remarkable given that both workers on the frontline of thefastest-growing Ebola outbreak on recordsaid they were not being paid.“I have been working since May and have only been paid for June,” said Bolombi, a hygiene worker who was among about 100 people who protested outside the Elikya treatment centreduring a strikelast month over unpaid bonuses.Kabundo said she was also missing wages. “We are not being paid and we want the government to provide solutions as soon as possible,” she said. “We are under immense pressure … We are exposed to the risk of infection, and our families and other loved ones may contract the disease because of us.”View image in fullscreenA health worker dries disinfected boots in Bunia.Photograph: Dieudonne Dirole/APUnpaid wages are just one of the factors – alongside misinformation, community mistrust and infrastructure deficits – hampering efforts to tackle the outbreak in the DRC, one of the world’s poorest countries.More than 2,500 people have now died in the outbreak, which ⁠is spreading exponentially in an ⁠area larger ​than France, the senior UNEbolacoordinator, Julien Harneis, said on Friday. Speaking on a video call from Bunia, Harneis called ⁠for more aid, saying the existing pool of funds would run out within weeks. He said 160 healthcare ‌workers had fallen ill with Ebola, and 43 of them had died.“The outbreak is growing faster and wider than the Ebola response,” he added. “And all of this is happening in an area that has had three decades of conflict and is generating huge humanitarian needs.”The World Health Organization estimates that the outbreak is on course to exceed west Africa’s2014-16 Ebola outbreakas the biggest ever globally. In the previous outbreak, more than 28,600 cases and 11,325 deaths were recorded across Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone,according to WHO data.View image in fullscreenHealth workers tend to an Ebola patient at the Rwampara treatment centre in Ituri province.Photograph: Moses Sawasawa/APThe infections in DRC are of the rare Bundibugyo species of the virus. There are no approved treatments or vaccines for the strain, but trials for both are under way.Bolombi said he was working seven days a week, with barely any time to see his family, as the outbreak was getting worse. “Logistics have improved compared to the early days of the response, but this is still not enough, as needs are growing as the disease progresses,” he said.Despite the enormous challenges and lack of renumeration, Kabundo expressed pride that there had been “a large number of recoveries” at the Elikya treatment centre. “This progress must be highlighted, but it is no excuse to rest on our laurels,” she said.The Congolese health ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment.View image in fullscreenPassengers on a boat intercepted by health authorities wait to be tested for Ebola in Kinshasa, the DRC’s capital.Photograph: Benoit Nyemba/ReutersEbola is transmitted to people from wild animals and then spreads between humans via direct contact with the organs, blood or other body fluids of infected people, including dead bodies. It can also be spread through contact with contaminated surfaces and materials, such as bedding or clothing.Initial symptoms can include fever, fatigue, muscle pain, headaches and a sore throat. These progress to vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, rash and symptoms of impaired kidney and liver functions.Widespread mistrust and misinformation have resulted in people with the virus not attending health centres for treatment until it is too late, as well as attacks on health facilities and ambulances.Dr Eddy Kambale Kahandukya, a deputy medical coordinator for the charity Médicins Sans Frontières in the DRC, said: “The lack of community engagement remains a major challenge in breaking this chain of transmission … For example, patients who suspect they have symptoms and are awaiting laboratory results seek refuge within the community and end up creating new clusters that further fuel the spread of the epidemic.”View image in fullscreenPeople dressed in protective gear lower a coffin containing Jeannine Katusabe, who died of Ebola, during a burial service in Bunia.Photograph: Dieudonne Dirole/APFear was a big driver of the lack of trust in the authorities’ response to Ebola, said Manon Dumortier, an emergency coordinator in Bunia for the aid group Mercy Corps.What is Ebola and why is the outbreak in DRC causing so much concern?Read more“It’s scary, right? … Suddenly there are so many people dying and you don’t know what it is about,” she said. “People are just disappearing, going to health centres and you cannot even see them before they are being buried. This is just raising a lot of speculation and rumours.”The WHO declared the outbreak apublic health emergency of international concernin May, but later said sequencing showed the outbreak had started months earlier in February.The virus has spread to six of the DRC’s 26 provinces, concentrated in the country’s north-east. More than 4,200 of the confirmed cases are in Ituri, which borders Uganda and South Sudan.Uganda reported 20 cases and two deaths, all in the capital, Kampala. The government declared the country Ebola-free on 28 July after the last Ebola patient, a Congolese national, was discharged on 16 July.Explore more on these topicsEbolaDemocratic Republic of the CongoAfricaInfectious diseasesEpidemicsGlobal healthfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: As Russian missiles rain down on Kyiv, casualties mount and the mood darkens | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Ukraine’s military has run out of US Patriot interceptors to repel ballistic attacks, which have one aim, the capital’s mayor says: to destroy morale
Author: Dan Sabbagh
Headline: Ukraine’s military has run out of US Patriot interceptors to repel ballistic attacks, which have one aim, the capital’s mayor says: to destroy morale
Content: Iryna Chechotkina, the co-founder of Rozetka, an e-commerce firm, by the remains of her firm’s distribution hub in Brovary, Kyiv region.Ukraine’s military has run out of US Patriot interceptors to repel ballistic attacks, which have one aim, the capital’s mayor says: to destroy moraleByDan Sabbaghin Kyiv. Photographs byJulia KochetovaSat 22 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 22 Aug 2026 03.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleViktor, 23, Sofiia, 18, and their dog, Teddy, were bedding down for the night on Thursday at the Dorohozhychi metro station three stops from Kyiv’s city centre. The couple have sheltered here “every night for the past three weeks”, Viktor said, as the missile threat to the city worsened; the dog, only three months old, has been with them a fortnight. Teddy lies quietly, knowing no different a life.View image in fullscreenPeople sleeping at Dorohozhychi metro station for safety.The atmosphere in the Ukrainian capital has shifted in the past couple of months as the war has returned more sharply to the home front. Russian high-speed ballistic missiles are routinely targeting the city and Ukraine’s military have run out of the interceptors from the only weapon system that can stop them, US-made Patriots. The anxiety that hangs over the wartime city has intensified.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreen(Clockwise from top left): Vitalii clears debris from around his damaged car with the help of a neighbour; the aftermath of a Russian night attack on Solomyanskiy district; a woman rests near the site of the attack.“Before, if you heard an air-raid warning you still had time to pack your stuff and get to the shelter. Now you have a warning and then in 30 seconds you have explosions, so you have no time,” Sofiia said. A night earlier,a wave of missiles targeted the citywithin minutes of the first warning, at 11.51pm. Sixteen people were reported killed after the missiles struck locations including residential blocks in the suburbs. Warnings of drone attacks followed for several more hours, fraying nerves after the opening hits.Russian ballistic missile attack sets Kyiv skyline ablazeCity dwellers had been fearing a big attack on Wednesday night. It had been a few days since the last one – and there were also reports that Russian Tu-160 strategic bombers were flying to the war zone. They launch cruise missiles, but their presence in the air heralds a wider missile and drone attack. The lower hall at Dorohozhychi metro was packed by 10pm that night, Viktor said, with tents or people lying on ground sheets, almost no space left for the couple as they arrived.Earlier on Thursday, in the morning, the grim aftermath of the missile strikes on residential areaswas clearly visible. Two missiles struck the Solomianskyi district west of the centre, one shearing off the top floor of a 10-storey apartment block, killing two people, the second crashing into a disused building in the centre of a car park, reducing it to a scatter of rubble, while local people tried to see if there was any hope for their cars – the ones that were not completely burnt out.Kyiv book market burns after Russian missile strikeThe rear end of Vitalii’s car was smashed in by the blast, and it appears to be a write-off. The 42-year-old said he works for an insurance company, yet admitted he had not insured his own vehicle. After a while, however, the car started, remarkably, its engine having faced away from the blast. At first the impact of the overnight attack may be financial, but Vitalii said its real effect will be psychological. “We are alive, our arms and legs whole. We will go on. But now it will be more scary.”View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenVitalii, a Kyiv resident, checks his damaged car; a woman rests and checks her phone the day after the Russian attack.Kyiv’s mayor, the former champion heavyweight Vitali Klitschko, arrived on the scene. “These attacks on the city have one aim – to drive people into depression,” he said. He is pressed about how many new bomb shelters the city has built, which might avoid people having to sleep in metro stations that reopen at 6am. He could offer no figure to one questioner.View image in fullscreenVitali Klitschko, Kyiv’s city mayor, talks to the media at the site of a direct hit.Ukraine’s military no longer announces how many ballistics come in because it cannot stop them, though hits can easily heard from bedrooms right across the capital. In July, the last full month for which figures are available, 437 civilians were killed across Ukraine and 2,610 injured according to UN figures – the highest number recorded killed since May 2022.Ukraine civilian deaths chartCauses of civilian casualties in UkraineThough it is August and the daily temperatures are frequently in the 30s, much of the talk is about the winter to come, when people expect to lose central heating and electricity as so many homes did last year when apartment temperatures in the worst-affected districts dropped to 4-5C. Kyiv’s infrastructure appears defenceless and those who can have long bought generators, batteries, electric radiators and anything else for emergency heating, but worries linger.View image in fullscreenA survivor of the night’s attacks holds a backpack containing her cat in Solomyanskiy district.“We are prepared to cope without electricity and without central heating – we did our homework, prepared the apartment and lasted last dreadful winter,” said Maria Hlazunova, who lives in the centre of the city. “But water … I’m afraid of lacking the opportunity to wash hands and food properly. Not to mention the toilet,” which she acknowledges is a particular source of anxiety. Residents know the city has only one wastewater treatment site, at Bortnychi. It has not yet been hit.Ukraine has defended itself by stepping up its attacks on Russia, long-range targeting first of the country’s oil refineries, leading to queues at petrol stations, and more recently by targeting warehouses, e-commerce sites that Kyiv says are also used by the military for logistics. It has been effective, though Russia has responded in kind – bombing and destroying warehouses just outside Kyiv, the medium-term economic consequences from the destruction uncertain.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenThe damaged Rozetka warehouse in Brovary, Kyiv region; a firefighter works at the warehouse after a Russian attack.Early on Thursday, a food distribution warehouse near Ukraine’s unused Boryspil commercial airport was completely destroyed by a missile attack. The fire spread because a succession of drone warnings – Shaheds were flying above – meant that emergency workers could not safely attend at first. When the Guardian visited in the afternoon, parts of the burnt-out site were still smouldering, and there were a handful of employees who recognised their jobs had disappeared in the wreckage.Viktoriia Ruban, the spokesperson for Ukraine’s state emergency services in Kyiv region, the area just outside the city, described a change in Russian military tactics. “Previously, the Russians would strike the Kyiv region at night. Now it’s three or four hours, then a strike; another three or four hours, then another strike. Whether it’s morning or daytime – it makes no difference now,” she said, and the observation applies also to the capital city where daytime alerts have become more common.1:12Barrage of Russian strikes devastates Kyiv – videoIryna Chechotkina, the co-founder of Rozetka, Ukraine’s most successful e-commerce distributor, showed a few journalists around the ruins of what was her company’s largest distribution hub near Brovary, north-east of Kyiv. It was a modern automated facility, built for $70m, capable of sending 100,000 parcels a day, and employing 1,000. But it was totally destroyed by three missiles on the night of August 4-5, the inferno so great that in places only bent-over cranes can be made out.View image in fullscreenIryna Chechotkina, the co-founder of Rozetka, inside her company’s burnt-out distribution hub in Brovary, Kyiv region.It was a clearly difficult visit for the businesswoman, amid worries that more of the company’s warehouses could be struck, affecting Rozetka and the 50,000 vendors who rely on its service. But the wider military reality is fragile.“How can a country defend itself against ballistic threats if we have nothing with which to shoot them down?” she asked. “It’s very hard for me; I’m a mother of four and I’ve sacrificed time with them to build this place. It’s my life’s work.” Breaking into English, she added: “This is not easy.”Explore more on these topicsUkraineRussiaEuropefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Canada vows ‘dollar for dollar’ response as US puts 50% tariffs on some goods | Canada | The Guardian
description: Collapse of trade talks could lead to job losses, but biggest impact on traditional allies is expected to be political
Author: William Christou
Headline: Collapse of trade talks could lead to job losses, but biggest impact on traditional allies is expected to be political
Content: The two sides blamed each other for the collapse.Composite: Dylan Martinez/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe two sides blamed each other for the collapse.Composite: Dylan Martinez/ReutersCanadaCanada vows ‘dollar for dollar’ response as US puts 50% tariffs on some goodsCollapse of trade talks could lead to job losses, but biggest impact on traditional allies is expected to be politicalWilliam Christou,Edward Helmoreand agenciesSat 22 Aug 2026 10.04 EDTFirst published on Sat 22 Aug 2026 00.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US has imposed 50% tariffs on some goods from Canada, andMark Carney, the country’s prime minister, has vowed to match them “dollar for dollar” after the collapse of trade talks.The tariffs came into force on roughly $20bn (£14.6bn) of goods – ranging from hockey sticks to tongue depressors – at 04.00GMT. Trade experts said the tariffs could result in some job losses, but the largest impact is expected to be political, driving a further wedge between the traditional allies.The trade row is the biggest rupture in recent relations between Washington and one of its closest allies and trading partners as Donald Trump’s bellicose foreign policy angered officials in Ottawa.The two sides appeared close to a deal on Friday to lower tariffs on steel, aluminium and cars, but the deal was scuttled at the last minute. The two sides blamed each other for the collapse.Canadian officials had worked hard in good faith but “last-minute changes in the US proposed terms were unfair, uneconomic and called into question the reliability of any deal”, Carney said in a statement. Carney recalled his negotiators asCanadavowed to match Washington’s tough approach. No further talks are planned.US officials accused Canada of collapsing the deal by seeking additional concessions at the last minute. The US tariffs will affect about $20bn worth of Canadian products, and the US trade representative, Jamieson Greer, said the breakdown represented a “missed opportunity for Canada”.Recriminations continued on Saturday with Carney accusing theTrump administrationof using “economic integration as a weapon” – and saying that his country had been “attacked” by the new US tariffs.Carney accused the Trump administration of adding last-minute terms that would have reduced tariff relief for Canadian-made vehicles, restricted Canada’s ability to strike trade deals with other countries and weakened protections for language, culture and sovereignty. He called the demands “unacceptable”.Carney said the Trump administration’s final demands went too far: “They asked too much and offered too little.”Greer said the US was compelled to act after a year of retaliatory measures by Canada. “We’ve said enough, and so we’ve taken countermeasures,” he told Fox & Friends Weekend. “Our interest is in protecting American workers and protecting American supply chains.”Greer said the US was offering to cut tariffs on steel, autos and lumber, “things that are sensitive for them”.“And they’ve always had the best deal, and they still would have an even better deal, but they didn’t want that,” Greer said.
