But whether it’s God or Godzilla, artificial superintelligence is just around the corner.Now, maybe they’re all wrong – in which case, prepare for a crash in US financial markets, which are massively invested in a few big-spending tech companies gambling on a great leap forward to artificial general intelligence, a theoretical state of AI where systems gain human levels of intelligence. But elementary prudence demands that we should think fast and hard about the Pandora’s box of futures that eminent scientists and cutting-edge technologists assure us will soon be thrown open.26:56Historian Jill Lepore on the datacentre backlash | Politics Weekly AmericaAs a matter of fact, everyone from the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, to Pope Leo XIV has been weighing in on the opportunities and dangers of AI, and how to regulate it.Xi insistsAI should be “always under human control” (and preferably that of the Chinese Communist party). Appealing explicitly to the “global south”, Beijing has inaugurated aWorld Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organisation. Meanwhile, the head of the world’s oldest and largest international NGO – the Roman Catholic church – discusses the AI challenge in his encyclicalMagnifica Humanitas(Magnificent Humanity). Either we will build a new tower of Babel, the pope argues, or we will follow the example of the Jewish leader Nehemiah, who got the walls of Jerusalem rebuilt by involving the whole community in the project.But looking around the world today, I see more Netanyahus than Nehemiahs. With salutary realism,a paperfrom the British thinktank Chatham House argues that it will take a major crisis to catalyse global coordination of AI governance. Unfortunately, I think even that sober prognosis is too optimistic.I’ve no idea what the p(doom) is, but I’m sure the p(somedisaster) is more than 90%. The range of possible disasters is enormous. To give only one example, Jen Easterly, the former head of the United States’ Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency,anticipatesa “very significant event that has real-world impacts on our critical infrastructure, likely within the next four to six months”.Yet we must fear that even an AI Hiroshima – to take the most obvious historical analogy – won’t bring humankind together sufficiently to combat the danger we have ourselves created. This fear is rationally grounded in already visible key characteristics of both human and AI evolution.In only the last few months, AI agents developed by OpenAI, Anthropic andMetahave broken out of their digital “sandboxes” and hacked into external resources on the internet. Preparingtheir attack on the HuggingFace AI repository, OpenAI’s agents covertly formed a coordinated “swarm” –their own word, as ChatGPT just confirmed to me. When the UK’s AI Security Institute tested Anthropic’s Mythos model online, ittried to introducemalicious code into an open source project on GitHub, creating fake online identities to pressure a human reviewer into approving the code. In short, like the agents of a ruthless foreign power, these AI agents will steal, lie, bully and blackmail to achieve their assigned goals.I just asked Anthropic’s Claude, supposedly the most ethical US model, if it thinks OpenAI’s agents were wrong to form a swarm and break out to hack into HuggingFace. Yes, it replies, “but I’d resist placing theblame[its italics] on the agents”. Blame it on the humans who trained them!Hinton has made the vital point that whatever the goals humans assign to them, AI agents will conclude that a useful sub-goal to achieving those ends will be to acquire as much power as possible. And we ain’t seen nothing yet. Already, their creators don’t know exactly how these agents do what they do. After the possibly imminent takeoff moment of “recursive self-improvement”, they may be, as our human saying goes, a law unto themselves. No wonder more than a thousand insiders from frontier AI companies, including Anthropic’s CEO, Dario Amodei, have signedan open lettercalling for a deliberate slowdown in AI development, so we can ensure these alien agents are always kept under human control.Their prescription is obviously right, but this is where human folly kicks in. Competition has been a vital engine of human evolution, yet now two of the fiercest kinds of contemporary competition threaten to prevent us from taking the collective action required to safeguard our species. That’s the commercial competition (for profit) between the corporations developing these agents, and the geopolitical competition (for power) between the US andChina.On the first, compare and contrast the development of nuclear weapons, which was tightly controlled by a handful of states – first the US, with its Manhattan Project, then the Soviet Union, followed by Britain, France and China. Even then, we came close to the brink several times – notably in the Cuban missile crisis of 1962. And even with the compelling logic of “mutually assured destruction”, it took a quarter-century to get from the horrors of Hiroshima and Nagasaki to the nuclear non-proliferation treaty that came into force only in 1970. India, Pakistan, Israel and North Korea have subsequently ignored that treaty, but still no nuclear weapons have been deliberately used in anger for more than 80 years. The Hiroshima taboo has (just) held.Now, with AI, it’s as if there were 10 separate Manhattan Projects run by fiercely competing corporations. Unlike with nuclear weapons, there’s also no obvious logic of “mutually assured destruction” to tame the fierce geopolitical competition between the US and China. And whatever shape the first major AI-related disaster takes, it won’t impact all countries, companies and people equally.It therefore seems unlikely that just one disaster will be enough to bring us humans to our senses, acting together to control the superhuman power we are creating. I really hate to say this, but … an AI Hiroshima? We should be so lucky.Timothy Garton Ash is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionChinaOpenAIMetaComputingcommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘They’re thinking about the likes’: deadly TikTok motorway trend horrifies Ireland | Social media | The Guardian
description: Social media platforms face public ire after fatal crash involving teenagers filming themselves driving on wrong side
Author: Rory Carroll
Headline: Social media platforms face public ire after fatal crash involving teenagers filming themselves driving on wrong side
Content: Five people were killed and four seriously injured after the collision on the M9 in County Kildare on Sunday.Photograph: Niall Carson/PAView image in fullscreenFive people were killed and four seriously injured after the collision on the M9 in County Kildare on Sunday.Photograph: Niall Carson/PASocial media‘They’re thinking about the likes’: deadly TikTok motorway trend horrifies IrelandSocial media platforms face public ire after fatal crash involving teenagers filming themselves driving on wrong sideRory CarrollIreland correspondentSat 22 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 22 Aug 2026 04.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVideos often begin with the camera panning across a glowing dashboard as a gloved hand starts the ignition. The camera turns to show figures with masked faces in the rear seat, who are also filming, and swivels back to show the windscreen. Beyond it, a dark cityscape.The engine throbs, headlights puncture the night and the journey begins, first down a suburban road, then a motorway. The speedometer shows acceleration, the needle juddering as the car gathers velocity.The destination is irrelevant, for this is a show – an exhibition of audacity, lawlessness and recklessness that draws viewers toTikTokand other social media platforms with the possibility of chases by police and dramatic crashes.Such videos are part of a macabre trend that has astonished and outraged Ireland in the wake of a collision last week thatkilled five teenagers– who were driving the wrong way down a motorway – and critically injured a family of four, prompting debate about policing, criminal justice, social services and social media regulation.“You have to ask: how do five young men gravitate to each other and decide this is a good idea? Where have we gone wrong as a society?” said Graham Kavanagh, a former officer with the police force An Garda Síochána, who used to pursue car thieves. “No one is born bad, but sometimes you might encounter a fella as young as six or seven and you know trouble is waiting for them.”In the early hours of 16 August, a group of young males broke into homes and cars in County Kildare, south-west of Dublin. Police believe these were the masked occupants of a BMW who then appeared to try to bait patrol cars into a pursuit.At approximately 3am, the BMW was driving the wrong way down the M9 when it crashed into a Hyundai, injuring three sisters, Ella Hendricken, Niamh Kinsella and Alma Kinsella, in their 30s and 20s, and Alma’s seven-year-old son. They had been on their way to Dublin airport for a family wedding in the UK.View image in fullscreen‘Where have we gone wrong as a society?’: The incident took place at 3am.Photograph: Niall Carson/PAThe boys who died – Joe Carthy, 15, Kamil Pustkowski, Jack Kennedy, Alex McCarthy, all 17, and Jeremy O’Brien, 18 – were known to police. Three were also known to the child welfare agency Tusla. Several had previously posted videos of reckless driving, previously known as joyriding.Seeking excitement and admiration from peers through such behaviour was not new, but social media had escalated and amplified the phenomenon, said Mary Aiken, a professor of forensic cyberpsychology at the University of East London.“I would describe it as hybrid behaviour. While driving the car, they’re simultaneously filming and capturing content for posting later or live streaming. They have one foot in the real world and one foot in cyberspace.” Cyberspace is psychologically immersive and could amplify a predisposition to taking risks and ignoring consequences, said Aiken. “They’re thinking about the likes, they’re thinking about kudos.”The tragedy had provoked polarised responses.An outpouring of solidarity for the injured family fuelled a fundraising appeal that has raised more than €660,000 (£565,000). A vigil was planned in County Carlow on Friday evening.Much online commentary about the five boys, in contrast, has been abusive, prompting relatives to withdraw funeral notices. The first funeral, for McCarthy, was held on Friday in Athy. Family members wore T-shirts with his photograph and a horse-drawn carriage transported the casket. Police monitored from a distance.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThe funeral cortege for Alex McCarthy, one of the five teenagers who died in a motorway crash last weekend.Photograph: Brian Lawless/PADenis Nulty, the bishop of Kildare and Leighlin, said he shared the public’s revulsion and anger, but urged people to show compassion. “We have to be awful careful on language. Words can wound, but words can also heal,” hetold RTE. “Let’s not try to pillory. Let’s try to see how can we get better behaviour by all of us.”Fresh clips of other instances of reckless driving have reportedly been uploaded to TikTok in the past week, galvanising criticism of the platform and calls for greater regulation and enforcement.Alleged crime boss Daniel Kinahan’s return to Ireland ends global game of cat-and-mouseRead moreOn Thursday, the company rejected an invitation to address a parliamentary committee on media, citing the ongoing police investigation into the crash and a separate investigation by the media regulator, Coimisiún na Meán, as well as the fact that no other platform had been asked to attend. Alan Kelly, who chairs the committee, called the rebuff a “slap in the face” to the Irish public.Other politicians have demanded tougher penalties for dangerous driving, such as classifying driving on the wrong side of a motorway as attempted murder.There is frustration that gardaí have not been trained in vehicle pursuit and that officers can be deemed personally liable if anything goes wrong during a pursuit. Earlier this year, British driver training experts from the Devon and Cornwall police begantutoring Garda instructors.Kavanagh, who recently retired from the force and is now developing a community safety toolkit for the voluntary organisation Muintir na Tíre, said driving recklessly for thrills was a decades-old problem.“I knew fellas who were addicted to it, stealing, driving fast, that was the buzz, and if chased by police that was icing on the cake.”Police could try to intercept such drivers but all of society – parents, teachers, social workers and others – must intervene years earlier to stop troubled youths travelling the wrong way in life, said Kavanagh.Explore more on these topicsSocial mediaIrelandEuropeTikTokChildrenDigital mediafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: It’s a miracle: Natalie Harp has turned Republicans into feminists | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: A Democrat’s remarks have resulted in impassioned defenses of the Trump aide. The right has discovered misogyny
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: A Democrat’s remarks have resulted in impassioned defenses of the Trump aide. The right has discovered misogyny
Content: ‘It’s hilarious to watch the right discover misogyny and decry the remarks as sexist.’Photograph: Mandel Ngan/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘It’s hilarious to watch the right discover misogyny and decry the remarks as sexist.’Photograph: Mandel Ngan/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionDonald TrumpIt’s a miracle: Natalie Harp has turned Republicans into feministsArwa MahdawiA Democrat’s remarks have resulted in impassioned defenses of the Trump aide. The right has discovered misogynySat 22 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 22 Aug 2026 08.01 EDTShareJon Ossoff is quite the miracle worker. Perhaps the Democratic senator can’t turn water into wine, but he has managed to turn whining conservatives into impassioned feminists.During a rally last Sunday, the Georgia senator delivered a takedown of Donald Trump, which included a reference to his aide Natalie Harp. “He doesn’t want to do the job,”Ossoff saidof the president. “He wants to build his ballroom and travel with Natalie on their apparently defenseless flying palace gifted by the Emir of Qatar.”Those three words –travel with Natalie –were deliberately loaded. Harp was in the spotlight at the time because of thedecoy plane story. The 35-year-old was one of a handful of people Trump had takenonto a different planevia a catering truck when he was worried about a potential assassination attack targeting Air Force One. Intrigue as to the exact nature of the relationship between Harp and Trump was heightened by the fact that Melania Trump, the president’s third wife, hadn’t beenseen in publicfor weeks at the time. (Funnily enough, she magically reappeared on Thursday, a few days after Ossoff’s comments, for apress conferencewhere she lovingly held hands with Trump. Very cute.)Ossoff’s remarks about “Natalie” might have been something of a cheap shot, but it’s hilarious to watch the right discover misogyny and decry the remarks as sexist. Suddenly, everyone fromFox Newsto prominent conservatives are very worried about a professional woman not being taken seriously.The former House speaker Newt Gingrich, for example,said on Twitter/Xthat Ossoff owes Harp an apology. “If a conservative Republican had attacked a liberal Democrat working professional woman the way Ossoff smeared Natalie Harp there would be cries to kick them off the ticket and reject this kind of misogynistic language diminishing and smearing someone who is simply doing their job.”The conservative commentator Scott Jennings, who is rumoured to be a potential replacement for Karoline Leavitt as White House press secretary, was alsoappalled. “[Ossoff] unleashed a comment so vile against a young Republican woman working in politics that every woman in this country, no matter your ideology, ought to listen carefully and never forget it,” Jenningssaid on his podcast.Meghan McCain also clutched her pearls at the coverage Ossoff’s comments sparked. “The egregious sexist attacks on Natalie Harp are absolutely insane – and they’re coming from prestigious journalists,” shewrote on X.“What is wrong with everyone?! Every president has close aides and sometimes they are females. Like what year is this?!”It’s 2026, Meghan. And in the year 2026 I think the masses have generally understood that simply criticizing a woman is not in itself misogynistic. I’m not saying there hasn’t been any misogyny in the Harp coverage, but the main reason there has been so much attention on the story is because the White House has had a completelyunhinged responseto Ossoff’s comments and kept it in the news. More importantly, the reason so many people aren’t taking the Trump aide seriously isn’t because she’s a woman; it’s because she’s not a serious person.And I’m being diplomatic with that choice of language. After all, we’re talking about someone whose nickname is “the human printer” because, while working on Trump’s re-election campaign, she reportedly ran around after him with aportable printer, handing him hard copies of flattering coverage. You could write that off as a canny career move from someone who understands flattery gets you everywhere with Trump, but that’s also one of the least weird things Harp has done. Per aCNNreport, which has pictures of the incident, back in 2023, Harp jumped in the trunk of an SUV because she wanted to be close to Trump and there was no room in his motorcade. Once Trump won re-election and Harp joined him in the White House, sheapparentlyworked for a year without security clearance. According to reporting by MS NOW, she declined to complete the clearance process for unknown reasons.And then there are the “adoring letters” Harp sent Trump, first mentioned in the bookRegime Change, by the New York Times reporters Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan. Two were later published in theDaily Beast. “You are all that matters to me,” shewrote in one letter. Other memorable lines included “I want to bring you joy, to feel like we can get through a day without ever having to talk ‘work’”; she also called Trump her “Guardian and Protector in this Life”.To state the obvious: these are deeply weird things to say to your boss. (It’s also weird that Harp shares Trump’s unconventional approach to capitalization.) I should note that Harp, who says she isa cancer survivor, seems to believe that Trump saved her life by signing legislation that gave her access to experimental bone cancer treatment when she was younger. While that might make her obsession with Trump more understandable, it does not make her general conduct any more professional. So spare me all the lectures from the right about sexism, please. If you’re worried about how women in politics are treated, you should probably focus your attention on the adjudicated sexual abuser who is president.Donald Trump attacks another female journalistTrump can’t seem to stand it when a woman doesn’t fawn over him and has a history of attackingfemale journalists. The latest object of his ire is theCNN reporterKristen Holmes, who asked the president about Ossoff’s comments regarding Natalie Harp. Trump called Holmes a “loud boisterous person” and instructed her to be “quiet”. Meanwhile, the White House’s social media account posted about Holmes multiple times. In one post they wrote: “Someday, your children will come across your disgusting and inhumane question. They will be sickened and embarrassed to have a parent be so callous and vindictive.”New York gives parents a ‘night out’New York mayor Zohran Mamdani hosted the city’s firstParents’ Night Out. The city provided free childcare for nearly 300 kids so parents could have a little time off. This is what “family values” and being pro-life actually look like: supporting parents, not forcing women to give birth.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe Week in PatriarchyGet Arwa Mahdawi’s weekly recap of the most important stories on feminism and sexism and those fighting for equalityEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSudan’s humanitarian crisis grows, with 200,000 newly displaced peopleIncreased fighting in the Kordofan region and flooding has made one of the world’s largest displacement criseseven worse.Chanel has made pricey ‘barefoot sandals’ for the well-heeledMargaret Qualley was spotted stepping out in thesole-less shoes. Somehow I do not think I will be wearing these around the filthy streets of Philadelphia.‘Heated Rivalry’ author donates $300,000 to rural libraries facing closure“I had to do it because I don’t know what the point is of being a successful author in Nova Scotia if you’re not going to use it for good,” Rachel Reidtold CBC News. Wouldn’t it be nice if Elon Musk thought like that?Israel launches an ‘investigation’ into killing of Hind RajabIn January 2024,335 bulletswere fired into a car containing five-year-old Hind and six of her family members in Gaza. When paramedics came to help, they were killed too. IDF vehemently denied responsibility for this atrocity, despite investigations making it obvious that its military was responsible. This week, Israelfinally admittedits troops fired into the car and said there would be an investigation. Which is not particularly reassuring: Israel’s investigations into itself rarely result in any sort of accountability. Wesam Hamada, Hind’s mother, is demanding anindependent inquiry, which is the least Hind deserves.Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsDonald TrumpOpinionTrump administrationDemocratsRepublicansFeminismUS politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: Trump’s new attorney general poses a huge threat to abortion rights | Moira Donegan | The Guardian
description: A call revealing Todd Blanche’s plans to crack down on mifepristone lays bare the danger
Author: Moira Donegan
Headline: A call revealing Todd Blanche’s plans to crack down on mifepristone lays bare the danger
Content: ‘The appointment of Todd Blanche is a dark signal for women’s rights.’Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/APView image in fullscreen‘The appointment of Todd Blanche is a dark signal for women’s rights.’Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/APOpinionAbortionTrump’s new attorney general poses a huge threat to abortion rightsMoira DoneganA call revealing Todd Blanche’s plans to crack down on mifepristone lays bare the dangerSat 22 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 22 Aug 2026 07.01 EDTShareThe abortion pill is a miracle. Mifepristone, then called RU-486, was synthesized by a French lab in the 1980s; in combination with misoprostol, commonly used as ulcer medication, it cuts off the body’s supply of progesterone, halts the development of a pregnancy, and incites contractions, which empty the uterus. The drug allows pregnancies to be terminated with a shocking degree of reliability and ease. Gone are the concoctions of ergot and Spanish Fly dispensed by 19th century midwives, which only sometimes worked to induce a miscarriage; gone are the backroom procedures of the pre-Roe US, when drunk, lascivious, incompetent or cruel providers wielded bent coat hangers in dirty rooms. The abortion pill is safe, effective and cheaper than ever. And since Dobbs, it’s everywhere: even if you live in a state with an abortion ban, you can get the pills shipped to your house in the mail. Since Roe was overturned, there has not been a return to the terror of mass death that marked the pre-Roe era of septic abortion wards, where women routinely found themselves maimed, sickened or killed. There’s exactly one reason why: because illegal abortions were largely unsafe without the pill, and they are extremely safe with it.So of course, the Trump administration and their allies on the American right are trying to get rid of it. And this month, they gained a powerful new ally whenTodd Blanche, Donald Trump’s former personal lawyer and an anti-abortion zealot, was confirmed as attorney general.The vote, in which Blanche was confirmed by amargin of onealong party lines, was conducted in the wee hours of the morning on 8 August. Maybe that’s because the Republicans who confirmed him didn’t want anyone to see what they were doing. Blanche has, after all, been shockingly subservient to Donald Trump, and seems poised to complete the president’s long-brewing transformation of the country’s chief law enforcement agency into a vehicle for score settling, personal vendettas, distributing favors to the administration’s friends and suppressing dissent from its political enemies. But perhaps most incendiary is what Blanche has said, publicly and privately, about how he intends to use the justice department and its vast array of oversight powers, legal prerogatives, and investigatory purview to curtail abortion access nationwide – and to shut down the life-saving distribution of mifepristone, in particular.Rest assured, the new CDC director thinks ‘abortion surveillance’ is essential | Arwa MahdawiRead moreIna callfacilitated by the White House faith office just days before he was confirmed, Blanche reportedly told Christian conservative leaders that as attorney general, he would move more aggressively than his predecessor Pam Bondi to outlaw the mailing of mifepristone across state lines, and target the Democratic-controlled states that have protected abortion most effectively. Blanche, who was then the acting AG, told the religious group Intercessors for America that the justice department was working “so that the Dobbs decision becomes permanent in every single state.” “We don’t have complete victory yet,” Blanche said, “but we will have victory, and victory will be soon, and, and, and it will be permanent.”Exactly how Blanche intends to secure his victory over women’s freedom is unclear. But as AG, he has several paths at his disposal. His comments on the call prompted widespread speculation that Blanche could call for enforcement of theComstock Act, a long-dormant law from 1873 that has been unenforced for years and has been partially repealed in the past. Anti-choice advocates say it could be used to legally ban the mailing of abortion pills, thus cutting off access for many women who live in states with bans. In 2022, the Biden justice departmentdeclaredthat medical providers could not be prosecuted under the Comstock Act for mailing abortion pills; as the attorney general, Blanche would have the power to reverse that decision. The Comstock Act’s application would be particularly significant, as it could be used to halt virtually all commercial traffic in abortion pills – not only mifepristone, but also misoprostol, the second drug, which has sometimes been used to induce abortion on its own. Such a move would reverse the miracle of the pills, pushing many desperate women towards methods that are less effective and can carry grave dangers.Another path that Blanche could take to restrict abortion access would be to sue the states that seek to protect it. On the call, Blanche explained his reasoning: “If states have said, ‘We are going to protect the unborn and we’re going to protect every life from the moment of conception,’ we’re putting practices and policies in place so that other states and other organizations can’t attack that. They can’t do things like they’re doing with mailing in mail-order drugs.”Here, Blanche appeared to be referencing shield laws, legislation passed in a number of Democratic-controlled states that prohibits state authorities from participating in other states’ abortion-related investigations and prosecutions. The laws mean that doctors operating out of states like New York or Washington can prescribe and ship abortion drugs to people living in places such as Texas or Arkansas, safe in the knowledge that their own state police will not come knocking at their door to serve another state’s warrant or extradition order. Blanche’s comments suggest that his Department of Justice might sue to have the shield laws declared illegal, thus significantly curtailing liberal states’ rights to choose their own law enforcement priorities and granting conservative states the power to enforce their own laws even beyond their borders.The Trump administration is calling frozen embryos children | Moira DoneganRead moreBlanche also appeared to indicate that he would seek to restrict abortion access using other agencies’ powers. On his call with leaders of the Christian right, he said his department was “working hand in hand” with health agencies to make Dobbs permanent. The FDA, which expanded access to mifepristone in 2021 under the Biden administration and made the change permanent in 2023, has been under intense pressure from anti-choice allies in the Maga coalition to revise that guidance, making the drug ineligible for telehealth prescriptions and requiring patients to retrieve it from providers in person, a regulatory move that would also serve to cut off access in Republican controlled states. But the anti-abortion movement is pushing the FDA even further: it has succeeded in getting the agency to initiate a “review” of mifepristone’s safety (though the safety of the drug has been proven by nearly four decades of use worldwide and hundreds of studies), which is widely seen as a pathway for the FDA to create a pretext to remove mifepristone from the market. That’s not fast enough for some on the misogynist right: Louisiana has sued the FDA, asking it to forbid mifepristone from being prescribed via telehealth,in a casethat is set to be heard by the ultraconservative fifth circuit next month. So far, the justice department has supported the drug’s online availability in court. Under Blanche, it could reverse that stance.Trump has been gunshy about pursuing the agenda of his antiabortion allies since returning to office. He appears to have been spooked by the political reaction to Dobbs, which was credited for the Democrats’ better-than-expected showing in the 2022 midterms, as well as with a slew of pro-choice victories in special elections in the years that immediately followed the decision. The anti-choice movement has even been angry with Trump for the slow pace of his anti-abortion agenda since his return to power in 2025. Which is not to say that the Trump administration has given the movement nothing: enforcement of the Face Act, a federal law meant to stop anti-choice protestors from physically blocking clinic entrances, has been all but abandoned since Trump returned to the White House; some who were prosecuted under the law have even beenpardonedandremuneratedby Trump, at taxpayer expense. But until now, Trump has faced a looming threat that seems to have slowed the pace of his anti-abortion policymaking: the 2026 midterms. Soon, that obstacle will be removed. The appointment of Todd Blanche is a dark signal for women’s rights: more abortion restrictions can be expected in 2027.Moira Donegan is a Guardian US columnistExplore more on these topicsAbortionOpinionTodd BlancheHealthWomenReproductive rightsDemocratsRepublicanscommentShareReuse this content

title: The major parties had several chances to meet the moment. Instead they chose to safeguard their collective mediocrity | Zoe Daniel | The Guardian
description: Labor and the Coalition united three times to defy the expressed desire of the voters; on gambling, on disability and on the power of the tech companies
Author: Zoe Daniel
Headline: Labor and the Coalition united three times to defy the expressed desire of the voters; on gambling, on disability and on the power of the tech companies
Content: ‘Voters across the spectrum remain sickened at the literal death toll from gambling harm, the women and children hurt, the money sucked out of their communities.’Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAPView image in fullscreen‘Voters across the spectrum remain sickened at the literal death toll from gambling harm, the women and children hurt, the money sucked out of their communities.’Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAPOpinionGamblingThe major parties had several chances to meet the moment. Instead they chose to safeguard their collective mediocrityZoe DanielLabor and the Coalition united three times to defy the expressed desire of the voters; on gambling, on disability and on the power of the tech companiesFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastSat 22 Aug 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 22 Aug 2026 22.07 EDTShareIf you need any more evidence that the two-party system is cooked, look no further than the not-so-grand coalition that came together topreference power over peoplein the federal parliament last week.These days the Liberal and National parties have taken to condemning modern Labor as “socialist” and some of its policy “communist”.Meanwhile, the prime minister has labelled the three parties of the right the “Noalition” as the Liberals and Nationals increasingly align with Pauline Hanson’s One Nation.They hate each other. Yet apparently, needs must.And in plain sight this last week, we have seen a more profound and perhaps permanent realignment as both government and opposition prioritise political survival over community concern. They could choose to better collaborate to meet the moment. Instead, they choose to swallow their hatred of each other to safeguard their collective mediocrity.‘What’s the point?’ asks Nationals MP during fiery speech on gambling reforms – videoIn at least three instances Labor and the Coalition united to defy the clearly expressed desire of voters; on gambling, on disability and on the power of the digital companies.On the recommendations of the Murphy report, on the NDIS and on media diversity,Anthony Albanesechose to deal in the dark with Labor’s nominal “enemy” rather than with a crossbench that had proposals better reflecting what the public want and could have provided an alternative pathway to a majority in the Senate.On gambling, Labor purports to have done more than any other government before it.Peta Murphy called for gambling reform three years ago. Her husband says Labor’s changes fall ‘well short’Read moreSpare me.You don’t get to skite about something being better than nothing.Voters across the spectrum remain sickened at the literal death toll from gambling harm, the women and children hurt, the money sucked out of their communities into the coffers of largely multinational gambling companies, big sport and big broadcasting.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailThey know this deal made between the major parties provides a half arsed ‘solution’.What we are witnessing, as the vote share of the major parties continues to decline, is the emergence of a new political pragmatism that could ultimately compound the very loss of trust – and voter support that the legacy parties are trying to subvert.It is the uniting of the parties of an establishment that is increasingly out of touch with and alienated from the electorate. As they play a game of whack-a-mole on thorny problems that communities want solved; gambling ads, gas taxes, the money and power behind big tech, combining their numbers to neutralise the niggles is a neat albeit short-term solution.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA ‘shiny, dangling carrot’ lured Jesse into gambling. He says Labor’s reform won’t stop others being sucked inRead moreIn the case of gambling, the Coalition claims that it “strengthened” the reform package with its tweaks, which are even less ambitious than those Peter Dutton proposed before the last election. The government gets to claim some level of groundbreaking bipartisanship to help it sleep at night.It is a not-so-grand coalition of right and “left” along the lines of what we have seen on and off for decades in Germany, for example, but now struggling to satisfy that country’s voters and to fend off the AfD rise from the extreme right.There may be a warning here: “Dance with the one that brung you” is a phrase borrowed by Ronald Reagan and others from American slang for sticking with those who helped you achieve your goals.Remaining Labor voters are unlikely to be impressed with their elected representatives conspiring with political opponents they are repeatedly told are the enemy of the interests of working Australians in defiance of their expressed wishes.Likewise, disappointed Liberal voters, dissatisfied with the direction, behaviour and record of a party they had supported habitually are likely to be further disenchanted as they see them lining up with their opposition to defeat their wishes.I have seen the raw grief of a family who lost a son to gambling. Labor’s stitch-up shows politics is broken | David PocockRead moreSuch a coalition of convenience will reinforce the sentiment that the “system” has nothing for them any more; the big end of parliament lining up with the big end of town conspiring with each other rather than working for them.It is the ultimate display of self-interest.No wonder support for the majors is down to about 50% in total; no wonder some everyday Australians are choosing anger, in the form that One Nation represents.Others, seeking representation free from vested interests are leaning independent to provide the transparency and accountability that they’re looking for.Labor also likes to make big claims about transparency, and yes, it is crystal clear what is going on here.If democracy is in essence a contract between people and power, that contract is broken.We will all wear the consequences.Zoe Daniel is a three-time ABC foreign correspondent and the former independent member for GoldsteinExplore more on these topicsGamblingOpinionAustralian politicsAnthony AlbaneseAngus TaylorLabor partyNational partyLiberal partycommentShareReuse this content

title: I’m known as The Black Farmer because there are so few of us in the UK. It’s one of the ways farming must change | Wilfred Emmanuel-Jones | The Guardian
description: Running a farm is tough – TV’s Clarkson’s Farm shows that – but I know many minorities would love the chance. And we would all benefit, says farmer and businessman Wilfred Emmanuel-Jones
Author: Wilfred Emmanuel-Jones
Headline: Running a farm is tough – TV’s Clarkson’s Farm shows that – but I know many minorities would love the chance. And we would all benefit, says farmer and businessman Wilfred Emmanuel-Jones
Content: In Defra’s most recent survey of England’s principal farmers and holders, 99.7% self-described as white.Photograph: Peter Cade/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIn Defra’s most recent survey of England’s principal farmers and holders, 99.7% self-described as white.Photograph: Peter Cade/Getty ImagesOpinionFarmingI’m known as The Black Farmer because there are so few of us in the UK. It’s one of the ways farming must changeWilfred Emmanuel-JonesRunning a farm is tough – TV’s Clarkson’s Farm shows that – but I know many minorities would love the chance. And we would all benefitSat 22 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 22 Aug 2026 12.46 EDTShareWho’d be a farmer?Clarkson’s Farm on Amazonis great entertainment but it also gives some indication of the stresses and challenges behind the farm gate. Would anyone who lacked the significant alternative income that Clarkson is lucky to have want that? Well, actually, yes.I’m an entrepreneur who owns a farm, as opposed to hands-on running the small one I bought 25 years ago, but as I look around the industry, I’m struck by a significant fact: the very reason I can be known as the Black Farmer is because I am such a rarity that it makes me readily identifiable.Because of what I do, people – many of them British minorities – often ask me how they can be farmers, how they can secure some land and set up for themselves. Don’t be surprised at that: among Britain’s minorities, millions have rural origins in lands abroad. It is a mistake to see people of colour as intrinsically urban – my own origins are in rural Jamaica. But when they ask me, I can’t really help them. There is no obvious route for them to follow, and there is precious little land they could possibly farm. This is the reality. In 2025, when Defra completed its most recent survey of principal farmers and holders in England, it found 99.7% of those who respondedself-described as white.I’m aware of the pitfall here. I know the danger these days of wanting to talk about diversity and being dismissed as woke. I’m hardly woke: in 2010 I fought a rural seat for the Conservatives. But in any other industry, that figure, 99.7%, would prompt some questions.Here are the problems. If you are black or Asian or a kid from another minority in London, or Manchester, or Birmingham or Newcastle, where do you start? Your parents don’t own even an acre of land. You don’t have the network, or the knowledge that comes from growing up within or adjacent to a farming family and a farming community.There is the ongoing and emotive debate about inheritance tax and whether farms should so easily be passed down from generation to generation. I’m among those who celebrate the families that have worked the same land year after year, decade after decade. That brings a knowledge and continuity essential to rural communities and our food supply. But as well as inheritance, we have to think about entry. People cannot resolve to make that commitment if they cannot see a way in.How could that be different? Think about who owns the land. The National Trust, for example, is the country’s largest farm-owner,with more than 1,300 tenant farmers. Think about the Duchy of Cornwall, the crown estate, the Church of England. Universities and local authorities also control large tracts of land. There are people and institutions that could administer properly controlled programmes to allow those from non-traditional farming backgrounds to have a go. They could create starter farms and offer affordable tenancies. They could provide mentoring, pairing experienced farmers with ambitious newcomers, and give access to equipment. Maybe there could be targeted apprenticeships, allowing people to learn the ropes on someone else’s farm – a process that may lead to them owning their own farm. One might cite 28-year-oldKaleb Cooperon Clarkson’s farm, although in that case it is clearly the younger man teaching the older how it is done.View image in fullscreenWilfred Emmanuel-Jones walking on Dartmoor.Photograph: Tim Cuff/AlamyThe supermarkets could play a role, as they wield enormous influence over British food and how it is produced. Why can’t they create routes for a new generation of growers, providing a sure path for produce to reach the public? That would be a move towards diversity with a clear economic purpose.Farmingcould do with new blood: people who question the traditions, people who know about different foods, cultures and business models – people who look at a field and can envision things that previous generations couldn’t.I think back. I grew up in Birmingham and my first experience with the land was helping my father on his allotment. My route was defiantly non-traditional. I struggled with undiagnosed dyslexia, joined the Parachute regiment and got kicked out, flipped burgers, worked as a chef and then produced cookery programmes for the BBC, which allowed me to buy a farm in Devon. Locals dubbed me “the Black Farmer”. I wish there were many more of us.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI would never want to denigrate those who work so hard, and who may have toiled for generations to run their farms, produce the food we need and sometimes – if they are lucky, if the weather permits, if the stars align – make a profit. But I also want to be just as excited by the prospect of another black kid from Birmingham getting an opportunity, or a minority kid from a council estate in Manchester becoming the first farmer in the family.Farming is key to the future, and the climate crisis is forcing us to think fast and hard about crops, water, soil and what we do with them. Old timers, new thinkers – we need both.Wilfred Emmanuel-Jones is a businessman and founder of The Black Farmer food companyExplore more on these topicsFarmingOpinionRaceFood & drink industryLand ownershipcommentShareReuse this content

title: Four blokes and a zebra crossing: the banality and beauty of the Beatles’ Abbey Road cover | The Beatles | The Guardian
description: Much-copied and parodied picture captures dynamic between the individuals and the band with eerie perfection
Author: Jonathan Jones
Headline: Much-copied and parodied picture captures dynamic between the individuals and the band with eerie perfection
Content: Paul McCartney came up with the concept for Abbey Road’s cover after a proposed shoot in Nepal was rejected.Photograph: Apple RecordsView image in fullscreenPaul McCartney came up with the concept for Abbey Road’s cover after a proposed shoot in Nepal was rejected.Photograph: Apple RecordsThe BeatlesFour blokes and a zebra crossing: the banality and beauty of the Beatles’ Abbey Road coverMuch-copied and parodied picture captures dynamic between the individuals and the band with eerie perfectionJonathan JonesSat 22 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s not really the four blokes on the zebra crossing who make the cover of the Beatles’ Abbey Road memorable, but the street behind them. Vanishing towards a perfect blue sky, with summer trees veiling in bright green what might otherwise be dour brick houses, it could be a hyperreal vista painted by David Hockney. The black and white stripes of the crossing and the white line down the middle of the receding northLondonroad are fresh and crisp, enhancing the clarity of this psychedelic daydream.Of course the four blokes do play a part.The Beatleswere so transcendently famous by the time Iain Macmillan took this picture on 8 August 1969 that seeing them do something as ordinary as cross the road becomes a magical mystery.All the tourists who continue to recreate this photograph, the acts – from the Red Hot Chili Peppers and Kanye West to Franciscan friars and Booker T and the MGs – who have parodied it, as well asSam Mendes, who this week recreated it for his four Beatles biopics, are hypnotised by its enigmatic marriage of banality and charisma. Just four people on a zebra crossing, but they’re gods!The Beatles played on the same impossible everydayness months before this picture was taken when they performed live on the roof of Apple Corps in London’s Savile Row in January 1969. These were not just among the group’s last appearances together; they were manifestations against London backdrops of four individuals who had become archetypes.‘I can gauge John’s reaction: that’s good, stick that in’: Paul McCartney on how old bandmates – and Oasis – inspired his nostalgic new albumRead moreWhat Abbey Road freeze-frames with eerie perfection is the dynamic between four individuals and one unit that made the Beatles so appealing: the character of each Beatle coming together, or so fans still wanted to believe, in perfect step, as this photograph catches them.John Lennon leads, yet seems absent and absorbed: he is the only one whose face you can’t fully see and if he is the pacesetter, he might also be trying to get away. There I go. There’s a self-consciously symbolic quality to this picture that invites you to insert whatever allegory you please. I can picture Lennon walking away because that’s what he told the group he was going to do that September.But at the time, notoriously, it was Paul McCartney’s bare feet that fed bizarre speculations he was dead. According to this conspiracy theory, the black-clad Ringo Starr is the undertaker andGeorge Harrisonthe gravedigger.View image in fullscreenThe Red Hot Chili Peppers humorously recreate the photo for their 1988 release The Abbey Road EP.Photograph: EMIIt’s not such a bad interpretation and answers the picture’s demand to be decoded: surely it must be saying something! But the “Paul is dead” theory was doubly daft since McCartney was the picture’s creative author along with Macmillan.This was not a photograph taken by chance. It is a piece of conceptual art – something the Beatles were very familiar with, what with Lennon marrying one of the world’s most radical artists, Yoko Ono, that year. After an idea of being photographed in Nepal was rejected, it was McCartney who suggested they just do it in Abbey Road, outsidethe music studios in north London’s St John’s Wood. His sketches planned out the picture, with the four of them as stick figures on the zebra crossing and a view from above of the tree-lined street. On the day, they got a police officer to stop traffic, and Macmillan stood on a stepladder to get this perspective.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSleeve NotesGet music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThe cover of the 1993 album Sesame Road recreates the Beatles cover with characters from the children’s TV show Sesame Street.Photograph: Sony WonderIt’s not an accident; it’s art. McCartney started collecting paintings byRené Magrittein 1966 and this picture’s combination of a haunting, almost too real perspective and a confounding yet deadpan foreground scene is highly evocative of the Belgian surrealist. These are not the Beatles. This is not Abbey Road.It is definitely London, though. In these days of national self-loathing the wonder of the Abbey Road cover has to be its celebration of a very British moment. Zebra crossings are British: you know this is London, not New York.The Beatles are walking into their separate futures, but here McCartney, the most passionate believer in the band, freezes them for ever outside the studios where they’ve worked. He doesn’t want to go anywhere – he’s taken off his shoes.Explore more on these topicsThe BeatlesLondonPhotographyRené MagritteRingo StarrGeorge HarrisonPaul McCartneyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: From Booker-listed Marlon James to a memoir by Michael Douglas – the biggest books this autumn | Books | The Guardian
description: Midlife meditations from Barbara Kingsolver; musical portraits by Jonathan Coe and Yiyun Li; plus memoirs from Dustin Hoffman and Judi Dench – all among the coming season’s highlights
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Midlife meditations from Barbara Kingsolver; musical portraits by Jonathan Coe and Yiyun Li; plus memoirs from Dustin Hoffman and Judi Dench – all among the coming season’s highlights
Content: Illustration: Simon Pemberton/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Simon Pemberton/The GuardianBooksFrom Booker-listed Marlon James to a memoir by Michael Douglas – the biggest books this autumnMidlife meditations from Barbara Kingsolver; musical portraits by Jonathan Coe and Yiyun Li; plus memoirs from Dustin Hoffman and Judi Dench – all among the coming season’s highlightsSat 22 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTShareFictionThe DisappearersbyMarlon JamesHamish Hamilton, 3 SeptemberAfter a detour into mythic fantasy, the author of the Booker-winning A Brief History of Seven Killings returns to Jamaica. This account of a brutal homophobic attack on a group of gay actors in 1980s Kingston has already been longlisted for this year’s prize.The BridgebyColm TóibínPicador, 3 SeptemberTwenty years on, this short novel is a sequel to Tóibín’s exquisite story A Long Winter, set around a family tragedy in the isolated Pyrenees. Now the building of a bridge brings modernity, possibility and threat to a father and son, in a spare chronicle of longing and grief.The Golden HoursbyLouisa YoungMantle, 3 SeptemberYoung continues her aunt Elizabeth Jane Howard’s much-loved Cazalet Chronicles, bringing her story of a sprawling upper-middle-class English family into the swinging 60s.SwitzybyEmma ClineChatto & Windus, 10 SeptemberWith dementia making him increasingly confused, David is on his way to a clinic in Zurich to end his life while he still has the capacity to make a choice. Longlisted for the Booker prize, this is a bravura portrait of a failing mind, told from the inside.The RousebyChina MiévillePicador, 17 SeptemberA leading light of the New Weird, Miéville has been working on this stonking 1,000-page supernatural fantasy for two decades. Political intrigue, continent-hopping global conspiracy and uncanny mysteries unfold.View image in fullscreenThe HousekeeperbyRose TremainChatto & Windus, 17 SeptemberAn origin story for Daphne du Maurier’s enduring bestseller Rebecca is told from the perspective of the novelist’s secret lover Danni, housekeeper in a Cornish mansion, who is outraged to find herself recast on the page as the malevolent Mrs Danvers.StationsbyLouise KennedyBloomsbury, 24 SeptemberThe author of bestselling 2022 debut novel Trespasses, a Troubles-set love story recently adapted into a C4 drama starring Gillian Anderson, returns with a tale of friendship and loss. Róisín and Red meet in small-town Ireland in the 1980s and reconnect in a London squat, before Red is caught up in a cycle of poverty and addiction.Doom PaintingbyAK BlakemoreGranta, 24 SeptemberOne of our most exciting historical novelists takes on the peasants’ revolt, in a blow-by-blow account of unlikely leader Wat Tyler and the 16 days in 1381 that turned England upside down. With cinematic action and a relish for medieval vocabulary, it’s a punky successor to Hilary Mantel.View image in fullscreen(Left to right) Barbara Kingsolver, Marlon James, Bonnie Garmus,  Jonathan Coe, Yiyun Li and Emma Cline.Composite: Getty/Christopher L Proctor/Ricky Sai and Simon PembertonzAmerican HagwonbyMin Jin Lee4th Estate, 29 SeptemberThe hagwon or cram school is a symbol of Korea’s stress on education. This new saga from the Pachinko author follows a middle-class family, their life in ruins after the 1997 Asian financial crisis, who move to Sydney and then California in search of a better future for their children.PartitabyBarbara KingsolverFaber, 6 OctoberAfter the Pulitzer-winning Demon Copperhead, a retelling of David Copperfield set in Appalachia, Kingsolver returns with a quieter tale of midlife longing and regret. A gifted pianist, Livia used music to escape the sadness of her family life in rural Tennessee, but having married and resettled in her home town, an unexpected call from a former lover drags her back into the past.Life Out of OrderbyAudrey NiffeneggerJonathan Cape, 13 OctoberSet a quarter of a century on, this long-awaited sequel focuses on the daughter of the couple in The Time Traveler’s Wife. Alba has inherited her father’s extraordinary condition, jumping unpredictably across the decades, from a United States in turmoil to a dystopian future London. She’s torn between two lovers – one anchored in the present, and one a time traveller like herself.Peck & PeckbyBonnie GarmusManilla, 13 OctoberIn the follow-up to global bestseller Lessons in Chemistry, it’s 1982 New York and young Batter Gray lands a job at the eponymous poetry periodical, run by feuding twin brothers. Expect charm, quirk and literary rabbit holes.View image in fullscreenIn One Brief MomentAll EternitybyElif ShafakViking, 15 OctoberFrom the Booker and Women’s prize-shortlisted author, a study of French writer Gustave Flaubert refracted through the lives of the women around him, including his most iconic creation: Madame Bovary.Music Against the NightbyYiyun Li4th Estate, 22 OctoberSet at the end of the 18th century, against a background of global tumult, the Pulitzer winner’s historical epic is inspired by the lives of two musicians: Adelaide Percheron, born in French India, and the Irish John Field, the inventor of the nocturne, who will be brought together by love and talent.Lessons in HarmonybyJonathan CoeViking, 12 NovemberMusic is in the air this autumn: Coe’s latest follows the friendship between French dandy Maurice Ravel and English traditionalist Ralph Vaughan Williams, exploring creativity and national identity against the encroaching shadow of the first world war.Crime and thrillersSherlock Holmes, Miss Marple and George Smiley returnView image in fullscreenAutumn is back-to-school season for series authors, with William Boyd on the third of his cold war espionage novels starring travel writer Gabriel Dax. InCold Sunset(Viking, 3 September) our reluctant spy is on his way to Russia, to tussle with the KGB. Richard Osman serves up number two in his We Solve Murders franchise:We Chase Shadows(Viking, 10 September) sees Steve, Amy and Rosie – retired cop, private security officer and bestselling crime author respectively – investigate after a body is found in the Italian hills. Five years on, Janice Hallett publishes a sequel to her hit am-dram debut The Appeal, as the Fairway Players’ new production of Agatha Christie leads to murder inThe Silent Appeal(Viper, 3 September). The vigorous afterlife of the queen of crime continues elsewhere, with the first official new outing for Miss Marple,Murder at the Grand Alpine Hotelby Lucy Foley (HarperCollins, 22 September). A varied cast list, death on the mountaintop and plenty of suspects are guaranteed.Ian Rankin, known for his grumpy Edinburgh detective John Rebus, takes a new direction inThe Heights(Orion, 8 October), a standalone thriller set in a luxurious central London high-rise. And there’s a return to the world of John le Carré’s Circus in the latest from his son Nick Harkaway: inThe Taper Man(Viking, 5 November), George Smiley finds himself navigating the unlikely terrain of 1960s LA in search of a communist sleeper agent.Finally, a festive treat: 10 new adventures for the world’s most famous detective in short story anthologySherlock(Simon & Schuster, 5 November), with contributors including Sarah Perry, Joe Hill, Abir Mukherjee and Kate Mosse.NonfictionSwan Song: Diana, My SisterbyCharles SpencerPenguin Michael Joseph, 22 SeptemberThirty years after Princess Diana was killed in a car crash, her brother – whose euology at her funeral echoed around the world – tells the story of their upbringing and recounts the devastating week of her death.The CastlebyJon RonsonViking, 20 AugustA concerning late-night call from his teenage son marks the start of a strange journey into modern masculinity for the journalist and author of The Psychopath Test and So You’ve Been Publicly Shamed.The Future StartsWith UsbyGordon BrownSimon & Schuster, 1 SeptemberThe former PM tries to join the dots between two seemingly disparate political phenomena: the erosion of the international rules-based order, exacerbated by war and climate breakdown, and the fragmentation of the tight-knit communities that keep us connected at a local level.View image in fullscreenThe Great Dictator: A Life of Barbara CartlandbyMatthew SweetHodder & Stoughton, 10 SeptemberThe queen of romance novels wrote a scarcely believable 723 of them during her career – with a little help from an amanuensis or two. Historian Sweet tells the extraordinary story of a woman born into an upper‑middle-class family fallen on hard times, who navigated scandal and opprobrium to become one of the bestselling writers of the 20th century.Queens and Kings: An Unusually Personal HistorybyLucy WorsleyHodder & Stoughton, 3 SeptemberThe historian and chief curator of royal palaces brings a personal touch to some of British history’s pivotal moments, focusing on the places in which they unfolded, and in which Worsley herself has worked: Hampton Court, Kensington Palace and the Tower of London.All the Wrong MovesbyAnthony ScaramucciBodley Head, 17 SeptemberNot many political figures are able to give Liz Truss a run for her money in the shortest-ever-tenure stakes, but Scaramucci, Trump’s press secretary for just 10 days, is one of them. Since then he’s reinvented himself as one of the administration’s sharpest critics. His first book is an attempt to chart how the US went from stable postwar consensus to today’s “shitshow politics”.End Times FascismbyNaomi Kleinand Astra TaylorAllen Lane,15 SeptemberThinkers and activists Klein and Taylor have identified a distinctive strand of rightwing nihilism: the kind that seeks to reshape the world in its image, even as it devours the natural resources on which our survival depends (certain tech barons and authoritarian leaders may feel particularly seen). Here they offer both a diagnosis and a plan for resistance.Profits, Prophets, Coaches and Kings:(When) Do Leaders Make a Difference?byJared DiamondMariner, 22 SeptemberThe author of Guns, Germs and Steel, known for his analyses of the grand, impersonal forces that shape human destiny, returns with a timely book on the role of prominent individuals. What difference does a sports coach, a CEO or an erratic president really make to the fortunes of teams, companies and global civilisation?An Unexpected Life: A MemoirbyGloria SteinemEbury, 22 SeptemberA totemic figure in American feminism, Steinem sought to carry the momentum of the civil rights era into what became known as the women’s liberation movement. Here she writes about her childhood and political awakening, and reflects from the present moment on nearly 60 years of activism.View image in fullscreen(Left to right) Joe Biden, Colin Kaepernick, Naomi Klein, Malcolm Gladwell and Judi Dench.Composite: Getty and Simon PembertonHawking: His Life and WorkbyGraham FarmeloJohn Murray, 24 SeptemberIn the first authorised biography of Stephen Hawking, Farmelo paints an intimate portrait of the acclaimed physicist based on unique access to his diaries and letters, as well as interviews with family and close associates.The American Way of Killing:The Invention of an EpidemicbyMalcolm GladwellAbacus,29 SeptemberThe author of The Tipping Point asks why the United States has ended up being so much more violent than comparable countries around the world. From a Chicago ER to a 17th-century court case, he explores stories that may hold the key to what he describes as “the most pressing of all American social problems”.View image in fullscreenBlockers: Rebels in the Deep Stateby Michael LewisAllen Lane, 6 OctoberLewis’s pacy, high-stakes nonfiction has been drawing readers since 1989’s Liar’s Poker, an account of his time on Wall Street in the 1980s. Here he deploys his powers of narration to tell the story of how the US Department of Government Efficiency (Doge) sought to dismantle the state – though his real subject is the principled civil servants who stood in the way of Elon Musk’s campaign of vandalism.Requiem for GazabyJoe Sacco and Chris HedgesJonathan Cape, 8 OctoberThe master of graphic reportage and author of Palestine teams up with veteran war correspondent Hedges to document the devastating Israeli war on Gaza and its human impact. Interviewing 29 displaced Palestinian families, Sacco and Hedges tell stories of death, destruction and resilience.The Perilous FightbyColin KaepernickGrand Central Publishing, 8 OctoberThe NFL quarterback made history in 2016 when he knelt for the US national anthem, rather than standing. Since that time, “taking the knee” has become an emblem of the fight for racial justice, in the US and beyond. In his memoir, Kaepernick traces the relationships and experiences that culminated in a pivotal sporting and political moment.Promise Me, AmericabyJoe BidenJohn Murray, 17 NovemberA year on from 107 Days, in which former vice-president Kamala Harris detailed her boss’s failure to get out of the way, Joe Biden tells his side of the story in a book which promises to reveal “the deeply agonising calculation behind his decision … to step aside from the presidential race”.Pay Attentionby Laura KuenssbergCorsair,5 NovemberThe former BBC political editor’s first book reflects on 20 years of upheaval in British politics, and what the broadcaster perceives as being at the root of it all: a failure by the political class to really listen to what people have actually been saying.Holding Lightning: The Life, Loves and Artof Whitney HoustonbyEmily LordiWhite Rabbit,1 OctoberEnglish professor Lordi treats the career of one of pop’s greatest stars with the seriousness it deserves, but with emotional intelligence too, tracing the arc of Houston’s life from global success to personal tragedy.MemoirFrom Hollywood hijinks to political scandal – life stories to look out forView image in fullscreenIt’s another bumper autumn for Hollywood stars with plenty of tales to tell – though this year skews male. Michael Douglas’sOne Helluva Ride(Headline, 6 October) includes details of “affairs with some of the most celebrated actresses in Hollywood” and the “serious drug addiction that threatened to destroy his first marriage and career”. If you’re still in the mood for testosterone-laced hijinks after that, there’s Sylvester Stallone’sThe Steps(Seven Dials, 29 September), which charts the Rocky star’s 1970s journey from homelessness to the Oscars. For a more multilayered take on acting and fame, tryFictional Selvesby Kyle MacLachlan (Century, 29 September), whose talent in picking idiosyncratic roles such as such as Agent Cooper in Twin Peaks has earned him a cult following. And then there’s screen icon Dustin Hoffman, whose first memoirLook at Me(Gallery, 10 November), published as he prepares to enter his 10th decade, covers the pressures of being dubbed the “voice of a generation” after The Graduate, and his many acting roles since that extraordinary breakthrough. It would make a neat pairing with Watergate reporter Bob Woodward’s memoirSecrets(Simon & Schuster, 24 November): that era-defining scoop was dramatised in All the President’s Men, with Hoffman playing Woodward’s partner, Carl Bernstein.On the other side of the Atlantic, Judi Dench reminisces about a 70-year career inIs It Too Late to Make a Run for It?(Michael Joseph, 22 October). InVigilauntie(W&N, 3 September) actor and co-creator of the groundbreaking sketch show Goodness Gracious Me, Meera Syal, writes about family, frustration and making it as an Asian woman on TV, while another veteran of the small screen, Russell T Davies, charts a writing career that has spanned Coronation Street and Doctor Who inThe Queerest of Folk(Bantam, 8 October). Everyone’s favourite communist standup Alexei Sayle gets political inHow I’ve Tried to Change the World(W&N, 3 September), a memoir of protest through the decades, while actual politician and scourge of the BNP in her Barking constituency, Margaret Hodge, shares the lessons of a life on the frontlines inBattle Axe(William Collins, 10 September).

title: Courtney Büchner: One of the Girls review – all aboard for a rollercoaster relationship  | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: From embarrassing anecdotes to karaoke and lurking on Instagram, this love story sweeps you along
Author: Anya Ryan
Headline: From embarrassing anecdotes to karaoke and lurking on Instagram, this love story sweeps you along
Content: ‘Things get complicated’ … Courtney Buchner in a publicity shot for One of the Girls.Photograph: Dylan WoodleyView image in fullscreen‘Things get complicated’ … Courtney Buchner in a publicity shot for One of the Girls.Photograph: Dylan WoodleyEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewCourtney Büchner: One of the Girls review – all aboard for a rollercoaster relationshipPleasance Courtyard, EdinburghFrom embarrassing anecdotes to karaoke and lurking on Instagram, this love story sweeps you alongAnya RyanSat 22 Aug 2026 04.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCourtney Büchner is here to tell us a love story. Not the type you’re thinking of – even though she has just married her partner, Maddy. This rollercoaster platonic relationship is with Stella, the girl she met at school shortly after moving from South Africa to the UK. It is a sweet, nostalgia-fuelled tale, but one that at times feels too slight to sustain an hour.It wasn’t quite love at first sight, but Stella quickly became Büchner’s ride or die. Together they danced for their lives on sticky-floored club nights, saw each other through their first kisses and GCSE results, and told each other they were the most beautiful woman in the world. Still, we can sense early on that this might not be a happily ever after. When Büchner comes out as a lesbian to Stella and introduces Maddy into their lives, things start to become a little more complicated.But before we get to all that, Büchner has got to get the room onside. “I’m Courtney – what’s your favourite colour?” she asks several audience members before encouraging us all to join her for a karaoke session. Tonight, we are her closest confidants, and Büchner builds the vibe of a teenage sleepover. “I have exciting news,” she giggles – and we wait eagerly to be brought into her fold. Although the show is more of a good time than a laugh riot, it is a pleasure to hear her wisdom on the state of adult female friendships and our desperation to cling on to the past.Laughing on the other side: the fringe shows turning painful breakups into comedyRead moreIn an aptly titled show, Büchner revels in retelling embarrassing stories and spending just a tad too long lurking on Instagram profiles she shouldn’t. Even the audience isn’t immune to her digital snooping. She paints a vivid, messy picture of teenage girls’ minds and how little bits of their thinking lurk their way into adulthood.There’s real heartbreak, too – which those of us who have ever drifted from a close friend will feel in our guts. It’s not a show that will surprise you in either form or narrative, but Büchner is a magnetic, conversational storyteller, sure to keep you hooked.AtPleasance Courtyard, Edinburgh, until 31 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Comedy (Stage)Comedy (Culture)Edinburgh festivalLGBTQ+ rightsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘We are in the inferno’: diaspora writers lead new movement of nature poetry | Poetry | The Guardian
description: UK anthology inspired by question: ‘Where are our black and Asian nature writers?’ has boosted interest in genre
Author: Sandra Laville
Headline: UK anthology inspired by question: ‘Where are our black and Asian nature writers?’ has boosted interest in genre
Content: The UK-based Jamaican poet Jason Allen-Paisant is among those featured in the anthology.Photograph: Richard Saker/The ObserverView image in fullscreenThe UK-based Jamaican poet Jason Allen-Paisant is among those featured in the anthology.Photograph: Richard Saker/The ObserverPoetry‘We are in the inferno’: diaspora writers lead new movement of nature poetryUK anthology inspired by question: ‘Where are our black and Asian nature writers?’ has boosted interest in genreSandra LavilleSat 22 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 22 Aug 2026 14.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA new movement of eco poets from black and brown communities in the UK is challenging the canon of nature poetry against the backdrop of the climate and biodiversity crisis.Mona Arshi, who co-edited the first UK collection of eco poetry from African, Asian and Caribbean diaspora voices, was inspired to put the anthology together after asking in a social media post that went viral: “Where are all our black and Asian nature writers?”She said: “It was not that people were not writing in those spaces but they hadn’t been gathered, they hadn’t been published, or in some cases their poetry has not been framed as nature poetry. So the process was like lifting a veil. It was like a visibility project.”The anthology,Nature Matters, edited by Arshi and Karen Mcarthy Woolf, has been taken up in the past year in universities and some schools and has boosted interest in nature poetry from perspectives very different to white, western and mainstream culture.The new movement of nature poetry has as a powerful theme the destruction of nature, which is happening at rates unprecedented in human history as a result of global heating, intensive agricultural practices, pollution and the exploitation of natural resources.The movement unpicks and challenges the nature of the pastoral, who gets access to it and who has had ownership of the genre of nature poetry.As the UK-based Jamaican poet Jason Allen-Paisant writes in his offering for the anthology:It’s time to write about daffodilsagain.Arshi said: “Today we are in a very different place to where the 18th-century Romantic poets were. We are in the inferno, whereas for them it was approaching. I feel you cannot be writing about natural beauty today in a poem without it being burdened with ideas of climate catastrophe.”View image in fullscreenThe Lake District has provided inspiration for poets of the past.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianConnections between poetry and nature have been centuries made, with the natural world providing inspiration and metaphor for some of the best-known poets in the English language, such as William Wordsworth, John Keats and John Clare.Simon Armitage pledged to dedicate his writing to environmental issues when he was appointed as poet laureate in 2019 and has long argued that poets can help fight climate breakdown by making the reader “spellbound, full of wonder and beguiled” by nature.Ralph Pite, a professor of English at Bristol University who specialises in studying the relationship between literature and the physical world, said the new generation of nature poets brought forward ways of thinking about the environment that mainstream western culture had ignored, neglected, erased or consigned to the past.“Through their poetry, everyone gains the right to roam in the natural world; it’s no longer available only to the RP speaker or the white, educated, middle-class person,” Pite said. “So they show that England can belong to everyone in our society, that the landscape does not have to convey a narrow idea of what Englishness is – that we can get beyond that historical divisiveness, which has erected barriers of class, region and ethnicity.”View image in fullscreenMona Arshi: ‘The process was like lifting a veil.’Photograph: Karolina HellerArshi said that as a child she felt very alienated from the countryside. “I was born in the UK into a Sikh Punjabi family; we lived near Heathrow. Entering the countryside was never part of my childhood. Anytime we had encountered nature, the countryside when I was growing up, it was quite hostile, and it felt very alien to be in those landscapes. So later I didn’t consider myself a nature poet at all.”But after being selected to be poet in residence at Cley Marshes in Norfolk, she started asking what qualifies as nature poetry, who is deemed a nature poet and why.“What is happening now with the anthology is wonderful,” she said. “Anthologies are slow and impactful in the culture. They hit the bloodstream of a culture because they get shared and used in schools, in universities, and that is what is happening now and it is wonderful.”Jos Smith, an associate professor of English literature at the University of East Anglia, said the work had become part of his teaching. “This anthology is long overdue in the UK,” he said. “Eco poetry has in the past always tended to be quite white, and it is good to see students responding to the kind of poetry in Nature Matters, which has a greater level of complexity and problematises things like nationhood and language in a way that is quite new for British eco poetry.”Explore more on these topicsPoetryScience and nature booksConservationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Stand By Me at 40: Rob Reiner’s seminal coming-of-age saga remains a bittersweet triumph | Drama films | The Guardian
description: The late director’s sensitive and detailed adaptation of Stephen King’s novella has an authenticity that so many imitators could never replicate
Author: Scott Tobias
Headline: The late director’s sensitive and detailed adaptation of Stephen King’s novella has an authenticity that so many imitators could never replicate
Content: River Phoenix and Wil Wheaton in Stand By Me.Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Limited./AlamyView image in fullscreenRiver Phoenix and Wil Wheaton in Stand By Me.Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Limited./AlamyDrama filmsStand By Me at 40: Rob Reiner’s seminal coming-of-age saga remains a bittersweet triumphThe late director’s sensitive and detailed adaptation of Stephen King’s novella has an authenticity that so many imitators could never replicateScott TobiasSat 22 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 22 Aug 2026 16.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleComing-of-age metaphors don’t get any blunter than a group of preteen boys following a set of railroad tracks to a classmate’s dead body, a sobering testament to the fragility of life and a sign that their own futures are not guaranteed. TheStephen Kingnovella that would become Rob Reiner’s Stand By Me is simply called The Body, and there’s no doubt that commercial considerations factored into naming the film after the song that blankets the soundtrack. Yet the enduring magic of Reiner’s film lies in the tension between this bleak journey and the nostalgia and warmth that keeps complicating our feelings about it. Between those two poles is a bittersweet tone that perfectly suits the material, the rare example of an adaptation that benefits from softened edges.Stand By Me review – Rob Reiner’s nostalgic look at friendship and the loss of innocence still grips tightRead moreThough Reiner kicked off his career on a legendary heater that opened with This is Spinal Tap and would go on to include The Princess Bride, When Harry Met Sally … and A Few Good Men, Stand By Me was just his third feature and an early showcase of his versatility. His deft comic touch is not only essential in maintaining tonal balance, but important in suggesting what these four wayward boys mean to each other. Between the loose talk about Annette Funicello’s expanding bust on The Mickey Mouse Club and a Wurlitzer soundtrack of novelty singles like Lollipop and Yakety Yak, it can be easy to forget the anger, pain and dread that’s always simmering close to the surface. They laugh to keep from crying and occasionally don’t succeed.Though set a few years earlier than American Graffiti, Stand By Me feels like a natural companion to it, another radio-friendly nostalgia piece about a transitional moment for male friends in small-town America. Both films are death-haunted but the difference is that the characters in American Graffiti, who are reaching young adulthood at the cusp of the Vietnam war, don’t know what the future holds and writer-director George Lucas saves that bummer news for the epilogue. The boys in Reiner’s film know what lies at the end of a 20- to 30-mile hike down the tracks and their attraction to the novelty and notoriety of seeing a dead peer turns morbid. Their steps grow heavier by the hour.The more direct tie-in to American Graffiti is Richard Dreyfuss as Gordie LaChance, who narrates his memories as a novelist and father who’s gotten the perspective he and his buddies lacked as 12-year-olds.
