Flashing back to Labor Day weekend in 1959, the film casts Wil Wheaton as young Gordie, whose intellect and storytelling wizardry already puts some distance between him and his three troublemaking friends, who are bound for trade school at best. There’s not much to do in the Oregon backwater of Castle Rock, so when Gordie’s pal Vern (Jerry O’Connell) overhears his older brother talking about where they found the body of missing boy, the group’s curiosity is piqued. The two other no-goodniks in the gang, Chris (River Phoenix) and Teddy (Corey Feldman), come from broken homes, so they’re all too happy to lie to their parents and join the hunt. They figure they’ll be stars on the local news.Even when he’s writing horror novels around this period, like the first half of It or 11/22/63, King’s affection for the late ‘50s and early ‘60s of his own adolescence is boundless and those fond memories flow through Stand By Me. (Between this and his 1990 adaptation of Misery, which plays off an author’s relationship with his fans, Reiner would become King’s unofficial screen biographer.) Small details like the boys singing the theme song to the TV western Have Gun – Will Travel or musing about cherry-flavored Pez or “what Goofy is” fill out the milieu before the fun pops like bubblegum. As Dreyfuss describes it, a jovial night around the campfire featured “the kind of talk that seemed important until you discover girls”.I watched Stand By Me with Rob Reiner. Both film and man changed my lifeRead moreReiner stages some fun scrapes along the way, like a confrontation with a notably meek junkyard dog and a mad dash across a bridge as a train unexpectedly bears down on them. His work with his exceptionally talented young cast, too, establishes a relaxed camaraderie that pays huge emotional dividends later, when they’re closer to the end of the line. Much has been made about how Feldman’s angst about his troubles offscreen feeds into his startling reserves of anger as Teddy, a boy whose father once held his face to the stove. Wheaton, too, has affecting moments as the lesser son of parents who grieve his late older brother (played in flashbacks by John Cusack) and make him feel like the wrong kid died.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: c Columbia/Everett/Rex FeatureYet Stand By Me is another reminder of how generationally special Phoenix was as an actor, here in just his second feature after appearing with young Ethan Hawke in Explorers a year earlier. His Chris is a tough kid who seems to fit the mould of a sadistic greaser like the one played here by Kiefer Sutherland, but Phoenix plays him with astounding sensitivity, especially when Gordie needs a lift. Chris, Gordie and their buddies are expected to mask their vulnerabilities, and one of the film’s most effective gambits is how it contrasts these boys with Sutherland’s gang, who are inevitably cowed by his leadership. Phoenix’s Chris charts a more empathetic course.There are times when Reiner tilts too far into sentimentality, especially when Dreyfuss’ narration reaches for emotions the film might better grasp without a personal story seeming like grist for a novelist’s mill. Yet Stand By Me does well to preserve the R-rated saltiness of King’s world – it’s always more bracingly profane than you remember – and that helps it land more authentically than popular TV imitators like The Wonder Years and Stranger Things. These innocent boys strike out looking for a taste of adulthood and the film captures the feeling in all its pungency.Stand By Me is available on HBO Max in the US, Now TV in the UK and Tubi in AustraliaExplore more on these topicsDrama filmsRob ReinerStephen KingRiver PhoenixfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Guide #257: What we lose when a medium ​built for the ear surrender​s to the camera | Culture | The Guardian
description: In this week’s newsletter: As platforms chase ​s​ubscribers, podcasts are losing their off‑screen charm​, leaving listeners to wonder whether the intimacy of audio can survive the studio lights
Author: Gwilym Mumford
Headline: In this week’s newsletter: As platforms chase ​s​ubscribers, podcasts are losing their off‑screen charm​, leaving listeners to wonder whether the intimacy of audio can survive the studio lights
Content: Seeing is believing … Amy Poehler and Olivia Coleman chat on Good Hang with Amy Poehler.Photograph: YouTubeView image in fullscreenSeeing is believing … Amy Poehler and Olivia Coleman chat on Good Hang with Amy Poehler.Photograph: YouTubeThe Guide newsletterCultureThe Guide #257: What we lose when a medium ​built for the ear surrender​s to the cameraIn this week’s newsletter: As platforms chase ​s​ubscribers, podcasts are losing their off‑screen charm​, leaving listeners to wonder whether the intimacy of audio can survive the studio lightsDon’t get The Guide delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereGwilym MumfordSat 22 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 22 Aug 2026 02.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis has been the year that podcasting properly, unapologetically “pivoted to video”. Yes, it’s been a progression that has been in the making for quite a while, arguably ever since Joe Rogan first trained a webcam at himself and whichever guest he was smoking weed with in his studio back in 2009 – but in 2026 the medium’s transformation from purely aural to audio/visual (often with more of an emphasis on the visual) is truly complete.In January, Netflix startedbroadcasting video versions of popular podcastsfrom The Ringer, iHeartMedia, Barstool and more, as well as continuing to make video pods of their own. That landgrab was a slightly desperate response to YouTube’s phenomenal success with visualised pods; after becoming the preferred podcast platform for most Americans in 2024, it managed the same featin the UK in 2026, overtaking Spotify. No wonder, then, that Spotify has – as part of a wider push to get people sticking to its platform for pods – continued to bolster viewing capabilities for its own pods too.Meanwhile, more and more podcast creators are running into the arms of video, wheeling cameras into studios that often resemble an Ikea showroom circa 2008, with their felt throw cushions and chairs that are absurdly poorly suited to facing someone and having an actual conversation with them. (I’m concerned about what all this pivoting to video is doing to these poor podcasters’ backs; they all seem to be sitting so uncomfortably, swivelling between guest and camera.)You might have guessed from the slightly sniffy tone that I’m not entirely on board with podcasting’s video pivot.Podcastshave long had a clearly defined role in my life: they are there for when I’m ironing, on my commute, at the gym or the ever-shrinking bit of time not glued to a screen. Adding video complicates that. If people are performing to camera as much as to microphone, you start to feel like watching them is the only way to get the whole picture. And some podcasters are just not suited to camera: I don’t want their true gift for audio to be diluted by them having to constantly think about the lens pointed squarely at their face. Let podcasts be podcasts, I say!But lately I’ve realised that my King Canute stance against this tide is futile. I need to learn to stop worrying and love – well, tolerate at least – the video pod. This is a permanent revolution – and one that does have its advantages. Making a show visual as well as aural allows podcasters to clip up their best bits and share them for potential new fans on social media, a crucial arrow in the quiver of smaller podcasts that lack the marketing budgets of their bigger competitors. It feels a bit churlish of me to deny them that out of sheer podcast purism.View image in fullscreenSee the shock … John Robins’s credit score meltdown from Elis James and John Robins podcast.Photograph: YouTubeWorse still for my militant anti-video pod stance, I have to shamefully concede that some of them work pretty well visually. Who would have thunk it, but it turns out that comedians, in particular, are good with a camera pointed at them: I’ll regularly try to catch a good moment from Elis James and John Robins that I enjoyed in audio form on video later on – just to see the redness of John’s face (pictured above), and the reality of his contempt as he embarks on awhite-hot rageat having a less than perfect credit score rating, say.Other podcasts, for example some of the Ringer stable, are starting to skilfully knit in clips and stills from the shows and films they are talking about, which is definitely an improvement over watching two people talk at each other over a desk for an hour. (The Rest is History’s own attempts – flashing up the odd picture of a historical figure mid chat – is a little less slick but just about does the job.)I still have quibbles. Many of these video podcasts will never look to me like anything other than bargain-basement daytime chatshows, causing them to shed the aura of their audio form. And I will never stop being infuriated by podcasters who forget that they have a listening audience as well as one watching on a screen. Gesticulations are completely useless to those who can’t see them, and please, if something funny happens in the studio, explain it to listeners rather than just bursting into guffaws and moving on. Maddening!skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhat I’m trying to say is: I still want most podcasts to stay podcasts, nattering away amiably in my ear while I’m at the supermarket. But I will concede that the video podcast isn’t a totally terrible idea, particularly when set against, say,AI-generated podcasts. But that’s a rant for another newsletter …To read the complete version of this newsletterplease subscribeto receive The Guide in your inbox every FridayExplore more on these topicsCultureThe Guide newsletterPodcastingPodcastsDigital medianewslettersShareReuse this content

title: From Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma to Brandon Flowers: your complete entertainment guide to the week ahead | Culture | The Guardian
description: A film-maker’s attempt to reboot a horror movie franchise is derailed by her wild relationship with its former star, and the Killers frontman gets rustic
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A film-maker’s attempt to reboot a horror movie franchise is derailed by her wild relationship with its former star, and the Killers frontman gets rustic
Content: Director’s cult … Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma.Photograph:  MUBIView image in fullscreenDirector’s cult … Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma.Photograph:  MUBIGoing out, staying inCultureFrom Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma to Brandon Flowers: your complete entertainment guide to the week aheadA film-maker’s attempt to reboot a horror movie franchise is derailed by her wild relationship with its former star, and the Killers frontman gets rusticSat 22 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleContents1Going out: Cinema2Going out: Gigs3Going out: Art4Going out: Stage5Staying in: Streaming6Staying in: Games7Staying in: Albums8Staying in: Brain foodView image in fullscreenGoing out:CinemaTeenage Sex and Death at Camp MiasmaOut nowJane Schoenbrun’s third feature builds on their interest in queer horror, with a story about the fictional Camp Miasma slasher franchise, set to be resurrected by an up-and-coming director (Hannah Einbinder), who enters into a wild relationship with the star of the originals (Gillian Anderson).MutinyOut nowJason Statham is back in his favourite niche of action thriller: one guy pitted against a system or conspiracy, which he will try to unravel, and when that doesn’t work, smash it to bits. This time, he’s framed for the murder of his boss. Annabelle Wallis and Adrian Lester also star.Spa WeekendOut nowA buddy comedy in the vein of Bridesmaids: Leslie Mann, Isla Fisher, Michelle Buteau and Anna Faris star in a tale of three childhood BFFs reunited for a fabulous weekend getaway, only to find a former friend, a total hot mess, gatecrashing their pampering sesh.Insidious: Out of the FurtherOut nowIn case you haven’t been keeping up, this is the sixth instalment in the Insidious franchise, which began in 2010 with a relatively simple haunted-house story. In this latest outing, a young mother discovers she can bring back supernatural demons. Spooksome.Catherine BrayGoing out:GigsView image in fullscreenArt on her sleeve … Rochelle Jordan.Photograph: Elise KRochelle JordanDublin,25 August; Manchester,26 AugustBritish-born, Canada-raised dance music maven Rochelle Jordan arrives in the UK and Ireland in support of last year’s excellent third album, Through the Wall. With a five-EP series of remixes slowly being released, expect these shows to be head-knocking, sweat-soaked affairs.Michael CraggTyler, the CreatorVictoria Park, London,28& 29 AugustThe mercurial rapper, singer, actor and fashion designer headlines two dates at this year’s east London-based All Points East series. Expect a zigzagging setlist careening between hip-hop, funk and electro, plus support across the two shows from the likes of Turnstile, Dijon and Rex Orange County.MCLondon Symphony Orchestra/PappanoSnape MaltingsConcert Hall, Snape,28 AugustThe Proms may be London’s symphonic main stage in August, but one of the capital’s finest orchestras is decamping to East Anglia, armed with Bruckner’s thrilling Symphony No 9 and Gubaidulina’s Viola Concerto. Antonio Pappano conducts, with Norwegian violist Eivind Ringstad.Flora WillsonTom Barford QuintetPeggy’s Skylight, Nottingham,22 August;East Side Jazz Club, London,25 AugustYoung UK musician Tom Barford won the prestigious Kenny Wheeler prize in 2017 for his edgily inviting compositions – but is just as notable for his sax virtuosity. Expect vivacious Barford originals mixed with hip tributes to the music of sax legend Joe Henderson.John FordhamGoing out:ArtView image in fullscreenSimón Vega’s Tourist Prospero Reflects, 2024.Photograph: Courtesy of Simón Vega and Elizabeth Xi Bauer, London.Our Place in These WorldsElizabeth Xi Bauer, London,to 27 SeptemberA roving, constantly evolving exhibition that has been growing and touring since 2023, featuring work about migration, colonialism and collective identity by artists Esvin Alarcón Lam, Antonio Pichillá Quiacaín and Simón Vega.Hot Snakes Night ClubTaco!, London,22 Augustto 13 SeptemberThis hip experimental gallery in south-east London is being transformed into a cabaret club by artist Chloe Langlois for three weeks of live performances, workshops and experimental music, starting with a 24-hour occult marathon.Gender StoriesWalkerArtGallery, Liverpool,to 31 AugustWith works by major artists such as David Hockney, Catherine Opie, Grayson Perry and Zanele Muholi, this show looks at how art can help us figure out the meaning of gender, and how it shapes our everyday lives.Simeon BarclayJohn Hansard Gallery, Southampton,to 29 AugustThe British conceptualist celebrates his nomination for this year’s Turner prize with a complex exhibition about barriers, gatekeeping, pop culture, fashion, bus seats and giant inflatable mascots.Eddy FrankelGoing out:StageView image in fullscreenUneasy listening … Frankie Thompson: Horrible Things.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianFrankie ThompsonBeside at Pleasance Courtyard, Edinburgh, to 30 AugustSomewhere between character comedy, performance art and drag, Thompson’s latest show, Horrible Things, is a riot of lip-syncing (often to unsettling archive recordings), audience interaction and contemporary clowning.Rachel AroestiA Slow FireJermyn Streettheatre, London, to 26 SeptemberThe UK premiere of Simon Stephens’s post-apocalyptic play stars a fierce trio of Irish actors and sees two men trapped in a bunker – before they meet a mysterious stranger.Miriam GillinsonSauna Sessions Arts ClubSummerhall, Edinburgh, to 31 AugustThis year’s Edinburgh festival fringe hosts the UK’s first arts centre set inside a sauna: the 80-seater venue will host a series of immersive performances – including a morning rave, a ritualistic storytelling experience and a reworking of Virginia Woolf’s The Waves, with towel-based choreography.MGDan Daw: ExxyKing’stheatre, Edinburgh,23 AugustExxy (it’s Australian slang for expensive) is the follow-up to the uncompromising and acclaimed Dan Daw Show, as seen at last year’s Edinburgh international festival. This year, the queer, disabled dancer and choreographer Daw returns, thinking back to his youth as an outsider in working-class South Australia.Lyndsey Winshipskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenStaying in:StreamingView image in fullscreenIt’s a knockout … Fightland.Photograph:  /Christopher Raphael/Starz, LLCFightlandSky Atlantic & Now,27 August, 9pmA Thousand Blows meets Top Boy in this 50 Cent-produced drama about the substantial overlap between London’s boxing scene and its criminal underworld. Howard Charles plays a heavyweight champ who returns to the UK to wreak violent revenge on his former promoter, a drug kingpin.The Airport ChaplainNetflix,26 AugustDramas that revolve round mavericks doing highly skilled jobs under enormous pressure are all the rage right now, and this Australian series about a man who isn’t afraid to ruffle feathers to ensure the smooth running of a busy airport is very much in that vein. Hugo Weaving and The Pitt’s Shabana Azeez star.Dog ParkU,24 AugustAlso from down under, this cute canine-dominated dramedy is TV at its most wholesome and nuanced. When Roland’s wife moves abroad, he’s left in charge of the family pooch and soon discovers his grouchy resistance to the hyper-friendly local dog-walking community may have been misplaced.Dark MatterApple TV,28 AugustBlake Crouch’s mind-boggling sci-fi about a physicist who split himself in two so he could enjoy family life and a stellar career (with, obviously, catastrophic consequences) returns. Joel Edgerton reprises the role(s) of Jason Dessen, who has peaceably reunited with his wife and child – but will the calls of the multiverse prove too strong?RAStaying in:GamesView image in fullscreenSuper troopers … Star Wars Zero Company.Photograph: EAStar Wars Zero CompanyPC, PS5, Xbox Series X/S, out27 AugustA single-player tactics game set during the Clone Wars, this XCOM-alike has you managing a group of misfits with a range of backgrounds and abilities. The story unfolds linearly, but your choices still matter in the complex missions.Resonance: A Plague Tale LegacyPC, PS5, Xbox Series X/S, out27 AugustThis prequel deviates from previous Plague Tale games, starring not stealthy noble children but combat-confident smuggler Sophia. Instead of hordes of rats you face the maze of Minotaur’s Island, and it’s back to ancient Minoan times to learn more about the mysterious Macula.Jordan Erica WebberStaying in:AlbumsView image in fullscreenMateria girl … Julia Holter.Photograph: Dicky BahtoJulia Holter – MateriaOut nowAfter releasing her sixth album Something in the Room She Moves in 2024, the US singer-songwriter turned her focus to its crystalline fourth track, Materia. On this follow-up she reimagines that song not once but twice, as well as pushing her sound into interesting new shapes on the tactile My Lost One.Sam Smith – Hazel EyesOut nowFor their fifth album, the singer-songwriter leans into a more rustic sound, eschewing the elasticated pop of megahit Unholy in favour of low-key romanticism. Oh Mother is head-spinning gospel, while the delicate When He’s Gone overspills with longing.Weezer – Weezer (Gold Album)Out nowPerpetual teenagers Weezer return with their 20th album, and their seventh to be self-titled but differentiated by album colour. With production by Swedish pop producer Klas Åhlund (Robyn, Katy Perry) and hip-hop wizard Kenny Beats, plus a guest spot from alt-rockers Wednesday, it’s another perfect mix of existential angst and frat anthems.Brandon Flowers – ThrasherOut nowWith Mr Brightside still bobbing around the UK Top 100, where it has now spent more than 500 weeks (!), the Killers frontman returns with a third solo album. While 2015’s The Desired Effect explored perky synthpop, Thrasher recasts Flowers as a country troubadour.MCView image in fullscreenRA Exchange.Staying in:Brain foodRA ExchangePodcastCelebrating its 25th anniversary, electronic music culture platform Resident Advisor releases a stellar lineup of in-depth discussions with leaders of the scene, from house and techno brothers Overmono to UK garage satirists Kurupt FM.Music-map.comOnlineIn an effort to make algorithms more playful, this charming site allows users to type in the name of a favourite artist and then navigate through a sprawling mind map of related sounds.Assignment: Brazil’s Gambling AddictionBBC World Service,25 August, 9.32amWith 2.1 million Brazilians currently reporting an addiction to gambling, journalist Camilla Mota goes in search of the reasons why betting has such a stronghold in the country and the psychiatrists trying to help.Ammar KaliaExplore more on these topicsCultureGoing out, staying inDanceTheatreTelevisionArtGamesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Hang Time review – a chilling picture of the horrors of racial violence | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Three men bicker and reflect like they’re chatting at a bar – yet this grimly beautiful piece of theatre at the Edinburgh international festival won’t let you forget their fate
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: Three men bicker and reflect like they’re chatting at a bar – yet this grimly beautiful piece of theatre at the Edinburgh international festival won’t let you forget their fate
Content: Full of life … Julian Rozzell, Bryce Foley and Kamal Bolden in Hang Time.Photograph: Danté Charles CrichlowView image in fullscreenFull of life … Julian Rozzell, Bryce Foley and Kamal Bolden in Hang Time.Photograph: Danté Charles CrichlowEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewHang Time review – a chilling picture of the horrors of racial violenceRoyal Lyceum theatre, EdinburghThree men bicker and reflect like they’re chatting at a bar – yet this grimly beautiful piece of theatre at the Edinburgh international festival won’t let you forget their fateMark FisherSat 22 Aug 2026 06.14 EDTLast modified on Sat 22 Aug 2026 06.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThree men are shooting the breeze. “We’re just talking – man to man to man,” says Slim (Kamal Bolden), an ex-con who believes in looking after number one. In a literal sense, he is right. They are just talking. In this short, grimly beautiful production, written and directed by Zora Howard for New York’sFlea theatre, they have the kind of all-male conversation you might hear in any bar – at turns needling, teasing, argumentative, romantic, trivial and spiky. They like nothing more than when an attractive woman walks by.Where Slim is always out for personal gain – a quick buck, a sexual misadventure – Bird (Julian Rozzell) carries the wisdom of age. He scorns Slim’s quick-fix philosophy, favouring old-fashioned values of loyalty, decency and privacy. Blood (Bryce Foley), the youngest of the three, is the romantic: the one who dreams of life beyond streets that seem to have stripped a community of ambition.Unhurried, they bicker about blues musicians: Slim is backingFreddie King, Bird sticking up forMuddy Waters, each winding the other up on a topic of little consequence. Their backchat is frequently funny, but they can be reflective, too: their failings as fathers and the role of the fathers who failed them. Most poignant is the talk about those they have lost. “A lot of ways to lose someone,” says Slim, whose time behind bars has made him a stranger to his family.Angels in America review – Tony Kushner’s five-hour fever dream predicts and reflects the US at 250Read moreAll this comes in bursts, as if we were overhearing snatches from afar. But although Slim is right to say they are just talking, in a theatrical sense, he is wrong. Thanks to the austere set design by Neal Wilkinson and the stark illumination of Reza Behjat’s lighting, we can never forget that these men, seemingly unknown to themselves, have beenlynched.Rigid and constrained, they dangle in space. At intervals between the conversation, Megan Culley’s sound design swells and the buzz of cicadas becomes a grating industrial ring. Their bodies droop and spasm. These men are at once full of life and deprived of life, killed by racist ideology. Hang Time is a dark and chilling testament.AtRoyal Lyceum theatre, Edinburgh, until 23 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026TheatreEdinburgh festivalRacereviewsShareReuse this content

title: The film Apollo 13 taught me how to survive heartbreak | Culture | The Guardian
description: After my engagement ended, I found myself repeatedly watching a movie about three astronauts trapped in a damaged spacecraft. It helped me see that sometimes the mere act of getting home is the success
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: After my engagement ended, I found myself repeatedly watching a movie about three astronauts trapped in a damaged spacecraft. It helped me see that sometimes the mere act of getting home is the success
Content: Illustration: Martin O'Neill/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Martin O'Neill/The GuardianMy cultural awakeningCultureThe film Apollo 13 taught me how to survive heartbreakAfter my engagement ended, I found myself repeatedly watching a movie about three astronauts trapped in a damaged spacecraft. It helped me see that sometimes the mere act of getting home is the successElf LyonsSat 22 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Failure is not an option” has always been my family’s catchphrase; it’s flight director Gene Kranz’s famous line in the film Apollo 13. When I tell people it’s our family motto, they often joke, “That’s healthy.” But it isn’t about being the best. It’s about refusing to stop being.I’ve loved Apollo 13 since I was a child. To me, Ron Howard’s 1995 adaptation of one of humanity’s greatest rescue missions is the perfect film to watch when you feel you might implode – because they got home. It is a film about a successful failure. When the Nasa director warns: “This could be the worst disaster Nasa’s ever experienced,” Kranz replies: “I believe this is going to be our finest hour.” Every time I watch that scene, I start crying.Since I was little, if I couldn’t understand an emotion, I used scientific examples and historical events as analogies and metaphors to explain my emotional state. For this reason, it was never the trapped floating astronauts led by Tom Hanks’s Jim Lovell who fascinated me. It was the white-shirted, spectacled, chain-smoking engineers and scientists in Mission Control.It was sexy, crew-cut Ed Harris saying: “Let’s work the problem, people. Let’s not make things worse by guessing.” It was Gary Sinise as Ken Mattingly refusing to take a break (“If they don’t get one, I don’t get one!”) as he tried to get his friends home.Mission Control embodied everything I loved about humanity and learning: teamwork, creativity, rationality, calmness and respect for the data and the facts. This was why, in 2025, when my own systems module exploded, Apollo 13 became my breakup movie. On a balmy night in Australia in April 2025, my relationship with my fiance ended in a concrete hotel room under a flightpathin Sydney, 15 minutes before I was due to perform to 2,000 people.double quotation markThe astronauts survive because they trust Mission Control … Mission Control became every WhatsApp group on my phoneInstantly, my brain shut down and went into survival mode. I moved into my own dreamlike Lunar Module (the lifeboat that saved the astronauts). I worked flat out but on reduced power. In 2025, that meant touring Australia and the UK with a show in which I pretended to be a horse, while also relearning three shows for the Edinburgh fringe.People suggested tragic weepies to watch: Call Me By Your Name, Twilight, Blue Valentine. They said: “You should let it out.” No, thank you. I have to be a horse later! Give me a film where there is categoricallyno chance of people having sex at all.I don’t need romance films full of tears. Words mean nothing to a depressed mime artist! Life isn’t romantic declarations. It is actions that matter. It is waking up, brushing your teeth and putting your clothes on. Survival is Ed Harris declaring, “We are not losing the crew!”The immediate explosion passed; survival mode lasted much longer. I was operational, but only just. The astronauts survive because they trust Mission Control. During the second half of 2025, Mission Control became every WhatsApp group on my phone. My friends and family made sure I ate, drove me to every show. My sister let me borrow and subsequently lose most of her clothes. My brother told me he loved me more than he had in his entire life. Everyone lied about my new haircut. They kept me on the right trajectory. They found the duct tape and rebuilt my lifeboat while I concentrated on putting one hoof in front of the other.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA kids’ film taught me the power of delusion – and helped me chase my standup dreamsRead moreWhenever I felt I couldn’t keep going, I returned to the film and revelled in the knowledge that it was based on truth. If Mission Control could get three men home from the other side of the moon, I could rebuild my confidence, travel the world as a horse and prepare for the Edinburgh fringe.Now, when people ask how I am, I tell them I’m like the crew of Apollo 13. I’m home. I had a rupture, but I landed – and, like Mission Control, I am focusing on the next mission.Because failure is not an option.Elf Lyons Is the Woman on the Edgeis at Pleasance Courtyard, Edinburgh, to 31 August.Share your cultural awakeningsYou can tell us how a cultural moment has prompted you to make a major life change by filling in the form below or emailing us on cultural.awakening@theguardian.com.Please share your story if you are 18 or over, anonymously if you wish. title: ‘Embryonic’: lost novel by French film-maker Éric Rohmer is republished  | Movies | The Guardian
description: English translation of Élisabeth, the New Wave director’s 1946 book about young lovers in prewar Paris, receives rave reviews as precursor to auteur’s cinematic work
Author: Xan Brooks
Headline: English translation of Élisabeth, the New Wave director’s 1946 book about young lovers in prewar Paris, receives rave reviews as precursor to auteur’s cinematic work
Content: ‘He was always hiding his profession from his mother’ … Éric Rohmer on the set of Full Moon in Paris in 1984.Photograph: Photo 12/Photo12/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘He was always hiding his profession from his mother’ … Éric Rohmer on the set of Full Moon in Paris in 1984.Photograph: Photo 12/Photo12/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesMovies‘Embryonic’: lost novel by French film-maker Éric Rohmer is republishedEnglish translation of Élisabeth, the New Wave director’s 1946 book about young lovers in prewar Paris, receives rave reviews as precursor to auteur’s cinematic workXan BrooksSat 22 Aug 2026 05.54 EDTLast modified on Sat 22 Aug 2026 05.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the dog days of the second world war, 24-year-old Maurice Schérer wrote a tale of young lovers in prewar small-townFrance. He described lazy August swims in the Marne River east of Paris. He wrote about age-gap affairs and semi-incestuous flirtations. Schérer gallantly used a nom de plume, Gilbert Cordier, to shield his Catholic family from scandal, but he needn’t have bothered as his concerns were unfounded. The finished novel, Élisabeth, barely made a ripple and quickly slipped out of print. Undeterred, Scherer adopted a second pseudonym – Éric Rohmer – and decided to try his luck as a film-maker instead.Now – eight decades on from its first publication, 16 years on fromits author’s death– Élisabeth belatedly returns from the cold. Republished in an English-language translation by Aaron Kerner, Rohmer’s book has been greeted with glowing reviews, hailed as a lost modernist classic and a crucial origin story for the award-winning director of Claire’s Knee, The Green Ray and My Night at Maud’s. “It would be a rewarding, exciting read even if the identity of its author were unfamiliar,” wrote Richard Brody in the New Yorker. The fact that it’s by Rohmer? That’s the icing on the cake.View image in fullscreenThe new edition of Élisabeth by Éric Rohmer.Photograph: McNally Editions“On the one hand, to be honest, the book is a footnote,” says the novelist André Aciman, a longtime Rohmer fan who wrote the foreword to the new edition. “But it is also embryonic and full of Rohmerian moments. It takes on all the themes that will become more developed, complex and impactful in his films.”Rohmer was working as a freelance journalist in Nazi-occupied Paris when he wrote Élisabeth, which follows a loose-knit group of dreamers in the pregnant summer of 1939. Stung by the book’s failure, he moved on to film criticism and finally to directing, becoming an older member of a generation of French New Wave film-makers that included Claude Chabrol, Jean-Luc Godard and François Truffaut. “I didn’t believe in literature any longer,” he would later say. “I felt its time had passed [and] that cinema had supplanted it.”Cinema, Aciman says, provided Rohmer with his natural home. Plot elements that feel formulaic in Élisabeth are more honest and lively in his films. “There is something in his work that has always captured me,” he says. “The study of human behaviour and our unpredictable natures. Two people who are dying to sleep with each other but don’t. That’s probably why I project myself on to every character in every Rohmer film. I think, ‘Oh my God, I could be this man or this woman. That’s what I’d do or say in that situation.’”The critic Adrian Martin, an expert on New Wave cinema, says that Rohmer’s use of improvisation helped give his films a sense of freshness and freedom. “He shot with a very small crew, sometimes three or four people,” Martin says. “And what was important to him was the spontaneity of the actors and the dialogue. He didn’t like to do multiple takes. He didn’t even like to direct the actors very much. Sometimes he’d be off in the next room while the scene was being shot. He’d yell: ‘Just do it!’ and whatever the actors gave him was mostly what he wanted.”In person, by contrast, Rohmer remained private and secretive. Sometimes he claimed that he was born in Tulle and sometimes in Nancy; sometimes that his real name was Maurice and sometimes Jean-Marie. “Basically he was always hiding his profession from his mother,” Martin says. “She would have been ashamed and seen film-making as a bit of a dirty profession. His parents thought he was a teacher and that was seen as OK and respectable. But they never knew that he was writing about films and eventually directing them. It’s mind-boggling to think of anyone doing that now. His whole adult life was a complete secret to them.”View image in fullscreen‘The missteps and confusions of footloose French youth’ … Éric Rohmer’s 1983 film Pauline à la Plage.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyRohmer’s best-loved works – Claire’s Knee (1970),Pauline à la Plage(1983), the Tales of the Four Seasons (1990-1998) series – chiefly focus on the missteps and confusions of footloose French youth. His people are articulate and self-questioning, invariably to a fault. “My heroes, a little like Don Quixote, take themselves for characters in a novel,” the director once said. “But perhaps there is no novel.” The republished Élisabeth at least puts that notion to bed. Filled with sparky dialogue and crisp stage directions, it is the literary ancestor of Rohmer’s arthouse filmography and as close to a screenplay as a novel can get.“The thing about Rohmer is that he dug his own field,” Martin says. “He’s constantly telling the same story, just with these little variations. It’s always about friendship, love affairs, games of desire and flirtation. It’s never simply a matter of one person loving another person. They’re thinking: ‘Do I want to love this person – and why?’ They’re hyper-rationalising all the time. That’s the same field that Élisabeth is digging. The basic dynamic is already there.”“I don’t think it’s a great novel,” Martin adds. “It might even be too much to call it a wellspring. But it’s still fascinating. It’s the seeds, germ and kernel of everything he went on to achieve.”Explore more on these topicsFilmEric RohmerPublishingFranceEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: The faces behind the feeds: Gen Z’s private lives and public posts – in pictures | Photography | The Guardian
description: For the first digital natives, there are two places to express yourself: in the comfort of your own room and online. Photographer Niccolò Rastrelli set out to find out how the identities compare
Author: Gabrielle Schwarz
Headline: For the first digital natives, there are two places to express yourself: in the comfort of your own room and online. Photographer Niccolò Rastrelli set out to find out how the identities compare
Content: Stevie, 20, Rome, photographed in his bedroom.Photograph: Niccolò Rastrelli/InstituteView image in fullscreenStevie, 20, Rome, photographed in his bedroom.Photograph: Niccolò Rastrelli/InstitutePhotographyThe faces behind the feeds: Gen Z’s private lives and public posts – in picturesFor the first digital natives, there are two places to express yourself: in the comfort of your own room and online. Photographer Niccolò Rastrelli set out to find out how the identities compareGabrielle SchwarzSat 22 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSocial media arrived just as I, a younger millennial, was on the brink of teenhood. My friends and I signed up for accounts on Facebook, Myspace and Twitter, as well as less remembered sites such as the now defunct Bebo. We didn’t know what we were doing; no one did. We posted indiscreet messages and photos on public feeds that we wouldn’t want any future employer – or really anyone, for that matter – to see. Then gradually we, and our parents and their parents, too, learned what it means to live with that world-changing phenomenon that we term social media. We started to find different ways to adapt, a process that is ongoing.But what is the experience like for gen Z, the first generation of “digital natives”, for whom the language of the internet is a mother tongue? That is the question that led the Italian photographer Niccolò Rastrelli to embark on the project IRL (the online acronym, of course, for a phrase denoting our offline existences: in real life).Rastrelli has long been interested in the way people construct their identities through self-presentation. “In the last few years, I’ve also worked a lot with younger people. I’m older and don’t have children, so I want to understand their point of view,” says the photographer, who was born in 1977, making him a member of generation X. Past works include a project exploring the rising popularity around the globe of the youth subculture of cosplay. Now he felt it was time to broaden his focus to a more ubiquitous experience: being on the “socials”.“I wanted to portray the diversity in gen Z,” Rastrelli says. He recruited subjects across the full span of the generation, from 14-year-olds to adults in their late 20s. Most were in Italy, but he also visited the UK, Morocco and France. Each portrait has two paired components. On one side the subject is photographed in their bedroom, whether in their family home or in a flatshare or university halls. They are intentionally posed, nearly always making eye-contact with the camera. S ome clutch their phones, or sit by a computer. Often there is the familiar sight of a tangle of cords and plugs in an extension cable by the bed.double quotation markWhen you’re young, your bedroom is such an important place. It’s really your first solo home“I decided to shoot in the bedroom because when you’re young it’s such an important place. It’s really your first solo home,” Rastrelli explains. “Before social media, it was also the main place where you could build your identity.” Your room and the things inside it – posters, paintings, books, an electric guitar, a barbell, a massivestuffed unicorn – tell a story about what kind of person you are and want to be.Nowadays, the same goes for social media. And so, alongside those portraits, Rastrelli asked each of his subjects to pick snapshots of their phone screens that represented their usual activity. Nearly everything is fromInstagram, one of gen Z’s main apps of choice – and many of the images are from temporary “stories” rather than posts on the feed. There are selfies with silly filters, casual snaps of friends and food, black-and-white portraits taken with film cameras. It was important to Rastrelli that the youngsters “co-curated” the selection, just as they had arranged and posed in their bedrooms.Rastrelli also gave his subjects a questionnaire about their relationship with social media. Many responses surprised him – for example, that they often maintain more than one account on a single platform. Lana, who is 16, has multiple Instagram profiles with varying levels of privacy. “Only on my most private account do I feel free to really be myself,” she told him. He was also struck by how many young people see social media less as a site of personal expression than as a work tool. The clearest example was 23-year-old web developer and social media manager Francesco, who doesn’t post on his own account. As Rastrelli observes, “It’s like when you meet chefs. They all say they don’t cook at home because they’re cooking all day in the restaurant.”Recent years have seen growing debate about the potential dangers of social media for young people. In the UK, a ban for under-16s is set to be enforced from next spring. (In Italy there are no such plans.) But from his conversations with gen Z-ers, Rastrelli doesn’t think they seem any more affected than their elders: “Many of them use social media less than people from my generation.” The primary difference is the platforms they go to. For example,Facebook, now associated with boomers, barely came up. It’s made Rastrelli consider repeating the project but focusing on the older generation instead: “We are all involved with social media.”Stevie, 20, Rome (main picture top)A student from Pennsylvania, Stevie is now studying abroad in Rome. He says he has two Instagram accounts: a public one and a private one, and tends to shift in tone and identity depending on which he’s using. He dreams of becoming a media personality.View image in fullscreenLana, 16, FlorenceView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenLana’s first smartphone – obtained aged 11 after longnegotiations with her parents – opened up a new world, from group chats to shared photos. Social media is integral to her daily life: TikTok is more of a pastime while Instagram is like a diary. Her bedroom is the place she feels most authentic, she says. She reads a lot, from YA novels to heavier authors like Dostoevsky and Freud, who help her better understand herself and the world around her.Sofia, 14,ArezzoView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenSofia attends an art school where she studies animation, a passion she discovered thanks to a digital creator who makes content about the history of cartoons. Her online life is limited: her parents have blocked Instagram and TikTok, so she uses WhatsApp to share drawings, homework and memes with friends.Roberto, 27, LondonView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenBorn in Italy to a Ghanaian family, Roberto has lived in London for the past eight years and currently works as a personal trainer and a bartender. He didn’t get his first smart-phone until around 15 or 16 – before that he used a basic phone so his parents could keep track of him. He is cautious about what he shares and views: mainly fashion and fitness content.Mark, 28, FlorenceView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenMark, who was born in Nigeria and raised in Italy, paid for his first smartphone himself aged 12, by doing odd jobs and reselling customised clothes. He used to alter his features in photos, removing elements like his nose to escape identity labels. Now, as a freelance creative, he mainly uses Instagram as a tool for research, and rarely posts.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMelina, 24, ArlesView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenMelina, who studied 3D animation, relies on Instagram for tutorials and discovering other artists. She also follows friends and humorous accounts. She shares infrequently, mostly drawings rather than photographs of herself, rarely edited beyond an occasional filter. She keeps a second account with no other followers, where she stores images to remember moments of her life.Anna, 23, GlasgowView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenWhat excited Anna most when she got her first phone, aged 11, was the ability to photograph and film the world around her. Now her dream is to work in film, and she says social media will be a useful way to share work and find opportunities. In the meantime, she uses Instagram mostly as a source of creative inspiration. When she posts, she likes to avoid putting herself at the centre of the image.Andrea, 22, FlorenceView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenAndrea maintains two separate Instagram accounts, a personal one and a professional one for his work – as well as appearing in a local theatre troupe he performs solo as a drag artist. He says his approach is consistent across both his accounts: showing himself without filters , whether beautiful or deliberately grotesque, retouching images in Photoshop only to make a scene more “editorial”.Ali, 28, RabatView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenAli’s first proper smartphone, after years spent using broken old ones, changed everything, allowing him to take and share photos for the first time. These days he works in social media marketing, helping companies and projects grow and gain visibility. He says that he sees his bedroom as a place to rest and think, while online is where he can express his personality and take inspiration from others.Silvia, 23, RomeView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenSilvia says she feels like herself both offline and online, in different ways. At home she is more quiet; on social media, more extrovert. She says her family hasn’t always approved of her lack of filter on the internet, but she continues regardless. Music is central to her life – she’s part of a techno collective and performs as a DJ.To see more images from Niccolò Rastrelli’s project, go to instituteartist.com.Explore more on these topicsPhotographySocial mediaInstagramFacebookDigital mediaSocial networkingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Dog Park: a delightful sitcom that will fill the Colin from Accounts shaped hole in your life | Television | The Guardian
description: This snort-aloud Australian comedy is sweet, hilarious – and a surprising examination of male loneliness and mid-life crisis. Who’s a good show then?!
Author: Rhik Samadder
Headline: This snort-aloud Australian comedy is sweet, hilarious – and a surprising examination of male loneliness and mid-life crisis. Who’s a good show then?!
Content: Park life … Grace Chow as Pamelia with little friend Big in Dog Park.Photograph: PRView image in fullscreenPark life … Grace Chow as Pamelia with little friend Big in Dog Park.Photograph: PRThe watcherTelevisionDog Park: a delightful sitcom that will fill the Colin from Accounts shaped hole in your lifeThis snort-aloud Australian comedy is sweet, hilarious – and a surprising examination of male loneliness and mid-life crisis. Who’s a good show then?!Rhik SamadderSat 22 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhenever I’m watching a programme that features an animal and I realise I’m expected to have a specific reaction to that animal, I run into a problem. I call it the Cuteness Assumptive Theory: Subjectivity inTelevisionissue (CATSIT for short). It boils down to this: if the success of your show relies on my finding your lead actor scrumptious-wumptious, you’ve already failed. We all like different things.The theory applies equally to humans. We all know that moment when some interchangeable heartthrob walks into the scene on a US sitcom. All the characters lose their minds, this being apparently the hottest person on Earth, while you’re sitting thinking, ‘Huh?’ It happens with child stars too. Casting directors have a narrow spectrum of children they think will elicit an “awww” response from audiences. The response usually elicited in me is “Couldn’t they find a better actor?” I’m not trying to be liked here! Anyway, it’s the animal version that came to mind this week, watching Dog Park.Dog Park(U, from Monday 24 August) centres on Roland, a misanthrope whose partner Emma has gone overseas for work. He’s been left in charge of their child, plus Beattie, a white poodle he never wanted. A neighbour, Sam, kidnaps Beattie to take her to the park to play with her friends. Roland’s wife has arranged this; she knows Roland will be a terrible dog-dad, only taking Beattie on joyless solo jogs if at all. Forced into the company of walkers, Roland comes to realise the importance of community and the joy of pooches. It sounds as trite as trifle, but hear me out.This downbeat comedy set in Victoria, Australia, is a surprisingly mature examination of male loneliness and midlife crisis. Roland is a borderline alcoholic grammar pedant who is quite literally running from depression. Working as a careers counsellor at a college, he encourages his young wards to write their future gravestones, a hilariously uninspiring exercise. He’s not thriving. You know how in Studio Ghibli films, you get interstitial shots of grass rustling or beetles creeping? Dog Park’s scenes are cut with moments of Roland getting annoyed at people in the grocery store or losing his rag at an Alexa. All worryingly relatable.His relationship might need one of those headstones. Roland and Emma are circling a breakup. They hurt each other and fumble to repair, while failing to hide this from their daughter. Rather than stock moments sketching such a breakdown, the show inhabits the barbed jokes, retyped texts, egg-shell conversations and frustrating phonecalls that feel painfully real. The show is sold as a comedy – and there are snort-aloud moments – yet more often I felt the prick of tears.View image in fullscreenJogging on … writer and co-creator Leon Ford as Roland in Dog Park.Photograph: PRBeing only at the start of the series, I don’t know if Roland and Emma make it. Perhaps theirs is a drawn-out game of fetch and return? However, I’m pretty sure his irascibility will be mellowed by the “dog park divas”, an eccentric band of gregarious day drinkers. Chief among these “dog tragics”, as Roland thinks of them, is Sam. Kind-eyed, gently provocative, she’s played by a radiant Celia Pacquola. If romance is in the air, it will surely come with a side order of pain and messiness. Or maybe Dog Park is playing a different game altogether.Writer and co-creator Leon Ford gives a thorny, moving performance as Roland, who distrusts joy and shuns friendship. “How’s your more interesting significant other?” joshes a colleague. “Dead, actually. She died,” he shoots back. This saltiness feels highly Australian. It put me in mind ofPatrick Brammall, who co-wroteColin from Accounts: another Aussie comedy about a dog I worried I wouldn’t find cute, the name of which I hated to boot. That show became my most beloved of recent years.And, actually, the dog is cute. Beattie has a sweet face, and ears that look like pigtails. I’m just delighted the show doesn’t rely on them. Unearned sentiment is what I struggle with, but Dog Park skips this hurdle, like an Australian kelpie at Crufts. Funny and frequently beautiful, it’s for dog people, but mostly it’s for people people. Who’s a good show? You’re a good show!Explore more on these topicsTelevisionThe watcherShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: The Voice gets a shake-up with new judge Kelly Rowland  | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: The Destiny’s Child star joins the hit singing contest. Plus: the essential BBC Four drama about America’s exit from Kabul. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: The Destiny’s Child star joins the hit singing contest. Plus: the essential BBC Four drama about America’s exit from Kabul. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Sing for survival …The Voice on ITV1.Photograph: Rachel Joseph/ITVView image in fullscreenSing for survival …The Voice on ITV1.Photograph: Rachel Joseph/ITVTV tonightTelevision & radioTV tonight: The Voice gets a shake-up with new judge Kelly RowlandThe Destiny’s Child star joins the hit singing contest. Plus: the essential BBC Four drama about America’s exit from Kabul. Here’s what to watch this eveningHollie Richardson,Hannah Verdier,Graeme Virtue,Ali Catterall,Phil HarrisonandSimon WardellSat 22 Aug 2026 01.15 EDTLast modified on Sat 22 Aug 2026 02.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Voice UK7pm, ITV1A new series calls for a new judge! Kelly Rowland will take a seat in the swivelling chairs for this year’s talent show, alongside Tom Jones, will.i.am, Tom Fletcher and Danny Jones. Emma Willis is back on hosting duties, though this could well be her last time. And there’s another fancy new feature: a “rewind” button that gives the judges an opportunity to bring back a contestant they regret letting go.Hollie RichardsonDeal Or No Deal: Celebrity Special6pm, ITV1Comedian and actor Katherine Ryan has faced the infamous Banker before, but she’s back again for more drama. With no shortage of celebrity friends and a history of taking home the cash for charity, she’s as ready as anyone to open those 22 red boxes in the right order as Stephen Mulhern tries to keep up.Hannah VerdierAlan Carr’s Picture Slam6.30pm, BBC OneEyes front for Carr’s breezy “say what you see” quiz in which competing duos must correctly identify images against the clock. If the aim is to get the entire family shouting at the telly, the show’s arbitrary pick’n’mix – from classic Hollywood to smartphone app icons – is its secret weapon.Graeme VirtueMarvin Gaye: A Tribute at the Proms8pm, BBC TwoView image in fullscreenLet’s get it on … Marvin Gaye: A Tribute at the Proms on BBC Two.Photograph: BBC/ Andy ParadiseEdwin Outwater conducts, and guest singers including Luke James are on tonsil duty for the BBC Concert Orchestra’s celebration of the soul icon. Andi Oliver hosts proceedings, with new arrangements of I Heard It Through the Grapevine, Sexual Healing and Ain’t No Mountain High Enough.Ali CatterallKabul9pm, BBC FourThis essential drama about the fallout from the American decision to abandon Kabul in 2021 continues. As panic spreads, Gilles attempts to negotiate with the Taliban – but with no trust on either side, it seems risky. Meanwhile, Amina decides to flee, but can she keep Nooria safe in the meantime?PHNigel Farage: Where Does the Money Come From?9.30pm, Channel 5Reform’s taste for litigation arguably makes idle speculation about this question unwise. But Channel 5 are up for it anyway in this documentary which puts Farage’s finances under the microscope, exploring his donors and examining his various lucrative sidelines as a broadcaster and speaker.PHFilm choiceWe Dive at Dawn,1.25pm, BBC TwoView image in fullscreenLife or death … We Drive at Dawn on BBC Two.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyDespite dutifully fulfilling its propaganda brief, this 1943 film from Anthony Asquith works superbly in its own right as a tense wartime thriller. John Mills, that era’s go-to everyman, stars as the captain of the fictional submarine Sea Tiger. Sent on a mission to attack a new German battleship, he and his crew find themselves out on their own in the Baltic, facing mines, undersea nets and destroyers. Naturally, a can-do attitude prevails, but the tangled personal lives of the crew provide a comic distraction to the life-and-death stuff of winning the war.Simon WardellDoctor Strange, 8pm, Channel 4This is the movie that, for better or worse, introduced the multiverse to Marvel’s superhero franchise. It also chucked magic into the otherwise muscle-based mix – as practised by Benedict Cumberbatch’s arrogant brain surgeon turned wielder of the mystic arts. This gives the film an enjoyably psychedelic feel, as Strange battles rogue sorcerer Kaecilius (Mads Mikkelsen), and is oddly reminiscent of Christopher Nolan’s Inception and Tenet (it was released between the two) in its architecture-twisting, time-reversing spectacle.SWLive sportTest Cricket: England v Pakistan, 10.15am, Sky Sports CricketDay four of the first Test.
