title: Elouise Eftos: Aphrodite review – ‘Australia’s first attractive comedian’ asks if love is real | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Heckling herself in character as the Greek goddess, the standup delivers an intelligent, in-your-face show about sex and expectations
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: Heckling herself in character as the Greek goddess, the standup delivers an intelligent, in-your-face show about sex and expectations
Content: Ticklish gags … Elouise Eftos at Sydney comedy festival.Photograph: Ashley MarView image in fullscreenTicklish gags … Elouise Eftos at Sydney comedy festival.Photograph: Ashley MarEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewElouise Eftos: Aphrodite review – ‘Australia’s first attractive comedian’ asks if love is realPleasance Dome, EdinburghHeckling herself in character as the Greek goddess, the standup delivers an intelligent, in-your-face show about sex and expectationsBrian LoganSat 22 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou can’t argue with the opening gambit of Aphrodite: “I’ve never been in love and I don’t think it’s real.” Consider me grabbed. This is the follow-up to Elouise Eftos’s fantastically provocative 2025 debut,Australia’s First Attractive Comedian, and it’s another intelligent, in-your-face hour about men and women, sex and expectations. OK, so it doesn’t administer the shock of the new quite like its predecessor, and Eftos’s argument about love is not as authoritative as her impossibly high status requires. But Aphrodite consolidates Eftos as a gripping new presence on the comedy scene.View image in fullscreenEftos ends Aphrodite by dancing with her audienceIt starts with a steamy pop video, with theGreek-Australian Eftosin character as goddess of love Aphrodite – who then heckles the comic in interrupting voiceovers for the remainder of the show. Eftos has an Aphrodite side, she tells us, but an Athena too –andshe wants to be funny. That’s a combination forbidden to women, she posits, certainly if they want to find love with (whisper it) heterosexual men. That latter disappointing category of human is mocked here for its privilege, its fear of dancing, and because “being a straight man is a little bit gay”.All of this is delivered with amusing hauteur by an act who styles herself as infinitely sexier and cleverer than we riffraff in the audience. There’s arresting material about the Eftos approach to flirting, the historical roots of misogyny (in medicine, in the church) and, as her tone turns more serious, about violent porn too. Visibly emotional, Eftos also tells the story of the life her grandmother led, one of brutally narrow marital and professional horizons.Courtney Büchner: One of the Girls review – all aboard for a rollercoaster relationshipRead moreThat tells a powerful tale of gender injustice, and contextualises the comic’s scepticism of romance in a world where true equality is beyond us. But that’s an argument Eftos never quite lands, as she insists on being both equalandworshipped, bringing the show to a slightly indistinct end. But if Aphrodite doesn’t scale Olympian heights, it does offer us trenchant feminist thinking, all sorts of sass, and lots of ticklish gags aboutGomez Addamsand the secret sauciness of bus travel.AtPleasance Dome, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Comedy (Stage)Edinburgh festivalComedy (Culture)FeminismWomen (Life and style)Women (Society)reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Island-hopping through stone-age history in Ireland, Wales and the Isle of Man | Heritage | The Guardian
description: Exploring prehistory sites around the Irish Sea – that were old even before the pyramids were built – throws a magical light on our ancestors
Author: Kevin Rushby
Headline: Exploring prehistory sites around the Irish Sea – that were old even before the pyramids were built – throws a magical light on our ancestors
Content: The Memorial Cross on a hillside on the Isle of Man.Photograph: Jan Treger/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe Memorial Cross on a hillside on the Isle of Man.Photograph: Jan Treger/AlamyGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.HeritageIsland-hopping through stone-age history in Ireland, Wales and the Isle of ManExploring prehistory sites around the Irish Sea – that were old even before the pyramids were built – throws a magical light on our ancestorsKevin RushbySat 22 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 22 Aug 2026 06.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe guide was adamant. “I’ve picked human teeth out of there and I’m not doing it again.” The small group of tourists looked suitably aghast, except the boy. He was jiggling the wellington boots on his feet and singing to himself. He looked about 14. I sensed that he was the catalyst, the one to make things happen.“So, if anyone is planning to leave human remains in this ancient place,” went on the guide, throwing the boy a stern look, “I say, DON’T.”We had arrived on the visitor centre bus from nearby Knowth, the first stop on our tour ofNewgrange Neolithic site, 30 miles (50km) north of Dublin. I was on a circuit of the Irish Sea, a ferry and road trip to see the best ancient sites that ring this salty mere at the heart of these islands. It was here, around 5,100 years ago, that a new people arrived and, capitalising on the sea as a cultural superhighway, constructed a dazzling array of stone monuments. Some of Europe’s finest Neolithic passage tombs are here, notably at Newgrange, the only one you can enter. But as the guide was sternly pointing out, some modern folk are irresistibly drawn to leave the ashes of deceased relatives inside, especially at Newgrange.View image in fullscreenNewgrange is more than 5,000 years old.Photograph: Ruben Galvez/AlamyThe plush visitor centre had been informative but had not conveyed the deep atavistic intensity that drives such tributes. There was magic here. I wanted to feel it. I had a hunch this boy was in touch with it.“As for pets,” said our guide, “I want no dog or cat ashes either.”The boy was drumming his hands on his knees, hearing an unheard rhythm. We were about to walk up to the hallowed tumulus with its 19-metre-long passageway that leads to the central chamber, but our guide was determined to get that boy’s attention. “There,” she shouted. The boy’s head shot up. She was pointing at a set of wheelie bins in the corner. “I can promise you,” she went on, grimly, “that if I find your granny’s remains inside my Neolithic chamber, then her last resting place will be that green wheelie bin.”There was a stunned silence among the tourists. But not the boy. He immediately ran over to the bin, opened the lid and stared inside.“Nothing,” he reported, slamming it down. “She’s not there.”The guide looked nonplussed, then marched away towards the hill that is a tomb. “Follow me,” she commanded. “Do not leave the path.”Everyone obeyed, except the boy. He ran in a great arc off the path, arms flapping like shamanic wings.We had started our huge circular journey around the Irish Sea at Pentre Ifan, a magnificent tomb from 3500BC, sited on the same Pembrokeshire ridge that provided the bluestone for Stonehenge. I was travelling with my partner, Sophie, and our dog, Stevie, who had gone through complex hoops to prove he was not carrying either rabies or tapeworm into Ireland. He liked the first ferry, from Pembroke Dock to Rosslare; it had an excellent pet lounge, but what fascinated him was the sea. He could not stop staring. His reaction made me pay more attention to him. Could dogs, I wondered, also help connect us with the deep past? After all, their wolf heritage is 30,000 years old, yet they relive it every minute of their lives. If anyone could remember the Neolithic age, it was Stevie.double quotation markInside, Newgrange looks haphazard, but is perfect, a Rolex assembled by FlintstonesHe had been well cared for initially. We stayed near Wexford, in a dog-friendly hotel,Marlfield House, with superb gardens. Then we toured the ruins of the greatest Irish saint of them all, Kevin. His sixth-century seat atGlendalough, in County Wicklow, is now a busy pilgrimage site. Twelfth-centuryTrim Castlein County Meath was next, followed by the Hill of Tara with its ancient standing stone, the Lia Fáil. Here all the pagan kings of Ireland were crowned, so the legend goes.At its base, visitors had laid a collection of apples, flowers and coins. That puzzled me. Were the apples significant? Or had that gang of girls carrying hurling sticks just donated their unwanted snacks? Some people, it was clear, wanted such places to mean something, not simply be dusty artefacts.I persuaded Stevie to lie down on a nearby grassy mound. Under us was theMound of the Hostages, a chambered tomb that was already ancient when the Great Pyramid was built. Time slipped away. Those Neolithic people are so distant and mysterious. What we know for certain is almost nothing. They had cows … and dogs. I opened one eye. Stevie had gone. He’d given up communing with the stone age and gone after the hurling sticks.That night, we stayed in another excellent dog-friendly hotel,Bellinter House, and visitedMarcie Regan’sin Trim, a vibrant, dog-loving pub. Not until Newgrange did we meet the dreaded sign, NO DOGS. I’d been forced to leave him in the car, my dæmon, my conduit to the ancient.Our guide stopped us at the entrance to the great megalithic structure, a turf-topped hill walled with white quartz. Discovered largely intact in 1699, the entrance was guarded by the same five-tonne stone that sits there now, covered in mysterious swirling patterns. Behind was a narrow entrance and a passage that lay under 200,000 tonnes of stone and earth.View image in fullscreenPentre Ifan tomb in Pembrokeshire, which is on the same site that provided the bluestone for Stonehenge.Photograph: Paul Williams/Alamy“If you get claustrophobic,” said the guide, “you can leave at any time. Do not touch the carvings.”Out the corner of my eye, I saw the boy come running. He had done a lap of the monument, chanting to himself, his little sister close behind. The guide bowed her head and disappeared inside. The boy ran his fingertips over the carvings and followed. I went in next. My unsatisfied desire for stone age magic was about to be fulfilled.The tunnel is slightly kinked and rises imperceptibly. You don’t see the final chamber. The mystery grows. There are patterns on some stones. A deep silence descends. I thought of Stevie back in the car. They found the bones of a dog in here, and its DNA showed traces of wolf from both Europe and Asia. Stevie’s Neolithic moment, however, would have to wait.At the end of the corridor, we arrived in a small chamber. Above, the roof was made of massive stones. In more than 5,000 years, it has not leaked. It looks haphazard, but is perfect, a Rolex assembled by Flintstones. The most impressive thing, however, was not understood untilProf Michael O’Kellycame and stood in this chamber on 21 December 1967. Our guide was now going to recreate that event, and what has happened at dawn on every winter solstice since about 3150BC.double quotation markManx ancient monuments do not come with visitor centres and guides, they come only with a cast iron sign, ‘Ancient Monument’We were in complete darkness. The boy had pressed himself into a niche where a huge stone basin sat. Human remains, ancient ones, had been found there. And then, the guide touched a hidden switch and a golden light came creeping up the passageway towards us, finally illuminating a triple spiral of megalithic art carved into one giant stone. It was like hearing a deep harmonic chord, or the haunting cry of a night bird, something profound and enigmatic. I forgave the bus, the tickets, the gift shop – all the paraphernalia of the tourism business – and saw the genius of this recreation.Light slowly filled the chamber. We were all dumbstruck, except the boy. He spoke out loud and bold. “Question. Are there aliens here?”The guide shook her head impatiently. “I won’t have any talk of aliens.”The boy nodded and turned to his little sister. “That means there are.”Then he was gone, scurrying down the tunnel in a half crouch, humming to himself.A huge storm came in that night, downing trees and flooding roads. We drove through it to Belfast and hunkered down in ourhotel.View image in fullscreenKevin Rushby’s dog Stevie on the Isle of Man.Photograph: Kevin RushbyNext day, thankfully in calm weather, we sailed for the Isle of Man. Landing here was like travelling back in time, to around AD1950. Manx ancient monuments do not come with visitor centres and guides, they come only with a cast iron sign, “Ancient Monument”. We climbed the highest peak, Snaefell, visited several fabulous Celtic crosses and spent ages in the wonderfulManx Museum.Then, one afternoon, we left the car and walked through fields to the island’s most important Neolithic monument,Cashtal yn Ard. It was in a tussocky field behind a kissing gate and a small sign. No ticket required, only some imagination and, if possible, a stone age scent hound. Behind were ranged the dark hills. The monument itself is a collapsed passage tomb that has left the ghostly imprint of its shape in rows of pale stones, marking the entrance, the tunnel, and finally, a low portal into what is left of the central chamber. Nevertheless, Stevie seemed to know the layout. He ran to the entrance, bounded down the tunnel, dodged through the portal and stopped dead. We lay on our backs and watched the skies. After a few minutes, I sneaked a look at the dog. He was curled up asleep at the exact centre of the vanished chamber.Travel was provided byDiscover Ferries, the industry body for 12 ferry companies.Irish Ferries sails Pembroke to Rosslarefrom £190 forcar plus two (pets travel free).Isle of Man Steam Packet Companysails Belfast to Isle of Man from £179.50 for a car plus two (pets in cars free, pet-accessible cabins £75).Taking a dog to Irelandrequires micro-chipping, rabies jab and tapeworm treatment (Stevie’s documents were checked at Rosslare).Further information fromTourism Ireland,Fáilte Ireland, Tourism Northern IrelandandVisit Isle of ManExplore more on these topicsHeritageIreland holidaysIsle of ManWales holidaysEurope holidaysPembrokeshire holidaysCultural tripsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Thomasina Miers’ recipes for spiced lamb-stuffed aubergine with aleppo chilli butter, and berry ripple ice-cream | Lamb | The Guardian
description: A meaty, Middle Eastern style stuffed vegetable feast finished off with an ice-cold berry dessert
Author: Thomasina Miers
Headline: A meaty, Middle Eastern style stuffed vegetable feast finished off with an ice-cold berry dessert
Content: Thomasina Miers’ spiced lamb-stuffed aubergine with aleppo chilli butter.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Mandy Thompson.View image in fullscreenThomasina Miers’ spiced lamb-stuffed aubergine with aleppo chilli butter.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Mandy Thompson.Thomasina Miers recipesLambThomasina Miers’ recipes for spiced lamb-stuffed aubergine with aleppo chilli butter, and berry ripple ice-creamA meaty, Middle Eastern style stuffed vegetable feast finished off with an ice-cold berry dessertThomasina MiersSat 22 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere’s something delightfully retro about stuffed vegetables. They take me back toDelia Smith’s iconic Summer Collection cookbook, which blew my tiny mind when it came out in my early teens. Too sheltered to know about the e rage that had inspired Delia, I delved into my mother’s vegetable crisper with reverence, stuffing courgettes, tomatoes and aubergines with a zeal that had escaped me at school. How could the roasting, reducing and condensing of ingredients create such explosions of flavour? I was hooked. I have recently been returning to this technique with glee, a simple solution for turning seasonal vegetables into feasts.Spiced lamb-stuffed aubergine with aleppo chilli butterWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appServe these richly seasoned aubergines with warm, herb-flecked bulgur, rice or flatbreads, and a parsley and onion salad.Prep15 minSalt20 minCook1 hr 30 minServes4-65 medium auberginesSalt and black pepperOlive oil400g lamb mince2 small onions, peeled and finely chopped2 garlic cloves, peeled and crushed1 green pepper, halved, stalk, pith and seeds removed and discarded, flesh cut into 1cm dice200g cherry tomatoes, chopped2 tsp ground cumin1 tsp ground cinnamon3 tspaleppo chilli2 tbsp Turkish red pepper paste, or tomato paste400g tinfinely chopped tomatoes1 bunchflat-leaf parsley, picked and chopped50g unsalted butter200gGreek yoghurt, to serveCut the aubergines in half lengthways, then slice a lattice of crisscrosses over the flesh of each cut side, being careful not to cut down through the skin. Lay the aubergines flesh side up on a baking dish, sprinkle generously with salt, and leave for 20 minutes. Meanwhile, heat the oven to 220C (200C fan)/425F/gas 7.Using kitchen paper, blot away any moisture from the aubergine flesh, then drizzle over a tablespoon or two of olive oil. Roast for 30 minutes, until browned and softened, then remove and leave to cool.Meanwhile, make the filling. Put a large pan on a medium-high heat, then add a tablespoon of olive oil and the lamb. Season generously with salt and pepper and saute for seven to eight minutes, until the meat starts to catch and brown. Stir in the onions and garlic, turn down the heat down to medium and cook, stirring often, for 10-12 minutes, until the onions have softened.Add the green pepper, cherry tomatoes, cumin, cinnamon and one teaspoon of aleppo chilli, and cook for another 10 minutes. Add the pepper paste and half the chopped tomatoes, and cook for a further 20 minutes. Taste and adjust the seasoning, then stir in half the chopped parsley.Carefully spoon the filling over each aubergine half. Mix the remaining half-tin of chopped tomatoes with 200ml boiling water and season with salt and pepper. Pour the mixture around the aubergines in the tin, cover with foil and bake for 20 minutes. Remove the foil and bake for a further 10 minutes.In the last 10 minutes of cooking, put the butter in a small saucepan over a medium-high heat. Once sizzling, cook for 30 seconds before adding a generous pinch of salt and the remaining two teaspoons of aleppo chilli. Pour the butter over the baked aubergines, sprinkle on the remaining parsley and serve with the yoghurt.Iced berry-ripple tahini creamWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appView image in fullscreenThomasina Miers’ iced berry-ripple tahini cream.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Mandy Thompson.An easy, no-churn ice-cream to finish; the tahini adds a nutty, salty note against the backdrop of intense berry deliciousness.Prep5 minCook25 minFreeze4 hr+Serves4-6200g mixed berries(blackcurrants, redcurrants, raspberries, say),thoroughly washed2 tbsp runny honey100ml tahini2 tsp vanilla essence150ml condensed milk200ggreek yoghurt400ml double creamTo serveYour favourite biscuits2 tsp toasted sesame seeds(optional)Pop the berries in a saucepan with the honey and cook over a low heat for eight to 10 minutes, until they start to break down. Take off the heat and leave to cool.Spoon the tahini into a small bowl and slowly whisk in the vanilla essence, followed by the condensed milk. Fold through half of the yoghurt, then fold in the rest.In a second bowl, whisk the cream to soft peaks, being careful not to over-whisk. With a large spoon, fold in the yoghurt mix little by little, until well combined.Spoon half the tahini cream into a freezable container, then pour over half of the berry sauce create a ripple effect with the blade of a knife. Repeat with the rest of the cream and sauce in a second layer, and ripple that, too. Freeze overnight, or for at least four hours, then serve with your favourite biscuits on the side and perhaps a sprinkle of sesame seeds.Explore more on these topicsLambThomasina Miers recipesFoodMeatMiddle Eastern food and drinkMain courseIce-cream and sorbetDessertrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Meera Sodha’s recipe for blackberry and almond cake | Food | The Guardian
description: Rich, velvety nuts are offset by zippy, seasonal berries in a cake for all occasions
Author: Meera Sodha
Headline: Rich, velvety nuts are offset by zippy, seasonal berries in a cake for all occasions
Content: ‘I never regret a slice’: Meera Sodha's blackberry and almond cake.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Mandy Thompson.View image in fullscreen‘I never regret a slice’: Meera Sodha's blackberry and almond cake.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Mandy Thompson.Meera Sodha recipesFoodMeera Sodha’s recipe for blackberry and almond cakeRich, velvety nuts are offset by zippy, seasonal berries in a cake for all occasionsMeera SodhaSat 22 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMost cakes I can take or leave, but I never regret a slice of almond cake. The density! The chewy crumb! The way it romances butter and other flavours! The ultimate almond cake, in the Sodha house, at least, isClaudia Roden’s orange and almond cake, which is made religiously for special occasions (of which there are many from December to March), but I wanted a more seasonal cake for a good friend’s August birthday. Blackberries are perfect (not least because we’re drowning in them right now), because they provide an excellent, zippy contrast to the almond’s velvety nature.Blackberry and almond cakeWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appPrep10 minCook1 hr 15 min, plus coolingServes8-10180g unsalted butter, melted, plus extra for greasing180g caster sugar150g ground almonds80g plain flour1 lemon, zest finely grated to get 1 tbsp1 tsp baking powder½ tsp fine sea salt500g blackberries, washed3 large eggs1½ tsp vanilla extract200g icing sugarHeat the oven to 190C (170C fan)/375F/gas 5, and grease and line a 20cm springform cake tin with baking paper.Put the sugar, almonds, flour, lemon zest, baking powder and salt in a bowl and whisk to combine. Sprinkle in 300g of the blackberries and stir to coat them in the dry ingredients. In a second bowl, mix the eggs, melted butter and vanilla extract, then pour into the bowl of dry ingredients and gently fold in until you have a smooth batter.Pour this into the lined tin, then bake for 45-55 minutes, until a skewer inserted into the centre comes out clean. Remove and leave to cool in the tin.While the cake is cooling, mash 150g of the remaining blackberries in a small bowl, then push them through a small sieve (or tea strainer) to extract the juice (eat or discard the pulp and seeds). Put the icing sugar in a small bowl, add three tablespoons of the blackberry juice, mix well until smooth, then mix in up to another tablespoon of blackberry juice, until the glaze is the thickness of double cream.Once the cake is cool, remove it from the tin and put on a plate. Slowly pour over the icing, then gently press in the remaining 50g blackberries to decorate. The cake will keep in the fridge for up to three days.Explore more on these topicsFoodMeera Sodha recipesFruitCakeBakingSummer food and drinkBritish food and drinkEggsrecipesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Perfect for kids’: the best (and worst) supermarket ketchup, tested and rated | Sauces and gravies | The Guardian
description: It’s a saviour at family mealtimes, but which bottle of red sauce does our reviewer relish the most? (Spoiler: it’s not Heinz)
Author: Tom Hunt
Headline: It’s a saviour at family mealtimes, but which bottle of red sauce does our reviewer relish the most? (Spoiler: it’s not Heinz)
Content: Feeling saucy? Not all tomato ketchups are created equal.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Loïc Parisot.View image in fullscreenFeeling saucy? Not all tomato ketchups are created equal.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Loïc Parisot.Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterSauces and graviesReview‘Perfect for kids’: the best (and worst) supermarket ketchup, tested and ratedIt’s a saviour at family mealtimes, but which bottle of red sauce does our reviewer relish the most? (Spoiler: it’s not Heinz)The best supermarket mayonnaiseTom HuntSat 22 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIwas that kid who put ketchup on everything, from fries to french toast, and if my parents wanted me to eat vegetables, they’d have to cover them in the stuff (the sugar cravings of my youth have subsided, but I still love ketchup mixed into peas). So I was pleasantly surprised by this test group, because even the most economical sauces performed well.Tomato content varied greatly (though not always in line with price), with the most tomato-heavy products containing almost twice as much fruit as the least. This information is presented in two ways: the first is the amount of raw tomato used before the sauce is cooked down into puree (more than 200g per 100g of finished product is high, less than 150g is low); the second is a straight percentage of tomato puree used, which is a more transparent measure (above 50% is high, while less than that I’d consider low, so check the label if you want more fruit in your sauce). Products made with fewer tomatoes are sometimes thickened with modified maize starch. I’ve also listed the total sugar content.Ultimately, every product did “what it says on the tin”, and while not necessarily delicious straight from the spoon, all were great with chips. Some of the top-end sauces suit a more mature palate, with a richer, spiced flavour, but they still have that classic burst of umami-sweet-sour tang.The best supermarket tomato ketchupsBest overall:Rubies in the Rubble Ketchup but GooderView image in fullscreen£3 for 485g at Tesco (62p/100g)£3.30 for 485g at Ocado (68p/100g)★★★★☆A squeezy bottle of vivid red sauce with a sweet and complex aroma. Contains a high percentage of fruit – 242g per 100g (tomatoes, plus surplus pears/apples) – which adds sweetness and a fruity depth layered with spice. Contains the preservative potassium sorbate and 20% total sugars.Best bargain:Bramwells Original tomato ketchupView image in fullscreen89p for 550g at Aldi (16p/100g), in store only★★★☆☆A squeezy bottle of thin and smooth puree, with a classic, inoffensive and unremarkable flavour profile (sweet-sour, tomato), making it perfect for kids. A simple, additive-free formula with 16.4% total sugars.And the rest …Co-op On the Side tomato ketchupView image in fullscreen89p for 550g at Co-op (16p/100g)★★★☆☆A squeezy bottle of thick, deep red sauce that’s sharp on the nose but with a tempting, savoury aroma. Sweet and easy on the palate, too, with a slightly higher total sugar content of 22% and a ratio of 167g tomatoes per 100g sauce.
